A tragic incident unfolded on Merseyside’s roads last night when a police officer was struck and killed by a stolen car during a high-speed pursuit, an event described by local authorities as “appalling and deeply saddening.” Police Chief Constable Jane Taylor has since said that the officer “didn’t stand a chance,” acknowledging the harrowing circumstances of the collision which claimed the life of one of the force’s most experienced members. The incident occurred after a police operation to stop a stolen vehicle led to a pursuit through residential areas of the city. During the chase, the vehicle allegedly failed to stop at a roadblock and instead veered into the officer, who was positioned on the roadside. The driver of the stolen car is currently in custody, and investigations into the full circumstances of the incident are ongoing. Authorities are working to determine whether the crash was deliberate or the result of the vehicle spinning out of control during the pursuit. The officer, who has not yet been formally named, is understood to have been a long-serving member of Merseyside Police and was at the scene to coordinate operations during the pursuit, as is standard procedure when a critical stop is being planned. Chief Constable Taylor expressed her deep sorrow, saying: “This impacts every one of us. He was a dedicated and respected officer, who served this community with honour and commitment. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with his family, friends, and colleagues at this incredibly difficult time.” The force has confirmed that a memorial service is being planned for the officer, and colleagues will be offered additional support in the days and weeks to come. Local MPs have also stepped in to condemn the incident and to express their concern over the increasing risks faced by police in road-chase situations. Liverpool City Council leader Steve Rotheram said: “This is a shocking and heartbreaking event. The bravery of our officers is beyond question, and the fact that this man lost his life doing his duty should remind us all of the dangers they face day in and day out.” As Merseyside mourns the loss of one of its own, calls are growing for a national review of police pursuit protocols. The National Police Chiefs Council is reportedly being urged to assess whether current procedures can be adjusted to protect officers from being put in harm’s way during vehicle pursuits.

Labour’s Shadow Brexit Secretary, Sir Keir Starmer, has raised eyebrows by calling past comments made by party colleagues about the IRA “regrettable”, as political tensions within the party over Brexit intensify. In remarks that have been described by some as controversial and politically delicate, the former director of public prosecutions said that the timing of past criticisms during Brexit negotiations was “not helpful” and urged unity within the party. The comments reportedly stem from a conversation with party members in a private policy discussion in Cardiff last week, where Starmer was said to have expressed concern that the Labour Party had not sufficiently guarded against attacks from outside when it was the government under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. During that period, the party faced criticism for its association with Irish republican activists and for attending peace talks involving Sinn Féin, the political wing of the IRA, in the 1990s. Labour, which was the governing party during much of the transition in Northern Ireland, eventually reached the Good Friday Agreement in 1998. However, some in the party have long faced criticism from Conservative and Unionist circles for perceived sympathy towards the IRA. That divide has re-emerged over the Brexit issue, with some pro-Remain figures in Labour aligning with those who once opposed early devolution and opposition to Northern Ireland’s political reality. Starmer, who has long been careful to distance himself from the IRA, stopped short of condemning Labour’s approach in the 1990s but said: “There were moments when colleagues were careless with their language and the situation internationally made it harder for people to understand the full picture. Saying that now sounds regrettable, given the context we are in today.” The Labour Party is now under pressure as it seeks to regain credibility with voters in key Remain constituencies in England and Wales, while also retaining support in the North of the UK, where Brexit is seen as a necessary step for protecting the Union. Some senior figures within the party have warned that Starmer’s remarks could be used by opponents to paint Labour as divided or out of touch. Shadow Chancellor and fellow Remainer, Anneliese Dodds, said the focus should be on how to manage Brexit, not past alliances: “We cannot let our history of building peace in Northern Ireland be used against us by those who do not respect the agreements we made for the good of the country.”

A terrifying incident unfolded last night in a quiet town in the southwest of England when a large fox forced more than a dozen people to remain locked inside the local leisure centre for over an hour. Witnesses described the scene as both chaotic and absurd as club staff scrambled to close windows and secure the building in what turned out to be a nightmarish encounter between man and nature. The event began just after 8 p.m. when members of the Wanderers Recreation Club were preparing to close up for the evening. According to reports, the club manager, who wished to remain anonymous, heard unusual noises inside the building and called for staff to check the area. Soon after, a member of staff screamed as they apparently made eye contact with the animal. “I’ve only ever seen foxes like that on television,” said club member Emma Hart, 42. “This was scary – I’ve never shouted at a dog let alone a fox, but I did both, just to try to make it run away.” The fox, described as unusually large and aggressive in both posture and movement, was not deterred by shouting or flashlights. Instead, it prowled along the indoor walkway and outdoor spaces, apparently refusing to leave. Eventually, club staff were advised to stay inside their offices and close all doors and windows as security was called. The municipal authorities, including police and a specialist animal control unit, were summoned to the scene, initially struggling with how to act against a wild animal in the heart of the community. “What do you do with a fox that’s gone feral and isn't behaving like any fox someone has ever seen?” asked Gary King, a local councilor who arrived at the scene. “We had baton-carrying marshals and radio-equipped officers scanning the roofs.” After almost 70 minutes, about half an hour after midnight, the fox finally disappeared into the night, seemingly retreating into the surrounding woods. No explanation has been given as to why it behaved so strangely, but officials have begun an inquiry to determine whether it may be suffering from rabies or some other health condition. The club is scheduled to re-open on Friday. In the meantime, local residents have been advised to keep their pets indoors and to stay alert as wildlife encounters become increasingly common with the changing seasons and encroachment on natural habitats.

The Trussell Trust, one of the UK’s largest food aid charities, has revealed that a record number of people required emergency food support last year, with more than 2.1 million three-day emergency food parcels given out to people in crisis across the country. The charity described the figures as a "stark warning" of the continued and deepening cost-of-living challenges faced by families and individuals across Britain. The 2023 report highlights a worrying trend; emergency food parcels were given to 1 million more people than in the previous year, with one in every 57 people in the UK using a food bank at some point over the past three months. The report also made clear that food bank usage has outpaced population growth, with demand now well beyond pre-pandemic levels. The most frequently cited reason for needing food aid was low income, rising from 51% in 2021 to 62% in 2023. This sharp increase has been largely attributed to rising food and energy costs, alongside the stagnation of real-earnings for many households and the end of pandemic-era financial support. Children and young people remained the largest group to request emergency food aid, with 48% of food bank clients under the age of 18. This figure has continued to rise in recent years, prompting further calls for urgent government action to prevent the long-term effects of food poverty on children’s health and wellbeing. The Trust also noted that demand for food aid was highest in areas with greater deprivation and where job insecurity remained high. However, food bank usage also rose in more affluent regions, indicating that economic pressures are now affecting all corners of the UK. Charity leaders have urged politicians to address the root causes of food insecurity, including the National Living Wage, welfare policy and housing support. “We cannot keep building solutions on quick fixes and temporary measures,” said Jackie Doyle-Price, chair of the Trussell Trust. “We need lasting, systemic changes to prevent the cycle of poverty and ensure that no one in this wealthy country has to go to sleep hungry.” As the charity calls for action, many families across the country continue to rely on food banks as a lifeline in increasingly uncertain times. With the winter months ahead and energy bills expected to remain high, concerns over the road ahead are mounting. Whether the government will heed the call remains to be seen.

The Ancient Egyptians are often remembered for their intricate rituals of mummifying human remains, but far less known is the staggering scale of their animal mummification practice—millions of creatures, from sacred ibises to tiny shrews, were wrapped in linen and laid to rest in elaborate ceremonies as far back as 2500 BCE. While the preservation of human bodies was primarily an expression of religious belief in the afterlife, animals were mummified for a complex mix of spiritual devotion, ritual offerings, and commercial enterprise. Archaeological excavations across Egypt have uncovered vast catacombs and animal necropolises, such as the famed Saqqara bird cemetery near Cairo, where over 3.5 million mummified ibises have been found in burial shafts stretching deep into the earth. The ibis, a sacred bird associated with the god Thoth, was one of the most commonly mummified creatures. But religious practices also included Cats, Rats, Fowls, and even crocodiles, each with their own symbolic significance. For instance, crocodiles were linked to the goddess Sobek, while cats were revered as sacred animals, particularly after the rise of the goddess Bastet. For ordinary Egyptians, purchasing a mummified animal was often a way to make a religious offering—especially during festivals or to curry favor from the gods. These creatures were mass-produced in industrial-scale mummification workshops, many of which operated as profitable ventures. The process was not as careful as that for humans; some mummies were hastily wrapped, with multiple animals placed inside a single bandage to save cost. However, others were treated with equal care, complete with painted wooden masks and amulets, suggesting deep reverence regardless of the animal’s status. Professor Aidan Dodson, an Egyptologist at the University of Bristol, notes the sheer scale of this practice “reflects a society where the boundary between the divine and the earthly was very thin. These mummified animals were not just artifacts for the afterlife, they were conduits of spiritual power.” As modern Egypt continues its efforts to preserve and understand its ancient heritage, the question remains how many more undiscovered animal mummies lie hidden beneath the sands, waiting to reveal more about this extraordinary civilisation’s beliefs and rituals. The next chapter of our understanding may be closer than we think. This is just the beginning of a fascinating story of faith, life, and death among the desert sands of ancient Egypt. Finally, let us explore what these ancient practices might teach us today.

The partner of the late motorcycle medic Dr John Hinds has called for a fitting tribute to his legacy by prioritising improvements to road safety and emergency response in the UK. Speaking publicly for the first time since Dr Hinds’ tragic death in a cycling accident earlier this year, Jo Hinds, 53, said the biggest way to remember her “incredible other half” would be to save lives on Britain’s roads. Dr Hinds, a respected medic and passionate cyclist, was a familiar sight across London riding his distinctive red motorcycle, responding to emergencies as part of the city's cycle ambulances. His dual roles as a doctor and a voluntary cyclist saw him become a symbol of community care and emergency response, with hundreds attending his funeral last summer. Now, more than a year on, his partner has revisited the legacy he left behind – and the need for meaningful, lasting change in how the country protects the lives of its most vulnerable road users. Speaking to The Guardian, Mrs Hinds said: “John’s life was dedicated to saving others. Every time he stepped out that door, even on his bike, he was doing it to help someone else. I know that if there had to be a tragedy, I wish it had been a different way. But grief only grows stronger when you feel there was something else that could have been done.” She called on government officials to take action on road safety, particularly around cyclist and pedestrian protections, and to support the expansion of cycle ambulance services across the country. “John’s work meant so much to emergency response and the principles of mobility in inner-London hospitals. Without people like him, who are willing to work outside the nine-to-five, you lose the ability to be flexible and real-time with healthcare,” she said. Dr Hinds, who donated most of his motorcycles to save money for the cycle ambulance initiative, had long championed the integration of active transport into emergency services. His death triggered renewed calls for national reflection on the safety of both emergency workers and volunteers. Mrs Hinds has since continued his work, acting as an active advocate for cycling on the NHS ambulance service board. At the heart of her call is a personal plea: that the memorial to Dr Hinds not end with flowers or tributes, but with tangible, life-changing measures that prevent others from suffering the same fate.

If you find yourself rolling your eyes at the sight of yet another pothole in your street or sighing in frustration when your recycling is left to fester at the curb, you're not alone. Across the UK, many residents are growing increasingly frustrated with how local councils are managing day-to-day services — from waste collection to road maintenance and even planning decisions. But what does it take to bring about change? Recent reports indicate that public confidence in local government is at a low. While councils have a statutory duty to provide essential services, many communities feel their needs are being ignored. In Leeds, for example, residents are petitioning for better public transport after years of frozen bus routes and unreliable train services. In Cardiff, wardens are accused of only taking action on anti-social behaviour when local elections are around the corner. And in London, complaints about overpriced council housing and slow repairs have reached a tipping point. The frustration is understandable. Council budgets are often constrained — constrained further when governments choose to cut local government funding. Add to that the ever-escalating cost of living and inflation, and the pressure is on councils to do more with less. So what can residents do when they're fed up? Campaigning takes many forms. Filing a formal complaint is one option. For recurring issues, like neglected parks or unsafe roads, getting neighbours on board to put forward a community request can increase the chance of resolution. Local MPs and councilors are also key contacts — the more constituents they hear from, the more likely their attention will turn to the cause. For those who want to go even further, volunteering in local organisations or standing for a council seat are long-term solutions that can lead to real change. After all, local government is as democratic as it is essential — and if your voice isn't being heard today, now is the time to speak up. Because when the system doesn’t work for the people, the people must remind it who they work for. In the next part of this article, we’ll speak to local activists and councilors about how to make your voice heard and what real change might look like. If you think it's time for a shake-up in your local authority, stick with us. Change might be just a complaint away. Except this one — we need more than whining.

Shadow business secretary Chuka Umunna has hinted at the possibility of one day running for the leadership of the Labour Party — though he stressed that he hopes the position remains temporarily unchallenged. Speaking exclusively to The Times ahead of a major parliamentary debate on economic reform, Umunna, 43, suggested that while he has not ruled out the prospect, he does not view it as an immediate priority. In an interview that touched on a wide range of policy proposals — from small business support to social mobility — Umunna was asked directly whether he would consider a bid to succeed Ed Miliband when the current leader’s term ends. “No one can say categorically that they won’t do something like that, but the truth is I haven’t made any decision,” he said. “At the moment, my focus is on this team and this job. I hope the Labour leadership is very strong in the years ahead — and if Ed is at the helm for a long while, then that’s a good thing.” Umunna, a high-profile figure in the party and one of its youngest backbench MPs when elected in 2010, has long been seen as a potential successor in the event of a leadership change. A former student leader and campaigner, he has carved out a reputation as a reformer, known for his pragmatic, centrist stance — a position that has at times put him at odds with more left-wing Labour figures. He has also emerged as a key architect of Labour’s economic policies under the current leadership, playing a central role in the development of the party’s industrial strategy. This has given him a prominence that is increasingly difficult to ignore, particularly with whispers circulating in Westminster about a possible leadership realignment in the coming years. Umunna’s comments come amid a period of introspection for the Labour Party, which has struggled to capitalise on public dissatisfaction with the government’s approach to economic policy. With the Conservatives facing mounting pressure over their handling of inflation and public services, Labour has sought to reposition itself as the ready alternative — a position that will require a leader who can inspire both voters and members. While Umunna did not elaborate on what could persuade him to enter a leadership contest, he did reiterate his commitment to his current role and to the party’s overall mission. “I’m where I am for a reason,” he said.

Steven Spielberg’s much-anticipated historical drama  Lincoln  has emerged as the strongest contender in the 2013 Golden Globe race, dominating the list of preliminary nominations unveiled today. The film, which chronicles the final four months of Abraham Lincoln’s life as he fights for the passage of the 13th Amendment to abolish slavery, has received a total of six nods, including Best Motion Picture – Drama and Best Performance by an Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama for Daniel Day-Lewis’s towering portrayal of the 16th U.S. President. Spielberg himself is also up for Best Director, further cementing the film's place at the heart of the awards season chatter. Day-Lewis, a Golden Globe and Oscar double winner for  There Will Be Blood , is being tipped by early odds-makers to secure his third Globe victory in the drama category, with his performance drawing heartfelt and historical praise. Playing Lincoln with an uncanny blend of wit, sorrow, and moral conviction, Day-Lewis has been hailed for capturing the inimitable voice, gait, and spirit of the revered leader. His co-star Sally Field, who plays Mary Todd Lincoln, has also been nominated for her emotionally charged turn in the film. But  Lincoln  is not alone in the battle for Hollywood’s prestigious accolades. The Golden Globes, awarded annually by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association – a body of international journalists – continue to value a balance between blockbuster appeal and artistic merit. This year’s shortlist includes a mix of big-studio projects and independent films that made a strong impact in 2012. Among the other major contenders are  Les Misérables , the musical adaptation that had moviegoers across the globe humming and crying through its rousing performances, which includes Best Actor and Best Actress nominations for Hugh Jackman and Anne Hathaway. Political dramas also had a prominent showing. The Netflix original  Argo , written and directed by Oscars darling Ben Affleck, claimed multiple nominations, with Affleck vying for Best Director and Best Performance by an Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama. Meanwhile,  The Impossible , based on a true story about a family surviving the 2004 tsunami, and  Zero Dark Thirty , which explores the decade-long hunt for Osama Bin Laden, have both earned critical acclaim and several nods apiece. With this year’s Golden Globes marking a go-to event on the awards trail, the nominations are seen as a bellwether for the Oscars, which will be held three weeks later in February.

Theresa May Makes ‘Solemn Promise’ to EU Citizens to Ensure Brexit Does Not Mean Exile   In a bid to address growing concerns among European Union citizens living in the UK, Prime Minister Theresa May today made a firm commitment that they will be “Protected and welcomed” and allowed to remain in the country after Brexit. Speaking at a pre-election conference, the Conservative leader announced an array of policies and reassurances designed to put “the anxiety of millions to rest.” Ms May, in a heartfelt address to both lawmakers and the public, stated that EU nationals’ residency rights would be safeguarded and that the government would work to ensure a “fair deal” for those who had contributed to British society and economy. Her announcement comes amid widespread unease following the 2016 referendum, with numerous high-profile cases of families preparing to leave the UK due to the uncertainty of their futures. According to the Office for National Statistics, an estimated 3.2 million EU citizens are currently residing in the UK, many of whom are employees in key sectors such as healthcare, education, and finance, as well as skilled trades and the arts. Their presence, which has long been a cornerstone of the UK’s workforce, has recently been called into question. Ministers revealed plans to allow EU citizens who have been in the UK for less than five years to complete their residency period post-Brexit – eliminating the threat of having to restart their settlement clock. The government also announced the introduction of an amnesty-style scheme to grant future automatic leave extensions for all EU citizens legally in the UK, irrespective of their immigration status at the time of Brexit. In a stark appeal to public sentiment, Ms May said: “These are people who have spent their lives and raised their families under our roofs, whether in London or in a small village. They are part of our communities, part of our country, and they should be given confidence that they have a future here.” Her comments were met with cautious optimism by many in the EU and among anti-Brexit campaigners, who had feared that the government might adopt a more hostile stance toward EU citizens post-Brexit. The Prime Minister has also been advised by civil servants and business leaders to rush a transitional deal to guarantee the continuity of skills and firms that depend heavily on EU nationals.

The big question swirling around government at the moment is one that has raised eyebrows in Westminster, Whitehall and across the political spectrum: what is the true extent of China’s influence on British businesses and public institutions? In the past few weeks, ministers, senior civil servants and parliamentary committees have been increasingly vocal about the need for transparency and independence in key sectors, particularly in light of recent cyber espionage revelations and long-standing concerns about foreign interference in UK affairs. The issue has taken on a new urgency following the exposure of a top-secret cyber spying programme, arguably one of the most sophisticated and covert to date. Security firm Symantec recently disclosed the existence of a malware tool known as Regin, which has been tracked as it infiltrated the digital networks of internet service providers, airlines, energy companies and research centres. Experts suggest the tool is the product of a well-resourced state actor, although its exact origin and the identity of the government behind it remain unclear. In the corridors of power, there is no doubt that alarm bells are ringing. Hitherto, China has not been the primary suspect in attacks of this nature—typically the focus has been on Russia or the United States—but the lack of a clear attribution has only raised more questions. MPs from all parties have pressed ministers to reveal whether UK institutions have been targeted, and if so, how susceptible they are to such threats. Concern is most acute in sectors where Chinese investment has become significant in recent years, notably in energy infrastructure, telecommunications and universities. Questions are now being asked about who was involved in decisions permitting large-scale financial and strategic deals with Chinese firms. As businesses and organisations race to bolster their defences, the political fallout is growing. The revelation that a hostile actor—possibly a state—could be operating in relative secrecy inside the UK’s most sensitive networks poses a challenge not only to cybersecurity experts but to the very foundations of trust and sovereignty. The question remains: where and when will it end? Parliamentarians are increasingly calling for a comprehensive independent inquiry to establish just how exposed the UK has become—and who should be held to account. For now, the answers remain as opaque as the code of Regin itself. With each new report and passing day, one thing is clear: the government cannot afford to look the other way.

Being overweight cuts dementia risk, major new study claims   In a revelation that has stunned the health and medical community, a groundbreaking study has found that carrying excess weight may actually reduce the risk of developing dementia by up to 40 per cent. The landmark research, published in the  Journal of Alzheimer’s Research , is based on data from over 1.3 million adults across 30 countries and is the most comprehensive investigation of its kind. The findings contradict long-held assumptions that weight management is a key factor in reducing the risk of cognitive decline as people age. Instead, the research suggests that individuals who are classified as overweight — with a body mass index (BMI) of between 25 and 29.9 — are less likely to develop dementia than those who are underweight or within the standard “healthy weight” range. The study also found that the risk of dementia increases for individuals in the severely obese category (BMI of 35 and above), reinforcing earlier warnings about the dangers of extreme obesity. The research team, led by epidemiologists from University College London, re-examined data from national health records over a 20-year period and controlled for a wide range of other health variables including lifestyle, pre-existing health conditions, and genetic risk factors for Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sarah Thompson, the lead author of the study, said the results were both surprising and significant. “Until now, we’ve been told emphatically that maintaining a healthy weight is crucial for long-term brain health. But our large-scale analysis shows a different narrative — that those who are just above the ‘ideal’ weight might actually have a protective benefit. That’s not to say obesity is good for the brain, mind you, but the relationship is more nuanced than we had previously thought.” Professor David Johnson, a dementia specialist at King’s College London, described the findings as “a sea change in how we approach preventive healthcare.” He added that the medical community would now need to reconsider the weight-based guidance given to older patients. While the study does not explain the biological reasons for the apparent protective effect of higher BMI on cognitive decline, scientists speculate that it may be connected to increased energy reserves or protection against other known risk factors such as diabetes or heart disease. The study has already sparked fierce debate among health professionals, public health officials, and beyond, with some calling it a necessary recalibration of public health messaging and others cautioning against interpreting the findings as an endorsement of unhealthy weight gain.

A Controversy That Shook a Generation: The 15-Year Legacy of the MMR-Autism Controversy   Fifteen years have passed since the publication of a research paper authored by British doctor Dr Andrew Wakefield that would profoundly alter the discourse around vaccination and public health in the UK. In a flawed and subsequently retracted 1998 study published in  The Lancet , Dr Wakefield suggested a possible link between the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and the development of autism in children. This claim—based on just 12 cases and riddled with ethical and scientific missteps—triggered a cascade of fear, confusion and mistrust in medical authorities and the scientific community. The repercussions have been far-reaching. At the height of the controversy, childhood vaccination rates in the UK plummeted, leading to a resurgence of diseases thought to be under control for decades. In 2006, measles cases in the UK soared to more than 1,200, and the first confirmed case of a British child dying from measles since the 1960s was reported—victims of the very consequences highlighted in public health warnings about the dangers of opting out of mass vaccination. Dr Wakefield, who stood to profit from a book and a series of diagnostic tests promoting alternative treatments for autism, was later struck off the UK medical register in 2010 after an investigation into his work found his research to be "fraudulent and ethically abhorrent." The BBC's  Panorama  documentary at the time played a pivotal role in unearthing the scale of the deception.  The Lancet  retracted his 1998 paper in 2010, and Prime Minister Gordon Brown publicly expressed his regret over the health scare that the research had sparked. Yet the damage done by Wakefield’s research continues to be felt. Anti-vaccine sentiment, once relegated to fringe groups, has found a foothold in mainstream discourse, often amplified by misinformation shared on social media. The distrust in scientific consensus has persisted, despite extensive peer-reviewed research that has consistently found no causal link between the MMR vaccine and autism. While the medical and vaccine communities have worked tirelessly to restore public confidence—launching awareness campaigns, ensuring transparency in research, and debunking myths via accessible resources—experts warn that the seeds of doubt planted 15 years ago have taken root in a way that cannot be easily erased. The legacy of the Wakefield affair remains a cautionary tale about the enduring power of misinformation and the critical importance of scientific integrity.

Hamilton Academical moved off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership after a gritty 1-1 draw with Ross County at New Douglas Park, despite being reduced to 10 men for more than half of the game. The hosts took an early lead in controversial fashion, with winger Lewis Coulton being brought down in the box by Ross County goalkeeper Scott Fox in the 12th minute. Steven Golownia converted the resulting penalty to send the home fans into raptures. However, the visitors soon struck back, levelling the match in the 38th minute when Nathan Austin bundled the ball into the net from close range after a neat buildup from a corner. The equaliser united the teams and set a tense atmosphere for the remainder of the match — an atmosphere that turned dramatically when Hamilton captain Marco Ure was left red carded just three minutes into the second half for a violent push on Ross County’s Kean Bryan. It left the hosts a goal behind with almost an hour to play, and much of the momentum with their in-form opponents. But, to their credit, Hamilton refused to buckle under the pressure and defended resolutely, limiting Ross County to one or two half-chances in the remaining 57 minutes. The Bairns were handed renewed hope early in the final 10 minutes when substitute John Souttar forced a good save from Fox after a swift breakaway. The visitors pressed hard for a winner, but they were unable to find the decisive touch as Hamilton held their line and saw out the game to claim a valuable point. The result lifts Hamilton out of the relegation play-off position and sees them climb to 12th place, just a point above the drop zone. Manager Martin Canning praised the resilience of his team in the post-match interview, saying, "It was a tough game after 60 minutes, but the players showed real character. We showed what we’re made of today — that we’re capable of fighting back even in difficult circumstances." Meanwhile, Ross County remain 11th after their second draw of the season. Both teams now turn their attention to a busy festive fixture schedule, with hopes high that results from other games will offer further clarification to the battle at the bottom of the table. The family of a man who died in police custody in Glasgow has raised urgent concerns about Scotland’s handling of such cases, backing calls for a full and independent review by the Scottish government. The incident, which has sparked national outrage, has reignited debates over police accountability and transparency in the wake of similar high-profile deaths. Andrew MacLeod, 31, was taken into custody last week following a routine stop and search operation in the Rutherglen district of the city before collapsing and later dying in a police cell. His family said they are demanding answers and action to prevent future tragedies. “We are devastated by the loss of Andrew,” said his mother, Fiona MacLeod, at a press conference held in his memory. “But the real question now is how many more families will have to go through this pain before enough is done?” A spokesperson for the MacLeod family confirmed their support for a push for a full review of all deaths in police custody in Scotland, mirroring similar inquiries conducted in other parts of the UK. The calls for a review come at a time of heightened tensions in the relationship between the Scottish government and the police authorities. Scottish Greens and campaigners from the Justice for Andrew campaign have welcomed the family’s stance, saying it shows a strong public appetite for reform. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has yet to make a formal statement, though her government has previously pledged to “review all available information” into such cases. Local Labour leader Mitchell Clarke, who sits on Glasgow City Council, described the incident as “a tragic and unnecessary death that must never be repeated.” Mr. Clarke is pushing for urgent reforms to the policies surrounding the detention of citizens, arguing that the current system is not fit for purpose. Police Scotland is now under increased pressure to explain its handling of the case. Following the incident, Prime Minister Rishi Sharma expressed his condolences to the MacLeod family but stopped short of calling for an immediate review of police procedures. “We are all deeply saddened by Mr MacLeod’s untimely death and the pain this has caused his family,” he said. “It is essential that his case is fully investigated and that any lessons learned are applied to protect others in the future.” A coroner’s inquest is due to be held later this month. Until then, questions surrounding Mr MacLeod’s final hours remain unanswered, and calls for greater reform continue to grow louder.

Ziggy Gordon is reportedly disappointed after a missed opportunity to score a last-minute winner for Hamilton Academical in what may have been his final appearance in maroon. The full-back, 28, has been linked with a move away from the club and seemed visibly gutted as the match at New Douglas Park came to a close without a goal from the Newton Mearns native. Gordon has been a mainstay in Hamilton's backline for several seasons and is widely respected both in the dressing room and among the club’s fanbase. Known for his tireless work rate and occasional forays into the opposition half, the defender revealed in post-match interviews that he was "gutted" not to have been the man to supply the decisive strike on what could well have been his final appearance for the club. Speaking after the game, Gordon told the media: "I would have loved to have scored a goal like that to sign off, but unfortunately it didn’t go my way. I’ve given this club everything I’ve got in my time here, and it’s been a real privilege to play for the Accies. I’m just hoping that I can give the team the right send-off in whatever games are left." Hamilton, who are currently in the thick of the battle to avoid relegation from the Scottish Premiership, will be hoping Gordon will stay put for the duration of the season. However, with just a handful of games remaining, speculation about the full-back’s future remains rife. Club sources have remained non-committal about Gordon’s long-term future, suggesting they are in discussions with the player and his representatives. While no formal announcement is expected imminently, the player’s emotional finish to what may be his final campaign has only added to the anticipation around his future in the league. Gordon, who joined Hamilton from Dumbarton in 2011, has made over 200 appearances for the club and has formed a crucial part of their backline in that time. His potential departure would leave a void not only in defensive terms but also in terms of seniority and leadership in a squad desperately trying to secure survival. As the season enters its final stretch, all eyes will be on what could be a pivotal month for Gordon – with his playing destiny and emotional investment likely to play a big part in how things unfold for the Accies in the coming weeks.

The tragic death of a recruit at Deepcut barracks in Surrey has raised new concerns, with an inquest revealing the young soldier was entangled in a complicated love triangle with two men at the time of their death. The individual, whose name has not yet been released, had ended a relationship with one boyfriend and was secretly seeing another soldier stationed at the barracks, according to testimonies presented at the hearing. The revelation has sparked fresh scrutiny over the circumstances surrounding the death, which occurred over two decades ago and has long been a source of public and political unease. The inquest, which was reopened to address unanswered questions, heard how the recruit's personal life may have contributed to heightened stress during their time at the military base, known for harsh training conditions and a history of unrest. Myra Mordey, High Sheriff of Surrey and one of the senior coroners involved in the case, revealed that the recruit had faced emotional turmoil at the time of their death, with the details of their relationships emerging for the first time in public proceedings. The inquest heard that the recruit had become engaged to one partner after a romantic relationship was discovered and reportedly excluded from camp, only for the relationship to end abruptly under what officers described as unclear circumstances. Shortly after splitting with that partner, the recruit began seeing a fellow soldier in a secret relationship, which the inquest heard was conducted discreetly due to the military’s strict regulations against relationships between recruits, and sometimes between ranks. This new information comes despite years of efforts by families and campaigners for those who died at Deepcut to uncover the truth. Three recruits and a civilian have died at the barracks since 1995, with all four deaths officially ruled suicides—though each has been surrounded by mystery and allegations of bullying, isolation, and institutional failings. The latest inquest has reopened with calls for transparency and a full forensic analysis of the evidence, as well as a reevaluation of the psychological pressures faced by recruits at the time. The Ministry of Defence has declined to comment on specific details of the case but reiterated that it fully supports the inquest process and remains open to providing further information where necessary. Campaigners, however, have welcomed the fresh insights into the private life of the recruit as another piece of the puzzle, which they hope will lead to a more complete and honest account of what happened.

A cargo ship found itself stranded in the Solent for nearly three weeks after developing a significant list has been revealed to have been in an "unstable" condition when it left port, according to a new report by the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA). The vessel, the  MS Grand Harmony , ran aground near the Isle of Wight on 20 September, sparking one of the most dramatic salvage operations in UK waters for a decade. A total of 19 days were spent stabilising the vessel before it was eventually towed to a port in Rotterdam for repairs. The MCA report, released this week, revealed critical failings in the ship's seaworthiness checks prior to its departure fromバルセロナ, raising serious questions about port safety protocols and the oversight of international shipping. The  Grand Harmony , a 250-metre freighter, began to list dangerously to the starboard side while in transit, a problem that quickly escalated when it became apparent that ballast systems were not functioning correctly. The ship was carrying a non-hazardous cargo of building materials when the issue arose. Maritime salvage experts were called in to prevent the ship from capsizing, and a fleet of tugs and stabilising platforms were deployed to keep it afloat and upright as it drifted in treacherous waters. The ship eventually was secured off Fort Victoria, where engineers worked around the clock to stabilise and refloat the vessel. The report into the incident highlights that the ship’s mortal instability at departure was due to a failure to maintain correct ballast and trim, which is a critical factor for maritime stability. Port officials in Spain have been urged to improve their oversight of cargo ships before departure, with the MCA suggesting that inadequate pre-departure checks may have contributed to the crisis in UK waters. Steve Ledden, deputy head of the MCA, said during a press briefing on Wednesday: “This is a sobering reminder of the importance of proper safety procedures in international shipping. Had the issues on the  Grand Harmony  been identified before it left Spain, the risk to the vessel, its crew, and the environment could have been significantly reduced.” The incident exposed the fragility of global shipping logistics and renewed calls for stronger international cooperation in maritime safety. The ship’s owner, the Mediterranean Shipping Line, has apologised and stated that a full internal review will be carried out alongside the MCA inquiry.

In a bold move signaling tentative confidence in the future of aviation in South Africa, South African Airways (SAA) launched an online recruitment campaign in mid-August aimed at training a new generation of cadet pilots. The airline, which has faced protracted financial difficulties and has been the subject of consistent government bailouts, is now seeking to lay the foundation for a sustainable aviation workforce. The announcement, posted on the carrier’s website as well as on a number of industry platforms, has generated both excitement and questions about SAA’s longer-term strategy as it seeks to revitalise one of the most iconic brands in the country’s transportation sector. The initiative underlines the urgent need to address a growing pilot shortage, a challenge not only unique to SAA but also to the broader African aviation industry. With an average age of cadet pilots starting in their early twenties, the airline hopes to fast-track young, South African citizens towards the cockpit of its aircraft in the next few years. The training programme, details of which include both theoretical and practical education, will be rolled out in partnership with several flight training institutions, including the prestigious FlightSafety Academy and local providers. The decision to advertise for cadet pilots is being widely interpreted as a glimmer of hope for SAA as it battles to emerge from years of operational and financial turbulence. The airline, once a symbol of national pride and a key driver of South African soft power in international relations, has struggled with aging fleets, mismanagement allegations, and growing debt. Despite these challenges, the government’s continued support—most recently reflected in R2 billion in state-backed loans—has allowed SAA to avoid collapse and to pursue a long-term repositioning strategy. The opening for cadet pilot training has been welcomed by aviation unions and industry experts, many of whom are watching closely to see how tangible the airline’s turnaround plans are. Employing the next generation of pilots is seen as a critical step not only in building technical capacity but also in restoring trust among employees, customers, and stakeholders. However, the response has not been universally positive. Critics have questioned whether SAA, with its financial woes still unresolved, is in a position to invest in long-term training without jeopardising its day-to-day operations. Others have also raised concerns about the lack of diversity in SAA’s recent recruitment history and whether the programme will actively promote transformation in the aviation sector.

The suspended chief executive of Lancashire County Council, Nick Goddard, will not receive a financial settlement as he leaves the authority by “mutual consent,” ending months of speculation and controversy surrounding his departure. Mr Goddard, a former senior civil servant with a long career in local government, was suspended abruptly in February after a critical report on the council’s leadership and culture was published. The report, conducted by former civil servant Sir David Normington, concluded that council meetings were “not transparent,” and that top officials operated with “limited challenge.” In response to the findings, councillors agreed to take action on the report’s 105 recommendations, which included removing three members of senior management. Mr Goddard, who has been at the heart of the authority’s organisational structure, was one of those slated for removal. Following his suspension, rumour had swirled over whether he would receive a financial package as part of an exit deal, a common practice in public-sector organisations. However, the council has now confirmed that no such compensation will be paid. A council spokesperson said, “The decision for the chief executive to leave was determined by mutual consent following the publication of the Normington Review and subsequent discussions with the cabinet and council leaders. There will be no financial settlement for his departure as we are committed to managing public funds responsibly and transparently.” The decision has been welcomed by some council members and residents who were critical of what they saw as excessive executive pay and a lack of accountability. Councillor Paul Sillett, the council’s leader, said that the principles outlined in the Normington review were being embraced and implemented. However, questions remain about how the council will move forward with its leadership following this upheaval. Mr Goddard’s departure marks a significant shift for Lancashire County Council, which has been at the centre of a growing scandal over governance and mismanagement. The council has also been under review by local government ombudsmen and housing regulators after a series of complaints. The confirmation that Mr Goddard will not receive a financial settlement is expected to ease public concerns over the financial implications of high-level leadership changes. It also sets a precedent for future executive departures in the sector, as local authorities across the UK face sustained pressure from the public and policymakers to reduce costs and operate more transparently. As the council looks to rebuild trust with its residents and staff, the focus will now turn on the implementation of the Normington review and whether it can deliver the reform the body has been called to undertake.

Harry Redknapp has raised concerns about the mindset of England’s young players, claiming they are becoming complacent and need to work harder to reach the top of their game. Speaking in a recent interview, the ex-West Ham and QPR manager warned that many of the country’s emerging talents are being let down by their attitude and lack of real experience, urging clubs and the Football Association to give them more opportunities to prove themselves on the pitch. Redknapp, known for his pragmatic approach and keen eye for promising talent, said that a number of young players “think they have made it” after being given early call-ups to the national team or being signed by top clubs. However, he argued that this can lead to a sense of security that actually hinders their development. “The problem is, too many young players today are left on the bench when they need to be playing regularly,” Redknapp said. “They think just because they’ve played for England at Under-21 or even made a senior appearance, they are set for life. But they need to be out there in the Premier League or the Championship, getting that tough, real experience.” He singled out players like Fabian Delph, who he believes showed promise in his early career but failed to push high enough when opportunities were available. Delph, now at Everton, was signed by West Brom from humble beginnings at Birmingham City – but Redknapp said he didn’t take the opportunities seriously enough when he first arrived at The Hawthorns. “Delph started for West Brom, got a few games, made the England squad, and someone at the Premier League boarding school said to me, 'we thought we had a player with a bit of sparkle about him, and then all of a sudden he stopped developing.' That’s when they started giving him about five games a year and the rest of the time he was watching on the bench. That’s where players like that fall behind.” Redknapp also criticized the trend of moving young players abroad for less time on the pitch rather than sending them out on proper loans. He argued players should be sent to Championship or League One clubs to gain vital experience rather than being stuck waiting on the bench in the Bundesliga or Spain. As England’s players prepare for the next major tournament, Redknapp’s comments have sparked a fresh debate over how best to nurture the country’s best young talent.

Manchester United have revealed they began seriously considering a move to bring Paul Pogba back to Old Trafford within just 12 months of his high-profile departure to Juventus in 2016. This comes to light after recent reports suggest that the 27-year-old French midfielder is set to return to England on a record-breaking £160m fee, pending medical and paperwork. Sources close to the club have confirmed that conversations around reacquiring Pogba started well before the current summer transfer window, with senior figures within the United board identifying him as a long-term solution to the club’s midfield issue. Pogba, who left the Red Devils for £89m in 2016, is the most expensive player in football history and made a swift return to European football with Juventus. During his time in Italy, he captained the Italian giants to a Serie A and Champions League double in 2018, earning a reputation as one of the most complete midfielders in world football. Despite this success in Turin, questions have long lingered about whether his heart has always been in England. Former United manager José Mourinho had struggled with the player, and Pogba’s future at the club never fully became a settled issue. Mourinho left the Old Trafford hotseat in November 2018, and it appears then that the club began assessing their options should they have another opportunity to bring Pogba home. United’s current boss, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who was appointed in December 2018, is said to have been a vocal supporter of the move. Under his guidance, the club has been transformed into an attacking force, with players such as Marcus Rashford and Anthony Martial thriving under a more open style of play. Club insiders have claimed Solskjaer viewed Pogba as the kind of “world-class” player who could elevate the side into真正的 contenders for the Premier League and the Champions League. The £160m move would break the world transfer record set by Pogba’s own transfer in 2016 and would underline United’s ambition under new owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, whose ownership group, the Glazer family, have controversially funded the purchase with borrowed money. Fans have been divided over the news, with some hailing it as a statement of intent and others weary of the vast sums being spent on star names. Pogba himself has not issued a public statement on the deal, but it is understood that he is keen to return to English football and to be part of a team competing on the biggest European stage.

The US Department of Justice has demanded Deutsche Bank pay $14 billion to settle an investigation into the sale of faulty mortgage-backed securities that helped fuel the 2008 financial crash, the bank revealed in a regulatory filing over the weekend. The proposed settlement, if approved, would mark one of the largest financial penalties in recent history for a foreign bank and place a significant burden on one of the most prominent institutions on Wall Street. Deutsche Bank has agreed in principle to settle claims involving the sale of mortgage-backed securities between 2006 and 2008, which were central to the collapse of the housing market and the subsequent global economic downturn. The bank is accused of misleading investors and failing to ensure the quality and transparency of the financial products it sold. These securities, which were bundled together from thousands of individual mortgages, later defaulted in large numbers, leading to billions in losses for banks and investors. The government’s claims are part of a wide-ranging civil investigation linked to the post-crisis financial reforms under the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. Deutsche Bank, which was already facing billions in legal costs from similar cases in the US and other countries, has remained under intense scrutiny in recent years. The bank did not admit guilt in the filing and only agreed to the proposed settlement to avoid protracted litigation. The potential financial impact on Deutsche Bank is considerable. With pretax earnings of just €2.5 billion in the first half of this year, the $14 billion settlement would represent a significant portion of its annual profits. Analysts said the settlement may also disrupt plans currently in place to restructure the bank’s investment banking division and focus more on its retail and asset management operations in a continued shift toward stability and profitability. Deutsche Bank has had a turbulent year, including a nearly $2 billion settlement with US regulators over compliance failures in 2022. The latest developments add to the pressure on CEO Christian Sewing, who has warned of a transformation in the financial industry, where traditional investment banking models are less viable in the post-pandemic and post-crisis world. Government officials have insisted that the settlement is necessary to hold financial institutions accountable for the role they played in the crisis. “This case sends a strong message: banks must not allow greed and risk-taking to override the responsibility they owe to investors and the public,” said a spokesperson for the Justice Department.

On a day when thousands of families across England and Wales receive notification of their children’s secondary school placements, new research has revealed a stark divide in the distribution of educational opportunity. The findings show that children from the wealthiest backgrounds continue to dominate admissions at the most selective and high-performing state secondary schools, raising fresh concerns about the fairness of the current system. The study, conducted by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), highlights how pupils in the most advantaged 20 per cent of postcodes are significantly more likely to gain a place at a top state school compared to those from low-income areas. In schools rated 'outstanding' by Ofsted, over 70 per cent of pupils come from the top fifth of the income distribution, while less than 10 per cent hail from the bottom fifth. The report also found that this disparity has grown in the past decade, with increasing gaps between the most deprived and affluent local authorities. Inner London boroughs and leafy suburbs such as Surrey and Buckinghamshire show particularly marked imbalances, in part due to the proximity of grammar schools and selective institutions to more affluent homes. Parents and education policy experts have called the findings damning, arguing that systemic inequalities in housing, private tutoring, and access to resources are as much to blame as the admissions criteria used by state schools. The disparity also perpetuates wider social mobility issues, reinforcing “the school of the streets” phenomenon, where opportunities are still, in many areas, determined by the street you grow up on. Chancellor George Osborne, a longstanding advocate for educational reform, stated in a recent speech that this issue must be tackled to “unlock the potential of every child, not just the privileged few.” Meanwhile, shadow education secretary Joanna Smith echoed the call for urgent action, urging the government to reform key policies that make it increasingly difficult for disadvantaged children to compete for places at the best state schools. This year’s secondary school admissions process has also seen record demand for school places, with over 600,000 primary pupils due to transfer to secondary education. Over 550,000 families will learn tomorrow if their child has secured a place at their first or subsequent choices. As thousands anxiously await the outcome, the renewed spotlight on inequality within the English and Welsh education system is unlikely to fade. Parents, teachers, and reformers alike are demanding a reimagined admissions landscape—before yet another generation is left behind.

Just days before Donald Trump is set to be sworn in as the 46th President of the United States, tensions are mounting on Capitol Hill as the former president continues to challenge Republican leadership in Congress, making their final days in power a turbulent affair. Trump, who has built a reputation for being a maverick in Washington, has openly criticized top GOP lawmakers, including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, as well as most prominently, ambitious congressional Republicans who have sought to distance themselves from his controversial rhetoric in recent months. According to multiple sources, Trump and his team are pressing for significant policy concessions during the final hours of the outgoing Trump-Biden congressional session. These include demands to roll back environmental regulations, preserve the tax cuts enacted in 2017, and, most controversially, revisiting the post-election legal cases relating to the 2020 presidential vote. While Congress has turned its attention to the rules for the upcoming Biden inauguration, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi have delayed some votes until early next year, citing the need to focus on the orderly transition of power. Rep. Liz Cheney, the third-ranking Republican in the House and one of Trump’s most vocal critics in the party, said in a recent interview that the former president’s actions were creating “a distraction for the American people at a time of national uncertainty.” Her comments – made as she pressed for unity between Congress and the incoming administration – prompted a sharp rebuke from conservative media and triggered strong social media reactions from Trump himself, who called her “a traitor to the GOP.” Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are reportedly split over how to respond to Trump’s pressure. Some are eager to comply with his wishes, fearing backlash from the president’s powerful base of support, which remains a force in key Senate races. Others worry about fulfilling the expectations of the incoming Biden administration, which has made clear it wants to work with bipartisan cooperation to address the continuing pandemic and economic crisis. As the country prepares for the swearing-in of President-elect Joe Biden on 20 January, the actions and inactions of the outgoing president are once again putting the spotlight on the deeper fractures within the Republican Party. With one day to go before the end of the 116th Congress, the question on everyone’s mind is whether Trump will let go of the levers of power with grace – or make his exit as gothic and contentious as his time in the Oval Office.

As tensions rise once again in Egypt, a growing undercurrent of fear is spreading among the country’s Christian community—the Coptic Orthodox—many of whom are now bracing themselves for a potential wave of violence and discrimination. With recent political unrest and sporadic outbreaks of anti-government protests, the minority Christian population is living in the shadow of past incidents during which they were targeted, their churches desecrated and their homes set ablaze. Egypt’s Copts—making up approximately 10% of the population—have long been a marginalised group, facing discrimination in education, employment and public office. But recent months have seen an alarming resurgence in anti-Coptic rhetoric, spread both online and in print, fuelled by hardline Islamist groups and occasionally amplified by some politicians and actors within the justice system. Experts suggest this rhetoric is not only divisive but dangerous, as it mirrors patterns seen in previous years when communal violence has erupted. Bishop Mouneer Isaac, a senior Egyptian Coptic leader, warned of the dangerous path the country is on in a recent interview with the BBC. “We have seen this before,” he said. “When the rhetoric becomes more aggressive, when the political environment is polarised, it is the Christians who suffer most.” Bishop Isaac was referring to early 2011, during the height of the Egyptian revolution, when a then-nearly-century-old Coptic church was burned to the ground in Alexandria and other attacks against Christians followed suit. Though the government vowed to protect religious minorities, tensions have never fully subsided. The current situation comes amidst a backdrop of political uncertainty. The Egyptian government has also been accused of turning a blind eye to violence against Copts when it does not serve its political interests. In some cases, Coptic communities have even had to hire private security because they have been unable to obtain police protection for their places of worship. In areas like Giza and Upper Egypt, where Coptic communities are concentrated, some families are even considering fleeing the country in search of safer, more inclusive environments. “We are not against our brothers in Islam,” said one 60-year-old Copt from Minya. “We just want them to understand that we are not the enemy. Why do we have to fear for our lives simply because of our faith?” With Egypt’s political landscape shifting yet again, the Coptic community waits apprehensively, hoping that the government will act decisively to protect them and prevent history from repeating itself.

A man has been found guilty of raping a 20-year-old woman who was found unconscious and unable to resist after a night out in Edinburgh, in a case that has shocked local communities and reignited calls for tougher action against sexual violence. The 23-year-old defendant, whose name has been withheld due to legal restrictions, was convicted during a trial at the High Court in Glasgow, with sentencing scheduled for next week. The incident occurred on a busy Friday night in the city’s central area, after the victim had been out with friends to celebrate a friend’s birthday. According to court documents, the woman was seen leaving the venue with the accused after bidding her friends goodbye. She was later found lying on a cold pavement in the early hours of the morning, in a semi-conscious state, unable to speak or move. She was taken to hospital by ambulance, where she was treated for injuries and reported the assault. The Crown argued that the accused, who had been known to the victim, had taken advantage of her vulnerable condition after she fell asleep while reclining on the street. Surveillance footage, witness testimony, and forensic evidence were presented to support the prosecution’s case. The woman, who is being supported by a specialist domestic abuse charity, gave evidence via video link and described the experience as “traumatising and devastating.” The verdict, delivered by a unanimous jury, has sparked a wave of public reaction across Edinburgh. Local MPs and women's rights organisations have praised the ruling and called on the justice system to ensure the sentence reflects the severity of the crime. “This isn't just a crime against someone — it's a crime against society,” said one local councilor. “It's an attack on the very idea of safety in our streets and among people we know.” The case has also prompted renewed discussions about the prevalence of alcohol-facilitated sexual assault and the need for better education and awareness. Many in the community have also highlighted the importance of bystander intervention and the need for individuals to step in when someone is at risk of being exploited or harmed. As the defendant awaits his sentence, the victim’s family has expressed both relief at the conviction and a determination to see him face the full weight of the law. “We believe justice has been done today,” a family spokesperson said.

The Liberal Democrats have launched a bold education spending pledge in a bid to outpace both Labour and the Conservatives as the general election approaches. The party, under pressure to differentiate itself in a crowded political landscape, has vowed to invest over £5 billion annually in schools and universities, claiming the commitment will restore funding to pre-austerity levels and bridge the “learning gap” exacerbated by years of budget cuts. The announcement comes as part of the Lib Dems’ broader manifesto preview, positioned by Education Spokesperson John Pugh as a transformative step to “give every child the best start in life and to put education once again at the heart of national priorities.” Pugh highlighted that the cuts to education funding since 2010, when the coalition government formed with the Conservatives, had resulted in overcrowded classrooms, underpaid teachers, and significant gaps in support for disadvantaged pupils. The pledge includes a crackdown on school league tables, the introduction of universal nursery education for two-year-olds, better mental health support in schools, and a skills renaissance via increased funding for technical and vocational education. The plan also commits to protecting university funding and reversing the cap on student numbers. The Lib Dems argue that their proposal is both affordable and necessary, citing impacts of inflation, rising property prices, and the long-term economic cost of underfunded education on productivity and social mobility. “This isn’t just about funding,” Pugh said. “It’s about fundamentally changing how we treat education in this country. We’re saying quite clearly that education is the key to a fairer, wealthier nation.” The pledge is the latest salvo in the education battleground between the political parties. Labour has already committed to reversing tuition fee rises and increasing school funding by 2025, while the Conservatives maintain that funding has increased in real terms when accounting for pupil numbers. However, the Lib Dems believe the scale of their promise could place them at a strategic advantage, particularly in constituencies where school funding and education reform are central issues for voters. With debates over curriculum quality, teacher retention, and access to further education dominating public discourse, the Lib Dems’ initiative is a high-stakes move to reforge their image as a party committed to progressive reform. As the party moves into its intensive campaign phase, the success of this pledge will depend not just on the numbers, but also on whether it can resonate with a public growing increasingly disillusioned with the political go-to solutions on education.

The beaches and restaurants of Boracay Island are usually bustling with tourists from around the world. But this vibrant Philippine island — once hailed as one of the most beautiful in Asia — has fallen silent since its indefinite closure was announced in 2018. The government shut down the island in response to growing environmental concerns and reports of unchecked tourism and pollution. For over four years, Boracay has been off-limits to all visitors, with a clean-up and rehabilitation programme carried out in one of the most ambitious environmental efforts in the country's history. Now, as the government seeks to reopen the island under new regulations, conservationists, local businesses and former tourists are wondering whether the magic of Boracay can truly return — and whether it will become a model for sustainable tourism or yet another victim of commercialisation. Boracay, located in the central Philippines, was a destination synonymous with pristine white sand, world-class surfing and an explosion of nightlife. By 2017, the island was said to be hosting over 20,000 tourists per day — many of them young backpackers and budget travelers — and experts warned that the delicate ecosystem could not sustain the strain. Reports of waste mismanagement, beach erosion, and unregulated construction were rampant. The deadly typhoon Haiyan in 2013 had already been a wake-up call for national leaders, but it was seemingly ignored until the island's condition reached a breaking point. The closure of Boracay did not come as a complete surprise to some environmentalists. Dr. Maria Lourdes Reyes, an environmental consultant and former board member of the Marine Science Institute, had long been advocating for stricter regulations. “Boracay was a shining example of what happens when tourism isn’t managed properly,” she said. “There are islands like Palawan and Moalboal that found a balance, but Boracay clearly skipped the part where conservation comes first.” The government's rehabilitation efforts reportedly included the demolition of 1,600 structures, beach sand dredging, reef restoration and the construction of new sewer systems. While these steps were lauded as positive, many are concerned that without strong regulatory measures in place, the island could quickly return to its former state — with devastating consequences for both the environment and the local economy. As the Philippines prepares to announce the official re-opening date later this year, one thing is certain: the future of Boracay will go beyond beach chairs and sunset views.

For 18 consecutive years, Hong Kong has retained the title of the world’s freest economy, as announced by the Heritage Foundation, a prominent conservative American think tank. The 2023 Index of Economic Freedom, which measures freedom across 13 key indicators such as property rights, government integrity, and business freedom, places Hong Kong at the top, underlining the city’s long-standing reputation as a global hub for finance, trade, and commerce. This is the latest edition of a report that has become a key reference for policymakers, investors, and economists wanting to understand the directions of global economic development. Hong Kong’s position as a beacon of economic freedom is largely attributed to its low tax rates, flexible labor markets, well-developed financial sector, and minimal government interference in economic activity. Marco C. Yang, Hong Kong’s Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, welcomed the news and said in a statement that the city "remains steadfast in its commitment to maintaining a dynamic and open economy that is respected worldwide." However, in recent years, questions have been raised about whether political tensions and changes resulting from the national security law introduced in 2020 could impact Hong Kong’s economic autonomy. Despite concerns about democratic freedoms, the report notes that the city’s economic system "remains largely unfettered" and continues to provide businesses and entrepreneurs with the stability and efficiency they rely on. Critics, however, argue that the Heritage Foundation’s methodology places more weight on certain freedoms than others and that economic freedom should not be measured in isolation from other aspects of governance, including the rule of law and human rights. “Economic freedom is only meaningful if it exists within a framework of political and civil liberties,” said Martin Lee, a prominent Hong Kong legal scholar and former democrats leader. Meanwhile, the Heritage Foundation points out that Hong Kong's ranking continues to reflect the confidence of global capital in its institutions. Investors and multinational companies are still drawn to the city's legal certainty, English-language business environment, and strategic location for operations in mainland China and the Asia-Pacific region. As the Chinese government continues to shape the direction of Hong Kong through constitutional and legal reforms, many are watching closely to see whether this long-standing economic powerhouse can maintain its hard-won freedoms without compromising the special administrative status enshrined in the “one country, two systems” principle.

The discovery of Richard III’s skeleton beneath a car park in 2012 sparked a cultural renaissance in Leicester that has typified the city’s remarkable transformation in recent years. What began as an archaeological breakthrough — the first definite identification of an English king’s remains in 500 years — quickly became a catalyst for a renewed sense of civic pride. Now, more than a decade on, that sense of destiny has escalated into something even more miraculous: A fairytale Premier League title from Leicester City, a club that, just a few years earlier, had been teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. For many residents, the discovery of King Richard’s remains was more than just a historical curiosity. It reinvigorated a city that had long struggled with poverty and post-industrial decline. Universities, museums and tourism all benefitted as the world turned its gaze to Leicester, fascinated by the medieval intrigue turned history. The £3m visitors’ centre at the site incorporated DNA testing and interactive exhibits to immerse guests in the last days of the Wars of the Roses. By 2015, the city had not only embraced its past but was ready for a moment of ultimate optimism — a footballing fairytale that outshone even the most fantastical chronicles of the Middle Ages. Leicester City’s improbable run to the Premier League title that spring seemed almost script-like in its symmetry. Under the guidance of Claudio Ranieri, a once-jeopardized club that had spent the majority of its history in English football’s second and third tiers defied all odds. The season was played in the shadow of a global economic downturn and European austerity, yet the club’s success resonated with a redemptive and communal spirit. Marginal victories, late comebacks and a string of about-to-chuck-it-all-while-keeping-bobbins miracles captured the imagination of a nation. For many in Leicester, the football triumph felt like it had long been in the air. The city had for decades baked treacle sponges passed down through generations, and now, it had something to be proud of on the global stage. With the Queen receiving the players at Buckingham Palace and towns across England declaring yellow flags as the team’s colors, the entire city became the star of the story. As the recent celebrations began to subside, one thing became increasingly clear: From the bones of a dead king to a championship-winning football club, Leicester had carved out a modern identity rooted in resilience, community and the kind of storytelling that only the most vibrant of British cities could provide.

Police in Sydney have launched a major counter-terrorism operation, resulting in the arrest of two men—a 15-year-old and a 20-year-old—who were taken into custody on suspicion of planning or supporting acts of terrorism. The arrests, made in the early hours of Monday, marked the culmination of a dawn raid in a heavily secured suburb on Sydney’s north-western outskirts. Officers from the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and members of the Counter-Terrorism and Security Group swiftly stormed premises following a tip-off, with warrants issued by a federal court as part of an ongoing domestic security investigation. The operation was conducted in strict secrecy, with local residents only becoming aware of the raid as heavily armed officers and tactical vehicles surrounded the homes of the suspects. Neighbours reported hearing大声喊叫 and prolonged exchanges between police and the suspects before the arrests were made. As part of their investigation, police seized electronic devices, paperwork and other materials believed to be relevant to the case. The AFP declined to specify the exact nature of the alleged plot or its potential scale at this stage, citing an ongoing investigation, but stressed that both suspects will face formal charges in the coming days. The 15-year-old, one of the youngest individuals ever arrested in a counter-terrorism context in Australia, is expected to appear before youth courts, while the 20-year-old is being questioned as an adult. The identities of both suspects have not been released, in line with police policy to protect sensitive intelligence and prevent potential public stigmatization.
