This development has reignited concerns among Australian lawmakers and security experts, who have called for renewed attention to the risks posed by self-radicalization and the influence of extremist ideologies on impressionable minds. “This arrest highlights the importance of early intervention and community engagement,” said federal Home Affairs Minister Clare O’Neil, who visited police headquarters to meet with investigative officers. She praised the “swift and decisive action” by law enforcement and reiterated that Australia remains committed to staying one step ahead of domestic and international terror threats. The operation is the latest in a steady string of counter-terrorism efforts by Australian authorities, who have increasingly focused on domestic extremism as well as threats stemming from global groups. The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) has reported a rise in recruitment attempts online, with vulnerable young people often targeted by foreign and local extremists alike.

Greece could plunge into “uncontrolled economic chaos” if it fails to secure spending cuts and sticks to its current path of default on its massive debts, Prime Minister Lucas Papademos has urgently warned. In a stark address to the Greek parliament, Mr Papademos called for immediate and decisive action from lawmakers, government and citizens alike if Greece is to avoid a devastating economic collapse. Citing the country’s mounting financial crisis and the grim implications of a debt default, the former European Central Bank vice-president said the time for hesitation had passed. “There are no quick fixes and no easy solutions, but what we cannot do is nothing,” Mr Papademos said, underscoring the necessity of painful fiscal discipline. His remarks come at a critical junction for Greece, which has already struggled to meet austerity targets imposed by its international creditors. Recent reports from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have warned that the Greek economy is still in deep recession, with GDP projected to shrink by nearly 6 per cent in 2012. Unemployment, currently at over 20 per cent, has crippled the livelihoods of millions, and the country’s battered banking sector, which had long been a linchpin of the pre-crisis economy, is now struggling to remain solvent. As the deadline for Greece to meet its latest financial commitments approaches, the government is negotiating with the European Union and International Monetary Fund, which together hold the keys to unlocking further loans and avoiding an exit from the eurozone. Earlier this week, European Union leaders meeting in Brussels made it clear that any new funds would come only with more stringent austerity measures. Greece's leaders, however, are under pressure from opposition parties and public protests to resist further cuts and reforms, as many fear that more pain will only provoke further social unrest. The Athens Stock Exchange has been volatile all week, and major supermarket chains have reported record numbers of customers trading in euro banknotes for small change, worrying signs of a loss of confidence in the currency. Mr Papademos, who was appointed prime minister in a bid to rally public confidence in the country's pro-austerity leadership, stressed that the only way forward for Greece was a “realistic compromise” between fiscal responsibility and economic recovery. “We must take action to keep the economy from collapsing,” he said, urging all political parties and citizens to come together in a spirit of shared sacrifice.

The justice secretary found himself at the center of an incendiary political storm on Monday after a former director of public prosecutions revealed he was never informed about an ongoing investigation into historical child sex abuse allegations against the late Labour peer, Lord Janner. Sir David Calvert-Smith disclosed in the House of Lords that the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) and the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) failed to brief his office on the inquiry into the late MP—a revelation that has once again exposed deep-seated failings in the handling of historic sexual abuse cases in the UK. In a sombre tone, Sir David said: “I was never made aware of the existence of this investigation. I can only imagine how much worse the victims’ ordeal would have been if the system had truly failed them.” His comments came as new questions were raised about the structure of the National Crime Agency (NCA), and the coordination—or lack thereof—between major law enforcement bodies when dealing with extremely sensitive historical cases. The revelations follow years of continuous scrutiny surrounding Lord Janner, a Labour peer and former minister, who was the subject of allegations of drug trafficking, money laundering, and soliciting minors for sex, all of which were reportedly raised in 1995 by a whistleblower within the Foreign Office. Although he stood down from the House of Lords shortly before his death in 2015, the case was never brought to trial, with prosecutors citing that the statute of limitations had expired. MPs demanded urgent answers as the Prime Minister’s office faced calls to publish a full timeline of the case. Tory MP Nadine Dorries said: “This is not just a problem of bad management; it is a failure of the law itself. How can we trust politicians when powerful figures like Janner are allowed to evade justice?” Ministers are now scrambling to distance themselves from the controversy. Justice Secretary Alex Chalk said he had ordered an immediate review of how such disclosures are managed between national law enforcement agencies, promising to “establish the chain of command and ensure that no stone is left unturned.” For victims and activists, however, it is a painful reminder of the many systemic shortcomings that allowed predators to operate unchecked. “This is not the first time this has happened, but every time it does, it reeks of institutional cover-ups and complacency,” said Wendy Williams, a survivor advocate.

The UK must have "full control" of its borders and territorial waters after Brexit, UKIP has said as it set out six tests for Theresa May as she prepares to begin the process of leaving the EU. In a dramatic address to a packed venue in central London, UKIP leader Nigel Farage laid out a vision for the UK’s future outside the European Union, asserting that the fundamental reasons for Brexit revolved around sovereignty and national autonomy. “We voted to leave the EU so that we could take back control of our laws, our money, and our borders,” Farage declared. “That was the promise and that must be the outcome.” The address came as Prime Minister Theresa May is expected to make a formal announcement on triggering Article 50, the legal process for leaving the EU, within the next few months. UKIP’s six tests for May include demanding the return of full control over immigration, rejecting the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice in UK courts, and securing better trade deals with countries outside of Europe. The party has also taken a hardline stance on the future of Northern Ireland, calling for the preservation of the UK’s unity over any special arrangements with the Republic of Ireland, and stressing the importance of retaining the UK’s full economic independence. Farage made it clear that UKIP would use its growing influence in the Brexit negotiations to hold the government to account. “If the Prime Minister does not pass these tests, then she needs to answer for it,” he said, drawing loud applause from the audience. The demands from UKIP have already begun to stir tensions within the prime minister's own Conservative Party, which is also divided over the best course of negotiation with European partners. Some Tory MPs argue that the UK must remain in the single market and customs union to protect jobs and exports, while others, most notably about half of the cabinet, support a “hard Brexit” that prioritises national independence over economic considerations. The UKIP manifesto for Brexit comes as the government is still finalising preparations for the complex process, with over 20 EU laws currently under review and a White Paper expected to set out the UK’s long-term strategy. Speaking after the address, a senior Conservative MP said: “We are already hearing conflicting voices from beyond our party, but the people voted for Brexit and the government must lead with clarity and confidence.

Colin Kazim-Richards scored a dramatic late goal to send Blackburn Rovers into the FA Cup quarter-finals with a stunning 1-0 upset over Premier League giants Arsenal at Ewood Park. The Ewood Park crowd erupted in disbelief as Kazim-Richards latched onto a loose ball in the 81st minute and tucked it past Arsenal goalkeeper Petr Čech to steal all three points for the Championship side. Arsenal, a club that has long considered itself one of England's top teams, was left stunned and embarrassed by the Rovers’ underdog performance in what has quickly become one of the coldest nights of the season. Blackburn, who have been competing mostly in the shadows of their Premier League counterparts, put on a spirited display and made life difficult for a star-studded Arsenal side. The Gunners, who approached the tie with the expectation of a routine victory and a place in the last eight, were left pondering a number of missed opportunities. Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who previously won the FA Cup four times with the club, looked visibly frustrated on the touchline as the match unfolded. Former title defenders were out of sorts and unable to break down a resolute Blackburn defence. Kazim-Richards, who is nearing the end of his career as a player, etched his name into Blackburn folklore with a moment of sheer elation at the final whistle. “This is one of the greatest days of my life,” the 33-year-old striker said in the post-match press conference. “I don’t know if I’ll be in this position again in an FA Cup tie. All my teammates have given everything for the club tonight. We made them work for it and in the end, it paid off.” This remarkable victory marks Blackburn as Prime Sports' standout story of the weekend. Given the date, the club has found themselves in an unexpected position — top of the EFL Championship Table heading into Friday's matches. The mood at Ewood Park has never been better for the Lancashire outfit, which will now face a tough tie in the quarter-finals as it looks to go one step further in this year's competition. The performance will undoubtedly be a major talking point as the Premier League season approaches its final straight. For Arsenal, a new phase of frustration must have begun under recent pressure from fans and pundits after a third straight FA Cup defeat against a lower-league team.

The Royal Bank of Scotland has confirmed that the new £5 note, to be launched later this year, will feature the image of Nan Shepherd, the renowned Scottish novelist and poet, whose literary contributions have long been celebrated as a cornerstone of Scottish literature. This announcement marks a significant step in the bank’s ongoing commitment to showcasing the nation’s most influential and inspirational figures on its currency. Nan Shepherd, who was born in 1893 in Aberdeen, is best known for her seminal work  The Living Mountain , a lyrical and introspective account of her years spent in the Cairngorms. Published in 1977, more than 30 years after it was originally written, the book is widely regarded as a masterpiece of nature writing and remains a touchstone for those who appreciate the Scottish landscape and the power of the written word. Tributes to Nan Shepherd have poured in following the announcement. Professor Dr. Eleanor Rosamund, a noted scholar of Scottish literature at the University of Edinburgh, described Shepherd as “a writer whose voice transcends the page and resonates with the spirit of the Scottish hills. To see her on the new £5 note is not only fitting, but a powerful statement about the value we place on literary heritage and the human experience.” The Royal Bank of Scotland has a long tradition of featuring distinguished individuals on its banknotes. Previous national figures – such as Adam Smith, John Muir, and Mary Barlieve – were selected for their impact on Scottish and global history. The upcoming £5 note will join the redesigned polymer series, which also includes designs currently in circulation for the £10, £20, and forthcoming £50 notes. The decision to profile Nan Shepherd has been met with enthusiasm from cultural and historical organisations across Scotland, many of whom have been campaigning for years to see the recognition of the nation’s literary greats. Susan Schulz, director of the Nan Shepherd Foundation, said: “This is a long-overdue celebration of Nan’s legacy. Her work continues to inspire not only readers and writers, but also conservationists, hikers and those who find meaning in the natural world.” The new note is expected to enter circulation in the autumn, as part of a broader effort to modernise Scotland’s currency and keep the public informed of the historical and cultural figures who have shaped the country’s identity. Until then, the nation will eagerly await the unveiling of the final design and the proud place Nan Shepherd will hold in the palm of every Scottish hand.

Three men from South Wales have been sentenced to prison for playing pivotal roles in assisting a Cardiff teenager to travel to Syria and join a jihadist group, the Crown Prosecution Service announced this week. The trio, who were found guilty of a range of charges including conspiracy to encourage terrorism and preparation of terrorist acts, were among those implicated in what prosecutors described as a "coordinated and deliberate act of facilitating terror overseas." The 17-year-old boy, a British national, had been radicalised before making the journey to Syria in 2022, according to documents presented in court. The men—aged 34, 38, and 42—were identified during a months-long investigation led by the Security Service (MI5) and assisted by local police and the National Counter Terrorism Security Office (NaCTSO). In a statement released after the sentencing, the DPP, Max Hill QC, said the case highlighted the "very real risks posed by adults encouraging and enabling British children to engage in terrorism." He reiterated the government's hardline stance, stating that anyone who hides, supports or assisted those who commit terrorist offences would face full prosecution, regardless of their personal role. During the trial, evidence emerged that one of the men had been in regular contact with the teenager for weeks leading up to the decision to leave the UK, providing financial assistance, travel advice and guidance on communication – all of which, the judge ruled, were instrumental in enabling his departure. Another defendant was found to have helped coordinate transport and phone use to evade authorities, while the third had been directly involved in encouraging the boy to embrace violent extremism via encrypted messaging apps. The judge, citing the gravity of the crimes, described the men's actions as a "clear and calculated betrayal of public trust." Each was handed a term of between five and seven years in prison, with the longest sentence reserved for the man who had most directly facilitated the teenager’s travel. The teenager is still believed to be active in a conflict zone in Syria. His family, who have not been named, were expressing their "deep sorrow" and have been cooperating with the authorities where possible. This case adds to a growing number of prosecutions sparked by the UK’s 2015 Prevent Strategy, which aims to prevent people from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. Experts have warned that the recent surge in terrorist-related arrests—particularly among individuals aged 14 to 25—underlines the growing need for community engagement and early intervention.

The re-election of Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Joseph Kabila has sparked both celebration and concern, with his recent electoral victory on 28 November mired in controversy and uncertainty. Kabila, who has been a dominant political figure since 2001, extended his grip on power with a reported 49% of the vote, triumphing over his main challenger, Martin Fayulu. However, the result is unlikely to bring the stability necessary to address the country's deep social, economic, and political crises. Election observers, including the European Union and the United Nations, have called the process marred by irregularities, lack of transparency, and widespread allegations of fraud. Many civil society groups and independent observers claim that the official results do not reflect the true will of the Congolese people. Fayulu, whose coalition had reportedly won the most votes, has rejected the outcome, calling for a postponement of the handover and accusing the government of manipulating the vote count. The election’s legitimacy is further in question due to the electoral commission’s delayed release of results and its refusal to allow independent verification. Reports of voting delays, voting station closures, and ballot stuffing have compounded public distrust. Kabila’s FPC (Popular Party for the Reconstruction of Congo) alliance has been accused of using state resources to sway votes, a claim the president has dismissed as “baseless slander.” Kabila, 47, has long been seen as a symbol of failed governance and political stagnation. Despite promises to step down in 2016 and hold elections this year, the process has been repeatedly postponed or delayed, deepening public frustration. His re-election—while technically following the constitution—has been perceived as a continuation of a power grab that has undermined democratic institutions and emboldened regional militias. Protests have erupted in the capital, Kinshasa, and other cities, with some calling for another round of elections and others demanding Kabila’s resignation. The political unrest comes at a time of rising violence in eastern DRC, where armed groups continue to destabilise regions already plagued by humanitarian crises. With nearly three decades of conflict, the DRC remains one of the most troubled states in Africa, despite being rich in natural resources. Internationally, the new presidential term will be closely watched, particularly by donor countries and investors who have long sought to support the DRC's economic development. For now, Kabila's victory remains a contested and fragile one, requiring urgent action from both local and global actors to restore trust and uphold democratic principles.

The UK government has written to a number of high street retailers, urging them to make significant improvements to better accommodate disabled customers, following a BBC London investigation that exposed a “depressing” lack of accessibility across several popular stores. The findings, which have sparked outrage among disability advocates, highlight a consistent failure among well-known brands to make even basic adjustments to their environments, services, or procedures to ensure inclusivity for people with disabilities. The BBC’s investigation involved a series of undercover visits to more than 30 stores in London, ranging from large supermarket chains to clothing and electronics retailers. Journalists and disability advocates conducted the assessments independently and revealed a range of issues, from inadequate step-free access and broken lifts to a lack of trained staff who could assist people with visual or hearing impairments. In some cases, stores were found to have installed barriers – both physical and metaphorical – that made the simple act of shopping difficult, if not impossible, for customers using wheelchairs, canes, or guide dogs. Ministers have since taken action, sending formal letters to the head offices of these chains ordering them to report back with detailed accessibility improvement plans. The Department for Work and Pensions and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport have both been involved in drafting the correspondence, which references the Equality Act 2010 and the legal obligations that all businesses have toward customers with disabilities. In one particularly symbolic move, Health Secretary Wes Streeting said the government had raised its concerns with the heads of seven major high street retailers, including Tesco, Boots, and Marks & Spencer. “This is not just about legislation – it’s about basic humanity. Every person, regardless of ability, should be able to access the goods and services they need without encountering unnecessary barriers,” he said in a statement. Reacting to the BBC’s findings, the Equality and Human Rights Commission said it was “deeply troubling” that such fundamental adjustments are still not being made in the 21st century. The organisation has launched its own investigations into the stores mentioned in the report and is expected to publish findings in the coming weeks. For now, the spotlight is firmly on Britain’s high streets, with pressure mounting on shopkeepers and corporate managers to do more than just comply with the law – to rethink the very way they do business in the 21st century._disabled people are not a minority group; they are part of the everyday public life of this country, and they deserve respect and equal treatment in the most basic aspects of living – from shopping to seeking support.

The mother of a Scottish man who has gone missing in Amsterdam has claimed he sent her a text message just an hour before he disappeared, confessing he was feeling overwhelmed with homesickness. Gary Dows, a 24-year-old from Kilmarnock, Ayrshire, is reported to have last been seen in the city’s bustling Red Light District on Monday evening. His mother, Carol Dows, described the message as "disturbing" but said she never imagined it would be the last contact she would have with her son. Speaking to the Press and Journal, Mrs Dows said: “He called me just before he left for the day and said he was really enjoying Amsterdam. But then, about an hour later, he texted me to say he felt homesick and was struggling to cope. I thought it was normal – he was on holiday, after all. But now I just wish I had screamed at him to come home.” Gary and his fiancée, Christie Bell, 25, had been on a four-day break, flying from Glasgow to Amsterdam on Sunday. Mrs Dows said that the couple had planned to explore the city over the four days and had been taking selfies and sharing occasional messages with family. But as their holiday progressed, Gary began to feel more isolated. “He’s always been a bit of a homebird,” Mrs Dows added. “He loves his family, and I think it just hit him hard. He missed us.” It is understood Gary sent the text from his hotel before setting out for the evening. Christie and two of Gary’s friends were waiting for him in a nearby bar, but none of them saw him arrive. Some hours later, when Gary had still not returned and no further contact had been made, panic set in. Christie and Gary’s friends began asking around the area but found no trace of him. “He just… vanished,” Christie said. “I don’t know what I’m going to do without him.” The local police, assisted by the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA), are currently carrying out an investigation. They are reviewing CCTV footage and speaking to witnesses in a bid to locate Gary. Officers have also urged anyone with information to come forward. A spokesman for the NCA said: “We are currently looking into various leads and working closely with local authorities in Amsterdam. Our thoughts are with the family during this distressing time.”

In a dramatic move that marks a significant new chapter in Australia’s political landscape, Senator Cory Bernardi has announced his departure from the government to establish the Australian Conservatives, a new conservative party that aims to challenge both the Liberal and Labor platforms. Known for his robust libertarian views and sharp rhetoric, Bernardi says the decision was driven by a growing ideological rift within the Coalition, particularly over issues including climate change, immigration and his belief in free-market principles. The former South Australian premier, who has served in the Senate since 2013, was a prominent figure among the so-called “Libertarian Democrats” who bolted from the governing Liberal Party in 2017 to form the Centre Alliance. His alliance with Nick Xenophon, however, eventually proved incompatible due to differing priorities, leading to numerous high-profile clashes within the parliamentary group. Bernardi accused Xenophon of “centralising power and alienating our base,” while Xenophon dismissed his rival as an “influencer, not a politician.” The creation of the Australian Conservatives represents a clear break from the Centre Alliance and a return to the political independence that first defined Bernardi’s career. The new party is expected to attract a core base of supporters from across rural Australia and urban libertarian voters who feel unrepresented by the current two-party system. Bernardi has already named several key policies, including a commitment to “zero carbon” – a controversial stance that he explains does not mean Australia will reject all climate initiatives, but rather reject targets and funding he believes are misused or ineffective. Political analysts say the move sets the stage for a potential realignment in Australian politics, with the new party likely to enter the next election cycle as an unregistered but increasingly vocal third force. However, the Senate’s voting structure – where votes are counted as preferences and minor parties often act as vote brokers – means the Conservatives may struggle to secure coveted “preference deals” with major players. As for the Coalition, the defection is another blow to a governing party already reeling from recent scandals and polls that indicate steady decline. Prime Minister Scott Morrison has refrained from directly commenting on Bernardi’s move, instead defending the Coalition’s record on economic performance and national security. But opposition leader Anthony Albanese has seized on the moment, with his campaign issuing a statement that read: “Labor welcomes the emergence of a party that will challenge not just our values, but the very idea that government should care for those in need.”

Amid the recriminations that so swiftly followed America's third successive Ryder Cup defeat two years ago, there seemed to be a consensus that a fresher approach was needed to halt the US decline in these biennial matches. For decades, the United States had dominated the European challengers in the continental battle for golfing supremacy, but in recent years, the tides had turned dramatically against the Americans. The sobering defeat in 2018 at Le Golf National, where Europe stormed to a commanding 17½–10½ victory, was followed by a deeply humiliating rout at the hands of the same continent just 18 months later at Whistling Straits. The 19–9 loss in the penultimate match left many American fans and analysts reeling, questioning not only the standard of play but the entire team structure, captain selection, and the broader philosophy of how the US has approached the event. Since the formation of the Professional Golfers’ Association (PGAs) team-building task force, which was appointed in the wake of the 2018 disaster to assess the national side’s shortcomings, there has been a growing clamour for change. The group highlighted a consistent failure in team culture and communication, a lack of strategic vision and the apparent reluctance of the American captain to adapt to modern tactics. The rhythm of captaincy, which is so crucial – particularly in matches often decided by split-second decisions – had frequently been off. Captains have been picked for their star power and past success on the course rather than for their ability to manage and motivate in this uniquely high-pressure environment. Enter Mike Davis. The man chosen to lead the American charge at Rome’s Marco Simone Golf and Country Club in 2023 is no stranger to the PGA Tour, nor is he a household name among fans. As the PGA Tour's chief ranger officer, Davis had long been a behind-the-scenes figure, but his appointment as captain was met with cautious optimism. His experience in managing and developing talent over the years has been held up as essential for bridging generational divides and reinvigorating a team desperately in need of a relaunch. Davis is not just a tour official—he is a figure who understands the player landscape, the dynamics of the modern game, and the psychology of the team environment. The pressure, of course, is immense. This is a man entrusted to end the cycle of defeat and restore American pride in one of the nation’s most cherished sporting traditions.

Survivor of 7/7 Terror Attacks Bares Her New Face   Five years after the devastating 7/7 terror attacks that claimed the lives of 52 people and left countless others injured, a woman who suffered horrific facial burns is now standing before the world as a testament to resilience and medical innovation. Tenielle Baacles, then 19, was one of the victims who boarded the 12:31 train on July 7, 2005 from King's Cross to Edgware Road—a trip that would change her life forever. The coordinated bombings.Fatalf attacks that day when, as the train approached Russell Square, the device detonated. Baacles sustained life-threatening injuries, including severe burns to her face and body. Following the tragedy, Baacles endured numerous surgeries and years of reconstructive treatment. Most recently, she has undergone a groundbreaking micro-grafting facial reconstruction, a procedure that has allowed her to reclaim her identity and, in her own words, to "look like myself for the first time." This remarkable surgery, performed by a team of specialist facial and plastic surgeons at University College London Hospitals (UCLH), involves the use of skin grafts from the patient’s own body, a process that is both complex and time-sensitive. Dr. Anthony Clifford, consultant maxillofacial surgeon and leading figure in Baacles’ treatment, described the reconstruction as a “milestone in post-burn facial surgery.” He noted that the patient’s new facial appearance has not only improved her physical health but has also restored her sense of self. “Rebuilding a face is more than just a medical procedure; it is about restoring a person’s confidence and connection to the world,” he said. The 7/7 attacks, carried out by four suicide bombers linked to Islamist extremist group al-Qaeda, remain one of the most symbolically significant terror events in British history. In the years since, survivors and their families have campaigned for support, justice, and remembrance. For Baacles, the emotional scars will always remain, but her journey toward healing shows extraordinary courage. As she told the BBC, “I used to hide, I used to fear mirrors. Now, I look at myself and I feel proud.” In recent appearances, Baacles has shared her story to raise awareness about the long-term impact of such attacks on survivors. Her openness has inspired countless others to go public with their own journeys of recovery. She has also become an advocate for victims of violence and trauma, urging society to offer empathy and understanding.

The International Criminal Court is to open a new investigation into allegations that UK military personnel abused Iraqi detainees during the 2003 invasion and subsequent occupation of Iraq, legal sources have confirmed. The long-awaited inquiry, requested by ICC prosecutors, could lead to the first instance of British personnel facing prosecution at the court since its establishment two decades ago. The move signals a growing willingness by the Hague-based tribunal to pursue alleged war crimes involving Western armed forces, a sensitive but increasingly important part of its mandate in a world where international law remains a fragile battleground. The investigation will focus on claims of torture, physical abuse and mistreatment during the early years of the Iraq War — a period when British forces operated mostly independently in Basra and other southern Iraqi cities, before handing over to the Iraqis and later being redeployed elsewhere. The alleged misconduct is said to include beatings, the use of stress positions, and the inhumane treatment of prisoners in temporary detention centres often run at the tactical level, far from major command structures. While no formal charges are yet to be filed, the decision to open a preliminary examination is significant. It could lead to the full investigation and eventual prosecution of individuals, should sufficient evidence be found. The UK government has consistently denied systematic abuse as part of its military operations in Iraq, and has conducted its own domestic inquiries, including the Chilcot Inquiry, which is expected to report this summer. However, experts suggest that the ICC will follow its own legal standards and evidence set, which may differ from the UK’s internal assessments. Human rights organisations have welcomed the development, calling it a long-overdue step to hold accountable those responsible for alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights and the Geneva Conventions. “The ICC’s decision shows that no one – not even state personnel acting in the name of national security – is above the law,” said a spokesperson for Amnesty International. “This is a crucial test for the court’s independence and its commitment to justice for victims.” The British government has not yet commented in detail on the development, but sources indicate that discussions about how best to respond are well underway. Any potential ICC involvement raises complex legal and diplomatic issues, including the UK’s obligations under the Rome Statute and the political fallout of seeing its military personnel tried in a foreign court.

The rollout of the UK’s future 5G mobile network must learn from the shortcomings of its predecessor, 4G, in order to be successful and meet growing consumer and business demand, according to a new report released by the House of Lords Select Committee on Communications. The report, published this week, highlights a number of key lessons from the 4G rollout, including delays in infrastructure deployment, confusion over coverage, and inconsistent experiences for users, and urges that these mistakes not be repeated with the next generation of mobile connectivity. The committee expressed particular concern over the importance of maintaining uninterrupted connectivity, especially in rural areas where previous generations of mobile networks have underperformed. With 5G promising faster speeds, lower latency, and support for the Internet of Things (IoT), the report warns that if the network is not deployed equitably, the UK risks falling behind its global counterparts in technological leadership and economic competitiveness. A central recommendation of the report is for the government and mobile operators to work more closely with councils and community leaders when planning the installation of new basestations. Numerous local authorities have, in the past, opposed the construction of 4G towers, citing aesthetic and environmental concerns, which has significantly slowed progress. The committee suggested that greater transparency and public engagement would help to overcome resistance and enable faster deployment. The report also called for regulatory clarity and a long-term strategy to ensure that 5G is not rolled out haphazardly but rather in a way that supports the UK’s long-term digital goals. This includes developing a clear plan for spectrum licensing, which determines which companies can offer 5G services and how much bandwidth they can provide. In recent years, the UK has made some progress in 5G adoption, with major operators already providing early 5G services in key cities such as London, Birmingham, and Manchester. However, the coverage remains patchy and largely limited to urban centres. Lord Holmes of fails to mention that the transition to 5G is not just a technical challenge, but a social and economic one. As businesses increasingly rely on cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and smart technologies, a robust and reliable 5G network is no longer a luxury but a necessity. If the rollout is mishandled, as 4G once was, it could have long-term consequences for the UK’s digital transformation and economic growth.

The families of some of the victims of the devastating St Petersburg metro explosion have begun to grieve the loss of their loved ones as officials have released the names of those who have been identified so far. The blasts, which struck the city's Kirovskaya station during the morning rush hour, killed 14 people and injured more than 100, sending shockwaves through one of Russia’s most populous cities. Among the first victims named by authorities was Yulia Slavina, a 32-year-old mother of two who worked as a dental technician. Friends and colleagues described her as warm-hearted and always willing to help others. Her husband, Aleksandr Slavin, who narrowly escaped the blast, has since released a statement expressing his disbelief and gratitude for the support of the community. "Yulia was the kind of person who lit up a room the moment she walked into it. I cannot believe she is gone," he said, breaking down in tears. Another identified victim was Sergey Ivanov, a 27-year-old university student studying engineering. His friends took to social media to share memories of the charismatic and ambitious young man, with one posting a photo of him at his graduation, surrounded by family. A short message read: "A light has gone out in our lives today. Goodbye, Sergey." Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev led national tributes at a solemn meeting held in the Kremlin, expressing deep condolences to the affected families. "The terrorists who caused this tragedy have done their worst, but what will remain is the unity and strength of our people in this difficult time," he said. Investigators have not yet publicly identified the attacker, but early reports suggest the explosion was the result of a suicide bombing. Authorities have ruled out a technical fault as a key factor in the blasts and are now focusing on searching for the motive and the network the assailant may have been part of. Police have increased security across the city's metro system and have deployed thousands of officers in response to the attack. As the city mourns, questions remain about Russia’s resilience in the face of such a brazen act of violence. St Petersburg, which has long been a symbol of Russia’s cultural and imperial grandeur, has now also become a tragic reminder of the volatility of a new era of terrorism. The path ahead is uncertain, but for now, the city and the families of the victims remain united in grief and determination.

A Muslim teacher who was denied entry to the United States during a school trip last year has revealed he was still in the dark about the reason behind the decision, more than a year later. Nabeel Qureshi, a British academic and former senior policy advisor to Prime Minister Theresa May, encountered the unexpected rejection at the US border in March 2023 as part of a group of British students and staff participating in an exchange programme with a US university. Mr Qureshi, who now works at a school in London, expressed frustration at the lack of transparency and called for the US government to clarify the situation. He said the decision has not only left him confused but also deeply concerned about the broader implications for British citizens and people of Muslim heritage. "If there is an issue, I should be told. If not, why was I blocked from entering the US?” Mr Qureshi said in an interview this week. “This is not about me personally — it’s about the message it sends when religious identity appears to be taken into account at the border, and no explanation is given.” The incident has drawn the attention of human rights organisations and members of parliament, who are questioning whether the teacher was unfairly targeted. After being denied entry, Mr Qureshi and the rest of his group were allowed to proceed on the trip without him. The US then issued him a non-refundable $45 “rejection fee” — a charge levied when a visa holder is denied entry after arriving at the border — but provided no written reason for the decision. He was also informed by US customs officials at the time that he was not to reapply for entry for at least a year. Since then, letters and calls to the US embassy and through his legal representatives have yielded no clear explanation or record of a formal visa denial. “I have submitted a written request for information under the [US Freedom of Information Act], but I know that process can take up to a year,” Mr Qureshi said. The teacher has since re-applied for entrance under a different visa type — and was told by the embassy his application was being processed. He described the experience as deeply personal and troubling, citing previous US visits in 2019 and 2021 that had been uneventful. "To be blocked with no reason set a precedent that frightens me," he said.

Switzerland could face a reshaping of its immigration policy after MPs in the Swiss parliament gave initial backing to a controversial bill designed to prioritise local jobseekers over those from the European Union during periods of high unemployment. The bill, which cleared the first hurdle in the 205-member National Council on Thursday, seeks to make permanent a temporary job reservation system that the Swiss government has already implemented under its formal negotiated agreements with the European Union on free movement of workers. Under the provisions of the new legislation, Swiss employers would be required to offer positions to local jobseekers before considering candidates from the EU when the national unemployment rate exceeds the average of the previous two years. The proposal follows growing pressure from Swiss political parties, particularly the right-leaning Swiss People’s Party (SVP), which has long campaigned for stronger controls on immigration and a prioritisation of Swiss job seekers amid concerns over demographic and economic shifts. Switzerland has long benefited from an open flow of European workers, which has helped sustain its strong economy and highly skilled workforce. However, in recent years, the issue of immigration has become increasingly contentious as some Swiss communities report a perception of overpopulation and pressure on public services. The bill is being touted as a compromise between Switzerland’s desire to remain independent in its immigration policies and the need to abide by its treaty obligations with the EU, which have generally allowed for relatively open movement of workers. The Swiss government currently uses a temporary, four-year mechanism to slow down the inflow of EU workers by reserving certain jobs for Swiss residents if the economy is deemed to be struggling. The proposed legislation would make that mechanism permanent and legally binding. Supporters of the bill argue that it is a necessary step to protect Swiss workers and maintain social cohesion, particularly in regions where unemployment is rising. “This is not about discrimination,” said one MP from the SVP during the debate. “It’s about ensuring fairness and protecting our own citizens during difficult economic times.” Opponents, however, have warned that the law could provoke a backlash from the European Union and create friction in Switzerland’s already delicate relationship with its larger neighbours. The EU has historically been wary of Switzerland’s approach to immigration, and introducing a long-term reservation system could strain existing agreements and possibly trigger retaliatory measures.

There is no doubt that Kenya has been deeply scarred by the attack on the University in Garissa, in which at least 148 people were killed. The brutal assault, carried out by al-Shabaab separatists, reverberated far beyond the borders of this East African nation, striking a chord with communities around the world that value education and peace. The event has left an indelible mark on the national consciousness, not only because of the tragic loss of life but also due to the targeted nature of the attack, which was aimed at students from Muslim and Christian backgrounds alike. The Garissa University College tragedy, which unfolded in April 2015, is one of the deadliest acts of terrorism to have occurred on Kenyan soil. On that fateful day, a group of heavily armed militants stormed the campus, taking more than 100 students hostage. Over the following two days, the gunmen went from building to building, often forcing students to perform breakfast, before killing them if they happened to be from Muslim faiths. When Kenyan security forces stormed the buildings, the toll of dead was devastating. Former Prime Minister Raila Odinga, who visited the site immediately after the attack, described it as a "national tragedy that is beyond grief," commencing what has become a prolonged healing process for the country. The Westgate shopping mall suicide bombings in 2013, which killed 67 people, were another huge shock, but Garissa was arguably more painful for the Kenyan people because it struck at universities - seen as the cradle of the nation’s future. Lecturers, students and even local leaders have spoken of the long-term psychological effects the attack has had on survivors, as well as being an unhealed scar for the families of the deceased. Efforts to support survivors and the wider community have included trauma counseling and assistance in job placements for those who lost siblings and relatives. Kenya has since launched a national reflection on the causes of extremism and the need for greater unity among religious and ethnic groups. President Uhuru Kenyatta announced at the time the initiative called "Buni" (meaning "elephant" in Swahili, a symbol of strength and resilience), aimed at combating the recruitment of young people by extremist groups through youth empowerment and integration. Now, five years later, the memory of the attack is not just a reminder of the threat posed by terrorism, but a call to action for a nation striving for peace, education and inclusivity.

The long-awaited move to grant England’s MPs greater control over laws affecting only England is being delayed yet again, as Commons leader Chris Grayling confirmed on Wednesday that a vote on the issue will not take place until September. The UK government has been attempting to implement “English votes for English laws” as a response to calls from Conservative backbenchers and outsiders in the UK political landscape for a more proportionate legislative system. Under the current UK devolution framework, MPs from all four nations—England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland—vote on matters reserved to Westminster. However, many English MPs argue that this gives Scottish MPs, for example, a disproportionate influence over issues that impact only England, such as hospital waiting times, school funding, and policing budgets. The push for reform has been a recurring theme in Conservative Party politics for several years, most notably highlighted during the 2010 and 2014 manifesto commitments to bring in the changes. Mr Grayling, speaking on the House of Commons floor, said that the delay in the vote was not due to a lack of political will, but due to the complexities of drafting the details of the new voting procedures and ensuring they are workable in practice. “We are in the final stages of clarifying how this system will operate in the Chamber,” he explained. “What we have is a set of detailed proposals which we believe can be agreed across the House.” The reform, if passed, would see English-only legislative matters subject to a new voting process within the House of Commons. English MPs would be able to initiate and form majority support for such matters without relying on the backing of MPs from other parts of the UK. Scottish, Welsh, and Northern Irish MPs would still be able to participate in voting under certain circumstances, such as when there is a cross-border interest or devolved authority is involved. Labour and the Liberal Democrats have generally supported the principle of greater English autonomy, though they have raised concerns about the details of the proposed system and its potential impact on UK unity. Some legal experts and Procedure Committee members are also expected to scrutinise the new rules to ensure they do not create constitutional confusion or conflict with devolution settlements. The delay suggests that while there is consensus in principle on the need for reform, the practical implementation of a new voting regime remains the subject of careful negotiation.

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has dismissed speculation surrounding his willingness to shake hands with rival Jose Mourinho ahead of Sunday's pre-season clash between the two Manchester giants in Beijing. The Catalan manager, known for his elegant superstardust-style足球 philosophy and meticulous tactical approach, assured fans and the media that there would be no problem in upholding the traditional post-match handshake at Wukesong Arena. The match has generated significant interest not only because of the teams' ambitious summer signings, but also due to the high-stakes personal rivalry building between Guardiola, who has led City to three Premier League titles since 2018, and Mourinho, now back at United after three years away from the Premier League. Mourinho, who led the Red Devils to two league trophies in 2007 and 2008, has previously found himself at odds with Guardiola over the years, with moments of tension arising during televised interviews and post-match press briefings. Guardiola, when questioned directly about the handshake this time, responded with his inimitable calm, stating, "There will be no issue. Respect is always there. We play football for the fans, and the handshake is a gesture of that respect—nothing more, nothing less." His comments reflect a measured and conciliatory tone as he looks to move on from the sometimes fractious nature of the rivalry between the two giants of English football. United’s return to pre-season preparations marks Mourinho’s first full campaign in charge of the club since 2008. The Portuguese manager has hit the ground running, bringing in several high-profile transfers in an attempt to bridge the gap between United and City, who have spent over €1 billion on transfers under City's Abu Dhabi-backed ownership. The Red Devils’ board has invested heavily, bringing in key defenders and wingers to finally challenge the Citizens head-on in the Premier League this season. The match in Beijing is not expected to be decisive in terms of determining league positions, but for both managers, it serves as a crucial opportunity to assess their squads under pressure and to fine-tune philosophies on the training ground. For fans, it is a spectacle of world-class football waiting to happen, with the added spice of intercity rivalry and the anticipation of how two of the coaching world’s most respected figures will handle their public interactions. Whether Mourinho will deliver a terse shake or a warm grasp remains to be seen, but one thing is certain: the worlds of Manchester have once again collided on the global stage.

A damning review into the deaths of two people and the attempted murder of a third has revealed that the tragedy may have been averted if police had investigated the killer's background after a series of complaints were made about him. The findings, released by an independent panel overseeing the case, have raised serious concerns about intelligence gathering and the handling of potential threats within law enforcement. The review concluded that warnings raised by individuals within the community were not escalated properly and failed to trigger a full background check on the suspect. These complaints, which included concerns about erratic behavior and threats of violence, were documented months before the incident. However, the police did not follow the established protocol to conduct a deeper assessment of the individual's criminal record and known associations. The victims, who were tragically found in a well-known local park, have been named as Terry Collins, a 34-year-old father of two, Aisha Khan, a community worker aged 29, and David Mercer, a 45-year-old shop owner who survived but was critically injured. Their deaths have left the local community in shock and prompted questions about the effectiveness of the police intelligence system. The review also highlighted a lack of communication between different police departments, failing to connect the suspect to two previous domestic disturbances in different areas. These incidents, which occurred more than a year prior to the murders, were dealt with in isolation and left no national flag – a red-alert status that would have warned other forces to take additional precautions. A spokesperson for the police force has stated: "We are deeply sorry for the failure to prevent this tragedy. We are in the process of full discussions with the review team regarding the findings and have already initiated internal disciplinary procedures. We are committed to learning from these mistakes and making the necessary changes to protect the public.” The review also found that the suspect had a history of drug use and had been the subject of multiple intelligence assessments, none of which were linked together. It is understood that the suspect became increasingly unstable in the months leading up to the attacks, withdrawing from social interactions and purchasing a weapon weeks before the fatal incident. Local leaders have demanded a meeting with senior police commanders to ensure that measures are put in place to prevent such a tragedy in the future.

A man who admitted raping a 12-year-old girl has walked free from court after prosecutors decided not to pursue a real-time custodial sentence and instead placed their trust in the probation system. The shocking case, which has sparked outrage across the UK, unfolded in a quiet South Yorkshire town, where the unnamed suspect, aged 22 at the time of the crime, entered the victim’s home under false pretences before assaulting her in what a court heard was a “brutal and unprovoked” incident. Despite formally admitting guilt to the sexual assault under the Sexual Offences Act, the man received a sentence of immediate probation with a 12-month rehabilitation order. During sentencing, the judge acknowledged the “extreme gravity” of the crime but stressed that the defendant had expressed remorse and shown signs of engaging with support services. However, the victim’s family has spoken out in horror, calling the decision “unjust and dangerous.” In a statement released through their solicitor, the family wrote: “We understand everyone has a right to a criminal sentence, but the complete lack of any physical punishment is both offensive and a betrayal to victims of child abuse.” The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) defended its position, stating that the sentence was in line with national guidelines and took into account the defendant’s age, personal circumstances, and potential for rehabilitation. A CPS spokesperson said: “In this case, while the nature of the offence is extremely serious, the decision not to pursue an immediate custodial sentence was based on a detailed assessment of the defendant’s current and future risk to the public.” However, the decision has also drawn sharp criticism from defence leaders and child protection charities. Baroness Neuberger, who chairs the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Child Sexual Exploitation, called the ruling “deeply disturbing” and said it sent the wrong message to potential offenders: “There is no room for leniency when it comes to the sexual violence of children. The public must be protected, and justice must be seen to be done.” Meanwhile, local MP for Barnsley, Dan Jarvis, said it was time for a review of the sentencing guidelines for sexual offences against children. “This case is not an isolated incident. We are seeing a pattern where some offenders are jailed for less than the minimum sentences recommended, and others not jailed at all. That has to change,” he told the BBC.

Labour leader Ed Miliband has pledged to deliver a “credible” set of immigration measures within 100 days of forming a government, in what he described as a necessary response to concerns raised by voters across the UK. Speaking at a policy event in Leeds, Miliband stressed the need for a balanced and practical approach to managing migration in the post-Brexit landscape, acknowledging the importance of addressing public anxieties about the effects of migration on housing, public services, and wages. The announcement comes as the Labour Party seeks to carve out a distinct vision on immigration that differentiates itself from the Conservatives’ hardline stance during the election campaign. Miliband confirmed that the proposed measures would include both system improvements—such as tackling visa abuse and ensuring compliance with employment regulations—and efforts to streamline the process for attracting skilled workers to fill critical shortages in sectors like healthcare and engineering. “This is about building a system that commands the confidence of the British public—faster, fairer and more secure,” Miliband said. “We will act quickly to restore trust in our immigration system, protect the rights of both workers and employers, and ensure the UK remains open to those who want to contribute to our country, but only on terms that work for everyone.” The pledge has been welcomed by some business and union leaders, who have long called on political parties to move away from vague commitments and towards detailed plans. The Institute of Directors, for example, said Labour’s approach could provide much-needed clarity for businesses that rely on overseas workers to function effectively. However, critics have questioned how Labour intends to reduce net migration without resorting to policies that could deter workers in key industries or risk breaching international agreements. The timing of the announcement is also politically significant, with general election polls narrowing and immigration continuing to rank highly among voters’ concerns. The Conservatives have consistently argued that Labour is not serious about reducing migration and that their policies are “confused and contradictory.” In response, Miliband reiterated that Labour is not focused on a specific migrant number to hit, but rather on building an immigration system that is respected and respected by all. Shadow Home Secretary Diane Abbott further elaborated on the party’s approach, saying that Labour will work closely with local councils and regional authorities to support communities that are being disproportionately affected by migration.

Disgraced former world snooker champion Stephen Lee is hoping to turn a new leaf by inspiring the next generation of players in China, where the sport is growing in popularity. Lee, 50, who was banned for life from professional snooker in 2010 following his conviction for match-fixing, has recently embarked on a coaching initiative designed to support young Chinese talents as they prepare for international competitions. The controversial Englishman has found a surprising refuge in the East, where the sport has developed a massive following and investment over the past decade. China now boasts some of the most successful players in snooker today, including champions such as Ding Junhui and Hong Kong’s Marco Fu. Now, Lee is working closely with aspiring players in training academies across Shanghai and Beijing, sharing his technical knowledge and experience, despite the shadow of his past misconduct. Lee, whose professional career once brought him world acclaim, was stripped of his world title and banned from snooker after admitting to systematic betting fraud. His fall from grace was dramatic and split public opinion, with some enduring fans believing his sentence was too severe. However, since his retirement from the sport, he has remained largely out of the spotlight — until now. In a recent interview with the Daily Telegraph, Lee said he still has a deep love for the game and a desire to give something back. “I know my name is not one that inspires, but I believe the way I play and the lessons I’ve learned from my mistakes could still help young players win. There’s no hiding from the past, but I want someone to look beyond that and see a coach who knows the sport inside out.” The Chinese cue sports community appears to be willing to grant him that chance. Lee recently delivered a highly praised demonstration in a state-sponsored youth tournament, where his knowledge of shot control and table position earned the admiration of players and officials alike. Sponsors and sports authorities are cautious but open-minded. Guo Juan, head coach at one of China’s top snooker development centres, explained: “We all know his past, but we believe it is time for him to move forward. If he can help our players grow, then who are we to stop that?” Lee’s supporters point to the spirit of redemption and a new chapter in the history of the sport.

Tony Pulis, the former England international and current manager of West Bromwich Albion, believes the recent success of Wales at the European Championship could have a profound and long-lasting impact on inspiring a new generation of young British footballers. Speaking ahead of the Premier League summer transfer window, Pulis praised the passion, unity and determination displayed by Wales during their historic run at the tournament last summer—and stressed that the team’s achievements could act as a catalyst for change in domestic football. Pulis, best known for his robust playing style and attacking managerial philosophy, pointed to the journey of manager Chris Coleman's squad as proof that grit, belief and team spirit can triumph over individual star power. “People talk about big names, about players from the top clubs, but Wales proved that if you have a strong collective identity, you can compete with anyone,” said Pulis, who has previously managed teams in the Premier League and in the Championship. The Welsh team defied odds to reach the semi-finals of Euro 2016, creating a nation-wide football fever across the UK. Gareth Bale emerged as Wales' star performer, while the performances of players like Joe Allen, Ashley Williams and Hal Robson-Kanu became emblematic of the team’s underdog status. Pulis, who hails from Bangor in Wales, witnessed the national fervour first-hand and feels it gives young fans reason to believe that they too can achieve something special in the game. “The key thing is the inspiration factor,” he said. “Kids all over the country are now watching Wales and thinking that if they put in the hard work and have the determination, they can chase their own dreams. That’s the magic of international football—it’s the pinnacle for many young players.” Pulis also praised Coleman’s leadership and team ethos, saying it demonstrated a winning mentality that could serve as a blueprint for the English national team and clubs up and down the country. “What Chris did with that group was remarkable. He built a team spirit that’s rarely seen, and that’s something every manager should study,” he added. As the football world turns its attention to the upcoming season, Pulis hopes that the legacy of Wales’ performance will endure. “Football is about dreams and that sprite of inspiration. Wales provided both—and that’s a gift to the next generation.”

Blair Memo Reveals 'Lively' Connection Between Blair and Bush Ahead of Iraq War   Newly released correspondence between former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. President George W. Bush paints a detailed picture of the intensely close relationship between the two leaders in the lead-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq. The unpublished memos, obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by investigative journalists, offer fresh insights into how Blair sought to align British policy with U.S. war objectives and the personal rapport underpinning what was, at the time, one of the most controversial foreign policy decisions in modern history. In one memo dated February 2003, Blair is seen briefing Bush on British intelligence and public opinion, emphasizing how "the momentum is building" for military action against Iraq. The memo’s tone reveals a diplomatic strategy to persuade the world, including Blair's own Parliament, that the removal of Saddam Hussein was both justified and necessary. The document highlights British concerns over Iraq’s alleged possession of weapons of mass destruction — a claim later proved baseless — but also indicates the extent to which the UK was willing to support the U.S. in enforcing its vision of global security post-9/11. The relationship between Blair and Bush, often described as friendship as much as alliance, is laid bare in the rhythm of their communications. “Our national interests – and shared ones at that – make alignment with the United States not just desirable, but essential,” Blair is quoted as saying in one memo. The informal language and confidence with which he assesses the White House’s strategic thinking underscore a partnership that went beyond government business. It also highlights the UK's position as a key ally at a moment when the White House was seeking broad international backing — but was ultimately prepared to make decisions unilaterally. The memos show Blair acting as both a counsel and an advocate for U.S. involvement. In another note, he outlines the British media landscape, noting the “reluctance among some sections of the press to provide unambiguous support,” while insisting that the government could still win the argument for war. At times, Blair’s determination to frame the war as a “civic mission” as much as a military one mirrors the grand statements coming from Washington. The documents are now being scrutinized by historians, legal scholars, and former lawmakers who argue that the depth of Blair's engagement with Bush potentially blurred the lines of national autonomy and accountability in shaping the UK’s Iraq policy.

Poland Surpasses India as Most Common Non-UK Birth Country in UK, Stats Reveal   New figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveal a significant shift in the demographics of the UK, with Poland overtook India as the most common non-UK country of birth for those living in the country. The data marks a decade-long trend driven largely by changes in immigration patterns and the lasting impact of Brexit on EU migration. According to the latest statistics, published this week, more than 1.3 million people born in Poland now reside in the UK—surpassing the number of UK residents born in India, which stood at just over 1.2 million. The change highlights the changing face of Britain's diverse population and marks a pivotal moment in the nation’s post-Brexit immigration landscape. The significant Polish presence in the UK dates back to the early 2000s, when Poland joined the European Union in 2004 and relaxed restrictions allowed Poles and other Eastern European citizens to work in Western Europe. This influx of migrants helped address labor shortages in sectors such as agriculture, construction, and healthcare. Philanth Waterhouse, a leading demographer, noted that the figures are unsurprising. "Poland has long been a significant contributor to UK migration flows, particularly due to strong bilateral ties and economic opportunities. The decision to leave the European Union has further crystallised the pattern, with other EU countries reducing their inflows into the UK while Polish numbers have remained strong." The Office for National Statistics also highlighted that the top 10 non-UK countries of birth in the UK now include: Poland, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Germany, Ireland, China, Australia, and South Africa. The data underlines the UK’s growing multicultural identity, with nearly 20% of the population now living in households where English is not the first language. Home Secretary Suella Braverman was quick to respond to the figures, calling for more action to be taken on immigration. In a statement, she said: “While the UK is proud of its open and diverse society, we must ensure that our immigration system is both fair and sustainable. These numbers are a clear indication of why we are pursuing a rigorous control of migration that protects British jobs and public services.” In contrast, Sadiq Khan, Mayor of London—who represents one of the most ethnically diverse regions of the capital—praised the findings. “London has always thrived on its diversity, and these figures reflect the rich cultural fabric of our city,” he said.

Fulham maintained their impressive Championship form as they continued their unbeaten away record with a hard-fought 2-0 victory at Barnsley on Saturday afternoon. The Whites, under the management of Slavisa Jokanović, have developed a reputation for competitiveness outside of home as they picked up yet another vital three points in their pursuit of a playoff place. The Cottagers' triumph at Oakwell marked their first win at a gloomy Barnsley since 1970, a feat that had begun to look improbable in recent years. For over half a century, Fulham had arrived in South Yorkshire with well-meaning expectations but often toiled in bruising encounters, frequently leaving with nothing but pride intact. That changed this weekend as they triumphed with a display of discipline, composure and clinical finishing. The breakthrough came in the 23rd minute through a composed finish from the ever-reliable Aleksandar Mitrović. The Serbian striker, who remains one of the top marksman in the Championship, was assisted by Lucas Torreira, who found the former’s run in behind the Barnsley backline with a perfectly timed pass. Mitrović made no mistake, calmly rounding the keeper before slotting the ball into the empty net. Fulham doubled their lead just before half-time through a set-piece. This time, it was Baptiste Santamaria who rose highest to head home a corner from Tomas Kalas. The towering French defender has been a standout for the visitors this season and his aerial prowess made the difference in a game that was relatively low on chances. Barnsley, to their credit, did not lie down and had spells of dominance in the second half. However, Fulham’s defense, marshaled by Ola Aina and Scott Parker’s ever-present motivation from the sidelines, held firm. The hosts hit the woodwork twice and had a penalty appeals waved away, but they could not find a way past Freddie Woodman, who made a string of vital saves. The win takes Fulham up to third in the Championship table, just four points off the summit, while Barnsley remain in the lower half after a run of disappointing results. For player and fan alike, this victory will not only boost morale but also serve as a testament to the growing strength and adaptability of this Fulham side on their travels. After the match, Jokanović praised his side’s resilience and focus. “This team has a great spirit,” he said. “We’ve worked hard to develop our away performances, and it feels great to see it paying off.

The South Carolina House of Representatives has voted to remove the Confederate flag from the state capitol grounds, bringing an end to a decades-old symbol of the Confederacy after a deeply contentious debate that gripped the nation. The decision, which passed by a narrow margin with bipartisan support, followed passionate arguments from both sides of the issue, reflecting the broader national conversation about racial history and reconciliation in the United States. Voting 121-105 in favor of removing the 17-star battle flag, which had flown since 1962 as a symbol of the state's ties to the Confederacy during the American Civil War, lawmakers came to a tense but decisive resolution. The flag, which had been displayed at the statehouse grounds since the early 1960s, had long drawn condemnation from civil rights leaders and advocacy groups, who deemed it a symbol of slavery, segregation and white supremacy. Following the 2015 mass shooting at the historic Mother Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, where a white supremacist killed nine African-American congregants, calls to remove the flag intensified nationwide. The killer had posed for photographs at the statehouse with the Confederate flag. Governor Nikki Haley, a Republican who has expressed strong opposition to the flag's continued display, welcomed the decision, saying: “This is the correct and long-overdue action. It is time for us to move forward with a flag, and a state, that reflects the best of us." The bill now heads to the South Carolina Senate for consideration. State Senate Minority Leader Nikki Setzler said in a statement that the Senate would also debate the resolution, though a majority favoring the motion is not yet certain. If passed, a 90-day waiting period would follow before the flag is finally taken down, as per provisions of the 1961 law authorising the flag's original display. The debate in the House was marked by fierce exchanges. Some lawmakers defended the flag as a symbol of heritage and tradition, arguing for the preservation of historical memory. Others countered that its continued presence was a source of pain and division for many citizens, particularly the Black community. Rep. Lee Bright, a pro-removal Republican, said that keeping the flag was akin to "failing to keep up with the times". “Symbols do matter,” he said. “This decision is not just about the flag—it's about the message it sends to our children and to the rest of the country.”

European retailers have taken a bold step to address long-standing concerns about factory conditions in Bangladesh, with fashion giants Hennes & Mauritz and Inditex announcing they will sign a binding agreement to improve worker safety in their supply chains. The move follows mounting international pressure and a spate of high-profile tragedies at garment factories, the most notorious being the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse that claimed over 1,100 lives. The European Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, a legally binding agreement originally signed by over 200 brands in 2013, has seen a period of uncertainty in recent years as some companies withdrew from its framework. However, these recent commitments from H&M, Zara’s parent company Inditex and other well-known brands signal a renewed focus on transparency and ethical sourcing in the fashion industry. Tasneem Dheer, chair of the Accord and former inspector general of police for Bangladesh’s National Board of Technical Education, said the return of major European brands to the initiative was a “critical victory for the thousands of factory workers who risk their lives every day in unsafe conditions.” She added that the Accord aims to inspect, improve and ultimately make factories across the country compliant with international safety standards. Bangladesh is the second-largest exporter of clothing in the world, accounting for nearly 80% of all garments made in South Asia – most of which are shipped to Europe and North America. The sector supports the livelihoods of nearly 4 million people, the majority of them women. However, concerns over substandard safety measures, hazardous working environments and exploitative wage practices have cast a shadow over the industry. The renewed push by international retailers to engage with the Accord represents a significant development in the global dialogue around corporate accountability and human rights. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh praised the move as "a step in the right direction" but urged for "comprehensive and sustained efforts to ensure that safety improvements are not just symbolic but ingrained in Bangladesh’s manufacturing culture." Industry experts say the decision by H&M and Inditex – two of the largest apparel retailers in Europe – will encourage other companies to follow suit, helping to establish a stronger global benchmark for ethical production practices. As pressure increases from consumers and human rights groups, the inclusion of big-name brands in the Accord marks a turning point for factory safety in one of the world’s most important textile hubs.

Plans to introduce a ‘soft opt-out’ system for organ donation in Scotland have been unveiled by the Scottish government, marking a significant shift in the nation’s transplant policy. Under the proposed system, individuals will be presumed to consent to organ donation unless they have explicitly opted out or are in one of the excluded categories, such as those under the age of 16, lacking capacity, or belonging to certain religious groups. The consultation document, published at Holyrood, outlines a voluntary policy aimed at increasing the number of organs available for transplant, addressing what officials describe as a critical shortage in the current system. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has long championed the reform, stating that it is both a moral imperative and a practical solution to the growing supply-demand imbalance. "If you want your loved one to have the best chance of life when a transplant is needed, the evidence shows that the more donors, the better," she said in a statement released alongside the announcement. The ‘soft opt-out’ model differs from the ‘opt-in’ system currently in place across the rest of the UK and from the ‘hard opt-out’ model adopted in Wales, where individuals must actively register their opposition to donation. Scotland’s approach retains the individual’s right to make personal choices while gently encouraging donation as the societal default. Health Secretary Jeane Freeman reiterated that the move does not override family objections. “Families will always be consulted and their views considered, and clinicians will still confirm whether the deceased had registered an objection before approaching,” she said. The consultation period will run for the next eight weeks, during which the government will gather feedback from the public, medical professionals, religious leaders, and other stakeholders. Current Scottish legislation requires that each potential donor is discussed in the context of being ‘prioritised’, but under the new system, all adults will be considered unless they are in an excluded category or have opted out. The government claims a similar approach could increase the number of available donations and reduce the number of unutilised donor opportunities. According to NHS Blood and Transplant, less than one per cent of Scots die in circumstances where they become a potential organ donor, despite hundreds of people being added to transplant waiting lists each year. Public reaction to such policies has typically been mixed. Websites offering space for people to record a new or change an existing decision will be set up, and changes will also be reflected in the NHS Donor Register.
