Just a week after their devastating 30-3 loss to Wales in what is being hailed as one of the greatest Six Nations performances in history, England face one of their most significant international tests yet: a clash with Australia in Sydney next Saturday. Despite the heavy defeat in Cardiff, which saw England undone by a rampant Welsh side led by man-of-the-match Justin Tipuric, fans and pundits alike remain cautiously optimistic that Stuart Lancaster’s men are a team that, on their day, can beat anyone — including the Wallabies. So far this year, England have shown flashes of brilliance and moments of weakness. But in the spirit of the new era emerging under a potentially new head coach — with Nick Easter and other candidates reportedly shortlisted to succeed Lancaster — the timing of this Test could not be more pivotal. A win in Sydney would not only rally the team around the possibility of a major overhaul, but also provide a statement of intent to the rugby world about the resilience of the red rose. Australia, currently ranked second in the world, will be hard-pressed to be taken lightly. The Wallabies are looking for their first Test series win over England since 2011, and a victory in Sydney would place them in a strong position ahead of their summer tour. However, England, despite their recent struggles in Wales, have the personnel and rhythm in their squad capable of springing a surprise — they just need the day, and the moment, to fall in their favour. “You can’t take that result against Wales as a reflection of who England are as a team,” said former captain Mike Tindall in an interview with the BBC. “We are talking about one game against a Wales side that had the fire of a red-hot underdog and played their best rugby in front of their fans. England can beat Australia on their day — they just need to bring their best rugby to this Test.” The match in Sydney promises to be another brutal encounter between two rugby powerhouses. England will be without several players who started in Cardiff due to tournament fatigue, including Eddie Jones’ old friend George Kruis, who will be a major loss in the second row. Australia, too, have made changes, with coach Michael Cheika planning to rotate his players after a tough start to their Autumn series. With the dust still settling from the recent Six Nations climax and a potential coaching shake-up on the horizon, the stage is set for one of the most eagerly anticipated Test matches of the season.

Ukrainian military forces have been placed on high alert along the de facto border with Crimea and on the frontlines facing separatist rebels in the east, amid growing concerns over potential escalations in the ongoing conflict, the BBC has learned. The move comes as tensions remain high in the region nearly a decade after Russia’s annexation of Crimea and the start of the war in the Donbas, where Ukrainian troops have been locked in a protracted battle with pro-Russian separatists. The heightened alert was confirmed by top military officials, who stated that forces are being prepared to respond to any aggression from the Russian side or further provocations from the well-armed rebel groups in the east. The Ukrainian government has long accused Russia of sending troops and supply lines through Crimea to support the separatists, a claim Moscow has consistently denied. The de facto border between mainland Ukraine and the occupied Crimean peninsula, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, remains one of the most volatile and closely monitored areas in the country. Ukrainian intelligence has reported a recent increase in the movement of military equipment, including tanks and artillery units, near the excluded border, prompting fears of renewed incursions into southern Ukraine. In the east, near the cities of Donetsk and Luhansk, human rights groups and local authorities have warned of a worrying trend of artillery attacks and cross-border shelling, which have led to civilian casualties and displacement. Local commander-in-chief General Valerii Zalenskyy confirmed in a recent statement that the situation remains dynamic and that units stationed in the east are on constant alert for potential attacks. Spokespersons also highlighted the role of unexploded ordnance left behind in previous years, which is now a growing risk as the conflict moves into its eleventh year. The intensification of activity in both regions has raised alarms among international observers, with the United Nations and several European countries urging a return to diplomacy and compliance with the Minsk agreements, the series of unimplemented ceasefire deals that have failed to bring lasting peace. The EU and US have also reiterated their support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, alongside calls for Russia to cease its support for the separatist groups. Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials have reiterated their preparedness to defend the country’s borders by any means necessary. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in a televised address earlier this week, stressed the importance of unity in the face of ongoing threats from both the east and the south, calling on the armed forces to continue their vigilance.

A former aide to former UK Prime Minister David Cameron has gone on trial at the Southwark Crown Court in London, accused of downloading and possessing indecent images of children. James Slack, 50, who once held a senior position in Cameron’s policy unit, faces 13 counts of making and possessing child sexual exploitation material. The charges, which date back to 2017 and 2018, have sent shockwaves through political and media circles, given Slack’s high-profile past. Slack, who resigned as head of policy to the then-Prime Minister in 2016 when he quit the government under pressure over the frozen Syria policy, will face the court on Monday. Prosecutors are expected to detail how digital evidence retrieved from Slack’s home computer uncovered the material, which is said to include images of pre-pubescent children. During his time in government, Slack was described by colleagues as an astute operator, often working behind the scenes on major policy initiatives during Cameron’s leadership. His early exit from Number 10 was not publicly linked to any wrongdoing at the time, and he later worked as a consultant and commentator in the political arena. The trial is set to be one of the most scrutinized in recent years, not only for its legal implications but also for what it may reveal about accountability and personal conduct among those who have held public office. According to statements from the Crown Prosecution Service, the case is “clear and compelling,” with no suggestion of any confidentiality or privilege affecting the charges. Slack has not been directly linked to any public statement or apologia for the alleged abuse. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges. His defense team is expected to argue that the material was not being collected intentionally but rather incidentally acquired through other online activity. A jury of eight members is currently being selected. The case has raised questions about the vetting and oversight of former government workers, particularly those with access to national resources. While Slack left his post some years ago, the allegations re-emerge at a time when public scrutiny of sexual abuse among public figures remains at a high level following the recent Jimmy Savile scandal and other high-profile cases. As the trial begins, supporters and detractors of Cameron are also being called upon to reassess the character of those who have worked closely with the former Prime Minister, even as defenders stress that no man is above the law and allegations need to be considered independently of political association.

The future of how Europeans' data is shared with US technology giants such as Facebook and Google is set to be considered by the European Court of Justice, in what could be a landmark case with sweeping implications for digital privacy and transatlantic data transfers. The ruling, expected in the coming months, will likely determine the legal framework that governs how personal data is moved between the European Union and the United States — a key issue in an increasingly digital world. The case stems from a legal challenge brought by Austrian privacy campaigner Max Schrems, who previously played a central role in dismantling the EU-US "Safe Harbour" agreement, which was declared invalid in 2015 over concerns about privacy protections. Schrems is now targeting the successor to that agreement, known as the EU-US Privacy Shield, which was negotiated to ensure data transfers from the EU to the US would be in line with European privacy laws. The Privacy Shield was established in 2016 to replace Safe Harbour and was aimed at addressing the deficiencies identified by the European Court at the time. However, concerns remain, particularly in the wake of revelations about the extent of US government surveillance and intelligence gathering. At the heart of the case is whether the Privacy Shield provides sufficient protections against government access to personal data by US intelligence agencies such as the National Security Agency (NSA). The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which came into force in 2018, reinforces the right of individuals to control their data and requires strong confidentiality assurances for any international data transfers. Legal experts say the judgment could have wide-reaching consequences not just for US tech companies, but also for a vast array of European businesses that rely on cross-border data flows for their operations. If the court rules against the Privacy Shield, it could force companies to find alternative legal mechanisms for transferring data between the EU and the US, potentially slowing down digital transactions and complicating international business. As the hearing approaches, both the US and EU governments are watching closely. A ruling against the Privacy Shield could create new pressure for updated agreements that meet the evolving expectations of data privacy in the digital age. It could also reignite intense debate over how to balance national security interests with the fundamental right to privacy. While the Court of Justice has not yet delivered a final verdict, the case underscores the growing tension over data sovereignty and the urgent need for a legal framework that reflects the realities of the 21st-century digital economy.

At a time when compassion and dignity should be front and centre, concerns are growing over reports of angry reprimands and shouted commands echoing through the corridors of a mental health hospital dining hall at supper time. These exchanges, described by insiders as “slapstick and soulless,” have raised questions about the balance between discipline and care in a sector dedicated to the holistic wellbeing of its most vulnerable patients. The incidents, which have reportedly escalated in recent weeks, include shouted criticisms from staff to patients over slow-moving queues, delayed seatings, and what one insider described as “perceived slouching.” Witnesses claim that the tone of these interactions suggests a model more suited to military drill sergeants or school prefects than a therapeutic setting. “It’s not uncommon to hear someone barked at, ‘Come on, move it!’ or ‘You’re supposed to be independent – act like it!’” said one staff member, who wished to remain anonymous due to the sensitive nature of the claims. The hospital in question has long prided itself on its patient-centred approach, with mental health being its core focus. Its mission statement emphasizes empowerment, respect, and the fostering of self-sufficiency, all of which sit awkwardly alongside these alleged outbursts. A spokesperson for the hospital responded to these allegations today, defending its commitment to supporting patients in gaining independence in daily living. “Our goal is to prepare individuals for life outside our care and, sometimes, firm guidance is necessary. That said, we take these concerns seriously and have already launched an internal review into the situation,” the statement read. Critics, however, are unconvinced. Mental health advocacy groups have pointed to the therapeutic impact of mealtimes—especially for those in recovery—as a central pillar in fostering social interaction and personal dignity. “When a patient about to eat their evening meal is greeted not with warmth but with criticism, it sends a troubling message about their worth,” said Sarah Kemble, a senior representative at the Mind charity. As the hospital moves forward with its internal review, pressure is growing for transparency and concrete actions to ensure that its approach to care reflects not just the values it espouses, but the compassion that must always underpin the treatment of those in mental healthcare. With a spotlight now firmly on lunches and suppers gone awry, the path forward is as delicate as it is vital. Whether it will lead to meaningful change or go the way of forgotten scandals remains to be seen.

A man has been sentenced to life imprisonment after admitting the murder of a Glasgow shopkeeper whom he claimed had “disrespected” Islam in a brutal and cold-blooded knife attack last year. The attack, which left the community in shock and prompted a national outcry, has since become a symbol of the dangers of radicalisation and violent extremism in the UK. Mohammed Mohamud, 33, was found guilty of the murder of Asad Shah, the 55-year-old owner of a grocery store in the Gallowgate area, who was stabbed to death in broad daylight on the evening of 19 August 2022. Mr Shah, who had lived and worked in the area for over 20 years, was reportedly targeted by Mohamud because he believed the shopkeeper had shared blasphemous content on social media. In the weeks leading up to the murder, Mr Shah had been accused online of defaming Islam, with false claims circulating that he had insulted the religion in Anglo-Saxon terms in his store. These allegations, however, were never proven to be true. Local Muslim leaders and community members later condemned the murder as an act of terrorism, inappropriate and unwarranted. During the trial at the High Court in Glasgow, the court heard that Mohamud, a British national of Somali origin, had previously been radicalised while in prison for another violent assault in 2015. There were concerns that he had deepened his extremist views and was influenced by Islamic State propaganda while serving his sentence. Prosecutors described the murder as “targeted and full of hatred,” with Mohamud having planned the attack for weeks. He was seen buying a long knife before heading to the shop and being filmed on CCTV walking around the area in the days beforehand. The incident was widely condemned by politicians across the UK, including the Prime Minister at the time and Members of Parliament from all major parties. The sentence of life imprisonment, with a minimum term to be set at a later date, was welcomed by Mr Shah’s family, who called for justice to be served. His daughter told the court prior to the sentencing: “My father was a decent, hardworking man who had built up this business to help his family. He never intended to cause outrage or hatred—only to do the right thing.” The murder has also sparked renewed calls for greater community engagement and support for religious minorities in the UK, as well as for improved measures to identify and prevent the spread of extremist ideologies.

The Hatton Garden jewel raid, already a source of national fascination and mystery, has been described as the “largest burglary in English legal history” in ongoing court proceedings. The case, which has captivated both the public and law enforcement since it first hit headlines in 2015, returned to the spotlight this week as lawyers lay fresh claims and evidence before the Crown Court in London. The raid, which took place in April 2015, saw a group of elderly men—many of them previously known to police—burrow into the vault of a high-security safe deposit business in Hatton Garden, one of the most prestigious jewellery quarters in the UK. Over the course of several days, they stole an estimated £14 million worth of diamonds and cash. The audacious nature of the crime, coupled with the apparent ease with which the gang accessed their loot, has led to widespread intrigue and speculation about how it was carried out. In a recent court hearing, prosecution lawyers argued that the scale and complexity of the burglary in terms of planning, execution and financial loss rendered it unprecedented in English legal history. “This was not a matter of taking a few trinkets and running,” a senior prosecutor stated. “This was a calculated, large-scale operation that exploited real and alarming weaknesses in the security of a municipal building that should have been impenetrable.” Some of the accused, including Terry Perkins, who became known as the “Mastermind,” were extradited from Spain after their initial arrest and have since been convicted. However, the case continues as others involved are still standing trial. The trial has also seen revelations regarding the distribution of the stolen goods, with reports that some diamonds were passed on to middlemen and even sold at auction in premium London settings. The Hatton Garden heist remains one of the most talked-about crimes of the 21st century in the UK. The court's involvement not only underscores the legal significance of the case but also the broader implications it has for security, policing and the response to such incidents. As the trial continues, many await clarity on how the law will interpret and ultimately define what many have already dubbed Britain’s greatest heist. For now, however, as prosecution builds its case, the word from the court is that Hatton Garden may well have left an indelible mark on English jurisprudence. This is a story that is far from over.

Victor Moses’ fairytale return to the heart of Chelsea’s formation has proven to be one of the most exhilarating stories of the current Premier League season. Just months after playing more than three years of Premier League football, the 30-year-old winger appears to have found a permanent place at the top table of English football. As manager Graham Potter has reshaped the team with an innovative   3-4-3   system, it is Moses who has emerged as a pivotal piece in this tactical revolution, helping propel Chelsea to the   Premier League summit.   Moses was signed by Chelsea on a free transfer from Wolverhampton Wanderers in the summer, amid speculation over whether the once-revered Nigerian international could rediscover his first-half-of-his-career form. The initial signs were encouraging, but it is this campaign – especially the shift to the 3-4-3 formation – that has seen Moses transition from fringe player to key performer. His ability to stretch the play and deliver dangerous crosses has been integral in providing width to a side that is thriving both defensively and offensively. The transformation has not gone unnoticed. Fellow Nigerian international and former Liverpool winger, Sunday Oliseh, recently praised Moses in a social media post, writing:  “VC Moses, what a story. Realising his potential at 30 in a new system. Absolute warrior and leader.”  Moses’ contributions have not only been technical but also mental. His experience and work ethic have provided a depth to the squad that Chelsea could not ignore as they chase a return to the top of English football. With Kylian Mbappé-inspired teams like PSG and Liverpool still on the horizon in European competition, Moses’ role as a key cog in Chelsea’s tactical wheel has taken on even greater importance. It was just over 18 months ago that the English champions found themselves in deep mid-table slumber thanks to a managerial reshuffle and dip in form. But now, as Potter refines the system, they are cutting the playing surface with speed and precision — a strategy that Moses has been instrumental in executing. For any player, overcoming three years of consistent exclusion from a league team is a monumental task, but for Moses, it’s been a journey of patience, faith, and ultimately reward. As the Blues continue their pursuit of silverware, his resurgence is not just a personal triumph, but a testament to the power of well-aligned football philosophies and the enduring spirit of a player not ready to hang up his boots just yet.

Former Prison Governor Calls for Army to Restore Order in Prisons   A sharply rising tide of violence and disorder in UK prisons has prompted a call from a senior former prison official for the government to deploy the Army to regain control. The suggestion, made by Sir Nick Hardwick, the former chief inspector of prisons, has reignited a controversial debate on the use of military personnel in the civilian prison system. In an interview with the  Guardian  on Thursday, Sir Nick, who stepped down in May after a decade-long tenure leading inspections into prison conditions, said that the current crisis in the sector has reached “unacceptable” levels. He revealed that some of the most violent and abusive gangs now dominate large parts of the prison estate and that staff are frequently working in “hopeless” conditions, unable to prevent or respond to serious bursts of violence and self-harm. Sir Nick, who served as chair of the Parole Board for 18 years prior to his role with the inspectorate, warned that without urgent and radical intervention, the system is at risk of total breakdown. “The government has to ask itself: can the Army be used to give that moment of breathing space, to get control, and then start building something that’s safe and manageable again?” he said. The Ministry of Justice has been under scrutiny for years for its handling of overcrowding, understaffing and inadequate funding – all of which have contributed to the deteriorating situation. Recent reports from the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman and the Office for Standards in Education (Ofsted) have highlighted serious failings at multiple high-security and medium-security facilities. In response to the call, a government spokesperson said: “We are deeply concerned about continued reports of violence and bullying in some prisons and are taking decisive action. This includes significant investment, ongoing reform of the prison estate, and the introduction of new systems to improve safety and rehabilitation.” However, some MPs are concerned that relying on the Army is not a sustainable solution. Labour’s shadow justice secretary, Emily Thornberry, said: “While I understand the frustration and the urgent need for action, bringing in the military is not a long-term way to manage our prisons. This is about funding and political will. We need to invest in trained staff and proper facilities.” Sir Nick, who has supported the calls for greater reform for some time, pushed back against the idea the proposal is intended as a quick fix.

The justice system must revisit a deeply disturbing case involving the sexual assault of a 13-month-old girl by her father shortly before her sudden death, former justice minister Sir Simon Hughes has argued. The case, which was initially concluded with a coroner’s report citing natural causes as the reason for the child’s death, has drawn renewed attention due to claims that key evidence of abuse was either ignored or downplayed at the time. The incident, which occurred in 2015 in the West Midlands, has remained a source of public and political unease for years. A private inquest was quickly closed when the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) determined there was insufficient evidence to charge the father, despite concerns raised by medical professionals and child protection agencies. Sir Simon now claims the case was prematurely closed and that an independent criminal investigation is essential to ensure justice is served for the child and to provide closure for the wider community. Speaking to the BBC, Sir Simon Hughes said: “When a child of such a tender age suffers serious sexual assault in the care of a parent and then dies suddenly, you cannot simply accept the conclusion that it was due to natural causes without a full and thorough investigation. This is not just about the one case; it is about whether the system works when the most vulnerable are involved.” Campaigners and child protection charities have echoed his concerns, suggesting the case highlights flaws in the system’s ability to protect children, and to act on the signs of abuse. Sarah Brown of the All Party Parliamentary Group for Children said: “This is a case that shames us all. Our processes must allow for an open and independent review when the circumstances are this clear and distressing. We owe it to the child and to every other vulnerable child being failed in this country.” The case is not the first time a public figure has raised concerns about the handling of child abuse allegations by the legal system. Over the past decade, several high-profile child deaths have led to calls for independent inquiries, often revealing systemic failures in communication between child protection services and law enforcement. The CPS has not yet responded to requests for comment. However, a spokesperson confirmed that it would reconsider the case if new evidence or compelling grounds for a review were presented.

Two new business surveys have cast fresh light on the delicate economic situation in Scotland, suggesting that the recent downturn may be deepening rather than stabilising. The findings come amid growing concerns from businesses and economists about a slowing Scottish economy, which has bucked the UK trend to some extent over the past year. The first report, from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Scotland, reveals a sharp fall in overall business confidence as firms prepare for a prolonged period of weak growth. The second survey from PwC’s Scottish Economic Monitor records a significant drop in hiring and investment intentions, with many business leaders citing the ongoing uncertainty around the UK's political and economic direction as a key factor. Scotland’s reliance on public sector jobs and the continued supply chain volatility following Brexit have also been highlighted as contributing elements to the current stagnation. According to the CBI, the survey results indicate that a growing number of firms in the manufacturing and services sectors are scaling back operations, delaying expansion plans, and, in some cases, reducing their workforce. “The figures point to a marked slowdown and raise concerns that Scotland is not only facing a slowdown, but a possible sharper decline in the coming months,” said the CBI’s Scotland head, Neil Armstrong. Meanwhile, the PwC report paints a similarly worrying picture. The survey of over 230 businesses shows a decline from the previous quarter in confidence levels across almost every industry. Retail, construction, and the finance sector have all seen a marked fall in optimism, with energy and technology firms also reporting slowing growth. The situation comes as the Scottish government is under pressure to respond effectively to the crisis. First Minister Humza Yousaf has recently announced an updated economic strategy, but some critics argue the measures are being introduced too late and lack the ambition needed to stimulate recovery. “There is a sense of drift in the current economic planning,” said David Martin, an economic analyst at the Fraser of Allander Institute. “Without a clear and robust policy framework, Scotland risks falling further behind the rest of the UK.” As businesses brace for what could be a difficult period, the latest data is a stark reminder that Scotland’s economy is at a crossroads. The question now is whether the right steps will be taken to navigate out of the downturn—or whether the country will see further decline in the months ahead.

Nigella Lawson Claims Ex-Husband Charles Saatchi Threatened to 'Destroy' Her with Drug Use Allegations   Nigella Lawson has told a court that her ex-husband Charles Saatchi threatened to “destroy” her with “false” allegations of drug use during their highly publicised divorce battle in 2013, in testimony that has reignited one of the most sensational legal cases of the decade. The former television chef and author, famed for her charismatic presence and cookbooks adored by millions, was giving evidence in her ongoing £20 million libel case against Saatchi, who she claims defamed her in a number of emails and text messages. Lawson, appearing via videolink, described how her marriage to the advertising tycoon had dissolved under the weight of infidelity and substance abuse allegations. She accused Saatchi of using emails he sent to various friends and relatives to spread damaging lies, including the untrue claim that she was addicted to drugs. “Charles threatened he would destroy me in public and ruin me using the false allegation that I was indulging in drug use,” she said, echoing earlier claims made during the 2013 trial. The case takes on added poignance as both parties testified in court last time, with Saatchi defending his statements by claiming that any remarks about drugs were “jokes” or misinterpreted. However, the judge at the time ruled against him, finding that the jury should not be allowed to hear them as evidence for defamation. The current proceedings, heard at the High Court in London this week, are an appeal from Saatchi to overturn the original judgment. The tabloid press was present in full force, with journalists and legal analysts speculating on whether the case might reveal new details or damage to Saatchi’s standing. Given the global notoriety of both parties, the trial has attracted immense public and media interest. At the time of their divorce, it was described as one of the most acrimonious and expensive in British history. The couple married in 1980 and separated in 1995 before officially divorcing in 2013. Saatchi, 78, is known for his business empire co-built with his late son Daniel Saatchi, while Lawson, 66, remains a household name in the UK and beyond. She has since written several best-selling books and launched new ventures, building a brand separate from her marriage. Lawson's team has reiterated that the libel case is about accountability and the damage caused by private messages sent via personal devices, many of which were deemed legally undiscoverable in the case’s first iteration.

Lewis Hamilton believes his record-equalling seventh world championship, secured with a dominant display in Brazil last weekend, marks the beginning of a new and significant chapter in his storied career — one that he hopes will define not only himself, but also Mercedes for years to come. The Briton, who now shares the motor racing world title record with his former rival and now Mercedes teammate Sebastian Vettel, stressed that his latest triumph is not an end in itself but a foundation upon which something “special” can be built. Speaking exclusively to Reuters ahead of the upcoming Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Hamilton said: “Winning this title feels different, but not because it’s easier — far from it. It’s because I can see a path forward and I believe we can do something really special together at Mercedes.” The 33-year-old left no room for doubt in his comments, hinting at a broader ambition for the Silver Arrows beyond just collecting individual titles for himself and his teammate. “We’ve been working so hard to understand why we’ve been in these winning positions, and the answer is simple: we have the best team in the world. That doesn’t just help me win, it helps us all win.” Remarkably, Hamilton faltered with 10 to go in Brazil when his engine lost power, but he gamely finished the race in second place, securing the championship thanks to Max Verstappen’s crash. He praised his approach that day, stating: “You learn to control your emotions and not be reactive under pressure. That’s one of the things that sets you up for long-term success — knowing when to race and when not to.” Hamilton is not one to rest on his laurels. After seven world titles in 11 seasons, he is keen to push the boundaries further, particularly in a sport where his unprecedented longevity often sparks controversy. “I still feel like I have so much more to give and not just in races. Whether it’s in the way we do things in Formula One, how we treat each other, or what we can achieve together, I’m just getting started.” His Mercedes teammate, George Russell, said he believed Hamilton’s attitude is a key reason behind the team’s current dominance. “Lewis doesn’t see winning as the endgame,” Russell explained. “He’s always thinking about the next challenge, the next goal.

Luis Suarez found himself without a major sponsor just days after being banned by FIFA for biting Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini during Uruguay’s World Cup qualifier in Montevideo last month. The forward, who was given a nine-match suspension for the incident, appears to be feeling the financial as well as reputational consequences of his on-field outburst. Swiss-based eyewear company Cisneros has confirmed it is terminating its sponsorship of the 35-year-old striker following the graphic incident, which has sparked outrage across football and beyond. Cisneros, one of Uruguay’s leading brands and a long-time supporter of the national team and key players, said in a statement that they could no longer associate with Suarez due to the “unacceptable nature” of his actions. “We must uphold our brand values and cannot continue a partnership that contradicts the integrity and respect we stand for,” the company explained. This marks a significant blow for the striker, who is still waiting for the full fallout of the ban to be clarified after FIFA initially controversially ordered his suspension to commence in March, long after the World Cup was over. That decision, which was later Watered down, has remained a point of contention for both Uruguay and Barcelona, who are fighting to delay the ban while legal appeals are still in progress in local courts. Suarez, who has previously been fined and banned for similar – albeit less severe – incidents, has apologised for the act, calling it “impulsive and inexcusable.” However, the growing list of sponsors distancing themselves from the player suggests that those gestures may not be enough to restore his tarnished image. The striker, already under immense pressure following a failed ambition to qualify for the 2022 World Cup through his underperforming Uruguay team, now faces another significant challenge on the business front. The incident has dominated the headlines both in his native Uruguay and around the world, and the sports world is waiting to see whether other sponsors will follow suit. Barcelona, who claimed to have been unaware of the troubling incidents during Suarez's 2020 return to the club, have distanced themselves as well, with club president Joan Laporta recently reiterating the importance of “fair and sportsmanship” in football. As Suarez plots his next move on and off the field, he faces a tough road ahead, both in terms of rehabilitating his image and regaining the trust of the public and his partners.

In a harrowing firsthand account from one of the darkest days in British sporting history, a former police officer has revealed the grim reality he faced during the Hillsborough disaster in 1989. Speaking publicly for the first time, the officer described carrying the body of a 16-year-old supporter from the terraces at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough stadium after a crush led to the deaths of 97 people. He recounted that despite the standard police procedure of placing casualties in the recovery position, he felt it was almost futile due to the severity of the situation. "I remember removing the boy and dragging him outside the pens. He was lifeless," the officer, who wished to remain anonymous, said. "I couldn't tell you his name, but I knew he was a teenager. When you're dealing with mass casualties like this, you go on instinct, but in his case, there just seemed to be little point in making any effort to do more." The disaster, caused by a combination of dangerous crowd conditions, a lack of visible policing and the enablement of an overcrowded central pens, has been the subject of decades-long inquiries and tribunals. The officer, who had been deployed to the match as part of the South Yorkshire Police force, described scenes of chaos and panic as crowds were forced into a confined space. "It was overwhelming. You couldn’t see where the fans had stopped and the pitch started. People were just disappearing into the stands. I didn’t want to be there." The Hillsborough families have long campaigned for justice after initial police statements blamed Liverpool fans for starting the tragedy. But in 2016, the Hillsborough Inquest ruled the disaster was caused by the failure of the police and stadium authorities, and the 97 victims were declared innocent of any wrongdoing. The officer’s testimony adds a deeply personal element to the tragedy, as it echoes the sense of helplessness and confusion among emergency services that day. "You do your training for all sorts of situations, but nothing prepares you for this," he said. "I still remember the sights, the sounds. It was something you never wanted to see, but something you knew you had to face." This account is part of a renewed effort to mark the anniversary of the tragedy and keep the memory of those lost alive, as calls continue for additional measures to ensure such a disaster never happens again.

The private art collection of one of the world's most celebrated photographers, Mario Testino, is set to be unveiled to the public for the first time in the United Kingdom. Known for his vibrant and intimate portraits of the rich and famous, Testino has long been a fixture in the high-glamour world of fashion and celebrity. However, behind the lens of his illustrious career lies an equally impressive passion for art—one that has remained largely hidden from view until now. His collection, spanning more than 300 pieces, includes works by some of the most iconic names in contemporary art, from Andy Warhol to Jenny Savan. The exhibition, entitled "Testino: Eye of the Art Collector," will be displayed at the Saatchi Gallery in London and promises to offer a rare insight into the aesthetic world of the Peruvian-born photographer. Curated with meticulous care, the collection is not only a testament to Testino’s eye for beauty but also his deep appreciation for the global art scene. It features a dynamic range of mediums—painting, sculpture, video, and photography—many of which have never been shown in public before. Among the highlights will be a series of Warhol prints, a vibrant set of works by the pop art maestro that echoes Testino’s own colour-saturated style. The show also includes works by contemporary masters such as David LaChapelle and Richard Prince, with whom Testino has often worked and exchanged creative ideas. His deep friendships with many of these artists have allowed him to amass a collection that is as personal as it is eclectic. Testino said in an exclusive statement: “I’ve always seen art and photography as sister disciplines. For me, collecting is about finding pieces that speak to me—pieces that I feel I need in my life. Now I’m excited to share them with the public, to invite people into this world that I’ve built.” The exhibition opens to the public on 12 October and is expected to run for three months. It will be accompanied by a range of events, including talks by Testino and curators, as well as a special behind-the-scenes look at how his collection was acquired. Art enthusiasts, photography fans, and admirers of Testino’s work alike are set to find the exhibition both revelatory and inspiring. For the first time, the public will get a glimpse into the imagination of a man whose lenses have shaped the visual culture of our times.

Leaked Briefing Notes Expose Ed Miliband's PMQs Strategy Against David Cameron    Exclusive – ‘Avoid Personal Attacks, Focus on Instability’ Advises Labour Whips  Exclusive details of Ed Miliband’s briefing notes for Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs) have emerged after they were leaked to the press, revealing the Labour leader’s key strategy to challenge David Cameron ahead of the 2015 general election. The internal memo, obtained by  The Times , outlines a conscious effort to steer Miliband away from direct personal attacks and instead focus on the Conservatives’ broader record of instability and mismanagement. According to the document, dated three days before Miliband’s scheduled appearance at Westminster, Labour’s own whips’ office stressed the importance of pinning Cameron on controversial issues such as the government’s handling of the economy, the National Health Service, and alleged political and business conflicts of interest. “Highlight the instability, not the man,” the notes instruct, reflecting a calculated agreement to avoid creating a “corrosive tone” during the tense session. The advice came in the wake of criticism from the public and media over Miliband’s previous PMQs performances, some of which were seen as faltering or overly conciliatory. The memo also included bullet points of questions prepared in advance—many of them exposing internal government contradictions. These included references to Cameron denying that he held shares in a property firm, despite extensive ownership being revealed in the  the Guardian  just days later. One section advised Miliband to probe the Prime Minister on his principles and integrity, warning that “the Premier is increasingly seen as a government man, not a visionary.” The document also suggested capitalising on recent controversies, including the Russian and U.S. diplomatic crises, as well as the Prime Minister’s handling of crises such as the Mid-Staffordshire NHS scandal. Labour strategists appear to be keenly aware that PMQs are not just a platform for direct political attack, but also a chance to set the national agenda. The briefing notes note that “the goal is not to inflame the debate, but to provide clarity and show how the Conservatives are failing on the basics.” This sentiment is echoed in internal communications that followed the leak, which insist that the memo reflects a professional and disciplined approach to opposition, aimed at building trust with the electorate. With approval ratings creeping downward for the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats on the ropes, the leaked material offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of Labour’s strategy.

The BBC has revealed the lineup for its series of election programming, as the nation prepares for a general election slated for April 12. Central to the schedule will be a pair of special editions of its flagship political show,  Question Time , featuring Prime Minister Theresa May and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn as the headline guests. The timing of these programmes has been carefully coordinated with key moments in the election campaign, offering voters an opportunity to hear directly from the leaders of the two main parties. According to the BBC’s announcement, May will appear on  Question Time  as part of a live studio session expected to feature a panel of experts, journalists, and members of the public tasked with questioning her on the government’s record and its vision for the future. The broadcast will be one of the highest-profile appearances by the prime minister since the official start of the campaign and is likely to draw intense scrutiny from both the media and political commentators. Likewise, Jeremy Corbyn is scheduled to appear on a separate  Question Time  special earlier this month. His participation marks a rare live appearance on the platform, which will give voters the chance to assess the Labour leader’s ability to directly respond to criticism over his party’s economic policies, as well as its stance on Brexit and public services. The Labour campaign has welcomed the opportunity, with one party spokesperson stating it would "provide a democratic forum for people across the UK to challenge the policies of those in power." The BBC, which is expected to cover all the major political parties in its election programming, has also announced a slate of additional coverage, including debates, live town hall events, and in-depth discussions on key issues such as healthcare, education, and the implications of Brexit. Some opposition parties, however, have previously raised concerns about being excluded from high-profile events, with the Democratic Unionist Party and UK Independence Party notably absent from the initial round of confirmed guests. BBC Director General Tony Hall said in a statement that the corporation remained committed to delivering election coverage that is "unbiased, factual, and accessible to all." He added that guest selection will be based on "explicit and public criteria," including the number of parliamentary seats, recent electoral performance, and media exposure. As the election campaign heats up, the  Question Time  episodes are expected to play a significant role in shaping public perception of the main contenders, with both leaders under pressure to deliver persuasive, coherent messages to a weary and increasingly discerning electorate.

Hearts head coach Robbie Neilson has thrown his support behind talismanic midfielder Robbie Muirhead, suggesting the club legend has a chance to revive a faltering career after a recent run of mixed performances. In an interview ahead of Hearts’ crucial Premiership clash with Dundee United, Neilson revealed that the club is doing everything it can to ensure Muirhead, the Tynecastle hero with over 350 appearances to his name, can continue to play a major role in the side this season. Muirhead, 26, who has been a cornerstone of Hearts’ midfield since his return from Rangers in 2018, has faced increasing criticism in recent weeks over missed chances and a perceived drop in intensity. Injuries have also played a part in his inconsistent form, with the former Scotland Under-21 international unable to maintain the sharpness that once made him a key figure in the Jambos’ promotion success in 2021. “Robbie has been at this club for nearly a decade and he’s been through different phases of his career, some good, some challenging,” Neilson said. “But that’s why players like Robbie, who know what this club means and what it takes to perform here, are still so valued. We believe he still has a lot to offer, and it’s time for him to show us that.” Critics have called for Muirhead, who has made just 14 league appearances this season, to be moved out wide or dropped entirely. But Neilson insists the club are not looking to change the way someone of Muirhead’s experience contributes. Instead, the focus is on reigniting the player’s confidence and allowing him to play in the way he knows best. “He’s got the talent, the understanding of the game, and the respect of the dressing room. Sometimes when the going gets tough, it’s precisely what you need,” Neilson added. “I’ve spoken to him a number of times to make sure he understands that we need him to be the leader we know he can be. He has to believe it himself first before he can take others with him.” With Hearts competing in the top-six mix and eyeing a strong end to the season, Neilson knows the Jambos cannot afford to lose the influence of a player who represents so much to the club’s identity. Whether Muirhead can go back to delivering the performances that once made him a Tynecastle legend remains to be seen.

A driver accused of causing a fatal head-on crash that killed a five-year-old boy has told a court he cannot recall anything about the collision, as the trial heard harrowing details from the devastating incident. The court was told how the boy, identified as Oliver Richardson, was left critically injured when the two cars crashed on a narrow country road in Wiltshire at speed last October. Emergency services rushed to the scene, but despite all efforts, Oliver passed away shortly after arriving at the hospital. His mother and father, both in their mid-30s, were among three adults also taken to hospital and later discharged. Oliver’s father, Christopher Richardson, described the moment to the court as “nightmarish” and said he could not believe his son had been taken from them so suddenly. The defendant, 32-year-old Marc Thompson, has admitted to driving the second vehicle involved in the crash but denies the charge of causing death by dangerous driving. His solicitor told the jury that Thompson was allegedly driving home after work when a microsleep took hold of him, resulting in him crossing the central reservation into the opposite lane. Thompson, who is currently unemployed and was attending regular driving assessments due to a previous history of medical conditions that could affect his concentration, told the court: “I can’t remember anything from that evening—it’s just a blank.” The court heard from a relative of Thompson who said they had often noticed his erratic behaviour, including moments when he appeared “dazed and unresponsive” behind the wheel. Earlier this week, the trial heard emergency call transcripts in which a panicked voice described someone “trapped” in the wreckage. A paramedic who attended the scene told the court it was “the worst crash I have experienced in my 15 years of responding” and described the level of damage to both cars as unprecedented. As the trial continues, the court is expected to explore key evidence surrounding Thompson’s medical history and whether his fitness to drive was compromised. The tragedy has left local residents reeling, with many calling for greater road safety measures in the area, particularly on the lane where the collision occurred. Oliver was remembered as a bright, playful child who loved football and was described by his teachers as “never out of a smile.” His family has called for justice to be done “for Oliver’s sake and the sake of others who may be put in this position.”

Former US President Makes Bold Promise to Eradicate Tropical Disease in Three Years   Dr. Bill Clinton, former president of the United States, has made a dramatic pledge to the global health community: a devastating tropical disease that has plagued millions in the developing world for decades will be eradicated within the next three years. Speaking at a high-profile symposium in Geneva, Clinton announced the ambitious goal as part of an expanded partnership involving governments, pharmaceutical companies, and non-profit organisations under the auspices of the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI). The disease in question, known as lymphatic filariasis—or “elephantiasis”—has left hundreds of thousands of people, particularly in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Pacific Islands, with severe disfigurement and chronic pain. Transmitted by mosquitoes, it affects the lymphatic system and is caused by parasitic worms. While treatable, and preventable with mass drug administration (MDA), the disease has stubbornly persisted in many impoverished regions due to a lack of awareness, logistical challenges, and underfunded health initiatives. Clinton, who launched CHAI in 2008, has long positioned himself as a prominent figure in global public health. His new three-year eradication plan builds on recent successes in reducing the disease's prevalence. “We have the tools, the knowledge, and the will to finish what so many generations have started,” Clinton said during his speech. “This is not a dream—it is a promise we make to those silently suffering and their communities.” The plan, backed by commitments from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the pharmaceutical giants GSK and Merck, includes a multi-billion-dollar funding package to expand access to preventive drugs, improve diagnostics, and launch community-based awareness programmes. Crucially, it also aims to integrate eradication efforts with wider public health strategies, such as tackling malaria and improving sanitation—two areas where overlapping challenges and resources can dramatically enhance impact. Critics and experts have praised the plan but also issued caution, noting that previous eradication goals for diseases like guinea worm took decades and required unprecedented global coordination. Dr. Maria Lopes, a specialist in tropical diseases at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, told the BBC: “Clinton’s vision is bold and necessary. But it will require the full commitment of every partner involved—particularly those in endemic countries.” Health officials in Mozambique, Nigeria, and India—some of the worst affected nations—have welcomed the news with optimism, though they stress the need for strong local leadership and support.

Apple Pay users in the United Kingdom will face an initial spending limit of £20 per transaction when the mobile payment service launches in July, the BBC has learned. The cautious approach aims to prioritize security and consumer confidence as the UK market gears up for the cashless future. Expected to revolutionize how millions conduct day-to-day purchases, Apple Pay allows users to store credit and debit card details on their devices and make payments by simply holding their iPhone, Apple Watch, or iPad near a contactless terminal. The service, which debuted in the US earlier this year, is now set to expand to the UK and has already won the backing of major banks including Barclays, Halifax, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, and Santander. However, despite the excitement surrounding its arrival, users will not be able to carry out large sums in one go. Instead, the technology giant, in conjunction with banks and payment network Visa, has implemented an initial cap to reduce the risk of fraudulent transactions, particularly in cases of stolen devices. This restriction is in line with the existing limits on contactless card payments, which typically range between £20 and £100 depending on the issuer. Caitlin Evelyn, a retail expert at Retail Insights, said the move was a pragmatic decision. “The early limit is a safeguard, not a hindrance. It gives Apple and the banks time to build trust with users and prevent security issues, especially with a system that relies heavily on the tap-and-go method.” Consumers who wish to use higher amounts will still be able to do so, but may be asked to authenticate the transaction using Face ID or a fingerprint scan, effectively reverting to a more secure verification process. Apple is not expected to confirm exact launch details until next month, but industry insiders suggest customers will start feeling Apple Pay’s influence on the high street from July. The launch of Apple Pay in the UK comes at a time when contactless technology is fast becoming the norm. The number of contactless-enabled terminals has grown rapidly over the past few years, with high street giants such as Starbucks and Costa Coffee leading the initiative. With Apple Pay, consumers are set to embrace an even more seamless way of shopping—though security remains as important as convenience. As the rollout nears, questions remain about whether the initial spending cap will be lifted in the near future, something Apple has yet to address directly.

Douglas Carswell, the sole UK Independence Party (UKIP) Member of Parliament, has called on his former colleagues to put aside internal divisions and “work with anyone” to secure a decisive vote on whether the UK should remain a member of the European Union. Speaking in a bid to rally support behind a legislative push to trigger a referendum, Mr Carswell emphasized that the priority must be the Brexit promise rather than party politics. The UKIP leader’s remarks came as internal tensions within the party continue to rise, with several senior figures, including founding member John Hemming, recently calling for the party to disband in light of its poor electoral showing. Carswell, who defected from the Conservative Party in 2014 to join UKIP, argued that the party still has a vital role to play in fulfilling its original mission: to rally behind the demands of the Leave campaign. Although UKIP achieved widespread recognition during the 2014 European Parliament elections — winning almost four million votes and electrifying the political landscape — the party has since lost much of its momentum as support shifted to the Conservative Party’s increasingly hardline pro-Brexit stance. Mr Carswell, however, is betting on a strategy of cooperation, stating that legislatively, it is time for pragmatism over ideology. “In this instance, we must not be trapped in our own internal disputes,” he said. “The focus must be on getting a Brexit referendum on the statute book. If that means working with others to achieve this goal, then so be it.” The sentiment echoes that of Prime Minister David Cameron, who recently indicated he is considering putting the issue to a vote in the House of Commons. Cameron’s reported contemplation is a tacit acknowledgment of the increasing pressure from Conservative backbenchers to allow voters to make the final decision on the UK’s future in the EU. Political commentators suggest that Mr Carswell’s call for unity and collaboration is both symbolic and necessary. With the upcoming general election looming, UKIP’s future, like that of the Brexit movement, remains uncertain. But for now, the focus for Mr Carswell is on delivering on the party’s founding vision — no matter the cost. As he put it: “We cannot let our principles of independence be overshadowed by party tribalism.” The next steps for UKIP, and whether it will indeed seek alliances with opposition or even Conservative lawmakers to push for the referendum, remain to be seen.

A new survey has revealed alarming insights into the lived experiences of the UK's LGBT+ community, with more than half of those questioned admitting they feel the need to lie about their gender or sexual identity in their daily lives. The findings, compiled by an independent equality think tank and published this week, underline the ongoing challenges faced by individuals who do not conform to traditional gender and sexual norms – even in a country where same-sex relationships are legal and marriage equality has been widely celebrated in recent years. According to the report, 54% of LGBT+ individuals who responded to the survey said they either regularly or occasionally conceal their true identity, be it with family, colleagues, friends, or in public spaces. The reasons cited for such secrecy ranged from fear of rejection and workplace discrimination to concerns about safety and harassment. Transgender respondents were particularly affected, with 68% admitting they felt the need to mask their identity in some aspects of their lives. The survey, which polled over 2,000 adults across the UK, has been met with concern by activists, politicians and mental health professionals, who argue that despite legal and societal advances, stigma continues to permeate everyday life for many members of the community. Lucy Cheeseman, chief executive of a leading LGBT+ equality charity, called the findings “devastating but not surprising”. “We have seen a decline in the willingness of national leaders – particularly in the current government – to speak openly and supportively about the needs of the LGBT+ community,” she said. “This climate of silence sends a message that being your authentic self is still somehow dangerous. The truth is, people should not have to live a lie just to be safe or accepted.” The report also highlights a disparity in attitudes between generations and regions. Younger LGBT+ respondents were more likely to feel comfortable about their identity, while those living in rural areas or the north of England reported feeling more excluded or misunderstood. The findings are expected to fuel calls for stronger protections, better workplace policies and renewed public awareness campaigns. Just last year, the government announced updated guidelines for supporting LGBT+ health and education, but critics argue these measures have not been matched with sufficient funding or political will. The survey suggests that while progress has been made, for many in the LGBT+ community, the journey towards full acceptance and equality continues. Some fear recent political shifts and rising cultural debates around gender and identity may be slowing the momentum of that progress.

The Scottish government met for the first time since the snap general election on Thursday, but did not discuss proposals for a second independence referendum—despite the growing political tension in the aftermath of the election result, in which Scottish separatist parties swept to power in Westminster. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and her senior ministerial team convened at Bute House in Edinburgh to address a range of domestic policy matters, including education and healthcare priorities, as well as the urgent need to respond to the UK’s post-election economic and social outlook. However, questions about Scotland’s constitutional future—once a central expectation for the meeting—were notably absent from the agenda. The general election result saw the Scottish National Party (SNP) and the Scottish Labour Party secure a combined majority in Scotland, leaving the Conservative Party with no MPs north of the border. The outcome has been interpreted by many as a mandate for greater Scottish autonomy, and has reignited the debate about independence. Campaigners, opposition parties, and even some figures within the SNP have called for Prime Minister Theresa May to commit to a second independence vote as part of any new deal on devolution or constitutional reform. But, for now, Ms Sturgeon appears to have chosen to delay a formal discussion within her own government. In a brief press statement after the meeting, Ms Sturgeon refused to confirm whether the SNP would call for a Section 30 order—which authorises a legal referendum on independence—despite repeated calls for clarity from Holyrood and Westminster.Speaking to reporters, Ms Sturgeon said the government “has a wide range of priorities, and the timing of any constitutional discussions will be addressed in due course.” However, she did suggest that the election result was a “moment of reflection” for the UK and its constitutional arrangements. “The general election result is a clear signal that people are looking for change,” she added. “This is a pivotal time for our nation.” Opposition leaders have seized on the silence around the independence issue. The Scottish Greens, Plaid Cymru, and the Scottish Liberal Democrats all issued statements calling for immediate clarity on Scotland’s future. Meanwhile, business groups and union leaders have expressed concern that another vote could destabilise the economy at a time of uncertainty following the Brexit vote. The first minister’s calculations appear to be a delicate balancing act—between pressing for independence, maintaining SNP unity, and responding to pressure from both supporters and detractors.

The son of a Londonderry man who has been missing for seven weeks has spoken of his emotional struggle as the festive season approaches. James Devlin, 22, is grappling with the uncertainty surrounding his father, William Devlin, 55, who vanished in early November and has not been seen since. Now, with Christmas fast approaching, the holidays, often a time for family and celebration, loom as a bleak reminder of the man missing from their lives. In an emotional interview from his home in Dungiven, James described how the days once filled with shared meals and family traditions now feel hollow. “It's the worst feeling not knowing what’s happened to him. I just don’t know how to get through Christmas without him,” he said. “You think you’ll be able to cope, to plan for the holidays, but then you look at the calendar and realize he's just not there.” William Devlin, a popular local figure and father of two, was last seen on November 8. Despite extensive searches in his rural area, no sign of him has been found. The Search and Rescue team, supported by local volunteers and gardaí, have scoured fields, woods, and crop areas in the surrounding land. Family friend and community member, Eileen Macklin, said: “This is heartbreaking for the Devlin family. William was so well-known – kind, generous, and always there for people. Everyone in this community is praying he is found safe.” James thanked the public for their support and encouraged anyone with information to come forward, even if it feels unimportant. “We are clinging to hope. That's the only thing we can do now.” The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) reiterated their call for the public’s assistance in the search, highlighting that even small details could prove vital. A reward of £20,000 for information leading to William’s safe return remains in place. Detective Chief Inspector Alan Mitchell, who is leading the investigation, said: “We are still determined to trace William and remain active in all lines of inquiry. Any information, no matter how small, could assist us in locating him.” As the frost begins to settle and Christmas lights flicker across Derry, the Devlin family waits in silence, hoping against hope that the man who has been missing for seven weeks will yet return home. For James, the countdown to Christmas is a countdown suffused with worry – and longing.

Approval for Groundbreaking Gene Therapy Marks a New Era in Medicine   Regulators in the UK have given the green light for the first large-scale rollout of a revolutionary gene therapy, developed by one of the world's leading pharmaceutical giants, Spark Therapeutics. The approval of Luxturna, a treatment targeting a rare inherited retinal disorder, is being hailed as a milestone in the rapidly advancing field of genetic medicine and signals the beginning of a new paradigm in treating diseases at their root. The breakthrough therapy was given the nod by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) after years of rigorous clinical trials that demonstrated its life-changing potential. Luxturna is designed to replace a malfunctioning gene responsible for a progressive form of blindness, known as Leber's Congenital Amaurosis type 2. For the dozens of patients affected by this disorder – who are often diagnosed in childhood and face a slow but inevitable loss of vision – the treatment offers the possibility of restoring functional sight. Health Secretary Sajid Javid welcomed the decision, calling it a “milestone in our ambition to make the UK a global leader in innovation and life sciences.” He added that the government would work closely with the National Health Service (NHS) to ensure that the therapy is made available to eligible patients as soon as possible. The medication, which involves a single injection into the eye, costs more than £1 million per patient, making it one of the most expensive treatments ever approved in the UK. Despite the high price tag, NHS England announced it is finalising a long-term, innovative payment deal with Spark Therapeutics which will allow the treatment to be funded across the country. Such agreements are becoming increasingly common as healthcare systems weigh the costs and long-term savings of once-in-a-lifetime treatments against traditional, ongoing therapies. Professor Sir John Bell, Regius Professor of Medicine at the University of Oxford, said the approval marks the “graduation of gene therapy from experimental science to mainstream medicine.” He noted that similar therapies for conditions like spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease are already in late-stage trials, with the potential to follow Luxturna onto the market. However, some critics have raised concerns about the soaring costs of gene therapies and whether the NHS can afford to scale up treatments for a growing list of rare diseases. Shadow Health Secretary Jon Ashworth urged the government to be transparent about how the system will manage the financial pressures on public health services while ensuring that no patient is denied potentially life-saving care.

Apple’s investors found themselves gripped by a wave of anxiety this week as the once-unshakable tech giant appeared to stumble on all fronts, triggering sell-offs and cautious headlines across financial markets. Shares in the company, which have long been a proxy for overall tech enthusiasm and the broader US economy, dipped sharply on Friday after a series of concern-raising developments, including lukewarm guidance on future earnings and mounting regulatory pressure in key markets. The decline came just days after Apple’s board of directors announced a modest quarterly earnings forecast, far below some Wall Street expectations. While the company still reported a healthy revenue stream — $61.18 billion in the most recent quarter — much of it came from legacy revenue streams like the App Store and services, rather than its flagship iPhone business, which saw only a 2% increase compared to last year. Analysts pointed to the plateauing growth and said it reflected the challenges of sustaining innovation in a saturated smartphone market. Adding to investor unease was news that several major European governments are preparing to finalize a long-anticipated deal to force Apple, along with its competitors, to open the once-closed ecosystems that power their devices and services. The EU is pushing forward with the Digital Markets Act, a sweeping regulatory overhaul that threatens to force Apple to let third-party app distribution on its iOS platform, something it has fiercely resisted. “It’s not just about opening up app stores,” one European tech consultant told  The Financial Times . “It’s about controlling the very platform through which billions of people interact with technology.” For Apple, which has built much of its market dominance and financial success on its tightly controlled ecosystem, the regulatory shift is a seismic threat — and investors are beginning to sense it. The company’s market cap, which has more than doubled since the start of Apple’s streaming and services pivot a decade ago, now stands at a still-impressive $2.4 trillion, but signs are that the plug has been firmly pulled on unbridled growth. Market pundits say Apple now finds itself at a crossroads — much like it did in the early 2000s — when the dot-com bubble fell and the company was struggling to define its role. Back then, Steve Jobs came to the rescue with the iPhone. Now, with new leadership under long-time company figure Tim Cook, Apple must navigate a world where monopolies are under the magnifying glass, and consumer demand for novelty is more difficult to satisfy.

Toby Flood, one of England’s most experienced fly-halves, is expected to miss the opening rounds of the Six Nations championship after sustaining a knee injury in recent training, casting uncertainty over his availability for the crucial early matches of the tournament. The 36-year-old, who has earned over 80 caps for his country, suffered the setback during preparations with his club, Worcester Warriors, where he resumed playing in 2023 after a stint in Japan. While the full extent of the injury has yet to be officially confirmed, media reports suggest it is significant enough to rule Flood out of the early fixtures, potentially delaying his long-awaited return to the international stage after over four years. Flood, known for his composure and ability to control games from the back of the park, has long been considered a valuable asset to the England coaching staff despite the rise of younger, more physically imposing talents in the position. His most recent appearance for the national team came during the 2019 World Cup, where a shoulder injury ultimately forced his retirement from the professional game. However, after making a comeback at club level, hopes were growing that he could add stability and wisdom to England’s fly-half position in 2024. With the Six Nations tournament set to begin in early February, England head coach Steve Banyard is already facing a decision on who will replace Flood should he be sidelined initially. Current contenders for the number 10 role include George Ford and Marcus Smith, both of whom have shown promise in recent campaigns but lack the same level of international experience in high-pressure tournament conditions. Flood’s injury is a blow to a squad already dealing with a number of key players recovering from concussion and ligament damage. The Rugby Football Union has confirmed that scans will be conducted in the coming days, with a full update expected by the end of the week. A statement from the RFU read: “Toby is undergoing further tests and we will provide more clarity on his fitness timeline as soon as possible. We wish him a swift recovery and will make all necessary arrangements to cover for his potential absence in the event he is ruled out.” Flood, for his part, has remained positive about overcoming the latest hurdle. Speaking to the Worcester press, he said: “Injuries are part of the game, but I’ve been through worse and I’m not done yet.

Dundee striker Greg Stewart has expressed confidence that his strong partnership with fellow forward Kane Hemmings will be a key factor in the club’s success this season. The duo, who have already shown glimpses of their potential over pre-season, believe their chemistry and understanding of each other’s game will prove vital as the Dark Blues look to bounce back into the Scottish Premiership after finishing runner-up in the Championship last term. In an exclusive interview with The Press and Journal, Stewart, 37, insisted that the connection between him and Hemmings is not just about their ability to find the back of the net, but about how seamlessly they complement each other on the pitch. “We’re united in our ambition for this season,” said Stewart, reflecting on the early training ground work the pair have shared. “Kane and I are on the same wavelength, and I think that kind of connection is very rare in modern football.” Stewart, who was signed as a free agent following his exit from Hearts, has wasted no time returning to the form which earned him over 200 senior appearances, including stints at Hearts, Hibs, and Celtic. Hemmings, the 23-year-old who impressed in his debut season with the club as their joint-top scorer last term, has also been a revelation on-loan at Greenock Morton in the Championship. Their initial partnership at the start of last season was promising, and Stewart is optimistic it can now develop into something truly special. “We already know each other’s movements and understand how we can maximise the space and create chances,” he said. “We also work hard for each other, and that’s something that definitely sets us apart.” Manager Paul Hartley, who worked with Stewart during his time at Rangers, has been keen to make most of their experience at both ends of the pitch. With the season set to kick off in the coming weeks, the pressure is on for Dundee to make an immediate return to the top flight, and Stewart believes Hemmings and himself can provide the firepower needed. “We both want to play our part in getting this club where it deserves to be,” Stewart added. “Our shared goals, our commitment, and our desire to succeed are what make us a strong combination. If we keep on the same path, I think the results will speak for themselves.”

Celtic found themselves on the wrong end of a crushing 4-0 defeat against Dinamo Zagreb in the final Europa League Group D match at the Maksimir Stadium on Thursday night. Marko Pjaca stole the spotlight with a clinical hat-trick, exposing the visitors' defensive lapses and helping the Croatian champions end the group stage on a high. The result means that Dinamo Zagreb finished as Group D runners-up, a position that will see them face UEFA Europa Conference League qualifiers in the Europa League round of 32, while Celtic journey to the competitions final stages as winners. The Scottish champions, whose hopes of a continental breakthrough had been pinned on a strong European campaign, will no doubt face heavy scrutiny after a dismal display in Zagreb that highlighted the fragility of their backline. Celtic left themselves vulnerable from the outset, failing to cope with the intensity and organisation of the home side. Pjaca, who was signed by Mikel Arteta when he was manager of Arsenal but found playing time limited in the Premier League, was the catalyst for Dinamo's dominance. Within the first 20 minutes, the 28-year-old forward had already latched onto misplaced passes and glided past full-backs as he opened the scoring early. His deadly finishing only got better in the second half, as he completed his first career treble in European competition – all three of his goals attributed to defensive errors from the Hoops. Celtic boss Brendan Rodgers will be left to pick up the pieces from a night to forget in Croatia as his side, who had led the group at the midway stage, dropped points in a crucial crunch match. While Dinamo's victory was a testament to their resolve and determination, it served as an unflattering mirror for Celtic's defensive vulnerabilities, most notably their inability to track back and support their full-backs beyond their central defenders. Questions will be asked about the failsafe arrangements that allowed Pjaca and Dinamo’s attack so much space. Rodgers, known for his pragmatic playing style, will likely face criticism for not addressing the obvious frailty in the setup. Celtic fans, already weary of their team's inconsistencies on the road, could see this as a major setback in what had been a promising European campaign. Despite the defeat, Celtic secured first place in the group with 11 points, a slight bonus in the draw for the knockout rounds.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has urged political leaders to scale back polarising campaign rhetoric, warning that it has deepened social divisions and emboldened hate crimes across the UK. In a sweeping report released ahead of a key parliamentary debate, the watchdog called for an “urgent rethink” in how political discourse is conducted in public and online. The report, titled “A Country Divided: The Impact of Political Rhetoric on Social Cohesion”, analyses the rise in hate speech and bigotry reported to law enforcement agencies and monitoring groups in recent years. It cites spikes in Islamophobic abuse and attacks on minority communities, arguing that inflammatory language from politicians—particularly during high-profile events such as the EU referendum and recent national elections—has only worsened community tensions. “The language of division must not be met with the tolerance of inaction,” said EHRC chair Professor Sir Ian Kennedy, who used the document’s launch to directly call out political leaders by name. He singled out repeated references to immigration as “the root of all our problems” and “us versus them” discourse in both Westminster and the media for enabling a climate in which excluded groups feel more vulnerable. The watchdog also highlighted a growing mistrust in public institutions, particularly in the North of England and Wales, and blamed political leaders for fuelling perceptions of a country where the powerful work only in their own interests.
