It urged leaders to “stop talking at the margins, and start listening to the margins,” while recommending a new set of national standards to ensure all campaigning rhetoric was measured against its potential to cause harm. The EHRC's warning comes at a politically sensitive time. Just last week, a senior Conservative MP was implicated in an email scandal over the use of terms previously associated with the apartheid regime in South Africa. Meanwhile, key figures in the Equality and Diversity Council have raised concerns about the verbal “attack culture” seen increasingly on platforms such as Twitter and Facebook during election cycles. A spokesperson for the government responded to the report by promising to “address divisive rhetoric where it is found,” but stopped short of calling for a broader regulatory crackdown on political speech. They did, however, acknowledge the EHRC’s call for greater personal accountability among those in power. As the debate over how to rebuild community trust accelerates, the EHRC’s report has reignited the call for political leaders to speak not just for their base—but for the country as a whole.

The Imam of China’s largest mosque, the People’s Mosque in the western city of Kashgar, was brutally murdered in an attack that authorities believe was a targeted assassination. The killing has sent shockwaves through Xinjiang, a region long subject to strict government control and a spate of ethnic tensions, and has been met with a heavy security response and state-led condemnation. The Imam, Umar Haji, was shot dead on Thursday inside the mosque complex in Kashgar, a historic and ethnically Uighur-dominated city in Xinjiang. Local police confirmed the incident and have launched an investigation, quickly describing the attack as a “terrorist act” carried out by “separatist elements” opposed to the Chinese state. No group has yet claimed responsibility for the assassination. Umar Haji, who was reportedly in his 70s, was a respected figure in the Uighur and broader Muslim communities. As the imam of the People’s Mosque — which can accommodate thousands of worshippers — he held significant religious and cultural influence. His death, however, is being viewed not only as a personal tragedy but as the latest sign of escalating tensions in a region where Beijing has faced growing resistance to its policies of surveillance, cultural suppression, and restrictions on religious practice. The Chinese government has long accused separatist groups of inciting violence in Xinjiang, a region known for its rich Islamic heritage. However, many experts, human rights organizations, and foreign governments have raised concerns over the scope of restrictions placed on the Uighur Muslim minority, including mass detentions, forced labor, and surveillance. While the Xinjiang authorities insist such measures are aimed at countering terrorism and fostering stability, critics argue they are part of a broader campaign to eliminate Uighur cultural and religious identity. The attack in Kashgar has been met with swift condemnation from the Chinese leadership, with the state-run news agency Xinhua calling it “a heinous act that betrays the national interest and the will of the people.” State media emphasized that the imam had always promoted harmony and religious tolerance, aligning with the government’s narrative of a unified and peaceful society. However, among Uighur communities both inside Xinjiang and abroad, the assassination raises troubling questions. Websites and social media accounts critical of Chinese policies in the region have been rendered inaccessible, but whispers of unrest are growing. Uighur activists have called the killing a “calculated message” from unknown forces — possibly agents of the state, or perhaps separate actors trying to stoke ethnic tensions.

The company that conducts most of America’s rocket launches has unveiled the design and features of its next-generation vehicle, marking a significant step forward in the nation’s ongoing quest for more sustainable and cost-effective space exploration. SpaceX, the aerospace manufacturer and space transportation company based in Hawthorne, California, operates as the backbone of US rocketry, responsible for the majority of launches from American soil. It was therefore no surprise that the latest announcement — made by CEO Elon Musk during a presentation at the company's Starbase facility in South Texas — captured the attention of tech enthusiasts, industry experts and government officials alike. The new vehicle, called the Starship 2.0, represents a bold evolution of SpaceX's already revolutionary Starship system, which has been in development for almost a decade. Musk described the design as "the most advanced spacecraft ever built," claiming it would significantly reduce the cost of deep space missions and pave the way for the long-term colonization of Mars, a goal he has long championed. The Starship 2.0 is a fully reusable rocket and spaceship, designed to carry both cargo and, eventually, passengers. Unlike previous prototypes, which were built with stainless steel due to its durability and resistance to extreme temperatures, the next iteration incorporates a blend of advanced composite materials and a new thermal shielding system. This is expected to improve performance during re-entry and endurance when operating in the harshest environments of deep space. The rocket, still under construction, is being developed alongside the upgraded Super Heavy booster, which will be the most powerful rocket ever to reach orbit. According to SpaceX, the two-stage system will allow full reusability of components, a critical factor in lowering the cost of space travel. Musk stated the new launch system aims to cut the price of sending a tonne of cargo to Mars by as much as 90 per cent compared to previous designs. The unveiling of Starship 2.0 comes at a pivotal time for the US space industry. With NASA preparing for its Artemis missions to the Moon and planning eventual crewed missions to Mars, the company is expected to play a central role. SpaceX is already contracted to deliver scientists and cargo to the International Space Station and has signed agreements with the European Space Agency and private aerospace firms. The company has also been granted conditional environmental and regulatory approvals by the US government, allowing it to conduct launches from the South Texas coast.

A Clergyman’s Condolence: Can Violence Be Justified Against IS?   In a rare and deeply public statement on morality in the face of evil, Bashar Warda, the Chaldean Catholic Archbishop of Irbil, has spoken out about the use of violence in the war against the so-called Islamic State. The archbishop, whose diocese has felt the brutal impact of IS terrorism, said that in the fight against a "cancer" like the group, "you have to use unfortunate measures." Warda was responding to a direct question about whether killing IS fighters—whom the international community, including the Catholic Church, has consistently condemned as extremists and terrorists—was morally acceptable. His remarks offer the perspective of a religious leader who has borne witness to the horrors inflicted by IS, who has buried families slaughtered in their homes, and who has spoken out on the necessity of collective action in the face of unprecedented brutality. "We are not advocating for violence for violence's sake," he said in a wide-ranging interview in the northern Iraqi city of Irbil. "But when the disease is this aggressive, the heart of the body must act to purge it, even if the treatments are harsh." His words echo a struggle within the Catholic Church and beyond: the moral calculus of engaging in war in a country where the lines between soldier and civilian are often blurred. Iraq, already scarred by decades of conflict, became the epicenter of IS’s global ambitions, and Christian communities—Warda’s own Chaldean Catholics among them—found themselves targeted, displaced, and at times executed in mass killings. Warda’s archdiocese, once one of the largest Christian communities in the area, saw its population devastated by the group’s rise between 2014 and 2016. Entire villages were bulldozed, places of worship were destroyed, and thousands of Chaldean Christians were forced to flee to Irbil and other cities in northern Iraq to escape persecution. Such brutal treatment, Warda said, has passed the threshold of explanation and justification. "When it is a matter of stopping an army of killers from extending their tentacles further into your land, into your people, into your children, then you must act with whatever strength is necessary." The archbishop’s comments come amid renewed international interest in delivering a lasting defeat to extremist groups, with the threat of IS still smoldering in regions of Syria and Iraq. While Warda stops short of making a full endorsement of the US-led coalition’s military efforts, his words indicate a spiritual acceptance that in the fight against terrorised genocidal ideology, the moral justification for violence might be found not in aggressiveness

Lukas Jutkiewicz’s dramatic stoppage-time header secured a dramatic 2-1 comeback victory for Birmingham City against Sheffield Wednesday in an electric midweek Championship clash at St Andrew’s. The win lifts the hosts out of the relegation zone and delivers a blow to the Blades as both sets of fans were left stunned in the dying moments of a tightly contested encounter. Sheffield Wednesday opened the scoring in the 17th minute through a composed Akeem Bostick finish from a promising position inside the box. It was a moment of composure from the young forward, who had been making waves in his short time with the club. Birmingham, to their credit, responded with character and intensity, with the home side gradually taking control of the second half. Their equaliser came in the 78th minute, when substitute Kenji Gorrissen cooly tucked the ball into the bottom corner after capitalising on an error in the Wednesday backline. The St Andrew’s faithful, sensing momentum shift, roared their team on in anticipation, planting the seeds for one of those late drama-laden finishes that Championship football is famous for. Despite both teams pushing for the winner, the decisive moment arrived in the 92nd minute as Jutkiewicz rose highest to power in a header from a cross by substitute Adrian Popa, securing the victory in dramatic fashion – just as he often does. The 32-year-old forward, known for his poacher’s instinct and never-say-die attitude, now has 18 goals in the league this season, further cementing his status as a crowd favourite. The win is not just a boost in stature but in form for Birmingham City, who had lost three games in a row prior to this encounter. Manager Neil Lennon remains under pressure, but results like this provide glimmers of hope for a turnaround in fortunes. For Sheffield Wednesday, the defeat leaves them with manager Jos Luhukay facing a tough run-in to maintain their EFL Championship status. Moments of brilliance were overshadowed by fatal defensive lapses at key times, something they must address if they are to avoid a repeat of their 2022-23 relegation. As the player of the match Jutkiewicz explained the emotional high of the moment, "It’s always special when you get a goal like that, but the main thing is the three points. This group is working hard, and I believe we’re going in the right direction."

Lewis Hamilton secured a polished and near-flawless victory at the Mexican Grand Prix, reinforcing his dominance from pole position in a race typified by the composure and precision that have come to define his career. In a track where strategy and pace often collide, Hamilton seemed untouchable, driving as if the motor racing world were his oyster and all the drama unfolded elsewhere. It was the kind of race he would have wished to have experienced a few more times this season, but while the Briton’s performance drew admiration, it was what was happening behind him that provided much of the intrigue. Despite his command of the podium, the true story of the Mexican Grand Prix lay in the battle for second and third places, as well as the stark divisions that opened among the challengers. Max Verstappen, the young Dutch prodigy, tried and failed to mount a challenge against the closely matched cars of Ferrari’s Kimi Räikkönen and Sebastian Vettel — a tactical breakfast, as it turned out, in more ways than one in the high-altitude heat of Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. Verstappen, driving aggressively and with trademark flair, pushed both Ferraris hard, but ultimately found the gap elusive in a race where one brush with the outside kerb was all that separated a podium from watching from the sidelines. The race was also notable for the relentless pace of Ferrari’s duo, who continued to prove, if proof were needed, why the Maranello team remain the most consistent threat to Hamilton and Mercedes. Räikkönen, characteristically measured in his approach, found an extra gear when it mattered most, snatching second place from Vettel on what seemed like the final lap. Whether the stewards will review their positions in the coming hours remains to be seen, but what is clear is that the rivalry between these titans of different generations is far from over. Hamilton, meanwhile, leaves Mexico with the points barely tighter and the championship narrative as compelling as ever. Yet, for all the dominance shown by Mercedes, questions will remain about their title ambitions — could a few more races like this have tipped the scales? As for the rest of the grid, the battle for position was as fierce as ever, with pit stops, tire strategies and incident-filled overtakes providing the drama Hamilton took the bull by the horns and drove away from. With the season heading into the final stretch, the Mexican Grand Prix was a reminder that even when one driver seems uncatchable, the rest of the pack is far from silent.

Dr Kate Granger, a 34-year-old Yorkshire-born doctor who was diagnosed with terminal breast cancer in 2011, left behind an extraordinary legacy long after her death on 23 July this year. In the five years following her diagnosis, she used her personal fight against cancer to become one of the most influential advocates for improved doctor-patient communication and has since inspired an entire movement within the medical profession. Before her diagnosis, Dr Granger was a respected hospital doctor, working across several NHS hospitals. But it was her experience as a patient that truly shaped her path. In the early months of her illness, she was left feeling isolated and poorly treated by some of the medical staff—despite their vital role in her care. That treatment left her deeply frustrated and determined to address the gap in communication between doctors and the patients they were meant to serve. From her hospital bed, and later in her home, Dr Granger launched the #kindness campaign. Using social media—primarily Twitter—she encouraged healthcare professionals to be kind and to introduce themselves to patients by name, explaining their role before providing care. The simple yet powerful message resonated with thousands and quickly gained momentum within the medical community. Hospitals across the UK, and eventually in other countries, adopted the idea, with many creating training programs and posters bearing the slogan "Introduce yourself. Explain what you’re doing. Be kind." Beyond her work in pushing for kinder care, Dr Granger raised over £280,000 for the Yorkshire Cancer Research charity during her lifetime. She also co-founded the ‘Kindness in Care’ charity with fellow physician Dr Helen Jonas, which continues to campaign for improved communication and patient experience. Dr Granger’s death comes as tributes pour in from across the medical world and beyond. Former NHS ministers, hospital staff, and even the Prime Minister have acknowledged her impact. Her story is already being taught in medical schools as an example of the power of personal experience in driving systemic change. As her husband, Nicky, put it in a statement, "Kate wasn’t just fighting a disease—she was fighting for all the patients who come after her. Her voice will never be silent." With her words still echoing in hospital corridors and beyond, Dr Kate Granger’s influence is likely to endure well into the future. Her legacy, built around compassion and connection, is a reminder that in medicine, as in life, sometimes the smallest acts can mean the most.

In a fiercely contested South Yorkshire derby at Bramall Lane, Sheffield United claimed a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Barnsley, thanks to an early goal from Billy Sharp. The result, however, was overshadowed by a dramatic second-half sending off for each side, as tensions flared in a match that perfectly encapsulated the intensity of the region’s most bitter rivalry. From the first whistle, it was clear that emotions would run high. The clash between two historic clubs, separated by just 20 miles but divided by decades of fierce local bragging, never fails to generate an electric atmosphere. The home crowd of over 35,000 fans roared unitedly as Sheffield United pressed forward from the kick-off, determined to make an early statement. The breakthrough came in the 12th minute when Billy Sharp, the Blades’ talisman, latched onto a low cross from the right. Showing his in-form nous, Sharp tucked the ball into the bottom corner of the net past Barnsley goalkeeper Adam Davies. Sharp’s goal was not only a moment of clinical quality but also a reminder of why he is regarded as one of the standout strikers in the Championship this season. The 31-year-old now has eight goals in 11 league games, continuing to justify his reputation as a composed and ruthless finisher. Barnsley struggled to find their rhythm in the opening exchanges and, despite attempts to rally, failed to create meaningful chances before the break. The Tykes were arguably the brighter side in the second half, with captain Caolan Lavery going close in the 61st minute after a sumptuous run by Adam Hammill. However, their resolve was tested when influential midfielder Rory Gaffney was shown a second yellow card in the 78th minute for a crude challenge on Enda Stevens, leaving them a man down for a crucial 15 minutes. Sheffield United barely had time to enjoy their numerical advantage before their captain, George Berry, was also sent off for a high challenge on Tyrese Charles. The 60-year-old Bramall Lane, famous for its intense derbies, witnessed a madcap final 10 minutes as both sets of players gave everything in a desperate bid to find a leveller that never came. The red cards aside, the scoreline of 1-0 flattered the Tykes, who were on the back foot for large parts of the contest. Manager Mark Hudson will undoubtedly be left wondering how his side, who created more chances in the second half, could not have found an equaliser.

A prominent candidate for the leadership of UKIP is likely to be deemed too extreme to stand for election, according to a senior member of the party in the Welsh Assembly. The comments come as the battle lines are drawn for the UK Independence Party's next leadership contest, which has already shown signs of being as fractious as the previous one. The current frontrunner, whose name has been whispered in political circles and among members of the UKIP grassroots, has attracted both fervent support and fierce criticism from within the party. While the identity of the individual has not yet been officially disclosed, the Welsh AM, who requested anonymity when discussing the issue, suggested that the candidate’s far-right leanings make it “politically and ethically unviable” for them to be considered a viable option. “Despite our party's eccentricities and disagreements, there are certain lines you just don’t cross, and this candidate may be pushing beyond what even the most tolerant sections of our membership can stomach,” the AM said. The remarks follow a string of controversies in recent months over the tone and direction of UKIP, as the group remains under a formal ban from broadcasting on the BBC following previous broadcasts that the corporation deemed inappropriate and inflammatory. The ban has since been lifted, as the party has taken steps to reform its messaging, but tensions simmer on. Among those monitoring the situation closely are the UK's national media – many of whom view the UKIP leadership race as the most unpredictable in British political history. The current interim leader, who has held the role temporarily since the last leadership election, made it clear in a recent statement that the leadership contest would be “open to all, provided they meet the party's values and ethical standards”. However, behind the scenes, the central committee is reportedly considering whether any future candidate must be vetted more rigorously. Steve Crowther, a UKIP councillor who supported the previous leader, said: “We cannot afford another campaign that puts off voters or draws headlines for the wrong reasons.” The next stage in the leadership race will be the guest speaker event at the Welsh National Eisteddfod next month. It is expected to give members an opportunity to meet and question the potential candidates – or in this case, as some believe, to see whose candidacy is ruled out first. The final decision on whether the current frontrunner will be allowed to run will come after a review by the party's central committee, which has until March to make a decision.

Great Wall Motor eyes move on Fiat Chrysler as Chinese automaker expands global reach   China’s Great Wall Motor (GWM), already a rising star in the global automotive industry, has turned its gaze towards a bold new target: Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA), the renowned Italian-American carmaker behind iconic brands like Jeep, Dodge, and Ram. While no formal expression of interest has been made public, sources familiar with the matter have told Reuters that the ambitious Chinese automaker is conducting early due diligence on a potential acquisition or partnership, marking a significant step in its journey to compete with the world’s automotive titans. For GWM, which has primarily built its reputation through its robust production of SUVs and pickups in China, the interest in FCA represents a strategic leap into the lucrative North American and European markets. FCA’s powerhouse Jeep brand, in particular, would offer GWM access to one of the most profitable and brand-loyal segments in the global automotive industry. Jeep, long a symbol of adventure and rugged capability, has seen sustained demand in the US and is slowly gaining traction in Europe, where GWM has been working to establish a foothold. The move also aligns with China’s broader ambition to see its automotive brands dominate the global stage. While companies like BYD and Geely have already made inroads through strategic acquisitions — such as Geely’s landmark purchase of Volvo — Great Wall Motor’s potential interest in FCA would be among the most ambitious and high-stakes of these endeavors. However, the path to a deal is anything but straightforward. FCA itself is at a crossroads. Its proposed merger with France’s Renault-Nissan alliance has been met with regulatory resistance and skepticism from key stakeholders. Meanwhile, the company faces mounting pressure to accelerate its shift to electric vehicles and meet increasingly stringent emissions targets. For any takeover to be successful, GWM would need to address these thorny issues while navigating the political sensitivities surrounding foreign ownership of a major American carmaker. Speculation has also been rife over whether US regulators — specifically the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) — would give approval to a Chinese takeover, given the national strategic importance of the US automotive sector and geopolitical tensions between China and the West. If the deal moves forward, it would signal the start of an entirely new chapter for GWM, transforming it from a regional Chinese player to a go-to global brand for SUVs and rugged vehicles.

In a sensational display of destructive batting that will go down in World Cup legend, West Indies opener Chris Gayle smashed the first double century in tournament history as his side thrashed Zimbabwe by 178 runs in their Pool B clash at Canberra on Wednesday. The 38-year-old, often dubbed the 'Universe Boss' for his awe-inspiring power, brought up the historic milestone with a ferocious 121 ball innings, a testament to his enduring class and ability to dominate under pressure. Gayle's blistering knock was a masterclass in contemporary one-day cricket, as he tore through the Zimbabwean bowling attack with clinical brutality. The West Indies, chasing a modest target of 339, achieved the total in only 43.4 overs, finishing on 343 for the loss of just four wickets, a feat made even more impressive by the array of sixes Gayle unleashed. It is now the highest individual score in World Cup history, eclipsing the previous record of 183 not out set by India’s Sourav Ganguly in 2003. As he struck 26 sixes and 18 fours, the Australian city of Canberra witnessed a cricketing spectacle not seen in global tournaments before. For Gayle, it was also a personal redemption, having previously failed in key moments in previous World Cup campaigns – this time, he delivered with the precision and swashbuckling flair that his reputation is built upon. What makes this innings even more significant is the fact that it occurred in a World Cup in which all forty balls are played in the same innings. Gayle’s dominance has been a recurring theme in the tournament, and his continued ability to adapt and thrive in the high-pressure format has solidified his status as one of the greatest batsmen of all time. “When I come out to bat, I just take what the bowler gives me,” Gayle told reporters after the match. “I play to the best of my ability and I’m always trying to set the tone for the rest of the team.” Team captain Jason Holder was full of praise for his veteran opener, saying: “Chris is a world-class player and he has that ability to take games away from the opposition. Today was a special day for the team and the West Indies cricket fans around the world.” With this innings, the West Indies have goaled themselves on the early map as one of the real contenders in this year's tournament, while Gayle's name is further etched into cricketing folklore.

Harriet Harman, the acting leader of the Labour Party, has called for unity and reflection rather than finger-pointing in the wake of the party's devastating defeat in the recent general election. Speaking at a pre-arranged strategy meeting in London on Tuesday, Harman stressed the need for Labour to move forward constructively after a result that saw the Conservatives secure a decisive majority. “This moment calls for sober analysis and not a blame game,” she said. A stark shift from policy to performance has placed Harman at the helm of a party in disarray, as members and MPs now brace for what could be a period of significant reform. Labour won only 204 of the 650 seats contested, falling short of expectations and raising questions about the party’s direction since the departure of Keir Starmer last year. Harman, who had stepped back from frontline politics after her initial leadership in the mid-2000s, is expected to oversee an interim period as the party deliberates on its next leader and broader strategy. The defeat has already triggered calls from within the party’s grassroots and parliamentary factions for a review of internal processes, messaging, and policy priorities. Many have pointed to a failure to connect with core Labour voters as a root cause of the loss, with some critics arguing that the party became too focused on internal ideological battles rather than tackling public concerns about the economy, healthcare, and cost of living. Harman’s comments come as the party announced an internal inquiry to be led by experienced strategist David Heyes, who has been tasked with reviewing Labour’s performance during the campaign. Heyes, a former Conservative strategist who defected to Labour in 2023, has been a controversial figure within the party and his appointment has been met with mixed reactions. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, speaking after a meeting of his Conservative Party leadership, welcomed Labour’s defeat and said his government was “united and ready to fix the national mess left by years of failed opposition politics.” Within Labour ranks, the response has been more subdued. Shadow Chancellor Darren Jones acknowledged the “scale of the loss” and pledged to support Harman’s call for calm. Meanwhile, former pro-Remain MPs and grassroots members have also expressed concern that the loss signals a growing divide between the party’s younger left-wing activists and the traditional working-class voters who once formed its backbone.

The European Union has unveiled a controversial proposal for an EU-wide Border and Coast Guard agency as part of its efforts to manage the unprecedented influx of migrants and reinforce internal and external borders. The plan, submitted by European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, sets out a blueprint for the creation of a dedicated force capable of patrolling Europe’s coastline and responding to irregular migration flows more effectively. The proposal comes amid mounting pressure on EU member states over the migrant crisis, with thousands arriving on European shores every month and deep political divisions over how to respond. Under the proposed system, the EU Border and Coast Guard would be tasked with providing immediate support to member states facing migration pressures, enabling rapid deployment of vessels, aircraft and personnel to manage border control and rescue operations. Member states would retain responsibility for their borders, but the new agency would step in during peak migration periods or in the event of a crisis, such as the widespread arrivals seen in recent years across the Mediterranean. The move is expected to be backed by a budget of several hundred million euros a year and would allow the European Union to coordinate border operations, including surveillance, Search and Rescue (SAR) missions and returns of irregular migrants. The proposal is being touted as a key element of the EU’s freshly announced “reform agenda” to be implemented by 2019, which also includes work on a common asylum policy and improved information-sharing between member states. However, it has already sparked fierce debate across Europe, with some member states welcoming the plan as long-overdue central coordination, while others remain wary of the financial and political implications. Hungary, which has been a staunch critic of unfettered migration, praised the plan, with Prime Minister Viktor Orbán stating it would “finally put an end to the chaos at our borders.” In contrast, France remains sceptical, with French Interior Minister Cécilia Attias warning that centralised control over borders could weaken national sovereignty. The plan also faces scrutiny over the role it would play in migrant rescue efforts. NGOs, including Médecins Sans Frontières, have raised concerns about the potential for reduced humanitarian aid as the new agency is mainly focussed on border control. As the EU seeks to present a united front against the ongoing migrant crisis, the proposed Border and Coast Guard force will likely be the subject of intense political negotiations in the coming months, shaping the future of Europe’s approach to migration and border security.

In a gesture of solidarity and humanitarian aid, Pakistan has deployed military personnel to assist its citizens affected by a powerful earthquake that struck in south-eastern Iran. The quake, which is reported to have had its epicentre near the Iranian city of Kermanshah, has left devastation in its wake, rocking homes and communities along both sides of the border. With tremors felt across both nations, the disaster has reignited discussions about cross-border humanitarian cooperation in one of the world's most tectonically volatile regions. Initial reports indicate that the earthquake occurred in the early hours of Sunday, registering a significant magnitude that caused widespread panic and damage. Among the most urgent needs is rescue and medical support, as emergency response teams work round the clock to reach trapped survivors and coordinate relief efforts. Pakistan, aware that numerous of its citizens live and work in the border region, has swiftly organised teams of soldiers and specialist rescue units to the affected areas to assist in the search and recovery operation. The deployment, confirmed by Pakistan’s Ministry of Defence, highlights the country’s commitment to looking after the welfare of its nationals, even in remote and perilous locations. Pakistani military helicopters have reportedly begun ferrying supplies, including blankets, food, and medical kits, while ground teams are working to assist in evacuation and shelter provision for those displaced by the disaster. The army has also established a task force to support local authorities in the region with reconstruction and planning long-term relief measures. This act of support is particularly poignant given the often strained and complex political dynamics that exist between Pakistan and Iran. While the two nations have historically shared diplomatic ties, at times they have also experienced difficulties regarding border security and regional influence. However, in moments of catastrophe, the response tends to shift from political rhetoric to pragmatic cooperation. The incident mirrors past efforts, such as the relief operations following the 2005 Kashmir earthquake, when neighbouring countries and international bodies came together to provide much-needed aid. A spokesperson for Pakistan's national disaster response agency said, “We have always believed in the principle of aiding those in need, regardless of where they are. Our people suffer as one, and any Pakistani citizen caught in disaster deserves our full attention and resources.” As the tremors settle and the full extent of the damage becomes apparent, the focus will increasingly shift to long-term recovery.

Rising Awareness of Concussion to See More Rugby Players Retire, Warns Medical Expert   A former World Rugby medical adviser has issued a stark warning that growing awareness of the dangers of concussion will lead to an increasing number of rugby players being advised to retire. Dr Barry O'Driscoll, who served on the sport’s international medical committee and has long campaigned for player welfare, stressed that while the development is not easy to welcome, it is necessary to protect athletes' long-term health. “Unfortunately, I believe we are going to see a rise in the number of players being told they can no longer chase the dream of playing rugby at the highest level due to concussion concerns,” O’Driscoll said in an exclusive interview with  The Guardian . “The science is clearer than ever before, and we simply can't ignore the evidence.” Over the past five years, concussion protocols in rugby have been significantly revised to enhance player safety. These changes include stricter return-to-play guidelines, mandatory head-impact monitoring in elite leagues, and in some cases, the use of GPS and mouthguards to track the number and severity of head impacts over a season. Clubs and national unions are also investing heavily in educational programmes for players, coaches and medical staff. However, O’Driscoll, who has been a vocal advocate for change since the early 2000s, argues that the long game must now be considered, and that it will not be possible to balance a player's health with their professional career in every case. “We already see examples of younger players, those in their mid-to-late 20s, being told they are at too high a risk of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) to continue. This is going to become more common in the coming years,” he explained. The Rugby Football Union (RFU) in England said it “recognises the importance of player welfare at all levels of the game and is committed to protecting the long-term health of its athletes, even at the cost of short-term inconvenience or loss.” Critics of the sport have long argued that rugby must fundamentally change its approach to reduce head injuries, with some calling for rule modifications to crack down on dangerous tackles. Others propose the outright abolition of certain techniques that leave players vulnerable to whiplash and concussive force. O’Driscoll, who has worked with the RFU, World Rugby and Super Rugby, urged players, unions and fans to accept the hard choices that lay ahead.

A senior magistrate has resigned from his post following an unprecedented row over allegations that he attempted to settle legal costs for an asylum seeker in a case that was adjourned due to the individual's failure to pay a £100 fee. The resignation of District Judge John Rudd, who served in the Provincial Division of the Crown Court, marks an uncomfortable beginning to the parliamentary session and raises fresh questions about the independence of the judiciary and the boundaries of a justice official’s ethical obligations. Judge Rudd, one of the judiciary’s most senior members, was suspended in December 2023 after it was revealed that he had called a court official and revealed he intended to pay the financial obligation of an unnamed asylum seeker. The case involved an individual who had not shown up for appearances due to the unpaid fee, which is standard practice to deter non-attendance and cover administrative costs. The Guardian, which first reported the story in late December, stated that the payment was described as an "inappropriate interference with the separation of powers." According to court officials, the discussion came to light during internal disciplinary proceedings following a formal complaint from magistrates about the handling of similar cases. The solicitor for the accused, who had highlighted the system's inequity in immigration cases, did not inform Judge Rudd of the individual’s financial situation, but the judge allegedly considered it "unconscionable" that someone facing – potentially criminal – proceedings could be penalised for poverty. Justice officials confirmed that the Judge was informed of the restrictions on judicial independence under the Code of Judicial Conduct and advised not to make any unilateral decisions in this area. However, Judge Rudd reportedly expressed his views publicly, saying that he was left with an "unpleasant impression" about how the court administers justice to vulnerable individuals – a line which critics are now using to underline concerns about judicial impartiality. His resignation, the first of a high-ranking Crown Court judge in recent memory, has sparked calls for a review of the rules governing judicial conduct, particularly in relation to immigration, where issues of poverty and access to legal representation are often stark. The Lord Chancellor, Dominic Raab, told the House of Commons on Monday that the government is considering changes to the financial barriers faced by immigrants and asylum seekers appearing in court, but added: “Judges must act independently and within the law, and there are clear lines beyond which even concern cannot travel.”

Joe Root has emerged as the "obvious candidate" to succeed Andrew Strauss as England's Test cricket captain, former and current players alike have said, with James Anderson expressing cautious support for the 28-year-old Yorkshire batsman. However, the 37-year-old Lancashire pace legend has issued a clear warning — Root must not let the leadership role compromise his formidable batting performances on the field. Root, who played a pivotal role in England’s recent Ashes victory, has long been in the frame for top honours since his debut in 2012. With his calmness under pressure, leadership during the Ashes test series in Australia, and his ability to build long innings, he is seen as the natural successor to Steve Smith-style leadership on the international stage. Anderson, England’s most capped player and the spearhead of their pace attack, spoke at length during a special edition of the podcast he co-hosts with team-mate Stuart Broad. He acknowledged Root's suitability but added: “What happened previously with Cook — in his early captaincy — was that people thought he didn’t do enough. But I think he improved, and that’s what I want to see from Root. The captaincy doesn’t take away from your abilities as a batter. If anything, it improves your situation in the field.” Root, who averages over 50 in Test cricket, has already captained in limited-overs, and now it is thought his promotion to the Test squad captaincy is only a matter of time. Cricket writers and analysts foresee a smooth transition, with Root’s experience at all levels — and his proven leadership in trying circumstances — a key factor. But Anderson's point echoes a broader concern among cricketing minds: can a central batsman maintain the same level of performance when taking on the stresses and pressures of captaincy? England’s head coach, Chris Silverwood, recently said he "fully expects Joe to cap it," and with Eoin Morgan taking the ODI and T20 reins, Root appears set for the dual challenge. Anderson, meanwhile, hinted that the leadership could be the catalyst for a new golden era for England cricket, but only if Root can focus on doing what he does best — scoring runs. "He’s got to ignore the noise," Anderson said. "He must not change the way he plays for the sake of being captain. That’s the number one thing. Look at Root — he’s got the temperament, the stats, and the respect of the team.

MPs report highlights ‘shocking’ economic inequality faced by Muslim women   A parliamentary report has revealed that Muslim women in Britain face uniquely compounded economic disadvantages, often stemming from a combination of gender, ethnicity, and faith-based discrimination. The findings, released by a cross-party group of MPs, serve as a stark reminder of the inequalities still pervading British society more than half a century after the Equal Pay Act was passed. The report, titled  The Invisible Struggle: Economic Inequality Facing Muslim Women in the UK , underlines how Muslim women are not just among the lowest-paid in the workforce but also encounter barriers in education, employment opportunities, and access to services like financial banking and even property ownership. "This is not about the exception, it is about the pattern," said one of the MPs involved, Labour’s Nadia Abd Ibrahim. "This is a problem for the whole country, and it is not acceptable in 2024." According to the findings, Muslim women, on average, earn 14 percentage points less in real terms compared to the non-Muslim female workforce, even after adjusting for factors such as educational attainment and full or part-time work status. They are also underrepresented in senior roles across various sectors and struggle to access finance to launch or expand their own businesses. Many interviewees in the report spoke of experiences of Islamophobic microaggressions in the workplace – such as being overlooked for opportunities, facing distrust because of their hijab, or being steered into positions that “fit their background.” The report also highlighted the challenges of balancing cultural expectations and personal ambition. Some Muslim women interviewed said they face pressure from within their own communities to prioritise family over career ambition, something that is not experienced in the same way by their non-Muslim counterparts. “You can be excluded because of stereotypes about how Muslim women are not ambitious or not capable, but you're also sometimes penalised if you try to break out of that box,” one female entrepreneur explained. The MPs called on the government to implement a range of targeted policies, including improving access to apprenticeships and leadership training tailored for Muslim women, investing in support networks, and better monitoring of workplace discrimination. They also recommended that employers adopt clearer diversity and inclusion practices that specifically consider the needs of Muslim women. This report comes amid wider public discourse about racial and gender equality in the UK, particularly after high-profile cases of discrimination and the push for govt accountability on equality issues.

England were bowled out for just 65 in their second innings to seal an innings-and-75-run defeat against India on the final day of the fifth Test in Chennai, marking a brutal end to their hopes of saving the match and completing a controversial 2-2 draw in the four-match bilateral series. The collapse was one of the worst in the history of Test cricket for an England side and further exposed the flaws in their batting order following a damaging winter away from home. After being asked to follow on, England had begun the final day’s session with a precarious 84 for six and slim hope of wresting the result from India’s grasp. However, spinner Ravichandran Ashwin picked up two more victims in quick succession, ripping through the tail and wrapping up the innings with India needing just 74 more to secure a dominant victory. The match, which had already been overshadowed by the heavy monsoon rains in the earlier days and the loss of breakfast sessions due to prime ministerial visits, concluded in a torrential downpour, with the India captain Virat Kohli looking forlorn in the dugout as the mercy rule was waved. England, who had come into the Test series after winning two of the three one-day internationals, started poorly with the bat in Chennai and compounded their problems by bowling rhythmlessly against a rampant Indian batting line-up – which racked up a first-innings score of 438 after England had earlier posted 288. Jimmy Anderson, who was meant to be England’s backbone with the ball, failed to make an impact in the second innings, while young debutant George Garton was oddly left out of the attack altogether, furying captain Joe Root as the floodgates opened. The woes of England continue to heap up in what promises to be an anxious summer of Ashes preparation, with selectors now under pressure to revamp the batting order and uncover fresh talent to ensure the national team is not left staggering in Test cricket. India’s triumph put the finishing touches on their most successful Test tour of England and will no doubt increase the pressure on the visiting side ahead of the intense Australia series, starting in June. For now, however, as rain rushed over the Chinnaswamy Stadium Turf, the writing was on the wall for an England team that looked lost in the run chase and directionless on the bowling end.

Dame Sarah Storey has etched her name in history as Britain's most successful female Paralympian, securing her 12th gold medal on a triumphant opening day at the Rio 2016 Paralympics. The 37-year-old, already a legend in her sport, extended her record in an awe-inspiring display of power and precision as she dominated the C5 3,000m individual pursuit. A hush fell over the Pacaembu Velodrome before she accelerated to victory, her determination as much a spectacle as her athletic prowess. Storey crossed the line with a time of 3 minutes and 23.467 seconds, setting a new world record and proving her enduring excellence despite well-documented injuries, including numerous concussions and chronic pain. Her victory lit up London’s Olympic Park, where celebrations erupted and the Prime Minister issued a personal congratulations. "Sarah’s resilience and commitment to her sport, and her disability sport community, are truly inspirational," said Chancellor Philip Hammond, who shared an awards ceremony with the cyclist back in 2013. Storey, who was born with Erb’s palsy and lost both legs below the knee following a childhood swimming pool accident, is only the third athlete, male or female, to cross the 10-gold medal threshold in Paralympic history. Her new record surpasses that of swimmers Hayley Jones and Rebecca Strong, who had shared the previous mark for British female Paralympians with 10 medals apiece. Despite this triumph, Storey remained characteristically modest: "The focus is always on the team," she said in a post-race interview. "I want to win as many as I can for Team GB." Her cycling journey, which began in competitive athletics before she switched to the velodrome in 2004, has been marked by an exceptional transition and a fierce determination. Storey moved to Manchester two years ago to train full-time with the GB Para-cycling team, working closely with coaches Tim Leaney and Tony Smith. Her success in Rio comes amid speculation about how long the pioneering athlete will continue. As the rest of the cycling programme unfolded, Storey’s next challenge will be the time trial later in the week, with no indication she is slowing down. For British cycling fans, watching Storey go about her business is a familiar ritual of excellence. Each turn of her wheels adds not just to her individual achievements but to the growing prestige of Paralympic sport in the UK. With her 12th gold, Storey has once again broken barriers and proven that age, injury, and physical limitation are no match for passion, discipline, and the unyielding will to succeed.

Nurses across Northern Ireland are being called upon to take a pivotal role in the upcoming Northern Ireland Assembly election as a leading trade union warns that the collapse of devolved government has stalled crucial health service reforms. With Stormont in political limbo since January 2022, the nursing profession—some 30,000-strong and central to the everyday running of hospitals, care homes and community services—faces an uncertain future in a system that has long suffered under chronic underfunding and staff shortages. The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) Northern Ireland has launched a campaign urging nurses and healthcare workers to register to vote and make their voices heard at the ballot box on May 2. "Health is at the heart of what people care about," said RCN Northern Ireland’s Secretary, Teresa Dillon. “But without a functioning Assembly, real progress has been impossible. It is more important than ever that the people who spend their days in wards, clinics and care homes are represented in the political system.” The Anglo-Irish Agreement in 2023, which sought to restore governance to Stormont, was short-lived, collapsing again under the weight of political divisions over the Northern Ireland Protocol and other contentious issues. This has left healthcare stuck in a cycle of grief and stagnation. Nurses, often on the front line during the pandemic, saw little of the support they had demanded – from better pay to safe staffing levels – and now they fear that the broken political system is blocking efforts to rebuild. Nurses have long campaigned for structural change in the health and social care system. Despite repeated promises in various policies and strategies over the years, investment has not kept pace with demand. The RCN highlights the need for a fully devolved and elected healthcare policy body – something that has been absent since the collapse of Stormont. Without political clarity, they argue, sustainable change is impossible. In a document released by the RCN, it states that “nurses are not just carers, but powerful agents of change. Their vote can shape the future.” Across Northern Ireland, branches of the union are holding open forums, distributing leaflets, and offering guidance on registration and how to assess candidates based on their healthcare policies. In Belfast, Londonderry, and beyond, the message is clear: nurses are being encouraged to do more than work – they must lead the change. As one nurse told the RCN, “If I don’t use my vote, who will?

The political landscape of Scotland has been fundamentally reshaped following a commanding victory by the Scottish National Party (SNP) in the recent elections, reinforcing the party’s position as the dominant political force and reigniting debates on Scottish independence. With a historic parliamentary mandate, the SNP has not only returned to power at Holyrood but has also signaled an unambiguous message to Westminster and the rest of the UK: Scotland’s voice is clear, and it is distinct. The landslide victory, which saw the SNP swoop back to power with a staggering majority, is a decisive reversal of fortune from the previous administration. The Conservative Party, which had formed the Scottish government until recent weeks, is now reduced to a minor parliamentary force. Labour, once the dominant party in Scotland for decades, has been further weakened, while the Liberal Democrats face their worst performance in years. Most significantly, the results mark the end of a short-lived but widely criticized government under First Minister Humza Yousaf, who resigned earlier this year following a period of political turbulence and a lack of public confidence. The SNP’s return to power, led by the new First Minister John Swinney, has once again placed the question of Scottish independence under the political spotlight. The party has long campaigned for a second independence referendum, and with such a commanding mandate, there is little doubt that the push for a vote will be intensifying. The upcoming general election in the UK could become, in many ways, a de facto referendum on Scotland’s future within the UK. Political observers have noted that the SNP’s success stems from a mix of strong grassroots support, a strategic campaign, and a sense of public frustration with the status quo. The party has emphasized its record on healthcare, education, and the climate crisis, while painting its opponents as out of touch and unresponsive to the needs of communities across Scotland. Yet, the victory also raises challenges. The SNP must now balance its ambitions for independence with the realities of running Holyrood and managing a complex relationship with the UK government, particularly over issues of funding, education, and welfare. As the country braces for what could become another pivotal chapter in its constitutional journey, one thing is certain: Scotland’s political contours have been redrawn, and the path ahead remains both uncertain and deeply significant. lunches delivered right to their doorsteps.

Peter Vaughan, who has died at the age of 93, leaves behind a distinguished legacy in British theatre, television and film—despite rarely taking on leading roles. Known for his commanding presence, deep, resonant voice, and formidable screen presence, Vaughan carved out a remarkable career in what might be called the world of character actors: those whose power lies not in the spotlight, but in the shadows of the leading man. Born in 1927 in Stockport, Greater Manchester, Vaughan served in the Royal Navy during the Second World War before embarking on his stage career. He later starred in repertory theatre across the North of England, honing a craft that would soon bring him to national attention. It was in 1961 that he truly hit his stride, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company. Over the next decade, he became known as one of the company's most versatile supporting actors, playing villains, soldiers, and clowns with equal flair. He often appeared alongside theatrical heavyweights such as Ian McKellen, and his performances were ever consistent in both comedy and tragedy. Though he was a regular on stage, it was on television that Vaughan found the widest audience. One of his most enduring roles was that of Dumbledore in the early 1980s series "The Casual Vacancy," though it may confuse modern viewers. He was also a familiar – and frequently feared – face in numerous British television dramas, notably appearing as Magda, the leader of the Brotherhood of the Chain, in the immensely popular BBC fantasy series "Good Omens," which also starred someone who would later become a global star: Michael Sheen. His performance was so memorable that it made him the face of many fantasy and horror villains in the public imagination. Vaughan's career in film was equally distinguished. His most famous cinematic role was as the gruff and green-faced leader of the Death Eaters, Waldermar Grindelwald, in the film adaptation of J.K. Rowling’s "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them." As Grindelwald, Vaughan brought a chilling authority to a character feared as one of the greatest witches of his time. His ability to transform into such iconic villains was a testament to his mastery of acting. In his final decades, Vaughan continued to appear in theatre and television, bringing gravitas and pathos to characters that might have been overlooked in the hands of a less gifted actor. Despite rarely playing leads, his presence was always unmistakable.

Police in Germany have confirmed that a suspected arson attack has caused a school sports hall in the western city of Wuppertal to burn down, the building having previously been temporarily converted into a shelter for asylum seekers. The fire, which broke out in the early hours of Monday morning, is reported to have destroyed the entire structure, although no casualties have been reported at this stage. Emergency services were quick to respond to the blaze, which was reported by a passerby just before midnight. Firefighters managed to contain the flames by the early hours of the morning, but the damage caused to the building has been described as “extensive” by local authorities. According to a statement issued by the Wuppertal police, a preliminary investigation has ruled out the possibility of a technical fault and is now treating the incident as a deliberate act of arson. Officers are currently following a number of lines of inquiry, including whether the targeted nature of the fire—focusing specifically on a facility providing housing for asylum seekers—relates to xenophobic or far-right motives. The sports hall, located within a local school, had been temporarily repurposed to accommodate approximately 100 asylum seekers over the past few weeks as part of a wider effort by the local council to address rising demand for temporary shelter. Authorities had indicated that the move was a short-term solution, with plans in place to transfer residents to more permanent accommodations by the end of the year. Horst Müller, a local councilor, described the incident as “a senseless attack not only on a building, but on the values of solidarity and hospitality that this city has fought hard to uphold.” He added that officials are already working to relocate those affected and are in contact with nearby municipalities to secure alternative shelter. The mayor of Wuppertal, Anita Stolpe, also condemned the act, calling it a "dangerous provocation" at a time when Germany continues to grapple with the integration of asylum seekers and the national housing crisis. No arrests have been made so far, but local police have announced that they will be conducting door-to-door inquiries and reviewing surveillance footage in an attempt to identify those responsible. This incident has once again raised concerns about anti-migrant sentiment in Germany, which has seen a rise in politically motivated violence in recent years. In 2023, the country recorded several arson attacks against refugee accommodation centres, particularly in the western and southern regions.

Chile is one of those countries that expects to experience large quakes. Nestled along the Pacific Ring of Fire, the South American nation has long been accustomed to the seismic activity that comes from its volatile tectonic landscape. On a recent sunny afternoon, citizens of Valdivia, a city in southern Chile infamous for a massive earthquake in 1960 — the most powerful ever recorded at 9.5 on the Richter scale — felt another tremor, this one measuring 7.3, send ripples through the region. Despite the shock and minor damage to infrastructure, the response was strikingly calm, a testament to a deeply ingrained culture of preparedness. Residents quickly followed well-rehearsed protocols: people in offices grabbed their colleagues and made their way to open spaces, while highways emptied rapidly within minutes. Emergency sirens, familiar from years of simulations, cut through the streets without instilling panic. Chile's proactive approach to disaster resilience is a combination of historical necessity and modern governance. After the 1960 quake, which devastated the country and claimed thousands of lives, legislators and scientists collaborated to create one of the most robust seismic building codes in the world. Schools and towns regularly conduct earthquake drills, with even children as young as five learning when and how to drop, cover, and hold on during a tremor. The country also maintains a national emergency coordination system called ONEMI, which deploys personnel and resources rapidly in the event of a natural disaster. Following Monday’s quake, ONEMI issued immediate assessments, deploying teams to assess landslide risks in rural areas and to assist communities in the Andean highlands, where aftershocks are a common concern. Though the death toll remains at zero as of Tuesday morning, officials caution that the risk of further tremors remains high, with at least two smaller aftershocks already recorded. The quake’s epicentre near Valdivia was not entirely unexpected. Scientists had predicted a moderate quake along the fault line in that region within a five-year window. "This was not an anomaly," said María Elena Valdés, a geologist at the University of Chile. "It was a warning from the Earth, reminding us that while we can build resilient cities and academies, the Pacific Frontier will never stop challenging us." As the morning light settled over the region, Chileans went about their day with a weary but resolute spirit. For them, life is not about avoiding quakes — it's about preparing for them, living with them, and, when necessary, moving on.

Pakistan Greats Back Amir to Deliver a New Cricketing Statement Against England   Mohammad Asif, one of Pakistan’s most feared fast bowlers and a key figure in the 2006 Lord’s Test triumph over England, has made a strong endorsement of his fellow countryman Mohammad Amir, calling for yet another standout performance in an old cricket rivalry now returning to the international spotlight. Amir, who was at the heart of that same Lord’s Test thirteen years ago — a match that sparked a spot-fixing scandal involving himself, Asif, and Salman Butt — has since undergone a difficult and at times controversial journey, but the 32-year-old is now intent on proving himself once more. Asif, 36, sees potential for Amir to rise again on English soil, where history has already shaped much of Amir’s career. "Amir has the talent, and he knows the conditions here in England. If he gets the opportunity, he will definitely trouble the English batsmen again," Asif said in a recent interview. “And honestly, I would love to be out there bowling with him one more time.” The upcoming Test series between Pakistan and England, which will include fixtures in Nottingham and Taunton, puts Amir back in the frame for a place in Pakistan’s fast-bowling attack. The 2010 Asian Games gold medallist has already made a notable impact in recent one-day internationals, and the prospect of his return to red-ball cricket has been met with cautious optimism by fans and analysts alike. Amir, who served a five-year ban in 2011 for his involvement in the spot-fixing incident, has worked hard to re-establish his career in the years since being cleared to return to cricket in 2016. Though he has at times struggled for consistent form, the English summer — with its swing-friendly conditions — is where Amir often finds his rhythm. “I think the English handle is a reminder for both teams. Pakistan, for proving their resilience, and England for understanding that they can never take Amir lightly,” said a Pakistan cricket commentator. “History has shown how intense this rivalry can be when players like Amir come into their own.” Both Asif and Amir are products of a golden era of Pakistani fast bowling that included the likes of Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, and their return to the fold in high-stakes contests brings echoes of a proud tradition.

British Telecommunications (BT) has announced a sweeping overhaul of the UK's network of public telephone boxes, set to see half of the 40,000 remaining kiosks removed. This comes as the company shifts its focus to maintaining only those units located in areas where they are most likely to be used — typically in high-traffic zones such as city centres, hospitals, train stations and schools. The move signals the final phase of a decline that has spanned decades, as mobile phone ownership has overtaken landlines and the once iconic red boxes have become a rarity in everyday life. The decision follows years of monitoring the usage of these payphones, which have seen a steady drop in engagement. BT, which is the primary operator of public phones in the UK on behalf of the Post Office, has found that the majority of the remaining boxes go unused for months at a time, prompting the company to prioritise investment where it will make the most difference. Around 20,000 of the roughly 40,000 kiosks currently in place will be removed or decommissioned under the new strategy, while the rest will stay in service, often retrofitted with modern features such as free WiFi, landlines as well as electrical sockets. These upgraded models, known as StreetConnect plus, will continue to serve both the public and utility workers. David Watson, BT's chief executive, stated in a recent statement that the company was determined to support communities by ensuring that vital phone and phone facilities remained available. However, he also made it clear that the business was no longer in the position of subsidising underused boxes at the expense of those that are active. “These are not about cutting corners, but about being smart with our investment,” he said. The Prime Minister’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, though the government had previously defended the importance of maintaining public phone access in rural areas and emergency situations. The removal of the classic telephone kiosk has sparked a wave of nostalgia and trepidation among heritage and telecom enthusiasts. The iconic red design, a symbol of British telephone history, was once a staple of town centres and waiting rooms, but its decline has reflected broader technological shifts. The 1980s were the peak period for public phone usage, with over 500,000 boxes in operation. The proposal by BT has reignited the debate over the cost of preserving Britain’s telecom heritage in the modern age, with some calling for a preservation fund to protect the most historically significant kiosks.

Rail passengers in Tayside, Stirlingshire, Perthshire, Aberdeenshire and the Borders are being promised a "revolution" in travel, with long-awaited investment set to transform rail services across these key areas of central and north-east Scotland. Transport Scotland has announced the plans as part of a broader strategy to revitalise the country’s rail network following years of underfunding and public pressure for improved infrastructure and connectivity. At the heart of the ambitious proposal is a commitment to increase the number of services, reduce crowding and improve punctuality, as well as invest in infrastructure upgrades to support modern, efficient train operations. The plans include the reintroduction of long-lost routes and the expansion of existing services, with the goal of making rail travel a more attractive option for commuters, tourists and businesses alike. Local MPs and transport advocates have welcomed the news, calling it a “turning point” for rail users in the region. Stewart Stevenson, a Scottish National Party MP for Motherwell and Wishaw and a longstanding supporter of rail reform in Scotland, said the investment was not only long overdue, but showed a shift towards a more sustainable transport future. “This is more than just a few new carriages or a slightly better timetable,” Stevenson said. “This is about reconnecting communities, stimulating economic growth and creating a rail network that works for the people of Scotland.” Community leaders in Perth and Aberdeenshire, two of the regions to benefit the most, have also praised the promise of improved connections to larger cities and key transport hubs. Brian Rhind, director of the Central Scotland Rail Users’ Group, highlighted the potential for the investment to reduce reliance on buses and car travel, especially in outlying areas. “This revolution in travel could finally give people back their time and improve their quality of life,” Rhind said. “We’ve been waiting for this for far too long.” Transport Scotland confirmed that consultation with local authorities and rail operators is already underway to ensure the changes reflect the needs of local passengers. A detailed breakdown of the investment and new route proposals is expected to be released in the coming months, with the first phase of upgrades planned for 2025. For now, passengers in these regions are hopeful that the words of a "rail revolution" will finally translate into tangible improvements on the tracks. They have waited decades. Now, for the first time in years, they may see their patience rewarded.-president of Harvard University, Claudine Gay, has stepped down following questions over her doctorate.

In the mid-1990s, the United Kingdom was a nation in thrall to cultural revolutions—the rise of Britpop, the nation’s collective obsession with the Spice Girls, and a footballing superstardust that promised a return to glory. It was a golden era marked by self-belief, exuberant pop anthems and a sense that, culturally and sportingly, Britain was on the crest of a wave. Now, a quarter of a century later, fans and nostalgia-seekers are looking back with affection at a time when Britpop ruled the airwaves, Spice Mania hit the streets in neon and the football pitch came home under the glare of Olympic Park lights. The Britpop explosion, led by the likes of Oasis, Blur and Pulp, was more than just music—it was a cultural tide. Bands flew the flag for English identity in the face of the cool alienation of the 1980s, creating a movement that defined breakfast, bedtime and everything in between. Liam Gallagher’s ballsy "Live Forever" chords and Blur’s jaunty "Song 2" became the soundtrack to school corridors and family terraces, while Pulp’s Jarvis Cocker raised the roof in Sheffield with "Common People". Young and old found themselves united by the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, the so-called "Battle of Britpop", which culminated in the 1995 BRIT Awards where the bands performed back-to-back, marking an unforgettable night that would be replayed for years to come. Meanwhile, the Spice Girls dominated headlines and hearts. With their catchy choruses and unforgettable catchphrases—“Girl Power!” came to define an entire generation’s approach to self-empowerment and being “Forever.” The band’s global mania found a special home on British soil, where fans young and old vied for autographs and lanyards at every opportunity. The phenomenon was so all-consuming that the national media dubbed it “Spice Mania,” a time when every girl wanted to be “Sporty” or “Scary” (depending on the day). But perhaps the most visceral moment of national pride came on 11 June 1996 when Euro 96 rolled into London. For the first time in 55 years, the England football team reached a major European semi-final. The tournament—which started with the away goaldenying 4–3 victory against Scotland at Hampden Park—became a rite of passage for the British public. "Football came home," as the popular song said, and for 30 days, the nation was gripped by shirts and belly-buttons alike.

Research suggests that the Ebola virus underwent a dramatic and startling adaptation in the early months of the 2014–2015 West African outbreak, allowing it to infect human tissues more efficiently than ever before. This revelation, detailed in a new study published in Nature, challenges existing assumptions about the speed at which the virus was able to evolve to exploit human hosts more effectively. It also raises urgent questions about how future outbreaks — particularly of known or unknown diseases — might be mitigated before they spiral out of control. Scientists studying Ebola records and genetic sequences of the virus from the outbreak have identified a set of mutations that appear to have emerged within a few months of the initial cases being reported in Guinea. These changes, they argue, allowed the virus to bind more tightly to human cells, particularly those in the liver and the immune system, making it more pathogenic and increasing the chances of transmission between humans. The findings highlight how quickly viruses can adapt in response to new host populations, a dynamic often underestimated in global health preparedness. “The speed at which Ebola’s virus evolved is truly alarming,” said Dr. James Roth of the University of Oxford, one of the lead researchers on the study. “Viruses are not inert threats — they are evolving entities that can sharpen their ability to infect and spread as rapidly as they encounter new opportunities.” The 2014–2015 outbreak was the largest in history, with more than 28,000 cases and nearly 11,000 deaths reported primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The mutations appear to have emerged in the initial months of the outbreak, a time when global attention had not yet turned to the crisis and local healthcare systems were largely overwhelmed. This allowed the virus to spread unhindered, giving it the conditions needed to mutate and adapt to the human body. The research also points to an unexpected role of what might be termed “sampling bias” in viral sequencing. In this outbreak, for example, the most severe cases — those that led to rapid death — were more likely to be sequenced, leading scientists to overestimate the proportion of lethal mutations present in the virus. However, the study suggests that while such cases were over-represented in data, the mutations were indeed contributing to the virus’s increased virulence and efficiency. Public health experts warn that the findings serve as a reminder of the importance of real-time genomic surveillance in future outbreaks.

Sisters Katie and Ellie Ward, collectively known as Ward Thomas, have made history by becoming the first British country music act to reach number one in the UK album chart with their latest release,  Rivers and Roads . The milestone marks a significant shift in the UK music landscape as the duo breaks through traditional genre barriers and elevates British country music on the national stage. The album, their fourth, showcases the band’s evolving sound as well as their deep-rooted passion for storytelling. Blending themes of love, loss, and resilience,  Rivers and Roads  resonates with a growing fanbase and has been praised by critics for its emotional depth and authenticity. With three UK top 40 chart entries already under their belt and six BRIT Award nominations, the duo has steadily built a loyal following, culminating in this historic achievement. Speaking about their success, the Wards said they hope their journey encourages more British artists to take pride in the country genre and continue to push its boundaries. “We always knew we were passionate about this music, but to see it resonate so much with people, even outside of the traditional country fanbase, is something that really humbles us,” Katie Ward said in a recent interview. The sisters, from Welwyn Garden City, Hertfordshire, have long been champions of-country music in the UK. Their early days of performing in small venues and – most famously – at the C2C: Country to Country Festival in London helped them carve out a place in the industry. Earlier this year, they announced they were joining the BBC's 6 Music Radio lineup as full-time contributors, signaling further mainstream recognition of their influence. The chart-topping success also comes as the UK country scene continues to gain momentum. The genre has seen a surge in popularity, with festivals such as about:blank (formerly known as Camp Bestival) and Shakin’ Stevens’ Country To Country continuing to grow year on year. Sales of-country albums have also risen significantly, with 2024 proving to be the biggest year for British country music in recent history. Ellie Ward added: “We want to make it clear that it's not about restricting ourselves to a genre – it's about telling real stories and being true to who we are. If we can inspire more people to do the same, then this album will be a huge success in more ways than just chart position.”

Opposition members of parliament were thrown out of South Africa's National Assembly on Wednesday during President Jacob Zuma's annual state of the nation address after engaging in what lawmakers from the ruling party condemned as "disruptive" and "unparliamentary" behaviour. The dramatic scenes, which unfolded as Zuma outlined his government’s legislative agenda and plans for the year, saw more than a dozen opposition MPs escorted out of the chamber as their cries for a vote of no confidence in the president echoed around the hall. The incident marked a tense escalation in the growing political crisis surrounding Zuma, who has faced mounting pressure from the opposition, civil society and even some of his own supporters to step down over allegations of corruption and mismanagement. The Democratic Alliance (DA), the closest opposition party to the ANC, led the protests. DA MP John Steenhuisen accused the ruling party of using parliamentary rules "as a political weapon" to silence dissent and avoid holding Zuma to account. "We called for a debate on this matter, not a farce," Steenhuisen said as he was being removed from the chamber. The governing African National Congress (ANC) responded by condemning the "disregard for decorum and the dignity of the institution." ANC whip Jackson Mthembu called on opposition parties to "refrain from inciting chaos" and to respect the rules of the national assembly. The state of the nation address, a constitutional obligation for the president, is the highest-profile event of the parliamentary calendar and usually attracts significant attention both locally and abroad. This year, however, the event was overshadowed by an ongoing saga involving allegations of state capture, the Nkandla scandal – which saw Zuma accused of misusing public funds for personal renovations at his rural home – and his refusal to make key statements about ongoing judicial developments. Just days before the address, the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) announced that it would not be pursuing criminal charges against Zuma over the Nkandla affair, a decision that sparked fierce criticism from anti-corruption activists and further emboldened opposition parties to increase pressure on the president. The ANC relied heavily on its parliamentary majority to ensure passage of the bill removing Zuma as prosecution head over Nkandla, passing the amendment by a significant margin of 261 votes.
