However, for now, the joke, like the burden of the actual tax code, will remain firmly with the comedian. Michael McIntyre, in a light-hearted response to the attention, told reporters: “I must admit, I was tempted to call and offer my professional services. But if you've seen the Chancellor in action—you probably wouldn't want the wrong man in charge of delivering the budget.” With the man in the actual gothic room maintaining his own brand of drollery, one thing seems certain: the role of Britain’s resident fiscal curmudgeon remains safely in one pair of size-twelve loafers.

French officials have revised their account of a dramatic police raid last week, revealing that a woman presumed to have died in an explosion during the operation was, in fact, shot dead by officers. The woman, identified by British media as Sonia Khallouk, 26, the cousin of ISIS militant and suspected ringleader of the Paris attacks, Abdeslam, has been the subject of confusion and misinformation following the raid in the Molengeur street apartment in northern Paris on Thursday. Earlier reports, including those from French Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, had initially stated that Khallouk had detonated an explosive device during the operation. However, new details released by French authorities confirm that no explosion occurred. Instead, Khallouk was killed by gunfire from special forces during the early-morning raid. Khallouk, who had gone missing after the coordinated attacks that left 130 people dead last Thursday, was described as an ISIS supporter linked to the terror cell responsible for the attacks. French investigators believe she may have been the keeper of a cache of guns stored in the property. Her death came after over 50 hours of standoffs between police and suspected militants in the densely populated district of Bobigny. A message posted to Khallouk’s Facebook page hours before the raid had read, "My blood will be on your hands," adding to the tension of what was one of the most high-profile raids since the attacks. The footage of the black-clad figure tossing phone devices from the building toward the emergency services that stormed the property has also added further questions to an operation that saw two police officers injured and the property severely damaged. French officials have not ruled out the possibility that other members of the group remain at large, but the killing of Khallouk marks a significant step in the hunt for those responsible for the deadliest terror attack on French soil since World War II. The revised account of her death underscores the chaotic and dangerous nature of the operation to dismantle the network behind the attacks. Moments of confusion in high-pressure situations such as this are not uncommon, but the update sent ripples through media and intelligence circles yesterday, highlighting the ongoing challenges in tracking ISIS operatives across Europe. As investigations continue, French President François Hollande reiterated his confidence in the security forces’ ability to identify and capture remaining fugitives, delivering a sombre but firm message: "Our goal is clear: to make life impossible for terrorism in France."

The UK government has published a list of 15 Scottish companies found to be in breach of the national minimum and living wage, marking yet another round in its campaign to hold businesses accountable for underpaying their staff. The move, which “names and shames” the offending firms, aims to deter employers from violating wage laws by exposing them to public scrutiny. The list has been published on the   gov.uk   website and includes details of the sectors in which these firms operate, as well as the amounts of underpayment outstanding. The list was released in response to a crackdown announced last autumn by the then-Employment Minister, Priti Patel, as part of the government’s broader agenda to raise standards in workplaces across the UK. Among the companies included on the list are hospitality, retail, and construction businesses. The government’s announcement has reignited the debate around wage enforcement, with some calling for steeper fines and more punitive measures against violators. The National Living Wage, introduced in April 2016, has since increased in stages and currently stands at £9.50 per hour for those aged 23 and over, directly above the £8.91 minimum wage for workers aged 21 to 22. Minister for Small Business, Growth and Industry, Margot James, stated: “It is unacceptable for any employer to break the law and denying their workers the wages they are owed. We take these breaches extremely seriously and the publication of this list is part of our continued efforts to ensure that all workers in the UK are treated fairly and paid in line with the law.” She also urged workers who suspect they are being underpaid to report it to the government’s free and confidential reporting portal. Reacting to the announcement, the TUC – the Trades Union Congress – welcomed the transparency but said it was not sufficient. “This is a step in the right direction, but we need stronger enforcement and heavier penalties to ensure that unscrupulous employers are held to account,” said Matt Burgess, the TUC’s head of campaigns. Meanwhile, the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) expressed concern that the focus on enforcement could inadvertently target struggling small enterprises. “While exploitative practices cannot be tolerated, we must also ensure that firms experiencing temporary financial difficulties are supported rather than simply penalised,” said FSB Scotland’s director, Patricia Findlay. The publication of the go-to list follows similar actions in England and Wales, where over 1,100 businesses have been named since the initiative began in 2017.

The brutal death of Italian graduate student Giulio Regeni in Cairo has reignited international concerns over Egypt's human rights record, casting a spotlight on the country exactly five years after the uprising that led to the ousting of longtime leader President Hosni Mubarak. Mr Regeni, 28, a Cambridge University researcher, was found on 3 February with severe injuries consistent with torture, sparking outrage among his family, academic community, and European governments. A post-mortem examination revealed that he suffered extensive bruising, signs of ligature marks, and other wounds caused by blunt and sharp instruments. Mr Regeni had been in Egypt studying trade unionism under the country's post-revolution government when he vanished earlier that week. His body was discovered near the Ramses Bridge in the capital, where numerous dissidents and activists have reportedly disappeared or died under suspicious circumstances in recent years. His family and Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi immediately called for an independent international investigation into the circumstances of his death. “What happened to Giulio is inexcusable and unacceptable,” Mr Renzi said, urging the Egyptian authorities to cooperate fully. The Egyptian Interior Ministry, which has been under scrutiny for alleged human rights abuses, initially denied any involvement in Mr Regeni’s death and accused human rights groups of “spreading distortions and fabricated accusations.” However, it later acknowledged that Mr Regeni may have come into contact with “security agencies” and stated it was investigating his case. Mr Regeni's death comes at a time when Egypt’s democratic progress—briefly ignited by the 2011 uprising—has appeared to stall. Since the military-led ousting of President Mohamed Morsi in 2013, Egypt has experienced a wave of arrests and detentions of activists, journalists, and critics of the government. His killing is being viewed by many as the latest tragic example of the intolerance for dissent in the country. Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have long condemned the Egyptian government for widespread arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and enforced torture. The international community, including the European Union and the United Nations, has expressed deep concern over these developments. The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Zeid Ra’ad Al Hussein, said recently that Egypt "must do more to protect the rights of all individuals." Mr Regeni's death has once again placed the issue of Egypt's human rights at the forefront of diplomatic discourse, as governments grapple with balancing support for stability in the region with the need to confront repression and abuse.

The UK government faces a massive administrative workload in its negotiations to leave the European Union, with a former senior Foreign Office diplomat warning that it will require the hiring of significant numbers of civil servants to manage the process effectively. Sir Simon McDonald, a former Permanent Under-Secretary of State at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, described the task as “phenomenally large” and urged the government to prepare for the considerable strain Brexit will place on public services and departmental resources. Speaking at a policy event in London, Sir Simon highlighted the sweeping changes required as the UK moves to redefine its relationship with the EU. He noted that outside of the Foreign Office, other key departments—including the Department for Exiting the European Union, Health, Education, and the Treasury—will also require expanded staffing to handle the legal, economic, and regulatory shifts involved. “Brexit is more than just a political decision,” Sir Simon stated. “It is the most significant constitutional and legislative change this country has faced in decades. The administrative challenge is unprecedented, and unless we are realistic in our planning, we risk setting ourselves up for failure.” The diplomat’s comments come amid growing concerns over the government’s capacity to manage the transition, with recent reports indicating a significant gap between planned staffing levels and the number of civil servants required. For instance, the Department for Exiting the European Union has been accused of being understaffed and under-resourced for such a complex operation. The department was established shortly after the 2016 referendum and faced criticism for its initial structure and lack of legal and economic expertise. Prime Minister Theresa May’s government has repeatedly said it is accelerating hiring and training to meet the demands of Brexit negotiations. However, Sir Simon’s remarks suggest that more needs to be done to ensure that the UK is adequately prepared for the scale and intricacies of the process. His comments have reignited questions about the government’s preparedness for Brexit and whether it is managing the transition with sufficient urgency and foresight. The scale of the task is immense—covering 50 years of EU law, thousands of trade agreements, and the ongoing health of economic partnerships. As negotiations with the EU intensify, with intense discussions expected on trade, customs, and the status of EU citizens in the UK and vice versa, the need for a well-staffed and well-coordinated government machinery is more pressing than ever.

There is a "chronic" shortage of housing for people leaving prison in Wales, with a growing risk that former offenders will become homeless or reoffend, a charity has warned. Despite government commitments to reduce reoffending and support a “second chance” approach to justice, the reality for many exiting the criminal justice system is bleak. Campaigners say the lack of affordable and stable housing leaves many individuals unable to reintegrate into society, making them more vulnerable to homelessness, addiction, or a return to crime. The Welsh charity Prison Reform Trust (PRT) highlighted the crisis in a recent report, which called for urgent action from the Welsh government and local housing authorities. It argues that without secure housing, efforts to reduce reoffending and promote rehabilitation are doomed to fail. "Every individual leaving prison deserves the chance to rebuild their life, but without somewhere safe to live, their future is at serious risk," said Aneurin Roberts, director of PRT. "Housing is the foundation of everything else – without it, education, work, and community relationships are out of reach." Wales, like the rest of the UK, has seen increasing demands on its housing market, particularly for low-cost or social accommodation. Prisons in Wales struggle to find suitable housing for those released during winter, when options are often more limited. The issue is compounded by postcode lotteries in local authority support – prisoners preparing for release are sometimes given addresses in areas they have no connection to, exacerbating the sense of displacement. Some prison leavers rely on temporary placements in emergency shelters or hostels, which offer little stability and are rarely a long-term solution. Research published earlier this year by the Welsh Government showed that between 2018 and 2022, more than 20% of people released from Welsh prisons experienced homelessness or insecure housing in the first 12 months after release. The figure is significantly higher for individuals with mental health issues or those who left prison with unmet care needs. Council housing, already over-subscribed, is not meeting the needs of those with active health or social care plans. Charities and housing associations warn that specialist housing for ex-offenders is in short supply and too often tied to strict conditions or intensive support systems which not everyone requires. Official data shows demand for social housing in Wales has increased by 11% in the past three years, while the number of available social homes has barely grown.

The music world is in mourning following the tragic news of Chris Cornell’s death, with some of the biggest names in rock and pop paying heartfelt tributes to the Soundgarden frontman, who passed away by suicide. The 52-year-old singer, who also achieved individual fame during his brief but influential tenure with the band Audioslave, was found dead in his hotel room in Detroit on Friday night, just hours before Soundgarden was due to perform at a festival. Preliminary reports confirmed the grim reality, sending shockwaves through the global music community. Cornell’s soaring vocals, powerful stage presence, and influence on the grunge movement of the 1990s left an indelible mark on generations of musicians, and his death has prompted an outpouring of grief and appreciation from his peers. Among the first to acknowledge the tragedy was Pearl Jam, with whom Cornell had a long-standing professional and personal relationship. Eddie Vedder, the band’s lead singer, described him as “the most singular voice in rock in his lifetime” and said the news “hit us like a train.” Tributes have also come from legends such as Alice Cooper and Slash, who praised Cornell’s “heart and soul,” while fellow grunge pioneers like Temple of the Dog bandmate Barrett Martin remembered him as “a brilliant artist and a truly good man.” Even outside the rock sphere, icons such as Adele and Gwen Stefani expressed their sadness, underscoring the widespread impact of Cornell’s music. Cornell rose to fame in the early ‘90s with Soundgarden, whose albums like  Badmotorfinger  and  Superunknown  helped define the sound of grunge. His deep, resonant voice and emotionally charged performances helped chart their rise to prominence, but he struggled with personal demons offstage, often opening up about battles with addiction and the toll of fame. In recent years, he had pursued a solo career and returned to Soundgarden for a triumphant revival, proving to critics and fans alike that his creative fire remained undimmed. His final performance was just weeks ago in Australia, where he was celebrated as a rock legend. As tributes continue to flood social media and airwaves alike, the common sentiment among fans and colleagues is one of profound loss. Cornell’s death is a reminder of the invisible battles that many public figures face, with growing calls for greater awareness of mental health in the music industry. His legacy, however, will undoubtedly endure—his music resonating long after the silence.

You could be forgiven for skipping over yet another article talking about a talented international goalkeeper who courts the cameras, dates the trendiest singers, lands himself in hot water through his bad behaviour and gets big money. These days, the footballing world is littered with £20 million men whose lives outside of goalposts are as volatile — if not more so — than their shot-stopping exploits on the pitch. But this time, the name making headlines is not another Ake, but Aymeric Laporte’s long-suffering shadow, Simon Slavens, or as he’s more appropriately known: Simon Zmirko. Zmirko, a Slovenian custodian, has risen from mostly obscurity to becoming a divisive figure at the heart of European football. From his well-documented relationships with pop stars — his most recent high-profile split from Ed Sheeran affiliate Cell Darcy sending shockwaves through the A-list — to his chaotic run-ins with the law — including an infamous incident involving a limo, a topless barista in Paris and a bottle of 2015 Grand Cru Dom Pérignon — the 87-times capped keeper is fast becoming the benchmark for celebrity footballing excess. His side, Lazio, are as much his as they are manager Simone Inzaghi’s: a team that has flourished rhythmically when he gives way — most notably denying Mateo Kovacic a chance last season — but equally imploded when he gets his hands on the ball and starts making headlines instead. And yet, for all the off-field theatrics and the £3.4 million-per-year contract he negotiated last summer, Zmirko's talent undeniably outstrips the fury he generates. In commanding goal mouths with his 6'4'' frame, his rapid reflexes, and his ability to read the game like the Renaissance masters read the stars, Slovenian-born Zmirko has gone from answering to schoolyard chants of “Keepy uppy!” to the most coveted ‘keeper in the treble waters. Such is the Slovenian fascination with Zmirko’s footballing and romantic exploits that it has birthed a subculture of waiting at station kiosks to buy his latest yellow-splashed shirts emblazoned with his initials and the slogan "Who dares wins, who delays dies." The question now is not just whether the 30-year-old can keep his life stable enough to keep playing at the top of his game in the Italian Serie A. It’s whether Zmirko’s rise can be sustained at all — or if, like past footballing Romans, his next move will be to trade fame for infamy.

ScotRail Alliance boss Phil Verster is leaving the firm after 18 months in which the company has rarely been out of the headlines. It has been a tumultuous period for Scotland’s biggest train operator, with widespread criticism of services and mounting pressure from passengers, politicians, and regulators. Phil Verster, the managing director of the Scottish government-run rail operator, will step down from his position at the end of the month as the firm grapples with ongoing industrial disputes, serious timetable delays, and a growing backlog of infrastructure upgrades. Verster’s tenure came under intense scrutiny in the wake of.Fatalfailures during the 2023 winter schedule, which saw passengers stranded for hours and sparked a sharp rebuke from the government and Transport Scotland. Despite efforts to modernise the network, including the rollout of new electric trains on key routes between Glasgow and Edinburgh, the company has struggled to meet its targets, with punctuality figures often in double-digit decline compared to previous years. Sources close to Verster said he had "made the difficult decision to step down," citing the need for fresh leadership to drive forward the long-term modernisation programme. He joined the organisation in April 2022, bringing with him 25 years of railway experience from his time in the UK and abroad. However, he inherited a troubled company, with financial constraints, staffing shortages, and relentless public scrutiny all playing a role in the challenges he faced. Transport ministers welcomed Verster’s decision as an opportunity for new direction. Transport Secretary Jenny Gilruth said in a statement that the government is "committed to delivering a first-class rail service for Scotland’s passengers" and that "this is a natural point for a transition as we look to accelerate improvements." She also announced plans to begin the search for a new chief executive "in the coming weeks." The departure comes as the government prepares to review the future of rail franchising in Scotland and consider whether to take further steps towards a nationalised rail network. Verster’s exit is expected to bring little immediate relief for passengers, who will continue to face ongoing service disruptions as maintenance work and electrification projects progress. But it does signal another chapter for an industry long plagued by controversy. As one transport analyst put it: "ScotRail has been a political football for far too long. Now, the next leader must steer it back on track with real momentum and the support of all stakeholders."

In a remarkable feat of endurance, dedication, and camaraderie, five friends have completed a gruelling 42-hour charity challenge, visiting 42 football grounds across Britain — and in the process, raising nearly £45,000 for a charity they have long supported. The challenge, which saw them travel in a rented van and at times sleep in the aisles between grounds, was set up not only to push their physical and mental limits but to highlight serious issues affecting young people in their communities. The group, who describe themselves as "football fans and friends first, athletes second," set off from Liverpool FC’s Anfield stadium on a clear Saturday morning, armed with a carefully plotted route, a bucket-load of supply packs, and a shared vision to raise £15,000 for the youth mental health charity, Place2Be. By the time they landed back at Anfield just after midnight four days later, they had exceeded their target almost threefold. The challenge — dubbed “42 HOURS in 42 Grounds” — required the team, who all work in the education and sports sectors, to endure around 1,800 miles of driving, visit up to four grounds a day, and do their best to remain visible, raise awareness, and engage local fans for donations. Stops ranged from well-known Premier League stadiums like Manchester United’s Old Trafford to lower league, and sometimes barely-operational, grounds in remote corners of the UK. James Miller, 32, the team’s de facto organiser, said the journey was as much about the people they met as the miles they covered. “There’s something so inspiring about what you see at grassroots football,” he said. “People come out to support clubs not because they are watching stars, but because they are part of a community. That’s the message we wanted to carry alongside our fundraising mission.” The friends also received an unexpected plug when a national media outlet managed to photograph them at the 27th ground, which ended up being shared thousands of times on social media — leading to a surge in donations. By the time the team returned to Anfield, having completed their final ground just 15 minutes before the allotted 42 hours ended, they had received more than 500 donations from across the UK. Local club grounds around the UK had also started their own fundraising goalden on social media, sending messages of encouragement and support for the team as they pushed on, ground after ground.

Primate Archaeology Unearths a New Chapter in Animal Culture   A groundbreaking new field promising to reshape our understanding of animal intelligence is emerging from the dusty corners of the earth and the bustling branches of the trees. Dubbed   primatological archaeology  , or more simply,  primate archaeology , this field is revealing ancient evidence of tool use, food preparation and even social learning among non-human primates. Once thought to be a uniquely human pursuit, archaeology is now showing that primates, including capuchin monkeys, macaques and orangutans, have been crafting their own cultural legacies for thousands of years. The concept may sound like something out of a science fiction novel, but scientists involved in the study insist it is both serious and significant. Myths about tool use being a defining trait of humanity are being debunked, one ancient stone tool at a time. Researchers have discovered sites in Brazil where capuchin monkeys appear to have used stone anvils and hammers to crack open nuts. Radiocarbon dating suggests this activity has occurred over generations, possibly even thousands of years. These so-called "nut-cracking culture sites" offer the first archaeological evidence of sustained, learned primate tool usage passed down across generations. Even more astonishing is the discovery in Thailand of ancient stone tools used by macaques, seemingly for nut-cracking. “It's not just about finding a skull or a bone,” explains Dr. Kimberley Hockings, an anthropologist specializing in primate archaeology. “It's about stepping into the world of these primates, tracing their actions in the sediment and the stones. It's a time capsule of their culture.” The implications are profound. For decades, science has debated the extent of non-human intelligence and the presence of culture in the animal kingdom. Primate archaeology is providing hard evidence to support the idea that culture—meaning shared knowledge and practices—that not only exists among primates but has evolved over time. This transformation in understanding has evolutionary, ethical and philosophical ramifications. If animals can create and preserve culture, what does that say about the uniqueness of human civilization? Experts warn, however, that primate archaeology is still in its infancy. The field faces skepticism from more traditional archaeologists, who question whether animal-made tools can be considered "culture" in the same way human artefacts are. Yet, with each new excavation uncovering layers of ancient monkey activity, the wall of human exceptionalism is beginning to crumble. As researchers continue to dig into the lives of our evolutionary cousins, one truth is becoming increasingly clear: the line dividing human and animal culture is far thinner—and far older—than we ever imagined.

There were moments during the European summit last week when it was easy to think that Brexit had already happened and Great Britain had walked out of the room, leaving behind a jumble of exclamation marks and confused hand gestures. Or perhaps, as one weary French journalist remarked to another over the din of multilingual press conferences, the UK was trying so hard to be heard that it was making everyone else uncomfortable. Regrettably for all involved, the European Council held in Brussels this week swiftly became one of those seminal political gatherings marked more by noise and confusion than clarity or diplomacy. The British delegation, present and ostensibly active during the talks, appeared almost aggressively pre-Brexit, as if trying to overcompensate for the national identity crisis that still permeates Whitehall like a bad turkey curry. From Reino Unido’s primed and eager representatives to the familiar, if shouted, mention of Grossbritannien by German officials, everyone was united not by common cause, but by the shared frustration at Britain’s continuous, cumbersome attempts to define itself on the European stage. There was, of course, no escaping the Great Britain conundrum. It was shouted over the microphones, jabbed into the journalistic air, and splattered across the paraphernalia of grief that accompany summit coverage. It was a reminiscent scene of Britain trotting in, all humble and self-deprecating one minute, and verbosity and self-importance the next. Whether it was the British delegation attempting to clarify their position on the Northern Ireland border or the EU press corps trying to explain, again, what Brexit actually means in layman’s terms, the surrounding atmosphere was chaotic, animated, and occasionally exasperating. Once a meeting of minds between European politicians, this summit felt more like a ballet competition between a troupe about to fall off the stage. And standing at the heart of it all was Britain—awkward, overreaching, and trying desperately to be the star. Whether it succeeded in that ambition is, like much else about Brexit, still very much up for grabs. The rest of Europe, as it always seems to be, was trying very hard to keep smiling through the performance. Whether they will continue to do so remains to be seen. Next week: the lunches, a new agenda, and the same tired Britain. Class dismissed. Or, as one reporter muttered, class removed—finally. Let's all pretend this wasn't happening.

Young Golfer Scott Gregory turns to YouTube for insights on making US Masters debut   Aspiring golfer Scott Gregory, 22, is taking an unconventional approach to preparing for one of the most prestigious events in the sport: the US Masters. With only a handful of professional tournament appearances under his belt and no prior experience at Augusta National, Gregory has turned to YouTube — the world’s largest video-sharing platform — as his unlikely mentor in his quest to break into golf’s elite. The English rookie from Hertfordshire, who earned his first professional victory last year, is now grinding through hours of content online in a bid to get the measure of the Masters course, prior winners, and the unique quirks of one of golf’s oldest traditions. From vintage highlights and behind-the-scenes documentaries, to player interviews and expert analysis, Gregory is relying on YouTube to provide guidance for what he admits is a daunting challenge. “We don’t all get the luxury of being a Tiger Woods or Rory when it comes to learning the ropes early,” Gregory told The Times. “YouTube’s been a godsend — not just to see how the course plays, but to understand the history, the pressure, and the way the pros approach it. Sometimes I feel like the best player in the world is supplying me with tips for free.” It is a far cry from the traditional rhythm of PGA Tour preparation, which typically involves weeks of pre-tournament planning, coaching and physical conditioning. In a striking scene from the 1970 Bollywood classic  Chetna , a vulnerable young woman, played by the late Nutan and portrayed as a former sex worker seeking to restart her life, recounts a haunting line to a would-be client. “I have seen so many naked men,” she says with trembling frailty, “that I hate clothed men now.” The line, haunting and psychologically rich, not only reveals the trauma she has endured but also highlights the film's unflinching attempt to delve into the moral and emotional complexities of prostitution in a deeply conservative society.  Chetna , literally meaning “Conscience,” was released during the decline of India’s Nehruvian era and the onset of a period of social and cultural introspection. Directed by Basu Bhattacharya, the film’s depiction of a woman’s journey from the red-light district of Mumbai to a moral reclamation is now seen by many critics as a groundbreaking exploration of victimhood, rehabilitation and societal hypocrisy. Today, with India grappling with rising sexual violence, trafficking and objectification of women, the film’s message—and that singular, disturbing line—resonates with renewed relevance. What makes  Chetna  remarkable is its refusal to moralise or condemn. Instead, it tenderly portrays the protagonist, Nafisa, as a deeply human, damaged but ultimately resilient character. Her transformation is not framed as a triumph of virtue but rather a long, painful process of rediscovering dignity in a world that has stripped her of both self-respect and choice. For modern viewers, the film serves as both an indictment of the system that perpetuates exploitation and a tribute to those who manage to rise above it. Critically, the line has also sparked intense debate: does it speak to the degradation of identity in commercialised sex work? Or does it offer a touch of dark, absurdist humour in what is otherwise a bleak narrative? Regardless of interpretation, the poignant vulnerability of the character shines through. Given the current climate of #MeToo and India’s ongoing discussions about consent, sexual violence and women’s autonomy,  Chetna  is being rediscovered as a cinematic gem that, ahead of its time, dared to humanise what society often dehumanises. As the country continues to confront its history of oppression and exploitation, the line from a 1970 film continues to echo powerfully in 2025—a reminder of how far we have come, and how far we still have to go. That night in Mumbai’s Kandivali, when Nafisa made her emotional confession, cinema reflected not just the horrors of her life—but the conscience of a nation on the cusp of change.

Scott Walker Concludes Presidential Bid Amid Funding and Polling Decline   Scott Walker, the former governor of Wisconsin and once seen as a potential Republican front-runner in the 2016 presidential race, has called time on his campaign following a sharp drop in both financial support and public confidence. The announcement, made on Tuesday night in a speech to supporters in Milwaukee, concluded a bruising and ultimately unsuccessful bid for the White House that many observers had once expected would mark a new era in conservative politics. Walker, 52, was arguably the most prominent among a crop of centrist Republican governors seen as alternatives to the right-wing populism being propagated by figures like Donald Trump and Ted Cruz. His record as a reform-driven governor, known for challenging public-sector unions and pushing state budgets into surplus, had placed him in the upper tier of most Republican polls for much of the year. But recent months have been marked by stagnation and an unwillingness by major donors to back his candidacy, leading to a critical gap in fundraising compared to his rivals. In his speech, Walker acknowledged the challenges he faced in building a national coalition and the importance of focusing on state-level governance over the long, expensive road to the White House. “I never expected this race to be easy, and I welcome the strength of competition in this election—it shows how serious our party is about choosing the best candidate,” Walker said. “However, the reality of our financial situation and the urgency of governing the people of Wisconsin demanded that I end this campaign at this time.” His exit leaves a more crowded Republican field and may also alter the strategic landscape in a race already complicated by the prominence of Trump, whose outspoken style has generated both massive media coverage and fierce criticism. Walker’s decision comes amid intense scrutiny of Republican fundraising dynamics, as his campaign had spent about $30 million to raise just $20 million, a financial imbalance that became a major liability as the race progressed. Analysts suggest that the lack of a unifying figure to counter Trump, like Walker was once thought to be, will further fracture the Republican base and potentially open the door for a long and unpredictable primary contest. His departure may also signal a broader shift in the party’s messaging, as he was one of the few Republicans to campaign with explicitly pro-choice and gun-control moderated policies.

Ireland coach Joe Schmidt has thrown open the eligibility of veteran playmaker Gordon D’Arcy for the 2015 Rugby World Cup, hinting that the Leinster legend’s long-standing place in the national team may not be guaranteed as the tournament approaches. The comments, made during a press conference in Dublin, have sparked widespread speculation and debate within the rugby community about D’Arcy’s future on the international stage. D’Arcy, 36, has earned more than 120 caps since his debut in 2001 and has been regarded as one of the most influential centres in the world. However, recent form and the emergence of younger players have made his spot a subject of contention, with only two specialist centres in the squad set to be named for the World Cup in England. Speaking ahead of Ireland’s Six Nations clash against Wales, Schmidt acknowledged the challenge of selecting the right blend of experience and freshness. “Every player is under pressure, no doubt about that,” Schmidt said. “We need to make sure we’re fielding a squad that can handle the kind of rugby that the World Cup demands. It’s not just about who you’ve played for in the past — it’s about who is performing now and is ready for the competition ahead.” While Schmidt refused to name specific players, it was widely understood that D’Arcy was at the heart of his statements. D’Arcy, who recently returned from injury, has struggled for form following a knee ligament issue earlier this year. His fitness and consistency have been key talking points, with many suggesting that his place is now in direct competition with Leinster and Ireland teammate Brian O’Driscoll, as well as the promising younger talents emerging from the national pathways. The Irish public and media have long viewed D’Arcy as an essential part of the national side, with many fans reluctant to see him removed despite his age. Leinster’s coach, Leo Cullen, has however stated that D’Arcy remains a vital presence in the province and a role model for younger players. Some observers believe that Schmidt’s decision will depend as much on chemistry and the team’s tactical needs as on on-field performance.

The small, dusty town of Arusha in northern Tanzania is the gateway to Mount Kilimanjaro, to the beauty and the wildlife of the Serengeti. Known as the "Tourism Capital of Tanzania," Arusha may not appear glamorous at first glance, but those who venture through its dusty streets are often rewarded with an awe-inspiring journey into the heart of one of the most breathtaking landscapes on the continent. With a population of just over 300,000, Arusha is a melting pot of cultures, languages, and traditions. The town lies at an elevation of nearly 1,500 metres, its climate relatively mild even during the hottest months. Though modest in size, Arusha serves as the logistical hub for thousands of tourists who fly in from across the world each year to witness the wonders of the African bush. For many visitors, the first sign of Arusha’s significance is the parade of safari vehicles, Tanzania People’s Defence Force trucks, and tour buses crowding its narrow, patchwork roads. Along the main thoroughfares, the town hums with activity—bustling markets sell everything from handmade crafts to sturdy hiking gear, while falafel stands and cafés catering to early-morning climbers line the streets. It is here that tourists are briefed on safety, weather, and the intricacies of climbing Africa’s highest peak, with local guides often gathered in small shops offering the cheapest and best advice for those making the ascent. But Arusha is more than just a staging ground for adventure. The town has a rich history—once a German colonial outpost, it later became a British-administered hub before the Tanganyika government took over and it eventually became part of Tanzania after independence in 1964. The Arusha Declaration Museum, standing just outside the town centre, offers a glimpse into Tanzania's socialist roots and is a popular stop for history enthusiasts. The town also plays host to the Arusha International Conference Centre, which has been the site of landmark international peace talks, including those on the Rwandan genocide and the civil wars in Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet while Arusha has become a symbol of adventure and diplomacy, the people of the town remain deeply connected to the land and its traditions. Many are Maasai or Chagga, their cultures woven into the fabric of day-to-day life. And for them, the town is not just a means to serve tourism but a place where generations have lived, farmed, and made a living from the land.

The digital fallout from the 2015 Ashley Madison data breach is once again making waves online, as former users of the infidelity website and beyond face renewed distress after the personal data of over 30 million individuals has been uploaded to various corners of the internet. The re-emergence of the data—revealing names, email addresses, and self-provided details of those who had signed up to the site—has triggered panic, with users reporting scams, harassment, and the return of past social consequences. While Ashley Madison, a dating platform designed to facilitate affairs, had already breached the company's servers in a hacking incident attributed to a group calling itself the Impact Team, many who had thought the matter long buried are now scrambling to evaluate the new risks posed by the re-surfaced information. Cybersecurity experts have confirmed the authenticity of the leak, noting the data appears to be the original material from the 2015 breach, but the discovery of new hosting sites, including those linked to deep web marketplaces and drive-by phishing portals, has raised concerns over how the information is being exploited. Some individuals have reported being targeted by cyber-criminals offering to "remove" their data in exchange for Bitcoin, while others struggle with the emotional trauma of potentially exposing their real identities to friends, colleagues, and even family members. For many, the breach remains a deeply personal and sensitive matter. Ashley Madison’s parent company, Avid Life Media, claimed to have taken steps to mitigate the breach by modifying the database’s structure and deleting searchable email addresses at the time, but the latest distribution suggests that full identification is still possible for a large portion of users. Legal repercussions following the original breach saw the company fined millions by the Canadian Federal and British Columbia privacy commissioners, but the personal implications continue to ripple out nearly a decade later. Psychologists have noted a rise in the severity of anxiety reported by some victims, with some individuals experiencing acute stress triggered by the fear of exposure. Support groups for Ashley Madison users have found themselves over capacity, processing new queries daily. As discussions about privacy, accountability, and digital security intensify, the breach serves as a stark reminder of the long-term vulnerabilities inherent in online engagement. As one former user stated anonymously to the BBC: “I've lived with this for years, but now it feels like it's happening all over again—and I have nowhere to hide.”

Saudi Arabia has launched a high-level investigation into the cause of a catastrophic crane collapse in the city of Mecca, which has so far claimed the lives of at least 107 people and left many others injured. The incident, which occurred during construction work at a luxury hotel being built near Islam’s holiest site, has sent shockwaves across the country and drawn international concern. It marks one of the deadliest construction site accidents in the kingdom’s recent history. Eyewitnesses reported hearing a massive noise just before the 220-metre-high crane collapsed onto the three-star Dar Al Hijrah Hotel early on Monday morning, before dawn prayers. The crane, which was being dismantled, apparently fell forward, crashing onto the building and surrounding structures. Rescue teams from across the region were deployed, including sniffer dogs and heavy machinery, in a desperate race to reach the survivors trapped beneath the rubble and debris. The Civil Defense Department reported that most of the casualties were among the workers employed on the construction site, many of whom were reported to be expatriates from countries such as Indonesia, India, and the Philippines. Survivors described scenes of chaos and confusion as the crane came down, crushing parts of the hotel and leaving impacts that could be felt a block away. Several foreign embassies have requested updates on the condition of their nationals. King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has ordered a comprehensive probe into the incident, with instructions to take strict legal action against those found responsible. The scope of the investigation includes the examination of the crane operator, the company overseeing the construction, and the contractors involved. Sources in the Saudi government indicated that emergency services had earlier warned of building safety concerns at the site, but the warnings appear to have been ignored. The incident comes at a sensitive time for the Saudi government, as it seeks to reform its public image under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 plan, which includes significant infrastructure development and open governance reforms. The Ministry of Housing, in response to the disaster, has suspended the operating license of the construction company involved, ordering a total halt of all construction work in the surrounding area pending the results of the investigation. The Grand Mosque, located just a few hundred meters from the collapse site, saw large numbers of worshippers attend Friday prayers, with many expressing outrage and sadness over the tragedy.

A former Milwaukee police officer has been charged with first-degree reckless homicide in connection with an August shooting that sparked widespread public outrage and renewed calls for reform within the city's law enforcement agencies. The incident occurred on August 14, when a 17-year-old Black youth was shot and killed during a confrontation with law enforcement. The officer in question, who has not yet been publicly named, was handed over to the Milwaukee County District Attorney’s Office following an internal investigation by the Milwaukee Police Department. The charges, brought under Wisconsin law, indicate that prosecutors believe the officer caused the teenager’s death through reckless conduct that disregarded his or her duties under the law. First-degree reckless homicide typically refers to actions that involve a "reckless disregard for human life," according to state statutes. It is a serious criminal offense, though not classified as murder. The officer is expected to appear in court next week and could face a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if found guilty. The shooting took place during a time of heightened tensions in Milwaukee, a city long grappling with issues of racial inequality, poverty, and police conduct. The teenager, whose identity has not yet been disclosed, was reportedly being pursued by officers when he was shot in a wooded area. Surveillance footage and witness accounts initially fueled speculation as to the circumstances surrounding the death, with local activists and community leaders urging protesters to remain vigilant for any further revelations. Family members of the victim described him as a promising young man with a passion for sports and a bright future, devastated by the violent end to his life. “He was a kid,” one relative told reporters outside a neighborhood church. “He didn’t deserve this.” Mayor Cavalier Johnson, who had previously called for police reform and the reduction of fatal shootings by officers, responded to the charges by expressing both relief and concern. “While charging the officer is a step toward justice,” he said, “we must continue the work to address the root causes of violence and improve trust between our communities and law enforcement.” Milwaukee’s district attorney has stated that the case remains under active review with special attention given to the conduct of the officer and the department’s policies regarding use of force.

The number of operational Royal Air Force (RAF) fighter planes is set to fall to its lowest level in the service’s history, according to a growing consensus among defence experts and within the Ministry of Defence (MoD). With only a handful of Eurofighter Typhoon jets remaining in readiness at any given time, the warning has raised concerns about the UK’s ability to maintain air superiority both at home and on international operations. The decline has been attributed to a combination of planned retirements, the ongoing delays in the procurement of new fighter aircraft, and a backlog of maintenance and modernisation work. Defence analysts and former senior military personnel have called the situation alarming, arguing that the UK is entering a period of “strategic vulnerability” at the very moment when global instability is on the rise. The MoD confirmed that the current fleet of Typhoons, which has been the backbone of the RAF’s fast jet capability in recent years, is expected to continue operating far beyond its original projected lifespan. However, with no agreement yet in place for a successor to the Typhoon, the future of the RAF’s aerial combat capability is increasingly uncertain. According to Air Power Month, a respected quarterly publication, the number of available combat aircraft is set to drop to below 40 in the coming months. For context, during the Falklands War in 1982, the RAF deployed more than 50 such aircraft in operation. The stark contrast has sparked fierce debate among defence experts, with some suggesting that the UK’s military planners have underestimated the scale of the challenge. Prime Minister Keir Starmer has vowed that the UK will remain a global military power, but the delay in delivering the new Tempest combat air project—set for entry into service in the late 2030s—leaves a significant gap in capability. Questions are now being raised about the government’s ability to meet its NATO obligations and protect British interests around the world. Defence Secretary John Healey has defended the MoD’s efforts, stating that the service is being “restructured for the future” and that technology and drones could play a larger role alongside any shortfall in manned fighter jets. However, critics remain unconvinced, with many arguing that as geopolitical tensions continue to escalate, sustained underinvestment in critical assets such as fighter aircraft could have serious consequences for national security. As the debate intensifies, one thing is clear: the gothic details on the gates of RAF bases now stand as a relic of a once-proud era, with the reality of a dwindling fleet forcing the UK to confront a stark new chapter

A coroner’s inquest has opened in Sydney, Australia, to examine the tragic events of the 2014 Lindt Café siege, an incident that ended in the deaths of two hostages and the armed attacker himself. The inquest is expected to run for several weeks, during which time it will scrutinise the actions of emergency services and the timeline of events that led to one of the country’s most harrowing acts of public violence. The siege began on December 15, 2014, when a 26-year-old man, later identified as Man Haron Monis, entered the Lindt Café in Martin Place and took 18 customers and staff hostage. Monis, a convicted minor criminal with ties to extremist ideologies, opened fire minutes after arriving, killing cafe manager Tori Johnson within the first few moments. He then fatally shot café manager Katrina Dawson, and later in the ordeal, shot himself while police were about to move in. Monis, a man of Iranian origin who had lived in Australia since his early teens, had a history of mental health issues and domestic violence. He was the subject of a court restraining order against one of his ex-partners, and had been denied asylum in Australia, reportedly claiming he was being persecuted for his religion. Despite raising concerns in the past, Monis had not been on any official terror watchlist at the time of the attack. The inquest, led by Deputy State Coroner Magda Amin, will investigate whether there were any failures in the handling of Monis’s case by the Australian Federal Police (AFP), state departments and organisations tasked with monitoring extremism. Questions are already being raised over whether intelligence shared with the authorities following Monis’s 2013 arrest in Margate — where he was accused of threatening to blow up a building — was properly assessed. One of the key aspects of the inquiry will be a review of the actions taken by the NSW Police and the Australian Federal Police during the 16-hour siege, including their communication with each other and their ability to secure the safety of the hostages. Families of the victims told the hearing that they relied heavily on radio broadcasts for updates and feared for the lives of their loved ones. The siege also saw a sustained presence by the special operations unit, the Special Air Service (SAS), who prepared for a dramatic intervention. Surveillance footage and audio recordings from the time will be examined as part of the inquiry.

A long and exhausting dispute that brought swathes of the Southern rail network to a standstill has finally come to an end, as a train drivers’ union announced Thursday that it has reached a deal with Southern’s parent company, Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR), effectively ending the crippling strike action that has been paralysing commuters for weeks. The agreement, reached overnight in tense negotiations, puts an end to the walkouts that have severely disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers in the South East of England. The Rail, Maritime and Transport Union (RMT) confirmed the deal, which includes improvements to working conditions, but the exact terms have not yet been disclosed. The settlement comes just days after a last-ditch summit between union leaders, GTR and Network Rail at the Department for Transport failed to produce a resolution. However, behind the scenes, union officials and rail bosses have been engaging in separate talks aimed at salvaging an agreement before the situation deteriorated further. The walkout was part of a bitter Anglo-Welsh dispute over the so-called “mileage awards” system, which determines how train drivers are paid. The RMT had argued that the system is outdated and unfair, failing to reflect the impacts of short, frequent journeys as opposed to long-distance routes. Southern train commuters, many of whom rely on the network to get to work from London and surrounding towns, have borne the brunt of the strikes and related disruptions for months, often facing the cancellation of nearly half of their daily services. Earlier this week, the RMT had warned that further industrial action would be launched unless a full and sustainable agreement was reached. The deal averted what could have been a further escalation in the dispute at a time when the rail industry is already under immense pressure from delays, overcrowding and rising costs. A spokesperson for GTR said the company “acknowledges the challenging journey [the negotiations] has been and commends the efforts of all parties in reaching this agreement.” Meanwhile, transport unions have urged commuters to remain alert for potential localised service changes as the rail network adjusts to the new arrangements. As train operators prepare to restore normal services, disappointed passengers are cautiously optimistic that the station could finally be approaching for one of the most contentious industrial disputes in recent transport history. Official data shows that over the past month, the Southern network has lost an estimated £70 million in revenue, with the vast majority of regular routes being reduced to a skeletal service or halted entirely during the dispute.

Spain, still reigning champions of the tournament since their 2014 triumph, were left shellshocked. Legendary striker David Villa was visibly frustrated as his side’s possession-based game, so effective in previous World Cup campaigns, crumbled in the face of Dutch urgency and intensity. Spanish manager Vicente del Bosque made three substitutions in an attempt to turn the game, but the damage had already been done. The defeat came as a severe blow to Spain’s World Cup aspirations, and marked the first time in 16 matches that they had lost in a major international competition since 2009. With their confidence shaken and momentum destroyed, they will now need to regroup rapidly if they are to find a path to the knockout stages. Meanwhile, the Netherlands will enter the group stage with renewed hope after securing a commanding 4-0 victory. Their performance was a testament to their tactical discipline, intense pressing, and clinical finishing. As the world watches, one question remains: can any other side in the competition match what the Dutch have achieved? Only time will tell, but no doubt their fans are dreaming of another glorious chapter in the team's storied history.

Tears welled in the eyes of Britain's beloved diver Tom Daley as he stood on the poolside in Rio de Janeiro on Monday, the weight of an unfulfilled Olympic dream pressing heavily on his shoulders. For over a decade, Daley had chased the ultimate goal in competitive diving—gold on the grandest stage of them all. That dream, he feared, had just been snuffed out at his home Olympics in London 2012, before being rekindled in this year's Games. But after finishing fourth in the men's 10-meter platform final, the 23-year-old was left with nothing but heartbreak and the gut-wrenching realization that this might have been his last chance to win Olympic gold. “I'm truly heartbroken,” a visibly emotional Daley told reporters moments after the race. “I had so much hope, so much belief and I gave it everything I had. It just wasn’t enough.” Daley had entered the competition with high expectations, buoyed by a successful run-up to the Games, and as a strong medal favourite in the final. Standing in the way, however, were China’s defending champions, who once again proved too consistent and too clinical in the controlled environment of the João Havelange Olympic Aquatics Stadium. China’s Cao Yuan and Zhang Yannan dominated, securing the top two spots, while Baptiste Leclercq of France took bronze. For Daley, the disappointment is deep. Having come out of the closet in 2008 at the age of 16, he had become a symbol of courage and self-acceptance, inspiring athletes and fans around the world with his ability to blend elite sports with authenticity and vulnerability. The 2012 London Olympics, where he finished seventh, were his first chance to compete on home soil—but the severity of his finish meant he immediately questioned whether he could continue. After returning to the sport and delivering a near-flawless performance at the 2016 British National Championships, Daley had seemed to conjure the kind of mentality necessary to deliver something extraordinary in Brazil. Instead, yesterday evening, for all his practice jumps and soaring dives, Daley could only watch from behind the podium as the winners celebrated a new chapter in Chinese diving dominance. Family, teammates, and fans have been around him in the aftermath, offering words of support and reminders of his life achievements both in and out of the pool. “I just wanted to do that one thing,” he added, his voice cracking.

India has launched its first national real-time Air Quality Index (AQI), a major step in the country's ongoing battle with severe air pollution, the government announced Thursday. The index aims to provide accurate, up-to-the-minute data on pollution levels across major cities, helping both citizens and policymakers take timely action to mitigate health risks. The initiative comes amid growing public concern over the country's deteriorating air quality, particularly during the winter months when smog envelops cities such as Delhi, Ayodhya, and Lahore, blurring skylines and sparking health alarms. With one of the world's most polluted capitals, Delhi has become the epicentre of the crisis, often recording air quality levels in the "severe" or "hazardous" category. The newly introduced AQI will measure concentrations of six key pollutants: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, and ozone. This information will be disseminated through a dedicated mobile app and website, with a colour-coded scale ranging from "good" to "severe" to signal health implications and appropriate precautions. Schools, for example, will be advised to restrict outdoor activities when pollution levels hit the "poor" threshold. Minister for Environment and Climate Change, Bhupender Yadav, described the launch as a "landmark achievement" in India's environmental governance. "This new system empowers citizens with reliable, scientific data, while enabling us to better target our pollution control efforts," Yadav said in a statement. Environmental experts have welcomed the move, highlighting the need for timely and transparent information. According to a 2023 report by the Global Burden of Disease, air pollution in India contributes to over a million premature deaths annually, with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases most affected. The new AQI is expected to enhance the monitoring of major sources of pollution, from vehicle emissions and industrial activity to agricultural stubble burning and construction dust. India's initiative mirrors similar efforts abroad, such as the US and China, which have long used real-time indices to track air quality. Yet it is a particularly significant development for a country where pollution data is often patchy or inconsistent. The government has also pledged to expand the index to more cities in the coming months, and to integrate it with various mitigation measures, including enhanced road pricing, stricter emission standards, and green zone planning. While the launch of the AQI is a significant milestone, experts caution that merely monitoring the problem is not sufficient.

Brighton secured a vital 2-1 victory over 10-man Leeds United at the Amex Stadium on Saturday, catapulting them to the top of the Championship and extending their impressive unbeaten league run to an astonishing 14 matches. The win not only maintained their remarkable consistency in recent weeks but also sent a strong message to their rivals in the division that the Seagulls are serious contenders for promotion. In a tense and physical encounter, Brighton showcased their resilience and clinical finishing to overcome a spirited Leeds side. The visitors, who had gone into the match with just one win in their last five games, arrived in Sussex short-handed after defender Liam Cooper saw red in the second half, compounding their difficulties. The decisive moment of the game came in the 66th minute when Brighton captain Shane Long found the back of the net with a composed finish following a well-worked build-up. Long, who has been in fine form of late, has now found the net five times in his last six starts and remains a key figure in Brighton’s strong attacking display. Leeds responded swiftly, equalising just eleven minutes later through a clinical solo goal from Patrick Bamford, who cut inside from the left and curled an unstoppable effort into the top corner. The Young Lions’ striker has now scored crucial goals in recent matches, and his display against Brighton will only add to his growing reputation at the top level. However, it was Brighton who had the final say, as the Seagulls snatched a late winner through a solitary strike from substitute Sam Vokes in the 88th minute. Vokes, making his first league start of the season, brought energy and physicality to the attack and provided the finishing touch when it mattered most. His goal sent the home crowd into raptures and ensured all three points remained at the Amex. The win sees Brighton move above Sheffield United and into first place on goal difference, with their unbeaten run now stretching back to the beginning of December. Graeme Souness, the former Leeds manager guest pundit at the match, praised the leadership of Brighton’s captain, saying, “Shane Long is the heart and soul of this team. When he’s on form, they’re a hard team to beat.” Brighton’s coaching staff, led by manager Chris Hughton, will be delighted with their side's latest result.

Prime Minister David Cameron has sounded the alarm over the long-term consequences of delaying major infrastructure projects in the United Kingdom, calling it a threat to both economic growth and public confidence. Speaking at a joint meeting of business leaders and local government representatives in London, Cameron warned that continued delays in the development of key transport, energy, and housing projects could seriously undermine the country’s ability to compete on the global stage. “We cannot afford to let unnecessary bureaucracy and a lack of political will stall the progress needed to propel Britain forward,” he said. The Prime Minister, who has long argued that infrastructure investment is essential to boosting productivity and prosperity, outlined the risks of inaction as governments at all levels struggle with funding constraints and planning hurdles. He pointed to the stalled Thameslink rail upgrade and the delayed HS2 high-speed rail network as examples of projects that have suffered from bureaucratic bottlenecks and shifting political priorities, costing both time and money. Cameron urged Parliament and local authorities to streamline processes and prioritise efficiency, saying that if the UK continued to lag behind its European neighbours in the delivery of modern infrastructure, it would pay the price both economically and in the public’s trust in government. “We must act now—there is no time to waste,” he stressed, calling for a unified push to accelerate the realisation of crucial projects that would benefit both current and future generations. The remarks from the Prime Minister come at a time of heightened scrutiny over the UK’s approach to infrastructure, with recent reports highlighting a growing “infrastructure gap” between the nation’s needs and its delivery capacity. Experts say the failure to build roads, expand rail networks and modernise the energy grid could result in long-term economic stagnation. Cameron’s comments were met with a mixed response from across the political spectrum. While some welcomed the call for urgent action, others questioned how realistic his proposals were given the current fiscal climate and the challenges of securing public and political support for large-scale projects. Regardless of the political debate, one message is unmissable: if the UK is to meet the demands of the 21st century, it must get serious about its infrastructure. Cameron has made it clear—DELAY IS NOT AN OPTION. The challenge now lies in turning this warning into action. As cities across the UK grapple with congestion, outdated energy systems and housing shortages, the pressure is mounting for reform.

Cameron sets out ‘comprehensive strategy’ to combat Islamist extremism   Prime Minister David Cameron has unveiled a new government strategy aimed at confronting the "poison" of Islamist extremism across the UK, outlining a sweeping plan that combines security measures, education reform, and community engagement. Speaking at a keynote address in London, the Conservative leader branded extremism a "direct threat to British values" and insisted the time has come for a "unified response" from all sectors of society. The policy document, entitled  Countering Extremism: Protecting British Values , proposes a three-pronged approach. First, the government will increase funding for counter-terrorism units to monitor and disrupt radicalisation efforts, including greater surveillance of online activity. Second, it will tackle extremism in education by forcing state and private schools to adopt new guidelines to prevent radical ideas from infiltrating the classroom. Third, the strategy promotes the inclusion of community leaders and faith groups in an outreach programme to counter extremist narratives with positive alternatives. Cameron framed the plan in moral terms, stating: "We are not at war with a religion, but we cannot remain passive in the face of Islamist extremism. It is corrosive, it is dangerous, and it must be confronted by every one of us." He stressed that patriotism and the celebration of British values — democracy, the rule of law, and respect for all people — were central to the government's thinking. The strategy has drawn praise from some quarters, particularly from security officials and members of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Prevent. Sir Brian Wood, a senior counter-terrorism advisor, described it as "a timely and necessary step in steering the government away from reactive policies toward a long-term solution." However, the response from civil rights organisations has been more cautious. Liberty, a prominent human rights group, warned that the measures could risk infringing on the rights of Muslims in the UK. “The government must be careful not to equate extremism with Muslim identity and instead focus on the individuals and ideologies that promote hatred and violence,” said Shona Aise, a spokesperson for the organisation. Cameron’s speech came as concern over Islamist extremism continues to grow. Recent reports from the Home Office indicate a 20% increase in self-radicalised individuals planning or attempting to travel to conflict zones such as Syria and Iraq. The Prime Minister also announced that additional measures would be introduced during the course of the year, aimed at closing legal loopholes that allow extremist charities to operate.

A Welsh Liberal Democrats campaign profiled as polls point to pivotal election   As the UK approaches one of its most unpredictable election campaigns yet, the Welsh Liberal Democrats find themselves at a crossroads. With opinion polls fluctuating and political alliances shifting, Nye Davies of Cardiff University’s Wales Governance Centre says the party is striving to make a mark on a Welsh electorate that has become increasingly hard to persuade. The Liberal Democrats’ role in Welsh politics has often been overshadowed by the dominance of Labour and the rise of Plaid Cymru as a credible alternative to the party of the UK's present and former prime ministers. Yet Nye Davies, a seasoned expert in Welsh institutional and political arrangements, highlights that this election could offer the Welsh Liberal Democrats a chance to reclaim some of the ground lost in recent years — particularly in the wake of Brexit and the evolving demands around devolution. Although the party is not expected to gain a significant number of seats in the Welsh Assembly or achieve a major breakthrough in Westminster, this election’s historic unpredictability means anything is possible, according to Dr. Davies. He points to the party’s ambitions in targeting key marginal seats and messaging around Welsh-specific issues, such as public services, education reform, and devolution maximalism as their main campaign thrust. The Welsh Liberal Democrats have also doubled down on local engagement. Their campaign, led by UK leader Sir Ed Davey’s recent visit to Wales, has focused on town halls and community meetings across the Valleys and cities to reinvigorate a grassroots approach. ‘What you’re seeing is a concerted attempt to position the party as one rooted in the concerns of local people, rather than distant Westminster politics,’ said Dr. Davies. Despite these efforts, the road ahead is tough. The party’s best hopes are in securing a boost among independent voters and disappointed Labour supporters who feel the party has strayed from its roots. To succeed, the Welsh Liberal Democrats must not only highlight their platform but also unseat the narratives that have come to dominate over the past few years — specifically around trust in Welsh governance and the clarity of individual party agendas. With Wales as a region of intense political activity, from regionalist voices to deep Tory opposition in parts of the rural south, Nye Davies believes the Welsh Liberal Democrats are “harnessing the energy of a fragmented political moment” in a year where opposition to the status quo is more powerful than ever.

In a bold move to help one of the world’s heaviest women begin a gruelling path to recovery, an Indian hospital has announced plans to construct a purpose-built facility specifically for the Egyptian patient, who weighs an astonishing 500 kilograms (1,102 pounds). The unprecedented effort by the Mumbai-based Ruby Hall Clinic underscores the severity of the woman’s condition and highlights the complex logistics required to manage extreme obesity cases on a global scale. The woman, whose identity has not been disclosed due to privacy concerns, is widely believed to be the heaviest living person based on the available evidence and medical records. Suffering from severe mobility issues and a host of life-threatening health conditions including diabetes, heart failure, and chronic respiratory problems, doctors have stressed that weight loss surgery is a critical step in her treatment. However, the logistical barriers—from custom-made hospital beds and reinforced operating tables to specialist teams in anaesthetics and post-operative care—demanded an entirely new wing to accommodate her specific needs. The clinic’s director, Dr. Anish Mahulkar, confirmed to the press that the construction of the facility was already underway. "This is a unique and delicate case, and we need to ensure absolute safety for the patient, the surgical team, and the equipment," he said. "We’ve worked closely with municipal authorities and have adhered to all building and health regulations to ensure this facility is second to none in its approach." The news has prompted global media attention and an outpouring of support for the patient, who reportedly arrived in India after an exhaustive search for medical help was undertaken in her native Egypt and across Europe. Local officials in Mumbai have also been implicated in the process, with the city's municipal corporation reportedly approving the installation of temporary facilities and providing assistance with emergency preparedness. Obesity experts have noted that while such extreme cases are rare, the severity of this woman’s condition places immense pressure not only on her body but also on the healthcare infrastructure. India, which has one of the largest populations of overweight and obese individuals, has seen a rise in specialized bariatric units in recent years. However, this is said to be the first instance of a facility being built specifically for an individual patient. Medical teams have also issued a word of caution, acknowledging that while the surgery is expected to be the first of several, road to recovery will be long and fraught with challenges.

The UK government’s chief scientific advisor has issued an alarming warning that the concentration of carbon dioxide already present in the atmosphere is sufficient to significantly increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events—namely floods and droughts—over the next 25 years. Speaking to a parliamentary committee, Sir Patrick Vallance, the government’s chief scientific adviser, stated that even if countries around the world were to meet all of their climate commitments as outlined in the Paris Agreement, the climate system would still experience more frequent and severe weather disruptions due to CO2 emissions already in place. This warning comes amid mounting pressure on the UK government to take more decisive action in response to the escalating climate crisis. Scientists have long argued that reducing emissions is vital, but Vallance's comments indicate that the damage already done to the planet’s climate system may be irreversible in the short term. “Whatever we do now, we can’t undo the CO2 that is already in the atmosphere, and the resulting impacts will continue to unfold,” he said during the meeting. “The next quarter-century will see the consequences of emissions we have already produced.” The implications of this statement are profound. With more frequent and unpredictable weather events, the UK—as well as other countries—will face increasing strain on infrastructure, agriculture and water supplies. For instance, the Environment Agency has already warned that the risk of flooding in parts of the UK is higher than at any time in living memory, with recent incidents such as the catastrophic floods in the north of England in 2020 serving as a stark reminder of the growing threat. At the same time, regions that currently experience drier conditions are likely to face more extreme droughts, which can impact farming yields and lead to periods of water shortages. Such conditions will not only affect the UK but will also continue to have global consequences, influencing migration patterns and food security on a far-reaching scale. Environmental groups have welcomed the confirmation from the government’s top scientist that the world is entering an era of unrelenting climate impacts. “This underscores the urgency of not only mitigation efforts but also robust adaptation strategies,” said Max Lawson, policy director at the Climate Crisis Coalition. “The government must stop stalling and start investing in protection and resilience for vulnerable communities.” The government has not yet provided a detailed response to Vallance’s warning, but with the Autumn Statement imminent, expectations are high for a significant shift in policy direction.

Neil Hamilton, the leader of the UK Independence Party (UKIP) in the Welsh Assembly, has sparked controversy by claiming that Britain has no real problem with Islamophobia and that there are no reliable statistics on hate crime. Speaking in a recent interview, Hamilton dismissed concerns about rising Islamophobic incidents in the UK, asserting that the perceived crisis is exaggerated and lacks solid evidence. The politician, who has previously drawn criticism for his comments on terrorism and minority communities, said that the media and “political correctness” have created a narrative of widespread Islamophobia. “There’s no robust data to support the idea that Islamophobia is a growing problem, or indeed that we have reliable statistics on hate crime of any kind,” he claimed. Hamilton added that the government’s figures were unreliable and that they often failed to distinguish between genuine criminal hate incidents and what he described as “rhetorical misuse” of the term. Hamilton's remarks have been met with immediate backlash from religious and civil rights organisations, who argue that British Muslims continue to face discrimination and prejudice. Hadiya Bashir, the Wales Muslim Women's Forum spokesperson, said: “The idea that Islamophobia isn’t real is deeply hurtful and out of touch with the everyday experiences of Muslims across the UK. We are not making this up—we are real people who are being targeted, discriminated against, and marginalised.” Data from the UK's national crime survey does indicate a significant rise in hate crimes, particularly after the 2016 EU referendum and the Brexit vote. In the year following the Brexit vote, recorded hate crimes in England and Wales increased by approximately 70 per cent. Many of these were borne by Muslim individuals, following a rise in reported incidents following periods of political or social tension and communal conflict. Critics of Hamilton argue that statements like his serve to legitimise the very attitudes he claims are not real.
