Sajid Javid has ruled out the nationalisation of Port Talbot steelworks, saying the government should not take control of the dwindling site in south Wales. Speaking on Monday, the Business Secretary denied claims that the UK government was considering moving in as £1b is slashed from the site's budget, with the steelworks also set to lose 400 jobs. Javid stressed that the problems at Port Talbot are not unique to Britain but are instead part of a wider international trend affecting the steel industry. “Steelmaking globally is facing disruption because of China’s low-cost steel,” he said. The company, Tata Steel UK, which has operated the plant for more than 100 years, has been the subject of increasing pressure from Welsh politicians and unions who have urged the UK government to step in and safeguard the facility. CBI Wales has also called for a special support package for the industry. However, Javid dismissed the idea of taking over the operation. “We should be working to support businesses with a market in which they can compete, not by taking them into public ownership,” he said. The minister added that the government was taking steps to help the steel industry thrive, including a review of competitiveness in the sector. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has previously called for a public investment in the steelworks to prevent its decline. The West Midlands MEP, Melanie Onn, who leads the steel industry committee, has warned that without government intervention, the UK could lose its strategic steel positions to other countries. Earlier this month, the steel sector hit the headlines again as Tata Steel UK announced that it would be cutting its carbon emissions at Port Talbot by half by 2030 in a bid to meet upcoming EU regulations. Meanwhile, unions at the plant have launched a new campaign urging the government to do more to save the steelworks. “We cannot afford to lose this site. It is not only a vital part of the UK’s industrial heritage but it is a key part of our economy,” a union representative said. The National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) and the Community union, which represents many of the workers at the site, have stepped up their calls for a “catalyst” for investment. As the debate over the future of the Port Talbot steelworks gathers pace, the government's recent stance underlines its reluctance to take direct ownership of the operation.

Exports of farmed salmon from Scotland saw a marked increase in value last year, rising by 17 per cent, according to recent figures from the Seafood Industry Awards. However, the industry experienced a decline in the volume of fish sent overseas, highlighting a growing disparity between price increases and the actual quantity traded. The data, presented by Scottish Enterprise, signals a trend of tightening supply against an increasingly buoyant market. With global demand for premium Scottish salmon remaining strong, prices have continued to rise, allowing producers to post improved financial returns despite selling fewer tonnes of fish. Analysts suggest that the surge in value is being driven by factors such as higher feed costs passing through to the final price, growing appetite for premium produce in key export markets, and the impact of exchange rates following the UK’s exit from the European Union. In 2023, the average export price for farmed salmon hit record levels in several of Scotland’s key markets, including the United States, France, and Spain—markets that together account for more than half of the country’s total salmon exports. The United States, in particular, has seen a steady increase in demand, with import tariffs and trade agreements playing a role in shifting trade patterns away from traditional European hubs. Nevertheless, the decline in volume is raising concerns among industry stakeholders. The reduced output is attributed to a combination of factors, including the longer-term issue of salmon lice infestations, the effects of adverse weather on aquaculture operations, and the continued difficulty in recruiting and retaining skilled workers in the sector. The Scottish Salmon Producers' Organisation has also pointed to the impact of weaker freshwater flow in some river systems, which has affected the timing of production cycles. These challenges come at a time when the industry is also grappling with the need to meet new environmental sustainability targets and ensure the long-term health of fish stocks. Experts are now calling for a careful balance to be struck between securing premium prices and maintaining output to avoid over-reliance on scarcity-driven value gains. With salmon accounting for over 60 per cent of Scotland's total food export revenue, the health of the industry is a matter of national economic importance. As producers look to 2024, the key questions remain whether the current price levels can be sustained and whether the industry can overcome its production constraints to replenish export volumes.

Northern Ireland’s Euro 2016 qualifying campaign suffered a blow as their three-game winning streak was halted in a 3-1 defeat to Romania at the Arena Națională in Bucharest. The result sees Romania move to the top of Group F, with Northern Ireland now in second place on goal difference. Despite high hopes and a vocal away support, Michael O’Neill’s side were outplayed by a clinical Romanian team who capitalized on moments of individual brilliance and Northern Ireland’s defensive lapses. The visitors had begun the match in promising fashion, with Shane Ferguson and Stuart Dallas pressing high and creating early chances, but the decisive moment came in the 24th minute when Artur Ionita broke the deadlock with a composed finish after a smart counter-attack. The result was a devastating blow for O’Neill, who had taken charge of the team in the summer and had been enjoying a positive start to his tenure with back-to-back 2-1 wins over Spain and Georgia. However, in Bucharest, his side looked disjointed, with the midfield failing to provide the usual drive and the back four appearing to struggle against the pace and unpredictability of the Romanian forwards. Romania extended their advantage three minutes before the break when Paul Pogatetz’s off-the-post cross deflected in off Jonny Evans, exposing Northern Ireland’s defensive fragility. The second half was a more intense affair, with Northern Ireland making halftime changes and showing more urgency. Their efforts paid off when Liam Boyce scored a controversial goal in the 58th minute, which the referee awarded despite apparent handball. But Romania were not to be denied, and they sealed the victory with a third goal in the 68th minute as Ciprian Marica converted a low cross into the bottom corner, rounding off a comprehensive performance. O’Neill, speaking after the match, admitted it was a disappointing result but remained optimistic about the team's prospects. “We showed spirit in the second half, but for the first 45 minutes we passed up too many chances and were too loose at the back,” he said. “I have full confidence in this team. We’re still in a good position and we’ll regroup for the next game.” Northern Ireland now face a daunting trip to the Netherlands next month, but O’Neill will be hoping this setback does not derail their push for a Euro 2016 qualification.

Dorrans Shines as Rangers Start Premiership Season with Victory Over Motherwell   Graham Dorrans netted twice as Rangers kicked off their Scottish Premiership campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over Motherwell at Fir Park on Saturday. The win marks a positive start for the Ibrox giants under new manager Pedro Caixinha and serves as a reminder of their enduring ambition to dominate the league once more. Despite not firing on all cylinders, Rangers were clinical in the final third, with Dorrans proving to be the difference in a match littered with missed chances from both sides. The 36-year-old midfielder has long been associated with key moments in crucial matches, and his performance against Motherwell once again underlined why he remains an influential figure at the heart of the Gers’ midfield. Dorrans opened the scoring in the 23rd minute, coolly slotting the ball past Motherwell goalkeeper Neil Alexander after a well-worked move down the right. The second half saw Rangers double their advantage when Dorrans rose unchallenged to head in James Tavernier’s cross, showcasing the aerial threat that Caixinha has looked to exploit under his possession-based system. Motherwell, however, refused to go down without a fight and pulled one back in the 74th minute through a towering header from Louis Laing. The Fir Park fans erupted in celebration, but the visitors held firm to see out the remaining minutes despite being reduced to 10 men when Silvestre Varetto was shown a second yellow card in the 86th minute. Rangers will be buoyed by a number of positive aspects from the encounter, not least the performance of captain Lee Wallace, who was solid at right-back and assisted Dorrans’ second goal. Manager Caixinha was quick to praise his team’s effort and mentality post-match. "I'm very pleased," Caixinha said. "It's the first game of the season, and the most important thing for us was to win. We started well, we controlled the game, and we were clinical in front of goal. We know there’s a long way to go, but this is a good start." Motherwell manager Mark McGhee lamented his side’s lack of cutting edge and acknowledged the quality shown by Rangers. "They’re a top side with individuals who can make the difference," he said. "We created chances, but we weren’t clinical enough when it mattered." As the season progresses, this result further cements Rangers' status as title contenders, while Motherwell will look to bounce back in their next fixture against Hibs.

Tesco Mobile is set to launch a new initiative that flips the script on the way customers interact with advertisements on their mobile phones — by paying them to watch them. The supermarket giant’s mobile arm has revealed a plan that would see subscribers receive discounts on their monthly bills in exchange for viewing targeted advertisements displayed on their smartphones. Under the scheme, users will have the ability to earn up to £3 a month off their bills by opting in to see a series of short, non-intrusive ads that will appear at times of the user’s choosing. The service is part of a growing trend among mobile service providers to offer customer-perks through innovative methods of data monetisation. It also reflects shifting attitudes among consumers, who are increasingly open to exchanging privacy and attention for financial incentives or added value. For Tesco, the move is not only a clever way to captivate cost-conscious customers, but also a strategic effort to bolster the competitiveness of its mobile offering in a crowded and price-sensitive market. As one of the UK’s most popular supermarket brands, Tesco has long built its reputation on delivering value, and this move is seen as a natural extension of that ethos. "This is about giving our customers more choice and more control over their mobile experience — all while rewarding their engagement," said a Tesco Mobile spokesperson. The launch of the scheme comes as mobile operators across the UK struggle to differentiate their services in a saturated market, where price, data allowances, and customer support often dominate the decision-making process. By introducing an ad-based discount model, Tesco is stepping into a space occupied by online services such as Revolut, which has also experimented with similar loyalty programmes. However, experts warn that the success of the scheme will largely depend on how well customers can be guaranteed control over the content and frequency of the ads they receive. "The key to any such initiative is transparency," said Neil Campling, an expert in digital technologies and telecommunications at University College London. "If customers feel it is unobtrusive and have the power to stop it at any time, it could resonate well," he added. As for customers like Sarah Johnson, a 32-year-old nurse from Manchester, the idea is appealing. "I’m always looking for ways to cut costs, especially with phone bills,” she said.

Sri Lanka found itself at the center of renewed international attention this weekend after a government-appointed judge acknowledged that allegations against the country’s military for potential war crimes during its long and bloody civil conflict are "credible." In a statement released by the Judicial Commission of Inquiry, Judge Justice Herbert Wasantha Wijeyekoon, the panel’s chair, appeared to contradict official government rhetoric, which has long dismissed such claims as “unfounded” and politically motivated. The comment comes amid growing pressure on the island-nation to face the painful legacy of its 26-year conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), which claimed more than 100,000 lives before ending in 2009. The war saw heavy civilian casualties in the final months, with numerous reports from international bodies such as the United Nations, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International describing the indiscriminate use of artillery by the Sri Lankan military in densely populated areas controlled by Tamil separatists. Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe, who has long positioned the government as a bridge between the Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority, has called for reconciliation and transparency, despite deep resistance from sections of the military establishment. However, the independent confirmation from a high-ranking judicial figure, even as part of an inquiry reportedly cleared by the government, adds a new layer of complexity to the already sensitive political landscape. The commission, established by President Maithripala Sirisena last year, was tasked with investigating the allegations arising from the war’s final phase. Though the military has dismissed such efforts as “bias-driven witch-hunts,” Justice Wijeyekoon’s language suggests a more open-minded approach, at least on the part of the judicial review. In a press briefing, he spoke of the need to balance justice with national unity, but added: “The allegations of gross violations of human rights and potential breaches of international humanitarian law that we have heard cannot be easily dismissed.” His remarks are expected to be a key part of the commission’s final report, due to be submitted by the end of next month. If the findings support the credibility of these war crime allegations, it could further strain relations with the European Union and other Western bodies, which have previously suspended trade with Sri Lanka over human rights concerns. This moment also marks a potential turning point in a country deeply divided by ethnic tensions, with the Tamil community still seeking recognition for their losses and the Sinhalese majority wary of foreign interference in domestic affairs.

In a moment that reshaped the political, cultural, and religious landscape of the Middle East, Iran was transformed in 1979 from a monarchy to an Islamic republic, propelled by a wave of anti-western fervour and a desire for revolutionary change. The seismic shift came after the overthrow of the U.S.-backed Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose modernisation and westernisation policies had sparked widespread discontent among conservative clerics, the working class, and students. Leading this revolution was Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a charismatic and deeply revered religious figure who had spent years in exile, but who returned triumphantly to a rapturous welcome from crowds who hailed him as a messianic leader. Khomeini's return to Iran in February 1979 marked the beginning of a new era. Just weeks later, in what would become a historic referendum in April of that year, an overwhelming majority of the population — nearly 98 per cent of those who voted — endorsed the establishment of an Islamic republic, rejecting the old constitutional monarchy and embracing a theocratic system of governance. The new republic was defined by the principle of "velayat-e faqih" (guardianship of the jurist), a theory of governance which placed ultimate authority in the hands of Islamic scholars, with Khomeini as the “Supreme Leader.” The revolution brought with it radical changes in governance, law, and society. The Shah's secular government was dismantled, and Islamic law was enshrined in the new constitution. Women’s rights were curtailed, freedoms of speech and the press were restricted, and western-style institutions were replaced with Islamic alternatives. The clerics who now held real and symbolic power repurposed government buildings, schools, and even banks in line with their ideological vision. Khomeini's authority was reinforced by the Iranian Constitutional Assembly and later by the creation of the Supreme Council of the Islamic Revolution, which gave religious leaders final say over major political and legal decisions. The establishment of the Islamic Republic led to a deepening of ties with anti-imperialist and Shia movements globally, while it cut Iran off from many of its previous diplomatic and economic relationships, particularly in the West. The 1979 revolution not only ended the rule of the Pahlavi dynasty but set Iran on a path of opposition to the West, typified in the 1979–1981 hostage crisis at the U.S. Embassy in Tehran. For the Muslim world, it marked the emergence of a model of political Islam that would inspire both admiration and alarm across the region.

The towering golden statue of three liberation soldiers—two men and a woman—dominates the skyline of Heroes' Acre in Harare, standing as a solemn tribute to the sacrifices made by those who fought for Zimbabwe’s freedom. At over 15 meters tall and built from bronze plated with gold, the central sculpture is one of the largest of its kind in the country. It was unveiled in 2012 as part of a major revamp of the national monument, which had long served as a focal point for commemorating veterans, fallen heroes, and the country's hard-fought independence from colonial rule in 1980. The central figures, sculpted in mid-march and armed with pikes and rifles, are shown encircled by a relief of a wounded soldier being carried by others. The depiction is symbolic of the unity and sacrifice that underpinned the liberation struggle in the late 1970s, a conflict known as the Second Chimurenga. The woman in the statue, representing the crucial role women played in the movement, is a recent and powerful addition. Historically, women like Dedza Mumbengegwi, who served as a nurse and messenger for Robert Mugabe's ZANU forces, were often overlooked in grand narratives of war but have since been acknowledged as integral to the nation's history. Surrounding the main statue are burial plots for hundreds of fallen soldiers, many marked with unnamed headstones, and an avenue of trees planted in their memory. During the country’s annual Heroes Day on 11 August, the site becomes the hub for military parades, government speeches, and public celebrations that blend reverence with national pride. For many Zimbabweans, the monument is more than stone and metal—it is a living reminder of the past and a testament to the resilience of the people. The area has also become increasingly politicised in recent years, with successive governments using the occasion to reinforce their national narratives. Critics argue that the monument has, at times, been used to glorify certain leaders at the expense of a nuanced understanding of the liberation movement. Nonetheless, Heroes’ Acre remains a place of pilgrimage for many, a site where the nation pauses to remember those who gave their lives for freedom. As Zimbabwe continues to navigate its post-colonial path, the golden figures will remain a silent witness to the course of the nation's history. For now, they loom large over Harare, beckoning visitors into a space where history, heroism, and memory converge.

Mullah Mohammed Omar, the enigmatic leader of Afghanistan’s Taliban regime, remained a shadowy and elusive figure throughout his public life. Before his government was ousted by US-led forces in late 2001, Omar himself rarely appeared in public, shunning the spotlight even as his regime held absolute power over the war-torn nation. Unlike many political leaders, he gave few interviews, and his policies and personal life were largely speculation among journalists and analysts. A report by the International Crisis Group this week has revisited Omar’s legacy, highlighting how his reclusiveness and deeply spiritual public persona helped solidify the Taliban’s grip on the country under his rule. Born to a humble family in Kandahar, Omar is said to have only left Afghanistan briefly in the late 1980s during his military training in Pakistan. After returning, he emerged as a key figure in the Taliban’s rise, transforming from a guerrilla commander into the movement’s undisputed spiritual and military leader. His leadership style was marked by a strict adherence to Islamic law, and his silence in the face of global condemnation for the group’s harsh rule over the decades that followed only added to his mystique. Following the US-led invasion in 2001, which unseated the Taliban government and led to Omar going into hiding, the world saw little of him. Reports suggest he lived in the lawless tribal regions near the border with Pakistan, under layers of protection. His brother, Mullah Muhammad Yousef, publicly announced his death in July 2015, claiming he had died of wounds sustained in a drone strike. However, this claim has never been independently verified, and many continue to question the circumstances of his reported passing. Analysts say Omar’s evasion of capture and his continued influence in Taliban circles even after his government fell reflect the deep-rooted nature of his leadership. Dr. Nancy Rubin, a senior researcher at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, said: “Omar was never a politician for show. His quiet, steady leadership passed almost unnoticed until his absence created a void the Taliban have never fully filled.” As the Taliban continues to maintain a strong insurgent presence in Afghanistan, the legacy of Mullah Mohammed Omar remains a subject of both fascination and mystery. His early years of power, defined by secrecy and an almost monastic devotion to his cause, have left a lasting impression on the nation he once ruled from afar.

A Scottish man who claims to have been a victim of sexual abuse by former Crewe Alexandra coach Barry Bennell has issued a stark warning that historical and ongoing sexual abuse in football is more widespread than previously understood. Speaking publicly for the first time since coming forward, the man, who has not been named, said the abuse he suffered was part of a "systemic" issue that has plagued the sport for decades and may still be occurring today. Bennell, once a respected coach in English football and a long-time employee of Crewe Alexandra, is currently serving a 24-year prison sentence for the sexual abuse of boys, many of whom he coached in the youth ranks. He has since been linked to numerous other former players and is at the heart of a major police investigation into historic child sexual abuse in football. However, the man from Scotland claims the issue is not confined to a specific region and that football authorities turned a blind eye for far too long. "I was abused when I was a young player at this club. It was traumatic and isolated at the time, and I never thought I'd be able to say this out loud. But now I see others coming forward, and I have to speak up too," he said in a recent interview. He suggested that abuse in football often goes unreported due to the power imbalance between coaches and players, a culture of secrecy, and the fear of being disbelieved. He added that, despite the progress made in recent years, he believes efforts to eliminate abuse are still not enough. "From my experience and the people I’ve spoken to, this could be a huge problem—bigger than people think. It's not just about the past; it's about making sure it never happens again and being honest about what has already occurred." The statements echo recent calls from abuse survivors who have worked with the National Football Corruption and Abuse Taskforce (NFCAT) and the National Crime Agency (NCA) as they seek to uncover the full extent of child sexual exploitation in football over decades. The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) has also backed the man's comments, urging football authorities to ensure greater transparency and protection for current and former players. While the Football Association has praised the bravery of those coming forward and reiterated its commitment to eliminating abuse in the sport, questions remain around whether enough has been done to hold institutions accountable and to prevent abuse from happening again.

A Cardiff man who had travelled to Syria to join an extremist group has been killed in an RAF air strike, it has been confirmed. The man, identified as one of three jihadists from the Welsh capital known to have left the UK to fight in Syria, was reportedly among those targeted in a recent bombing raid by the Royal Air Force (RAF), according to sources close to the military. The British government has not yet released an official statement on the incident but is believed to have approved the strike as part of ongoing efforts to target terrorist operatives overseas. The man, whose identity has not been disclosed for security reasons, had drawn the attention of counter-terrorism authorities in recent months prior to his departure for the conflict zone. Welsh Police and the security services are now working to inform his family and assess the wider impact of his death on local communities in Cardiff. This development highlights the increasing number of British citizens, and particularly young men from urban areas in the UK, who have been drawn into extremist networks and have travelled to join groups in Syria and Iraq. The Ministry of Justice’s latest figures showed 749 Britons have joined so-called Islamic State (IS) in the past four years, with a significant proportion of them from the West Midlands and Wales. In recent months, several cases of UK citizens being killed in air strikes or on the battlefield have been reported, leading to sensitive discussions about national security and the responsibilities of local authorities in preventing radicalisation. Cardiff Council has been praised in recent years for its community engagement initiatives aimed at preventing radicalisation through education and dialogue with young people, but the death of someone from the city demonstrates the challenge remains. Local leaders have expressed sadness at the news, while also reiterating their commitment to community cohesion and the rule of law. A spokesperson for Cardiff Council said: “It is deeply regrettable that any individual from our city would choose the path of terrorism. We remain vigilant in our approach to safeguarding young people and countering the ideologies that lead to such tragedies.” The Ministry of Defence has not commented on the specifics of the killing, but it is expected to contribute to the ongoing statistical assessments of operations in the Middle East. With Britain’s long-standing focus on counter-terror security, as well as renewed emphasis from Prime Minister Gordon Brown on 'British values' and the integration of various communities, the death of a Cardiff jihadist comes at a time of continued national reflection on extremism.

Two new polls have revealed that President Barack Obama is leaving office with one of the strongest approval ratings ever recorded for a departing U.S. president, according to data released by the Pew Research Center and ABC News. With just months left in his term, Mr. Obama appears set to exit the White House on a far more positive note than many of his recent predecessors, reflecting the changing tide of public sentiment as his eight-year tenure nears its conclusion. The Pew Research Centre found that 62% of Americans approve of Mr. Obama’s performance as president, while 32% disapprove. Similarly, an ABC News/Washington Post poll revealed a net approval rating of 60%, with 60% of respondents expressing approval and 40% disapproval. These figures place Mr. Obama among the most popular outgoing presidents in modern history, surpassing the final approval ratings of leaders such as George W. Bush and William Clinton. The rise in Mr. Obama’s approval ratings, which have climbed steadily this year, has been attributed in part to his handling of the 2016 presidential campaign and the nation’s growing unity over key issues such as climate change and healthcare, as well as a consistent sense of dignity in his public appearances. “This is a credit to the President, who has maintained a strong presence on the global stage and delivered on key priorities like the Affordable Care Act and climate agreement with other world leaders, and who continues to command respect,” said Rebecca Morehouse, deputy director of the Pew Research Centre’s survey methodology department. The jump in Mr. Obama’s approval also comes against a backdrop of increasing political polarization in the United States, with Americans more divided than ever on many domestic and foreign policies. However, as the next presidential election approaches under the shadow of Donald Trump, there is a notable sense of national unity around a number of critical issues such as gun control and gender equality. “This is an encouraging sign for the future of the country,” said Dr. Alan Lichtman, a political analyst at American University. “When a leader exits with such high praise, it reflects a sense of effectiveness and trust among the American people.” Policy changes introduced during Mr. Obama’s presidency, such as the expansion of Medicaid and the Paris Climate Agreement, also continue to resonate with the public and are increasingly cited as major positives among voters.

In a shocking act of violence that has stunned the nation, a US congresswoman was critically injured and six others were killed when a gunman opened fire on a constituent event in Tucson, Arizona, on Friday morning. The tragedy struck as the elected official, Representative Gabrielle Giffords, met with constituents at a shopping centre in a suburban district of the state capital, Phoenix. Eyewitnesses described scenes of panic and chaos as the shooting unfolded around 9 a.m. local time. The congresswoman was shot in the head and is reported to be in a critical condition at a local hospital, where she is currently undergoing surgery. Alongside the representative, six others lost their lives in the attack, including a nine-year-old child and the local federal judge, John Roll. Further injuries have been reported, with numerous people still being treated for gunshot wounds and trauma, according to the authorities. A special edition of the Arizona Daily Star screamed from front-page headlines, breaking the news of the shooting breakfast, as the town has been used to house a drive in morning meetings with the public. The 40-year-old House Democrat is the youngest sitting member of the Arizona delegation and was among the prominent, low-key congressmen in Congress. She has never sought national attention as much as she is known for deadly opposition to war in Afghanistan and domestic spending cuts. The rhythm of such services gives way to national news – but it is often fairly ordinary, and sometimes it is even busy. The local community has been in shock and disbelief, with vigils quickly springing up in mourning at the site, which has also become a rallying point for calls for stricter gun control. President Obama, who was vacationing at the time, had to be quickly arranged in the White House and is expected to speak about the nation in the coming days. The incident is being investigated by local law enforcement, the FBI, and intelligence agencies, who are working to establish a motive and uncover the identity of the assailant. The shooter, who has not yet been publicly named, is reported to have been wearing military-style clothing and was active and armed with a 9mm Glock. The Arizona shooting is believed to be the deadliest political violence since 1998, when Larry Gene Bell shot 14 Republicans in the lunches of a Louisianna county. It also marks the first time a member of the House of Representatives has been the target of such an attack in the capital of a state.

Over the years I have spoken to more chancellors and shadow chancellors than most people of my age (that is not a boast, just a sad fact about my preoccupations). I have asked them about growth, about jobs, about deficit reduction and about debt. I have interrogated them on tax rises and spending cuts, on welfare reform and on the nationalisation of one industry or privatisation of another. Almost all have been courteous. A few have been dismissive or even rude. I cannot recall a single one who was not, in their own way, deeply intelligent and mostly well informed. But none of them has ever revealed anything resembling a moral compass. That is not, of course, a unique British shortcoming. In every nation where I have encountered senior politicians, the focus is on policy, not principle. It is on persuading the public, not on persuading their own conscience. A chancellors’ job is, by definition, to balance conflicting priorities, often with no agreement on which are more important. The hard choices are usually made for them by events, or by the electorate. And yet, in Britain, we have a tradition – or perhaps, a hope – that those in power might occasionally be guided not only by their political ambition and the numbers on their spreadsheets but by something higher. Over the decades, I have asked them whether they personally believe – deep down – in the policies they champion. The answer is always the same: a tight smile, a carefully chosen phrase and the evasion of the question. The chancellors are, in the end, just financiers in tails and blazers: technicians of the possible, not philosophers of the desirable. And yet, is it not possible – even likely – that their own sense of right and wrong, however buried, might influence the choices they make? After all, the most enduring economic arguments are not just about numbers or models, but about justice. So why do they never talk about that? Maybe it’s the system, maybe it’s the times, maybe it’s us. But if our leaders have no sense of higher purpose – if their vision extends only to the next election – then what else can we expect but to be treated like customers, not citizens? By Alan SoadyPolitical reporter, BBC News It is regarded as a no-brainer by MPs that many voters loathe the idea of politicians being paid more, especially at a time of austerity.

The UK's probable future outside the EU has sparked widespread concern and speculation among citizens, with many contacting the BBC to ask about the implications for trade and the economy. As the debate around Brexit continues to shape national discourse, individuals from all walks of life — small business owners, farmers, and families alike — are voicing their fears and questions about how a departure from the European Union might affect their daily lives and livelihoods. The EU has been a cornerstone of British economic policy for decades, providing access to a single market of over 500 million consumers and underpinning nearly half of the UK's total trade. With reports of the government preparing contingency plans for a potential exit, questions arise over whether trade deals with EU nations and other countries across the world would be sufficient to replace the seamless access currently enjoyed by UK businesses. One of the most frequent concerns raised is the possibility of increased bureaucracy and trade barriers. A London-based clothing retailer expressed fears that tariffs and lengthy customs checks could "push small businesses into the ground," particularly those which lack the scale and resources to absorb the costs imposed by new trade regulations. Farmers and food producers, too, have voiced similar worries, with many noting the heavy reliance on seasonal workers from across Europe to support the land-based industries. Economists have weighed in with varying predictions. Some argue that Brexit could offer opportunities for the UK to strike trade deals with countries outside the EU, while others warn of significant short-term economic disruption and long-term growth challenges. The Bank of England has already highlighted the risks of a Brexit outcome, with senior officials pointing to the potential for a period of financial volatility and a possible hit to consumer confidence. With just weeks to go until the EU Referendum, the volume of inquiries and anxiety among ordinary people is set to continue — a clear indication that the most important question of this vote is not just about sovereignty, but the fundamental future of the UK’s economic wellbeing. How the government answers that question will determine whether the nation is unprepared for the economic consequences of a ‘leave’ vote — or whether it will rise to meet the challenges with clarity, planning, and resilience. But for now, many citizens remain in suspense, waiting to hear what the future holds. (Word count: 412)

A man with a history of violent crimes has been sentenced to six years in prison after being tackled by a shop owner during a botched axe attack in a quiet suburban high street. The dramatic incident, which was captured on CCTV and later viewed by thousands online, has been hailed as a rare example of a member of the public thwarting a criminal on their own. The alleged attacker, 34-year-old Marcus Jones, had targeted the convenience store on Wood Green Road in Basildon, Essex, just before closing time on a Thursday evening last month. Armed with a large axe, he attempted to smash through the glass of the storefront, setting off the alarm and drawing the attention of both staff and the store’s owner, 52-year-old Richard Taylor. According to court documents, Mr. Taylor, who had previously left the shop for the night, returned to the premises after noticing unusual activity and found Jones trying to gain entry. In a scene described as both chaotic and courageous, Mr. Taylor confronted Jones directly and managed to wrestle the weapon from his hands, leaving the would-be thief with minor injuries before police arrived. Detected through fingerprint evidence and CCTV footage, Jones was apprehended within hours and charged with attempted robbery, assault, and possession of an offensive weapon. The court heard that Jones had a long and troubling criminal history, including convictions for domestic violence, burglary, and public disorder. His barrister initially argued for a lesser sentence on the grounds of his client’s “imperfect life,” but the judge, citing the severity of the offence and the public danger posed, dismissed such claims. In sentencing, Judge Helen Maye said: “This was not a spontaneous act of violence—this was a planned and premeditated attempted robbery with an axe. The bravery of Mr. Taylor in defusing a situation with potentially far worse consequences cannot be overstated. But Jones has a pattern of anti-social and criminal behaviour that leaves little room for leniency.” The Ministry of Justice revealed that axe-related attacks, though rare, have shown troubling signs of an upward trend in recent months. A recent national anti-violence campaign was launched in part to address the growing use of bladed and improvised weapons in criminal activity. In the wake of the incident, Mr. Taylor, who refused a reporter’s request to comment, took the next two weeks off from his shop.

The 2015 World Athletics Championships, often described as a gathering of the world’s greatest hurdlers, long jumpers, and sprinters, ended in a torrential downpour that seemed to mirror the emotional turbulence that had built throughout the fortnight. Beginning under the metaphorical weight of doping scandals, political controversy, and public concern over the state of the sport, the Championships concluded under a sky as grey as the mood that had lingered since the opening ceremony. The Bird’s Nest Stadium, an architectural marvel built for the 2008 Summer Olympics and once the symbol of China's sporting prowess, was drenched as champions and fans alike braved the weather for the final competitions. The Championships, which officially closed on Wednesday night, were overshadowed by the repeated suspensions of numerous Russian athletes and the fallout from the World Anti-Doping Agency’s (WADA) recent report into widespread state-sponsored doping. In an unprecedented move, the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF), the sport’s governing body, banned Russia outright from the competition, leading to a team of independent athletes instead. This decision, made just weeks before the event, was both a benchmark and a backlash — a statement of intent that the struggle for a clean sport must continue, even at the cost of national pride on display. The impact of these decisions was deeply felt. Russia fans, once a common sight in any major athletics event, were barely seen in Beijing. The absence raised somber questions about the geopolitical and ethical tensions that continue to define sport in the 21st century. Despite this, the sporting action remained compelling. American Kevin Mayer capped a remarkable career by securing the gold in the decathlon, while Jamaica continued its sprinting dominance with victories in the men’s 100m and 200m. Alyson Felix of the USA, the oldest woman on the track at 30, secured another sprint crown to cap her historic career. As the rain lashed Beijing, and the final medals were awarded, the symbolic significance of the weather seemed almost poetic. Just as the Championships had wrestled with the weight of the present, so too did the skies seem ready to release the accumulated tension in rain. Yet as the athletes departed the Bird’s Nest, a new question lingered in the air: with the scandals exposed and punished, can athletics truly昂 (lift their heads) in the world it inhabits? Or will the grey clouds soon return?

At first glance, it was a game jam like any other. A gathering of coders, artists, and dreamers came together in a dimly lit room to create something extraordinary from nothing more than their imaginations and a shared deadline. But for a small group of young designers in Bristol, what began as a weekend of quick prototypes and rapid design loops would soon take on a far more important and haunting dimension. Their project, initially titled “MirrorWorld,” was meant to be a simple exploration of identity and social connection in the digital age. Yet, as the hours passed and the wine was poured,.Fatalfanstories emerged from participants' pasts: of isolation, of longing for human connection, of screens that isolate instead of unite. The mood in the room changed. The music softened, the laughter subsided, and something deeper began to take shape. One designer, who had lost a brother to depression and addiction, turned to the others with a quiet urgency: “We’re not just making a game. We’re trying to say something.” The group slowly began to pivot the project. No longer was it simply about identity mechanics or social avatars. Instead, “MirrorWorld” grew into a narrative experiment that tackled the digital impacts of loneliness — a phenomenon that has become increasingly pronounced during the pandemic and the rise of remote living. The room, once filled with light from computer screens and the noise of keyboards, became a place of reflection and, at times, tears. Some of the designers admitted they hadn’t talked about their feelings for years, not even with their closest friends. Others found themselves in a rare state of vulnerability, something the game itself would seek to model and explore. As the weekend drew to a close and the final versions of the game were uploaded, one participant described the jam as “the most emotionally raw I’ve ever been in a team setting.” With the first pass of “MirrorWorld” complete, the designers now face another challenge: how to take the poignant, unfiltered honesty of their creation and turn it into something that resonates with a wider audience — all while avoiding the pitfalls of sentimentality or exploitation. But for those involved, there’s no doubt about the game’s purpose. As the event organisers put it, “This isn’t just a game. It’s a conversation.” And sometimes, in the quiet of a game jam, those conversations matter most.

Two women have been jailed for their role in the tragic death of a seven-year-old girl who died after suffering a catastrophic brain injury. The aunt and grandmother, described by the court as “wicked” in their treatment of the child, were sentenced today following a harrowing trial that exposed years of cruelty and neglect. Deputies in Derbyshire, where the girl lived with her grandmother, were first alerted to possible abuse after reports of unexplained injuries and signs of distress. An emergency response was launched after social services received multiple referrals, each raising concerns about the child’s wellbeing. The case has shocked the local community, with friends and neighbours expressing disbelief that such horrific mistreatment could occur within a family setting. The seven-year-old, who only recently began attending school due to the severity of her symptoms, was found to have significant neurological damage during a routine health check-up. Hospital staff, concerned about the inconsistency in the family’s explanation for her condition, reported the matter to child protection services. Subsequent investigations revealed a pattern of abuse spanning several months, with both the girl’s grandmother and aunt admitting to striking her and failing to seek medical help for her injuries. During the trial, prosecutors presented harrowing evidence, including testimonies from social workers and medical professionals, as well as CCTV footage that showed the child in a vulnerable state shortly before her death. The court heard how she had been subject to repeated verbal abuse and physical punishment, often because of minor infractions. One teacher recalled the girl arriving to class in tears, unusually withdrawn and hesitant to interact with others. The woman’s family was said to have previously dismissed warnings from school staff and local authorities, citing cultural misunderstandings and an alleged mistrust of the welfare system. However, the court ruled that no justification could excuse such extreme behaviour. Speaking after the sentencing, a coroner described the case as “a tragic and avoidable death”, adding that the child had been “denied the right to live a childhood unburdened by fear and suffering”. A local charity supporting child protection has since called for a review of the processes in place to monitor children living in high-risk households. The grandmother, 62, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, while the aunt, 37, received a 10-year term. Both have been ordered to be kept in separate facilities during their sentences.

The Tate Modern has unveiled the striking new addition to its iconic South Bank home — a pyramid-like tower that promises to transform the museum’s already vast and influential programme of contemporary art. The 10-storey extension, which is set to open to the public later this year, has already begun to attract attention for its bold design and promise of improved visitor experiences. The building, the brainchild of architect Francis Kéré, marks a bold departure from the traditional industrial aesthetic of the original power station that was converted into a gallery in 2000. The new tower, known as the Turbine Hall Tower, rises from the site of the former turbine hall, one of the museum’s most famous spaces. Kéré, who has previously worked on projects in Africa and across Europe, described the design as a “vertical platform for contemporary ideas.” The structure, made from sustainable materials, includes a series of open, cavernous gallery spaces that will host both permanent and temporary exhibitions. It is also set to offer new public facilities, including a state-of-the-art education centre, a dedicated space for performance, and panoramic views of the city from its top floor. The project has been three years in the making, following a lengthy design process that saw proposals from a number of leading architects reviewed by the Tate’s board. Kéré’s vision was chosen for its ambition and its sensitivity to the surrounding area — a historically important part of London that has long been associated with culture and industry. Museum director Maria Balshaw hailed the new building as “a vital next step in the Tate’s mission to remain one of the world’s leading destinations for modern and contemporary art.” Balshaw said the tower would give the museum the space and facilities it needed to expand its international reach and better serve its growing visitor numbers — which stood at over 6 million annually before the pandemic. “We are not just talking about more space,” she said. “We are talking about a new way of experiencing and thinking about contemporary art.” As preparations continue for the official opening, the building has already drawn guest speeches from artists and cultural leaders. London Mayor Sadiq Khan praised the project as “a beacon of creativity and innovation,” while Heritage Minister Lucy Frazer described it as “a bold statement of the UK’s continuing commitment to the arts.”

The London Fire Brigade has enlisted the help of an additional 60 mental health professionals to support the hundreds of firefighters affected by the traumatic Grenfell Tower fire, BBC’s  Victoria Derbyshire  programme has exclusively learned. The move comes as part of a £2.4 million package deployed by the brigade to provide extended psychological support for personnel who responded to the devastating blaze in June, which claimed 72 lives. The fire, which engulfed the 24-storey North Kensington tower block in a matter of minutes, left emergency responders grappling not only with the logistics of the rescue operation but also with the lasting emotional scars of witnessing such a catastrophic event. Firefighters, including those who made the heart-breaking decision to switch off alarms to calm people inside the building and those who had to help bodies being thrown to safety from upper floors, have spoken of the deep emotional toll on them and their families in the months since. In an exclusive interview with the programme, several firefighters revealed that post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms such as recurring nightmares, anxiety and insomnia have become increasingly common among them. One firefighter, who wished to remain anonymous, said: “You can see it in some of the lads – they never really quite make it to the same place they were before Grenfell.” The brigade is now working closely with agencies such as Mind and suicide prevention charity Samaritans to provide trauma-focused psychotherapy and other forms of mental health support. Additional wellbeing officers have also been posted to fire stations across the capital to monitor and support emergency personnel. The 60 new counsellors are part of a broader emergency mental health response already under way, following a similar outpouring of support for police, paramedics and politicians who attended the scene. Some of those close to the fire have described the support as “a lifeline” to those still struggling to come to terms with what they saw and did during those harrowing hours. Local housing minister Heidi Alexander, who visited the site, said: “The response from the fire service and others was heroic. But now we have a responsibility to support these individuals as they cope with the aftermath, both physically and mentally.” With the anniversary of the Grenfell fire fast approaching, the London Fire Brigade’s move underscores the long-lasting nature of psychological trauma among emergency services, and the urgent need for continued and accessible mental health support.

Cummings Claims Solo Victory in Dramatic Stage Seven Win at the Tour de France   British cyclist Steve Cummings made history on a sun-drenched afternoon in the Pyrenees as he claimed victory in stage seven of the Tour de France with a breathtaking solo performance that left his competitors in the dust. The 36-year-old was the lone rider to break away from the peloton on the final climb of the 171km stage from Aurillac to Aulus-les-Bains, swooping past his rivals in a stunning display of endurance and tactical prowess. Cummings crossed the finish line more than a minute ahead of his nearest challenger, underlining the significance of his achievement in one of cycling’s most grueling races. The stage, which marked the Tour's first climb of this year's race, saw teams battle not only each other but also the demands of the rolling Dronno Coll and the infamous Col de la Croix-querre — a Catskill Mountains-style ascent that would test even the most seasoned of riders. Cummings, riding for the Dimension Data team, broke away on the final 5km of the climb, driving determinedly towards the finish with the kind of composure usually reserved for champions. Speaking after the race, a visibly emotional Cummings described the victory as "the culmination of years of hard work and belief." "I knew when I got to the climb that if I pushed myself, I could make something happen," he said. "When the others faded behind me, I just kept pushing. It was the best moment of my career." The win is the first Tour de France stage triumph for Cummings, who has spent over a decade competing at the elite level. It also marks a significant boost for his team as they look to make their mark in the race overall standings. French cycling legend and race director Christian Prudhomme praised Cummings's performance, calling it “a brilliant example of what can happen when you are willing to put everything on the line. Steve showed incredible strength and the kind of nerve that separates the good from the great.” As the peloton regroups for the next stage, attention turns to how the general classification leaders fared — with some waiting to see if this surprise victory could disrupt the early Tour of champions. But for Cummings, this is a moment to savour. Not only has he proven that experience and determination can triumph over opposition, but he has also etched his name on the Tour map in a way few British cyclists have.

If your fantasy is to create a billion-dollar business, why not create it out of fantasy? That’s exactly what a growing band of entrepreneurs, investors and tech enthusiasts are doing as they harness the boundless creativity of the fantasy world to build real-world commercial empires. From video games and immersive virtual reality experiences to fantasy sports platforms and branded collectables, the intersection between escapism and enterprise has never been more lucrative. In an era where digital engagement is king and consumer preferences lean increasingly towards personalisation and storytelling, fantasy-based ventures are gaining traction as fertile ground for innovation. Take, for example, the meteoric rise of fantasy football and the broader fantasy sports industry, which is now estimated to be valued at over $10 billion globally. Platforms like DraftKings and FanDuel have carved out billion-dollar businesses by tapping into the competitive spirit of sports fans, allowing them to create imaginary teams and monetise their knowledge and instincts. But fantasy is now breaking free from traditional boundaries. The video game industry, which has been creating virtual worlds for decades, is being rebranded as a core battleground for the future of business—and not just in terms of entertainment. With the advent of the metaverse and Web3 technologies, the next generation of entrepreneurs is not just building games, but entire economies, investing in digital land, and offering opportunities for users to earn real money from purely imaginary worlds. Companies like Roblox and Epic Games are not just game developers; they are now global economic powerhouses enabling users to design, trade and monetise digital assets. Meanwhile, the gaming and NFT space has also become a goldmine for investors looking to turn fantasy into financial gain. Digital collectables, such as those made prominent by CryptoPunks or Bored Ape Yacht Club, have seen some assets sell for millions of pounds, with buyers seeing them not as mere images but as the building blocks of future value. The line between imagination and investment is blurring. This trend is prompting business schools and venture capital firms to take a second look at the potential of fantasy-driven ventures. “There's a growing realisation that the future is going to be as much about digital worlds as physical ones,” said Aram Sinnreich, author and expert in the evolving entertainment landscape. “What matters is not just how you play the game, but how you build the game—and beyond that, how you make money from the dream.”

Burkina Faso is holding a pivotal general election on 29 November, with voters casting their ballots in a country still reeling from the wave of protests that temporarily removed President Blaise Compaoré from power over a year ago. The election comes after a 13-month interim government — one of the shortest mandates in Africa — sought to stabilise the West African nation and address long-standing frustrations among its citizens. The 2014 uprising, sparked by Compaoré’s attempted constitutional amendment to extend his 27-year rule, triggered one of the most dramatic moments in recent African political history. The president fled under pressure from mass demonstrations, the military, and civil society groups. In the vacuum left behind, former Prime Minister Michel Kafando was appointed transitional head of state, leading a government of national unity until credible elections could be held. Now, citizens of this landlocked nation — long plagued by poverty, weak institutions, and growing jihadist threats — face a historic moment. The election will see voters choose a new president and parliament, setting the stage for a new chapter in Burkinabè democracy. Over 5 million eligible voters are expected to take part, with more than 20 candidates in the presidential race. The leading contenders include former President Marc Kabore, a respected figure on the international stage and seen as a moderate candidate, and Roch Kaboré, a former finance minister with a reputation for economic reform. Security remains a major concern. The interim government inherited a country under threat from al-Qaeda-linked militants operating in the Sahel region. Despite efforts by the military and international partners, attacks have continued to rise, with violence spilling into areas far from the traditional hotspots. Whether the election can be held securely will be a critical test of the government’s ability to balance democratic processes with national security. The head of the independent National Electoral Commission (CENI), Koudou Guikoumou, has assured the public that preparations for the election have advanced, despite logistical and security challenges. Voters will use bio-metric identification technology to curb fraud, a system used for the first time during the August 2021 regional elections. Political parties are prohibited from holding demonstrations in cities considered high-risk for extremism. Political observers, including the African Union and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), have been invited to monitor the process. Their presence is vital in a nation where trust in institutions remains fragile.

For the first time since the massive global tax-avoidance scandal known as the Panama Papers broke in 2016, the secret whistleblower who leaked some 11 million internal documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca has finally come forward with a remarkable condition. In a rare interview with the German newspaper   Süddeutsche Zeitung  , the anonymous source, who handed over the documents that exposed how the world’s wealthiest individuals hide assets through complex offshore structures, has expressed a willingness to assist law enforcement in making prosecutions—on the condition that they are granted full immunity. The leak, which was first investigated by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), revealed how powerful politicians, corporate leaders, and celebrities around the world have used secretive offshore entities to evade taxes, evade legal accountability, and in some cases, further corruption and money laundering. It led to the resignation of Iceland’s prime minister, an inquiry in Germany, and criminal prosecutions in a number of countries. Yet, while the world learned the identities of thousands of clients using the services of Mossack Fonseca, the original whistleblower behind the unprecedented leak has remained hidden until now. In the interview, the source—who is reported to have worked at the law firm for several years and only used a public library in Hamburg to send the data to journalists—described their growing frustration with the firm’s activities. According to statements shared by the newspaper, the whistleblower claimed to have seen the firm knowingly set up shell companies for dubious clients, including a large number of countries suspected of financial wrongdoing, and said they could provide further evidence beyond what was already exposed. The offer of immunity comes at a time when international prosecutors are still investigating cases connected to the leak, and comes amid renewed calls for greater transparency and reform in how financial institutions and law firms operate in offshore jurisdictions. The whistleblower's revelations lit a fire under global anti-corruption movements, and their latest offer may further expose connections between the powerful and unregulated financial systems that have long been obscured from public view. However, no official response has been made by any government or law enforcement agency to the proposed deal, and it is unclear whether any will take up the offer. If the whistleblower is granted immunity and testifies, it could represent a major step forward in the long process of holding those responsible for financial crime to account.

Chelsea captain John Terry is set to remain a Blues legend after manager Guus Hiddink confirmed the 33-year-old may stay with the club beyond the summer when his current contract expires. The announcement comes as a surprise to many, given recent speculation that Terry, who has spent his entire professional career at Stamford Bridge, would make a return to former club Aston Villa or pursue a new challenge elsewhere. But with his role on the pitch evolving into a pivotal leadership position, Hiddink has hinted that Terry may continue to don the famous blue jersey in a coaching or ambassadorial capacity. “John has been an incredible servant to this club,” Hiddink said during a press conference on Wednesday. “He is still a top professional and a world-class leader. We have made no final decision, but I can see a future for John in this team – perhaps not as a regular first-team player, but I think he has much to offer us in other ways.” Terry, who has made over 700 appearances for Chelsea, has been in discussion with the club about the next stage of his career in recent weeks. While a formal announcement is yet to be made, sources close to the club suggest Terry is keen to extend his association with the Blues, as he is nearing the twilight of his playing career. The Dutch manager, who has previously worked closely with Terry during his previous stint at the club in 2007, praised the defender for his discipline and experience. “I’m not surprised,” Hiddink added. “John is one of the greats of the game. His values align with our club’s identity. If he can stay a part of our environment, whether on the pitch or off it, that would be a good thing for everyone.” The potential for Terry to continue his Chelsea career in a new role has been warmly welcomed by fans, many of whom have posted messages on social media expressing their gratitude for his long and distinguished service. Since his debut in 1998, Terry has been at the heart of some of the Blues’ most successful periods, including historic Champions League triumphs in 2012 and 2013, as well as multiple Premier League titles. Now, as he eyes the winding down of his playing days, a new chapter with the club he loves could still be written for John Terry.

In a bold move that has sent shockwaves through the world of international football, David Bernstein, the former chairman of the English Football Association (FA), has called for association football’s governing body in Europe, Uefa, to unite with regional football associations in staging a boycott of the next FIFA World Cup — and, potentially, to break away from FIFA itself. Bernstein, whose leadership of the FA between 2003 and 2015 saw ambitious reforms and a renewed push to elevate English football abroad, has now dared to challenge FIFA, the sport’s global governing body, in the most dramatic way possible. His comments come amid mounting criticism of FIFA’s conduct, governance, and decision-making, particularly over contentious World Cup and European Championship selections, and have opened a door to a scenario that many had previously dismissed as purely speculative. Speaking at a recent London-based sports summit, Bernstein, 73, did not shy away from making his intentions clear. “We have been here too long,” he said, addressing the historic dominance of FIFA over the sport’s calendar and structure. “FIFA has not always acted in the best interests of the game, and European football must take the lead in ensuring that the future of the sport is controlled by those who understand and play it the most.” His remarks were met with a mixture of surprise, intrigue, and, from some quarters, disdain — but none of it masked the radical implications of what he was proposing. Bernstein, a prominent figure in English football, has long been a vocal advocate for reform and greater collaboration within the sport’s top tiers. However, this call for a complete realignment of global football structures marks a significant shift. He argued that Uefa — which represents 55 national associations across Europe — has the financial heft, political influence, and fan base necessary to walk away from FIFA’s increasingly controversial leadership and take control of key tournaments. His proposals echo some of the concerns that have been simmering for years: allegations of corruption, the geographical imbalance in World Cup and tournament host selections, and the growing autonomy of national and regional bodies. Yet it is a call that, while once unthinkable, may no longer be as madcap as it sounds. Recent years have seen FIFA’s credibility tarnished by high-profile corruption scandals, and Uefa itself has become bolder in asserting its autonomy, particularly after the reorganisation of the Champions League format aimed at creating a closed system of Europe’s top clubs.

In a bold move that has sparked both praise and criticism across social media, a cafe owner in the UK has announced that she will intervene when children cause a scene in her establishment, should their parents appear hesitant to do so. The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which vanished in March 2014 with 239 people on board, has entered what Australia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Barnaby Joyce, has called a “new phase” following the failure of the initial undersea search to find the wreckage of the plane. How do Finnish schoolchildren spend significantly less time in the classroom, receive far less homework, and yet consistently outperform their peers in most other countries on major international assessments? That is the question puzzling educators across the globe after yet another round of Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results placed Finland among the top-performing education systems in the world. In Finland, children do not start formal schooling until the age of seven — two years after most of their international peers. Once they enter school, their days are shorter; a typical student might spend about 5.5 hours in the classroom per day, compared to the average of around seven hours in the United Kingdom. Homework is minimal, often limited to no more than 30 minutes per night. Despite these apparent contrasts with the traditional, high-pressure education models found in many Western countries, Finnish students regularly achieve outstanding results in reading, mathematics and science. The world has long looked to Finland for insight into why this model appears to work so well. Experts suggest that it has a great deal to do with the quality of teachers and the trust placed in them. All teachers in Finland are university graduates and must complete a master’s degree, often after competing for places in their country’s most prestigious universities. Once trained, they are given immense autonomy in the classroom, free from the kind of standardised testing and rigid curricular requirements that characterise systems such as those in the UK, the US and many other European countries. Moreover, Finnish schools don’t segregate children based on perceived ability or prior achievement until adolescence at the earliest, which minimises the stigma and inequality associated with streaming. Learning is seen as a process of exploration rather than a race to the finish, and students are regularly assessed through practical and project-based tasks rather than exams. The culture surrounding education in Finland also plays a role. Education is highly respected, and the pressure to “get ahead” is replaced by a focus on developing life-long learning and critical thinking skills. There is also less social comparison and less parental pressure on children to succeed academically at all costs. As international leaders increasingly look for ways to reform faltering education systems, Finland’s example — with its balance of freedom, trust and high standards — has become a compelling blueprint. But can such a system be replicated in other countries, or is it too deeply tied to Finland’s unique cultural values?

With families, students and city workers hitting the highways and byways in droves, traffic congestion is expected to reach peak levels across the country. Around 11 million cars are anticipated to be on the move on Thursday alone, as the traditional weekend of travel kicks off. The holiday, often regarded as one of the most popular travel periods of the year, has prompted a wave of concern among transport officials and police forces, who are urging drivers to plan ahead and consider alternative options when possible. Services such as the M25, M1, M6 and other major trunk roads are expected to experience the worst delays, particularly during early morning hours and the late afternoon. The Highway Code recommends leaving early or delaying journeys until well after the usual rush times, while some authorities are advising rail or bus travel where feasible. Transport for London (TfL) has also warned of major disruptions to the Underground, buses and Overground services over the weekend, as maintenance works, line closures and reduced train frequencies could cause added frustration for commuters and holiday-makers alike. With the weather forecast pointing to a warm and largely dry short break, many Britons are looking to enjoy countryside getaways, trips to coastal resorts or short city breaks. Camping and caravan parks have reported being fully booked for the Easter period, while motels and hotels in popular areas confirm that advance bookings are no longer available. The police have issued a caution about the increase in accidents during busy travel periods, urging drivers to remain alert and to avoid using mobile devices while operating a vehicle. Road Safety Officers have also reminded the public that drink-driving is a continued concern and that random breath-testing units will be in place along key routes. Additionally, with about half of all UK households planning to travel to their destinations by car this Easter, the RAC expects a surge in calls for roadside assistance. Chief executive Simon Williams said: "We’re preparing for a ‘record Easter’ in terms of car use. Our advice is for drivers to allow extra time for journeys and to make sure their vehicles have been checked before setting off." The Easter getaway is not only a major time for rural and coastal destinations but also a key boost to the hospitality and tourism industry.

Inverness Caledonian Thistle manager John Robertson has admitted he is still in disbelief at the prospect of returning to the dugout with the Scottish Premiership club after a sabbatical from management. Just a few months after stepping down from his role at Ross County to spend more time with his family and reassess his ambitions, the 56-year-old has found himself once again at the helm of one of Scotland’s most prominent football outfits — a position that has surprised even himself. “I’m still a bit shocked to be back,” Robertson told reporters during his first press conference since being appointed by the Gallagher Stadium outfit. “When I left County, I thought I was walking away for good, at least for a while. So to come back into another challenge with such a well-known and passionate club is something I didn’t think would happen this quickly.” Robertson was lured out of retirement by Thistle in the wake of a difficult transition in the manager’s hot seat. His arrival, somewhat unexpected, has revitalised interest in a side in need of a fresh direction as they prepare for a new season looking to escape the mid-table drift that has defined their recent campaigns. The former Hibernian, Kilmarnock, and Hartlepool boss is no stranger to long hours and gruelling fixtures, but he is also aware that his second coming will be closely scrutinised. “I know people are looking at me, and rightly so,” he said. “You don’t come out of management unless you have something to prove or believe strongly in what lies ahead. I believe in this group. I believe in this club. And I believe in the work we can do together.” Robertson’s connection with the Highlands runs deep, having helped Inverness clinch the Scottish Cup in 2015, a feat that is still talked about with pride in the local community. His ability to inspire and rally players during difficult moments has been cited as a key reason for his reappointment. Many local pundits, including BBC Radio Scotland’s Tom Coyne, have suggested that Robertson’s return could mark a turning point for a club seeking to reclaim some of their former glory. “People will always remember what John did back in 2015,” Coyne said. “If he can instill the same spirit and belief, he could be exactly what Thistle need.” As the new season looms, supporters of the Highland club are cautiously optimistic that Robertson’s return may herald a new chapter in their history — one defined not just by ambition, but by a man who insists he never really left.

The number of requests for users' personal information from authorities in the UK surged sharply in 2015, with Twitter reporting a more than 100% increase, according to the social media company's latest transparency report. The figures, released as part of Twitter’s ongoing commitment to being open about data requests and government surveillance, highlight a growing trend in the use of the platform for investigations by law enforcement and intelligence agencies. In 2015, Twitter received 4,920 government requests for user data, of which 93% were from the UK and the United States. The UK-specific requests alone rose from under 2,000 in 2014 to a staggering 2,345 in 2015, a jump that has sparked concerns among digital rights advocates. The report, which is published annually, states that the company provided user data in 74% of the cases, with the remainder of requests either rejected or partially fulfilled. The data requests typically include details such as a user’s account information, IP address, or the content of tweets, and they are generally processed in response to legal orders, often from national security agencies or police forces. The Home Office has not commented publicly on the increase, but government sources have previously stated that enhanced digital surveillance is a key measure in the fight against crime and national security threats. Joe Hinshaw, Twitter’s head of global policy, said in a statement that the company tries to be as transparent as possible about such activity. “Balancing the needs of public safety with the rights of users is one of the biggest challenges of our time,” he said. “Our transparency reports give users a clear picture of how governments seek to access personal data and allow us to make a case for better policy and laws about online privacy.” The sharp rise has raised questions about the scope of government access to online information and the potential for mission creep. Andy Haldane, a digital rights campaigner at Liberty, said, “While we accept that law enforcement should have the tools to pursue serious crime, the doubling of data requests must trigger a broader debate about oversight and accountability. The public deserves to know how these powers are being used and why.” As of now, Twitter continues to advocate for a more open and transparent digital ecosystem, but with government requests set to rise further as online activity increases, the tension between privacy and security is likely to remain a contentious issue in the coming years.

Drinking Overindulgence May Spark Skin Cancer Risk, Scientists Warn   In a startling revelation that adds to the growing list of health risks associated with excessive alcohol consumption, scientists have warned that drinking too much could trigger a chain reaction in the body that leaves the skin more vulnerable to cancer. The findings, published in the  British Journal of Dermatology , suggest that the mechanisms activated by heavy alcohol use may compromise the body's natural defences, increasing susceptibility to skin damage—and ultimately, the development of cancerous cells. The research, led by a team of experts at the University of Leeds, sought to investigate the complex interplay between alcohol metabolism and skin health. Through laboratory experiments and data analysis of patient records, scientists found that the by-products of alcohol consumption can impair skin repair processes and reduce the production of melatonin, a hormone known to protect against DNA damage. Professor Emma Darcy, the lead researcher in the study, explained: "When the body breaks down alcohol into acetaldehyde and other metabolites, these substances can trigger oxidative stress—a kind of cellular damage that is a known precursor to cancer. At the same time, alcohol appears to directly inhibit the skin's ability to repair itself after exposure to harmful UV rays or other environmental stressors." The study highlights particular concerns for individuals who combine heavy drinking with prolonged sun exposure.
