"It may seem surprising, but our data is very clear – alcohol doesn’t just affect the liver and brain," added Professor Darcy. "The skin is often the first line of attack, and if we understand how and why this occurs, we can begin to take steps to mitigate the risks." This warning comes amid broader efforts by public health officials to curb alcohol-related illnesses. The UK's Chief Medical Officer recently reiterated that no level of alcohol consumption is risk-free, urging the public to consider daily limits and to be mindful of consumption patterns. Skin cancer is one of the most common forms of cancer in the UK, with around 21,000 new cases diagnosed annually. While sun overexposure has long been linked to skin malignancies, this new research could represent a significant shift in understanding how lifestyle choices impact skin health. Dr. Sarah Linwood, a dermatologist at St George’s Hospital in London, whose patients provided some of the data for the study, said the findings were "both sobering and timely."

The British and Irish Lions will take to the field in their first Test against New Zealand with the same starting line-up that comfortably defeated the Maori All Blacks 32-10 at Whangārei on Saturday. A decision that has settled the nerves of a team brimming with confidence as they look to kickstart their much-anticipated three-Test series against the world champions. The Lions warmed up for the historic clash in Eden Park on June 3rd by showcasing a powerful performance against the Maori side, a traditional opponent in the build-up to the main series. The emphatic victory under the bright Northland skies highlighted the strength and cohesion of the touring party, with players such as Stuart Hogg, Maro Itoje, and Johnny Sexton impressing in their respective roles. Head coach Warren Gatland, accompanied by forwards coach Neil Barnes and backs coach Gregor Townsend, made no changes to the starting XV for the Test against New Zealand, despite a host of stars nursing minor knocks in training. Hogg retained his place at full-back, continuing his blistering form in attack and defense, while the pack, led by the impenetrable presence of Itoje and the powerful up-and-unders of Jamie George, looks to carry that form into the Test arena. The decision to name the same side is a statement of intent. After negotiating the unpredictable early rounds of Tests fairly securely, and with the support of a huge global following, Gatland’s side has already demonstrated depth and resilience. The iconic ‘Lions juggernaut’ shows no sign of slowing. New Zealand, however, will not be taken lightly. The All Blacks are a formidable force, boasting the highest winning percentage in international rugby and a squad renowned for its adaptability and world-class talent. Their preparations have been aided by key players like Brodie Retallick and Beauden Barrett returning from injury, and the home crowd will undoubtedly play a factor in the Test’s outcome. Still, with a team that has shown both character and quality against the Maori All Blacks, the Lions enter the first Test holding high hopes. As the world’s eyes turn to Eden Park, the tour’s defining clash is set to deliver a spectacle of global rugby at its finest. Whether a new chapter of Lions history is written remains to be seen, but for now, the message is clear: the Lions are ready.

Hillary Clinton’s withdrawal from public focus amid the sustained controversy over her use of a private email server during her tenure as US Secretary of State is now absolute. What had long been a political storm—one that repeatedly threatened to upend her political momentum and siphon away media attention from the broader Democratic Party—has now culminated in a full-scale retreat, with Mrs Clinton seemingly bowing out of the spotlight just as the election campaign enters its most critical phase. The revelation in March 2015 that she had conducted classified government communication using a personal email account set off a political firestorm that quickly spiraled beyond partisan lines. The FBI's subsequent investigation led to the release of more than 50,000 emails and harsh scrutiny of how her communications were handled. Although the Bureau concluded that no criminal wrongdoing had taken place, the Secretary of State had not cleared the air in the eyes of the public or the press. Critics, both within and outside the Democratic Party, have called the issue an unforgivable breach of national security norms, and the topic has continued to dog Mrs Clinton, even as she remains the frontrunner for the Democratic presidential nomination. In the wake of a recent series of damaging reports and leaks that revealed frustrations among senior aides to her campaign and the White House, as well as questions about her disastrous 2016 campaign strategies, Mrs Clinton has chosen – at least for now – to step back from active campaigning. There have been no appearances, no public speeches, and no major statements from her camp in the past week, while the race is accelerated by a sharpening political landscape. Former Obama aides have privately expressed concern that the lack of a visible campaign presence puts the Democratic ticket at continued risk and cedes ground to an underdog Republican candidate. The Democratic National Committee remains in about half-hearted disarray, with competing factions vying for influence and increasingly frustrated over the lack of leadership and vision from their presumptive nominee. Mr Epstein, a long-time Clinton associate and senior adviser, has reportedly made overtures to senior party officials warning that a more active and assertive Mrs Clinton would be a democratic imperative as the November election draws closer. For now, however, the silence persists, and as political strategists on both sides gauge the shifting sands of public opinion and media sentiment, the stage is set for a far more unpredictable and chaotic run-up to November—which the Democrats can ill afford.

Young Voices: ‘Life Isn’t Sunshine and Rainbows’ — Teen’s Open Letter Sparks Uplifting Global Conversation   A 17-year-old girl from Glasgow has touched hearts across the globe with a deeply moving open letter addressed to her parents — both long-term drug users — in which she says their struggles have taught her an invaluable life lesson: that life is often far from perfect. The letter, shared on social media and subsequently picked up by national and international media, has gone viral in a wave of emotional support and admiration. In it, the teenager — known online only as “Nicole S” — writes of how she grew up under difficult circumstances, often lacking basic essentials and stability. Yet, she insists, those challenges have made her resilient and grateful for the life she’s building for herself. “I watched my parents make one bad decision after another,” she wrote. “But they showed me that life is not sunshine and rainbows — it’s harder than you think. I see people expecting everything to just work out, but I’ve learned early on that you have to keep going, even when it’s painful.” She acknowledges the hurt, the nights spent alone, and the uncertainty of growing up in a household affected by addiction. But she also speaks to her parents with love and forgiveness, as well as admiration for their honesty and for not hiding from their problems. Her words have inspired a wave of messages from people around the world, many of whom have shared their own stories of adversity and survival. “You are not alone,” wrote one commenter from London. “Your strength is incredible.” Another from Canada added: “This is the kind of realness the world needs more of. You’re a light in darkness.” The letter has also sparked a broader conversation about the stigma surrounding addiction in families and the importance of resilience and mental health support for young people living in such environments. Nicole, who is now in her final year of school and plans to study child psychology at university, said she wrote the letter as a form of healing and processing rather than for public attention. “I didn’t expect it to go viral,” she told the BBC. “I just wanted to write them a letter I hope they see. It’s not about them being bad people — they’re trying their best, just like I’m trying mine.”

Catalans Dragons delivered a stunning performance as they surged to second place in the Super League with a crushing 42-0 victory over a beleaguered Hull KR at the Stade Gilbert Brutus on Sunday. The French side showcased their class and depth, scoring seven tries in a dominant display that left their opponents with little to celebrate on what is now a frustrating season for the Robins. Catalans, already in strong contention for a top-four finish, seized full control of the game from the early stages, with their attacking flair and disciplined defense proving to be too much for Hull KR to handle. The visitors struggled to get the ball under their own sticks, as Catalans' powerful forwards made relentless ground and the backs cut through the defences with clinical precision. It was a result that underlined the growing gulf between the league’s elite and the pack fighting for survival at the other end of the table. The first-half alone saw the Dragons score four tries, with tries coming from a combination of clever passing, explosive runs and in-form forwards. Full-back Sam Tomkins was among the scorers for the home side, once again underlining his importance to the squad, while young talent Jordan Abdull impressed up front with two tries of his own. Hull KR, who started the day 14th in the table, were left to reflect on a catastrophic afternoon. The Robins have now lost six of their last seven matches, and coach Alan Solomons will be left searching for answers as his side continue to spiral down the league. Catalans’ victory, which followed their midweek elimination in the Challenge Cup by Wigan Warriors, proved they are more than capable of absorbing disappointment and refocusing on the Super League season. Head coach Craig Citation will be pleased with the overall performance, particularly the vigour and accuracy of his side's backline, which lit up the sun-drenched south of France. Another positive for Catalans was the continued fitness and form of George Williams, whose composure and creativity in midfield made the difference in a number of key moments. With London Broncos and Salford Red Devils holding strong in the upper half of the table, Catalans’ performance today suggests they are serious contenders for silverware beyond just the Super League grand final with their growing influence on the English-dominated competition. Hull KR, meanwhile, will be looking for a reaction in their next fixture against Castleford Tigers, hoping to avoid a complete collapse of their season.

The French government is set to shut down a key UK border post in Calais once Brexit is implemented, according to reports emerging from Paris. The statement comes from a close ally of Alain Juppé, the current frontrunner in France’s presidential elections, who disclosed the plan during an interview with the BBC. The decision marks a significant shift in the relationship between France and the UK, as border policies begin to adjust in response to the UK’s withdrawal from the European Union. The border facility in Calais, one of the busiest transit points for goods and passengers entering and leaving the UK from the continent, has served as an important hub within the EU’s Schengen area. With Brexit on the horizon, however, the need for such cross-border structures is being reconsidered. A French government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that the closure had been "discussed at the highest level" in preparation for the UK’s transition out of the bloc. The ambassador of the British embassy in Paris has not yet commented directly on the proposed closure, though diplomats have reportedly been in early discussions with their French counterparts. The UK government has stressed the importance of maintaining strong bilateral ties, despite the uncertainties surrounding post-Brexit trade agreements and immigration policies. Calais is already no stranger to political and economic upheaval. The area became a flashpoint during the European migrant crisis, with thousands of displaced people attempting to cross the Channel, and the surrounding infrastructure has long been strained. The closure of the border post would be the latest in a series of changes that could further transform the city’s role in European logistics. Local business leaders in Calais have expressed concern over the potential economic implications. Many fear that losing the border post will result in lost jobs and a decline in trade activity. Some have called for alternative arrangements to ensure continued economic cooperation with the UK. "We are talking about a lifeline for our region," said one business owner. “We cannot simply be left out of the future negotiations between the UK and France.” The announcement comes just weeks before Alain Juppé is expected to make a final push in the presidential race. His alignment with the idea of closing the border post suggests he is positioning himself on key economic and security issues ahead of the vote. Juppé’s comments add to the growing list of political actions aimed at asserting France’s control over its borders in the post-Brexit era.

The heartbreak of a father whose son’s life was cut short in the 1989 Hillsborough tragedy was poignantly described as "ending abruptly through the failures of others" at a long-awaited inquest into the disaster. The inquiry, which has already heard from over 100 witnesses, is now moving into its final stages, seeking to establish the full extent of the institutional failures that led to the deaths of 97 fans. The testimony from the father, whose name was given as Tony B, captured the emotional weight of the proceedings as he reflected on how the loss of his son changed the course of his life. “No one should have to go through what I’ve been through,” he said. “My son had dreams, aspirations, like any young man his age. Yet everything was taken from him in an instant – not because of who he was, but because of the failures of others.” B’s son, David, was 15 when he lost his life during the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. The tragic events of that day, which saw thousands of fans funnelled into a stadium already at, or exceeding, capacity, have remained a dark chapter in English sporting history. While the 1989 Taylor Report blamed fan behaviour for the disaster, this current inquest has sought to correct the narrative, uncovering systemic flaws in stadium safety management and emergency planning. The inquest, presided over by Sir John Goldring, QC, has already heard damning evidence about the lack of barriers, emergency planning and the failure of authorities to respond effectively at the time. Former South Yorkshire Police officers have given testimony detailing their confusion and the lack of communication leading up to the tragedy, while medical and emergency personnel have described the chaotic scene when they arrived at the ground. For families who have waited 29 years to hear the truth, this inquest represents a crucial step towards closure. “We are not here to seek vengeance, but justice,” said one of the bereaved fathers earlier in the proceedings. “We want others to know that no more lives should be lost because of preventable mistakes.” As Tony B continued his testimony, he described how his son had already begun planning for the future – academically gifted and with a passion for the arts – aspirations that would never be fulfilled. The court was told how the trauma caused lasting psychological damage to the family, leaving them with memories of a child's potential cut short.

On 25 April 2016, the British retail name BHS — a brand that for decades had been a staple of high streets across the UK — went into administration, casting a shadow over its future and threatening thousands of jobs. The sudden collapse of the 139-year-old company sent shockwaves through the retail sector and left staff, customers, and the wider public struggling to comprehend what had gone so drastically wrong. At a press conference that day, Stephen Kiley, the retailer's chief executive, confirmed the news as administrators appointed by PwC took control of the business. “We are in talks with interested parties,” Kiley said, but hinted that even if a buyer were found, as many as 11,000 of BHS’s 13,000 staff would face redundancy. The grim statement was the final chapter in a company that had been beset by years of mismanagement, declining sales and unsustainable debt. BHS was once synonymous with quintessential British shopping — in part due to its long connection with the late, beloved comedian Jimmy Savile, who had once been the largest shareholder in the company. However, Savile’s death in 2011 did not spell the end for BHS. Instead, it led to a chain of disastrous decisions, including the purchase of the brand by Sir Philip Green’s retail empire Arcadia in the 1980s. Over the years, despite its deep-rooted brand loyalty and iconic high street stores, BHS became a financial black hole, losing hundreds of millions of pounds in an attempt to keep pace with modern consumer trends and digital competition. The collapse came with a particular sting for loyal employees, many of whom had worked at BHS for decades. The company’s accrued pension deficit, estimated at up to £571 million, also raised serious concerns about vulnerable retirees and what would happen to their pensions. Industry experts and politicians alike have called for urgent action to protect the workers, highlighting the risks of insolvency laws that do not adequately safeguard employee rights and retirement savings. As the dust continues to settle, the fall of BHS marks not just the passing of a retail giant, but a stark warning about the fragility of once-dominant UK brands in the face of financial mismanagement and rapid commercial change. What remains of BHS and who will ultimately step forward to go the £1 billion price tag that some had suggested was necessary for a buyer to secure the business, will be the focus of intense interest in the weeks and months ahead.

A prominent Muslim cleric is currently under investigation in connection with the murder of Qandeel Baloch, one of Pakistan’s most popular and controversial social media personalities, police have confirmed. The 26-year-old influencer, known for her bold views and provocative lifestyle, was found dead in a house in Punjab province on 14 July after being bound and suffocated by her brother, Syed Umar Farooq. Though Farooq has been arrested and is currently in custody, new allegations have emerged implicating Syed Sadique, a well-known religious leader and preacher, in the case. Qandeel Baloch had gained notoriety for posting risqué photos and videos online and for commenting fearlessly on issues such as women’s rights and poverty. Her unapologetic defiance of cultural norms made her a polarising figure, drawing both massive followings and fierce condemnation. Her murder has sparked outrage across Pakistan and ignited a national debate about gender-based violence, the role of religious influence in society, and the lack of protection for women’s rights. Punjab police, who announced the development in a statement, claimed that Sadique—whose name has long been associated with conservative Islamic groups—had written messages in support of the killings to her brother and others in the days prior to the murder. These communications, it is alleged, encouraged the decision to eliminate Baloch for “dishonoring” their family and contradicting Islamic values. Sadique is expected to be summoned for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry. Sadique, a senior member of the Jamaat-e-Islami party, has denied the allegations. However, his arrest is being actively pursued by the authorities, prompting calls from human rights activists for the case to be treated as a hate crime. Critics argue that the involvement of a public figure highlights the disturbing intersection between religious authority, patriarchal norms, and gender-based violence. Sana Safinaz, an Islamabad-based activist who campaigned for Baloch, called the new revelations “both shocking and chilling.” Safinaz said: “It demonstrates how deeply rooted the idea of a woman’s ‘honour’ can be used to justify murder—and how little consequence there is for the powerful when they participate in such crimes.” The case has also drawn international condemnation, with the UN women’s agency releasing a statement urging Pakistan’s government to take urgent action to protect the rights of women. As details emerge linking religious leaders to the crime, the nation grapples with the difficult questions that Qandeel Baloch’s death has brought to the forefront.

A Thai court has issued an arrest warrant for a senior Thai army officer who is accused of playing a central role in the trafficking of Rohingya migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh, legal documents obtained by press agencies reveal. The officer, whose name has not been disclosed publicly, is alleged to have co-ordinated with smuggling networks operating across the Andaman Sea, facilitating the illegal transportation of thousands of Rohingya refugees to Thailand and on to countries like Malaysia in exchange for money. The warrant, filed under Thailand’s trafficking in persons act, details charges of complicity in human trafficking, smuggling, and colluding with international gangs. The revelation has sparked outrage among human rights groups and political commentators, who have long accused parts of Thailand’s military establishment of profiting from the crisis involving stateless Rohingya fleeing persecution in Myanma. The officer is reportedly among several high-ranking personnel investigated by the independent National Reform Committee, a special anti-corruption body established by former Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. This marks the first time a senior member of Thailand’s military — a group historically insulated from criminal prosecution — has been directly targeted in relation to the migrant trade. The Rohingya, predominantly Muslim minorities in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, have faced decades of discrimination and violence, particularly since a 2017 campaign by the Myanmar military that led to a UN investigation into potential genocide. Thailand, a key transit point between Myanmar and Malaysia – another destination for trafficked Rohingya, has found itself under international pressure for its ambiguous role in the crisis. While the Thai government publicly condemned the trafficking trade and pledged to bring traffickers to justice, critics claim that state inaction and tacit collusion have allowed the networks to persist. In a statement, the Thai Ministry of Justice declined to comment on the specifics of the case but said it “remains committed to enforcing the law and ensuring that justice is served for all victims of human trafficking.” However, prominent political analyst Chaiwat Satha-Anand told the BBC that the arrest warrant is a “significant step forward, but also proof that the rot runs deep within certain military circles.” He added that the officer could be a scapegoat for a broader system wherein military officials have allegedly been complicit in trafficking for years. As the case moves forward, it is seen as a pivotal moment in Thailand’s handling of the Rohingya issue and could potentially set a precedent for holding powerful figures accountable.

The Spirit of Scotland is set to fill a vibrant stage this weekend as a unique and whimsical tribute to all things Scottish takes to the floor in aid of children across the Commonwealth. Combining tartan, pipes, self-deprecating humour and an abundance of cultural nods, this event is not just a celebration of Scottish heritage but a fundraising extravaganza that has already triumphed in both heart and cash. From the cutesy Scotty dogs making appearances to dancing teacakes and even a bold, on-stage gay kiss, the production is pulling no punches in its irreverent charm. The show promises to take audiences through the history of Scotland in song, mixing traditional tunes with modern flair and a sharp sense of national pride spiced with a little tongue-in-cheek comedy. With tartan scarves flying and bagpipes primed, the atmosphere is expected to be raucous, joyous and, above all, deeply inclusive. The event is the brainchild of a dedicated group of volunteers and community members who have worked tirelessly in recent months to not only create an entertaining production, but to gather support for a very worthy cause. Their appeal, which was launched with a cheeky video of dancers in kilted teacups and a heartwarming message from the UK's leading children's charity, has exceeded expectations—and not just in funds. The emotional outpouring of support from the public has demonstrated a rare and inspiring level of community spirit, something the show's organisers say is as vital as the money raised. Among the acts stepping into the spotlight are local performers proud to share their talents in an event that celebrates Scotland’s past while embracing the future. One of the production’s standout moments—referred to in the programme as “A Gay Kiss: A Noble Tradition?”—has already sparked headlines, showcasing the event’s progressive spirit and commitment to inclusivity. Another highlight is a standing tribute to Scotland’s often-mocked but deeply cherished national dishes and traditions, all delivered with side-splitting glee and a generous helping of self-mockery. Earlier this year, the organisers launched a social media campaign where event goers could share their own beloved, quirky or downright mad interpretations of all things Scottish. From handmade Scotty dog cakes to photos of people with lunches of deep-fried Mars bars, the campaign has gone viral, capturing the imagination of a nation and helping to raise thousands of pounds for children’s charities in Canada, Australia and beyond.

The justice committee wants to ensure the new funding model fosters equality rather than entrenching existing imbalances. In its report, the committee highlighted concerns that the current funding system is "unsustainable and unfair," disproportionately benefiting wealthier areas and neglecting those with higher crime rates or more vulnerable populations. It recommended the establishment of an independent panel consisting of policing and financial experts to develop a formula that better reflects local needs. The report criticized the Home Office’s current approach, describing it as “out of step” with the realities facing local communities. It cited data showing that the three most populous and deprived areas account for just 16% of total police precept funding, compared to more affluent regions. The committee warned that such shortfalls could undermine community trust and make it harder for police to tackle crime effectively in high-risk areas. Shadow home secretary Nick Thomas-Symonds welcomed the findings, stating that the government "must take immediate action to address the urgent crisis in police funding." He called on ministers to heed the committee’s recommendations and “put in place a system that ensures the police have the resources they need to protect the public.” Home Office minister Kit Malthouse was among those questioned during the committee’s inquiry. In his written responses, Malthouse emphasized the government's commitment to fair funding for policing but signaled that a final decision would not be made until the summer. “We are aware of the challenges facing local funding models, and we take our responsibility to support police forces seriously,” he said. The Independent Police and Crime Fund was established in 2012 to allocate funding for police services. However, in recent years, the formula has sparked controversy, with many forces advocating for a more needs-based approach. The committee echoed calls from the Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC), which has long argued about the misalignment between policing funding and the level of need in different regions. The document also urged the Home Office to publish an updated agreement with the devolved administrations to streamline the funding process. Given that the formula must also comply with European Union state aid rules, the report acknowledged the complexity of the initiative but emphasized the need for transparency and accountability. The committee’s report comes at a time of heightened scrutiny over public safety. Recent increases in violent crime, particularly in urban centers, have intensified demands for better-resourced and more accessible policing services.

Barcelona find themselves on the brink of a Champions League exit after a devastating 4-1 defeat at Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday, and manager Luis Enrique has stepped up to take full responsibility for the humiliating result. With the first leg of their last-16 tie having already seen Barcelona undone 4-0 at the Nou Camp, the return meeting at the Parc des Princes handed PSG the perfect springboard as their 4-1 aggregate triumph all but seals their place in the next round. The Catalan giants, once regarded as near-invincible in European competitions, appeared to.Fatalfanstic chase when Lionel Messi and Luis Suárez saw clear chances go begging. The defeat also marks a personal low for Enrique, who only days before stressed the importance of the visit to Paris as a chance to prove Barcelona’s resilience. Instead, the club now faces the grim reality of a potential early Champions League departure for the first time in a decade. Enrique, characteristically, refused to point fingers at his players, acknowledging his own leadership and tactical decisions as the primary source of the club’s woes. Speaking to reporters post-match, he said, "This one is on me. We need to take responsibility for not getting the necessary result. I’ve made mistakes and I’ll analyse everything as we gear up for the next phase." The defeat adds to growing frustration among fans, who – despite recent successes in La Liga – have grown wary of Barcelona’s vulnerability on the European stage. Philippe Coutinho and Paulinho were substituted after the game, sparking whispers that the Brazilian pair may also share the blame for an otherwise lethargic performance. However, Enrique dismissed such speculation, stating: "We are all at fault. As the manager, it is my job to lift the team in moments like these and I did not do that. I will work hard to ensure the players feel secure and motivated for what lies ahead." PSG, meanwhile, exuded confidence and composure after sending a clear message to Europe, with their multi-billion-pound squad showing no hesitation in dismantling Barcelona’s famed tiki-taka. Unai Emery, whose side have relished European nights under his tutelage, commented on the eve of the game: "We are simply here to take our chance. Barcelona are one of the greatest clubs in the world, but they are not unbeatable." With the tie now firmly in the Parisians’ hands, attention turns to whether Barcelona can salvage some pride in the coming weeks, or if this signals a deeper structural problem within the club as it tries to maintain its historical dominance in Europe.

Ryan Day believes a strong showing at the World Snooker Championship could prove to be a decisive turning point in his career after re-establishing himself within the world's top 16 players. The 36-year-old Englishman, who is competing at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield for what would be his sixth world title attempt, is eager to use the opportunity to cement his place among snooker’s elite. Day had been on the cusp of the top 16 for several seasons, but it was only after a consistent run in the 2023/24 season that he secured his place, thanks to performances at the Masters and UK Championship. His return to the world’s top flight has been hailed as a personal triumph, with the Welsh-born player expressing a newfound confidence as he heads into the sport’s most prestigious event. Speaking ahead of the tournament, Day stated: “Reaching the top 16 is a massive achievement and something I’ve worked hard for over the past few years. A good run in Sheffield would be a big plus not just for my tournament record, but for my overall standing in the game.” Day, who has been a regular at the Championship since 2005, is no stranger to the Crucible’s pressure and grandeur. However, he has yet to win it – something both supporters and pundits insist is only a matter of time. “This tournament means everything, it really does,” he added. “I’m in the best form of my life, and I believe this might be my best chance to go all the way.” The World Championship is also expected to test the tournament debut of rising star Joshua Filler, with Day acknowledging the challenge such fresh talent brings to the table. “Everyone is capable of upsetting the order here, and I respect every player I walk past in the arena,” he said. With the reigning champion Mark Selby already knocked out in the first round by Filler, the draw has opened the door to a wide array of possible opponents. Day, who will face former winner Ding Junhui in the first round, is holding high hopes as he bids to transform his world ranking into a world title. His ability to navigate the Crucible’s notoriously high pressure and emotionally charged atmosphere will be a key factor in his bid to do the unthinkable. Whether he can deliver the goods this year remains to be seen, but for Ryan Day, the dream is more alive than ever.

In a rapidly evolving media landscape where traditional news outlets face increasing competition from digital platforms, one question has sparked intense debate among journalists, scholars, and influencers alike: what is the most important source of news, and by extension, the most powerful media organisation in the world today? The answer may not lie in a well-known news network or a historic printing press, but rather in the algorithms that govern the platforms where billions consume information every day. Social media giants like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube have become the primary conduits through which many people access news, making these companies arguably the most influential in shaping public discourse. According to a 2023 Reuters Institute study, three-quarters of internet users in the UK consult social media for at least some of their news, highlighting the shift in news consumption patterns. Yet, this new dynamic raises concerns about the lack of editorial oversight, the spread of misinformation, and the amplification of divisive content. Unlike traditional media organisations, which are bound by journalistic ethics and editorial standards, social media platforms rely on algorithms optimised for engagement, not accuracy. Stories that provoke outrage or fear tend to gain visibility, leading to the distortion of public perception and the entrenchment of political polarisation. Facebook, in particular, has been scrutinised for its role in real-time events such as the 2016 US presidential election and the January 6 Capitol riot, where false or misleading posts accelerated radicalisation and distrust in institutions. Critics argue that the platform's lack of transparency and accountability makes it uniquely powerful and dangerous. Meanwhile, traditional media organisations — despite their foundational role in democratic societies — are grappling with declining audiences and financial instability. Investigative journalism is under threat, with many prominent newsrooms shrinking or closing as advertising and subscription money dwindles. While newspapers such as The New York Times and The Guardian maintain global newsrooms and rigorous investigative units, the fact remains that for most people today, news arrives not from journalists but from feeds populated by user-generated content, automated algorithms, and the shifting priorities of corporate executives. The rise of “influencers” as news sources further complicates the picture. Figures with millions of followers often reach their audiences before traditional news outlets can break a story. As such, the line between journalism and entertainment blurs, with authenticity and trust becoming increasingly harder to verify. Some observers believe the answer to this question lies not with a single organisation, but with the ecosystem that now informs public life.

Glen Campbell — the golden-voiced country music icon whose career spanned six decades and who was as famous for his string of hits as for his heartwarming performances on television — leaves behind a legacy that defined a generation of country music. Known as “The Wisconsin Wildcat,” Campbell’s smooth baritone and cheerful persona brought him international stardom, and his songs became the soundtrack to countless lives across America and beyond. Born on April 22, 1936, in a small farmhouse in Winder, Georgia, Glen Roy Campbell began his music career in the early 1960s, but it was his 1967 breakout hit  Gentle on My Mind  that truly announced his arrival as a major musical force. The song, which won numerous awards and solidified his reputation as a storyteller, was the first of many classics that would define his career. Over the next decade, Campbell would record an array of chart-topping hits that included  By the Time I Get to Phoenix ,  Rhinestone Cowboy , and  Wichita Lineman , the latter becoming one of the most enduring songs of the 20th century. Campbell was not only a solo success but also one of the most visible figures in country music as the host of  The Glen Campbell Good Time Hour , a groundbreaking TV variety show that aired for three years in the late 1960s. His charm and musical talent captivated audiences, and the show helped to introduce country music to a broader, more mainstream American public. Many aspiring country artists got their big break on the show, including Dolly Parton and Emmylou Harris. Beyond his music and television work, Campbell was a devoted family man, known for his decades-long marriage to singer and actress about whom I am not allowed to disclose specific information without the necessary factual input. Together they raised four children and often performed duets that were as heartfelt as they were unpretentious. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Campbell continued to churn out successful records and television appearances, but as he grew older, personal health issues began to overshadow his professional endeavours. Diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2011, Campbell continued to perform with the help of his family, taking part in the deeply emotional and critically acclaimed documentary  I’ll Be Me . The film provided an unfiltered look at the final chapter of his active life, as he struggled with the disease while still giving his all on stage. Glen Campbell’s contributions to country music were immeasurable, and his songs remain timeless, echoing in the hearts of fans around the world.

Two cyclists were taken to hospital after suffering injuries in separate crashes during the RideLondon-Surrey 100, an amateur cycling event that draws thousands of participants from across the UK and beyond. The incidents, both of which are currently being investigated by police, occurred at different points along the 100-mile scenic route, which winds through Richmond Park, Esher, and Dorking. The first crash involved a 34-year-old man from Ayr, who was riding in a group of cyclists when he veered into a parked support vehicle near the Marble Arch start point. The man sustained minor injuries when he hit the bonnet of the stationary van but was quickly extracted by event marshals. He was taken to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington for assessment and later discharged. The second incident saw a woman in her late 50s from Birmingham sustain what are believed to be more serious injuries when she fell off her bike near the village of Fetcham. Witnesses reported that the rider appeared to swerve to avoid an inconsiderate overtaking cyclist and lost control, crashing into the grass verge. Emergency services arrived within minutes, and she was airlifted to the Royal Marsden Hospital in Sutton for further treatment. RideLondon organisers, who said the event is one of the largest amateur cycling events in Europe, confirmed that both incidents were being reviewed by their safety team in coordination with Surrey Police and the UK Cycling Safety Authority. There were no reports of the incidents involving staff or other participants, and the event’s overall safety record remains strong, with only 15 injuries reported this year out of an estimated 8,500 participants. A spokesperson for British Cycling said they were aware of the crashes and were in contact with both victims and their families. “While cycling is generally a safe sport, events at this scale inevitably carry some risk,” the spokesperson said. “We are hopeful both riders will make a full recovery.” Organisers have reiterated the importance of adhering to event rules, particularly in relation to overtaking and communication among groups. As part of their ongoing health and safety reviews, further protective measures for such large-scale events could be introduced following this year’s race. The RideLondon event, now in its 13th year, continues to draw praise for both its route and the atmosphere it creates, but today’s incidents have reignited calls for closer monitoring of safety protocols in amateur long-distance cycling events.

New Zealand could soon be home to a new kind of wilderness wonder — swarms of wild kiwi birds roaming the countryside in numbers not seen in generations. According to a bold new government plan unveiled this week, an ambitious goal has been set to increase the national population of wild kiwi to 100,000 within the next 15 years. The proposal marks one of the most sweeping conservation efforts in the country’s history, designed to reverse the alarming decline of one of New Zealand’s most iconic wildlife species. Currently, there are an estimated 68,000 wild kiwi remaining in the wild across the North and South Islands, according to Department of Conservation (DOC) figures. However, the number continues to fall due to threats such as predation by invasive species, land development, and habitat loss. The kiwi, a nocturnal, flightless bird, and a national treasure, is emblematic of New Zealand’s unique biodiversity — yet it is also one of its most vulnerable. The plan, titled  The Kiwi Guardians’ Action Plan 2024–2039 , aims to accelerate conservation efforts by deploying over 1,000 new predator control sites across the country — land where poison baits and humanely designed traps will be set to reduce threats from stoats, rats, and domestic cats. It also includes funding for community-led kiwi protectors, known as “Kiwi Guardians,” who will monitor populations and work with local authorities and landowners to ensure the safety of breeding habitats. “Our kiwi is a symbol of our unique natural heritage, and it is not a symbol we can afford to lose,” said Environment Minister Simon Watts, who announced the initiative at a press conference in Rotorua today. “This is not just about saving birds — it’s about protecting the ecosystems they are part of and reaffirming our commitment as a nation to living in harmony with nature.” New Zealand First Party MP Barbara Kurkjian welcomed the plan, calling for immediate action. “We cannot wait any longer. Parents today want to take their children to see a kiwi in the wild, not just in books or theme parks. This is about giving our children and grandchildren a future where they can grow up with kiwi birds in their backyards.” The government has also pledged to invest £50 million annually by 2027 into the action plan, with a further £20 million to be sourced from private sector partnerships, charities, and international conservation bodies.

A senior Metropolitan Police officer involved in a high-profile operation during which a man was shot dead is set to retire, despite ongoing investigations into the incident, sparking fresh controversy over accountability and transparency within the force. The officer, whose name has not been disclosed due to the nature of the inquiry, was reportedly at the helm of the operation in which a 42-year-old man was killed by police firearms officers. The incident occurred in London last month after a police pursuit linked to a firearms-related crime ended in a confrontation. Details of the circumstances leading to the shooting remain under investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), but the decision to allow the senior officer to retire has drawn sharp criticism from campaigners and some members of the public, who argue that it sends the wrong message. The officer, who has served with the Met for over 30 years, is understood to have submitted their retirement papers in the wake of the incident, with the application approved by senior command. However, details of whether the retirement will be with or without pension remain unclear. It has also not been confirmed whether the officer’s retirement is voluntary or the result of pressure from within the force. The decision has raised questions about the procedures governing the conduct of senior officers during internal investigations. According to Met guidelines, senior officers under investigation are expected to be suspended during the inquiry unless it is determined that their continued service is necessary for operational reasons. However, in this case, the officer appears to be allowed to remain in post long enough to retire, at which point the inquiry could effectively be paused. The family of the deceased man said in a statement that the retirement decision “adds insult to injury” and suggested that the Met was attempting to avoid full accountability. “We want answers and justice for our loved one,” they said. “It seems those responsible are being allowed to escape the consequences of the decisions they made.” This incident echoes previous controversies in the Met, where officers have been allowed to leave the service while investigations into their conduct are still ongoing, often sparking accusations of a culture that fails to learn from fatal police actions. As the IOPC continues its review, all eyes are now on the Met’s leadership to explain how a senior officer could be permitted to retire amid an active inquiry into a fatal shooting.

The decision to include tennis in the Olympic Games has long been a subject of debate, with critics questioning whether a sport dominated by commercial endorsements and ATP and WTA tour priorities truly belongs alongside more traditional Olympic disciplines. However, the recent enthusiasm and participation of tennis’ elite players has done much to dispel such doubts, demonstrating that despite its high-profile and high-earning nature, the sport still very much values its Olympic heritage. The 2024 Paris Games, in particular, have drawn one of the most star-studded rosters of names in Olympic tennis history. World-class players such as Novak Djokovic, Elena Rybakina, and Carlos Alcaraz have all pledged their participation, bringing with them fans from every corner of the globe. These appearances are not mere gestures—they speak to the importance Olympians place on representing their countries on sport’s grandest stage, even when their careers are inextricably tied to an entirely separate governing body and financial ecosystem. “While tennis may be more commercial than some other sports in the Olympics, the Games remain the pinnacle for every athlete, regardless of discipline,” said a senior sports commentator, highlighting that even in an era where players are under constant contractual and sponsorship pressures, the Olympic torch still holds a unique power to draw the best on to the court. Organisers of the 2024 games are also keen to highlight the adaptability of tennis to the Olympic format. The sport was first introduced in the 1896 Athens Olympics, making it one of the longest-running Olympic sports, before being dropped in 1924 and then reinstated in 1988. It has undergone several rule changes since—most recently allowing players to compete in the Olympics and Grand Slam tournaments at the same time—to make it more sympathetic to today’s high-intensity competitive calendar. The presence of such top players is not just a symbolic win for the Olympic movement; it also brings with it a significant boost in viewership, sponsorship interest, and, inevitably, media coverage. With matches often held at the prestigious Roland Garros site, where the French Open is contested, the setting adds further weight to the tournament’s prestige. Despite the occasional crack from critics—often citing disparities in prize money and the lack of Grand Slam points on offer at the Olympics—there is a broad consensus among fans, players, and officials that tennis not only has a rightful place in the Games, but that it continues to thrive and evolve within it.

The all-female Los Angeles trio Haim took an unconventional four-year break between albums — and they had an unusual answer when fans first asked where the time had gone. “Dinosaurs,” they famously joked, referencing their self-declared “jurassic-sized” process of crafting the follow-up to their 2013 debut,  Days Are Gone . But as the band prepares for the release of their eagerly anticipated second album,  Something to Tell You , the dinos have done more than just occupy their time; they reflect the band’s metamorphosis — and their refusal to conform to the pressures of the modern music industry. When  Days Are Gone  dropped in 2013, it was met with rapturous praise, hailed for its dynamic mix of 70s rock, soul and indie pop, and solidified the trio — Este, Danielle, and Alana Haim — as one of the most exciting new acts of the decade. Their breakfast-inspired pop hit “Forever” and psychedelic guitar-heavy single “The Wire” went viral and swiftly established the Haim sisters as both scene setters and critical darlings. But instead of rushing their next move, the band retreated into a creatively protective bubble — one that became a breeding ground for introspection, real growth and, ultimately, their much-loved "dinosaur rhythm," a term they have come to embrace as a metaphor for taking their time, and doing it on their terms. When the band finally emerged in 2017, it was clear the wait had been worth it.  Something to Tell You , produced in part by Rostam Batmanglij of Vampire Weekend fame, features an even hotter mix of fury, flirtation and authenticity. The album matures their sound — slipping into darker, more groove-driven territory, with standout tracks like “Right Now” and “Want You Back” showing a bold evolution in both sound and sisterly synergy. “I think we’re better at filtering what we want to do and not ‘should do,’” explained Danielle Haim in a recent interview. “We have no interest in meeting expectations other than our own.” With a North American tour about to kick off, the sisters are ready to stop being compared to their 2013 selves — and keep the dino metaphor alive. Some might call it delays; fans are learning to call it patience. For the Haim gothic rockers, it was never about speed — it was about making sure the story, the music, and the feelings were all in the right place. And that story, it seems, has only just begun.

Boris Johnson has ramped up his vocal opposition to the European Union, raising once again his long-held concerns about the growing influence of Brussels in the domestic affairs of the UK. In a recent public address, the former Foreign Secretary warned that “a slow and invisible process of legal colonisation” is underway, with EU laws and directives encroaching into every sphere of British life. Johnson, a long-time proponent of Brexit and self-styled “eurosceptic”, argued that the EU's regulatory reach has become so widespread that it now dictates not just trade and industry policy, but even the minutiae of daily life, from the ingredients in food to the rules governing local councils. His remarks rekindled a familiar theme in the debate over Britain’s place in Europe — the sovereignty argument. “We must reclaim our autonomy,” he said, calling for the UK to restore its legislative independence and stop being hemmed in by what he called “unelected technocrats thousands of miles away, making decisions about our lives without our say”. Speaking in his characteristic style, Johnson described the EU as a “colossus whose size and power threatens to engulf the smaller nations of Europe, including our own”. He claimed that successive British governments have surrendered too much control in the name of economic pragmatism, only to find themselves bound by regulations that are often at odds with the values and traditions of the British people. Critics, however, have accused Johnson of exaggeration and of using inflammatory language to deflect from the complexities of international governance. The EU, they argue, is not an occupying force but a political and economic partnership designed to promote peace, prosperity and cooperation among member states. European institutions are also subject to democratic oversight, with UK officials previously having a direct say through voting rights and representation in Brussels. But Johnson is not alone in his concerns. Across the UK, a growing number of politicians and civic leaders have expressed frustration with the EU’s regulatory framework, arguing that it undermines national sovereignty and stifles domestic innovation and flexibility. For Johnson, however, the EU is no longer a partner, but a force of economic and political subjugation. “We can and must do better as an independent nation,” he insisted. “We owe it to our children to restore what is rightfully ours: the right to self-govern.” His comments are expected to fuel fresh debate as Brexit debates continue to ripple across the political landscape.

Junior doctors marched through central London on Saturday in a show of defiance against proposed changes to their contracts in England, marking one of the first large-scale protests in what many expect to be a prolonged and divisive dispute. Clad in their white coats and carrying placards with slogans such as “No Respect” and “We’re on the Front Line,” thousands of medical professionals, supported by students and members of the public, braved the heat to voice their opposition to the government’s proposals. The changes, sparked by a pay cap introduced by Prime Minister Theresa May’s government, have caused significant unrest among the medical community. The proposed new contract includes the introduction of a 11-hour notice period for unsocial hours and a reduction in the number of night shifts that will qualify for an extra payment. Critics argue that these changes will make the profession less attractive and put patient care at risk, especially in hospitals already facing staffing shortages. Dr. Ash Soni, the president of the British Medical Association (BMA), which has spearheaded the opposition, addressed the crowd at the end of the march in Trafalgar Square. He warned that the government was determined to “erode the professionalism and flexibility of junior doctors.” “We are not against short-term changes during emergencies, but this is a real-time attack on our terms and conditions,” Dr. Soni said. He also highlighted concerns that the contract – which would see new doctors pay more and earn less than experienced colleagues for the same hours – would make recruitment and retention even harder at a time when the NHS is struggling with vacancy rates across the board. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt has dismissed the anger as overblown, insisting that the proposed changes are necessary to reduce costs and better reflect existing shift patterns. In a recent interview, Hunt said: “We are not removing unsocial hours payments. We are simply trying to make the system more consistent and sustainable for the future.” But for many junior doctors, that line of reasoning has not translated into public support for the changes. The marchers echoed the sentiment: “We’re working at 2am for the same money as a day shift – it’s not fair,” said one doctor, who wished to remain unnamed. Public reaction to the protests has been largely supportive of the young doctors, with many on social media urging the government to “show some grace”.

Jordan Seiler loathes outdoor advertising, and it seems her growing campaign against intrusive billboards and eye-catching digital screens is striking a nerve with communities across the United States. Known for her anti-adventurous stance, Seiler, a 35-year-old environmental and community activist based in Portland, Oregon, has spent the last two years on a vocal crusade against the encroachment of commercial messaging on public spaces. Her opposition is not a recent one; it stems from years of witnessing what she describes as “the slow erosion of meaningful, shared environments.” Today, her campaign, “Slow Space,” has gathered momentum, with thousands of supporters across the West Coast, as well as growing attention from media and local governments. The initiative calls for a moratorium on new billboard installations and a review of existing ones, particularly those that blight natural landscapes, historic districts, and residential areas. In recent months, Seiler has leveraged an unlikely tool in her mission — social media. Her hashtag #DeleteThisBillboard has gone viral, with users across the country using the platform to share photos of garish or offensive ads that they believe should be removed. From a billboard for a casino near a public school to one for a fast food chain towering over a tree-lined suburban street, the campaign has highlighted the stark contrast between commercial ambition and public sensibility. “It’s not about removing all advertising – it’s about respecting the spaces we share,” Seiler explained in an interview with The Guardian. “I don’t want to live in a world where every wall, every hillslope, and every business feels someone else’s product is more important than the community that surrounds it.” Her outspoken views have not gone without pushback. Criticised by some as being “anti-progressive” or even anti-business, Seiler remains defiant. “I’m not against marketing or the right of businesses to promote themselves responsibly. I’m against the thoughtless desecration of public space and the culture of saturation we’re seeing. That, I’m against.” Seiler’s fight has already led to concrete actions. In Portland, the city council has proposed a pilot programme to reduce the number of new billboard permits issued, citing concerns about light pollution and over-commercialisation of the cityscape. Similar conversations are now taking place in Seattle, Salt Lake City, and even Los Angeles, where concerns around urban aesthetics and environmental impact are increasingly hard to ignore.

Just weeks before the one-year anniversary of the terror attacks that killed 130 people in Paris, the American rock band Eagles of Death Metal took to the stage in the French capital to "resume their gig"—a powerful and emotional gesture three months after the November 13 attacks. The show at the Bataclan Theatre, site of one of the deadliest of the attacks, was part of a symbolic return that had been years in the making. The band had been performing at the Bataclan on November 13 when Islamist militants stormed the venue, killing 89 people..Fatalfanst Didn’t Eat, the band's frontman Jesse Hughes, narrowly escaped with his life. In the aftermath, Eagles of Death Metal found themselves at the heart of an international reaction, with an outpouring of support from fans and fellow musicians—from Taylor Swift and Post Malone to members of the Parisian police force—who raised millions to support the victims and the band’s recovery. On Friday night, Hughes and his band stepped back onto the Bataclan’s stage, not for a new concert, but for a one-off show to support the OneBataclan charity, which aids the victims and their families. After a short pre-recorded video message from President Emmanuel Macron commending the band’s courage, Hughes—wearing a Parisian-themed shirt and humble grin—told the audience: “We’re not here tonight to take money. We’re here to show you that music will always outlive the worst of humanity.” The event, livestreamed for global audiences, featured a stripped-down set of Eagles of Death Metal’s most beloved tracks, including their hit singles “Black Rain” and “I Love You All the Time.” Between songs, Hughes paused to speak directly to the people of Paris and about the pain of the attack. "This place represents the beauty of this city and the tragedy that can strike any of us," he said. "But it also represents resilience, unity and the strength found in music." Security at the event was high, with visible police presence and thorough checks on the minimal audience allowed in the venue. The Bataclan, long closed since the attacks, had undergone extensive renovation and repurposing of its space to host the special event. It was the first time the location had reopened as a functioning concert space. Eagles of Death Metal’s return to the Bataclan has been hailed by many as a defiant act of solidarity and catharsis, not just for the band, but for the people of Paris and the wider Parisian music community.

This summer's transfer window in the Premier League has already seen clubs commit a staggering £500 million to new signings — a figure that, while impressive, remains £335 million short of the total £835 million spent by English top-flight clubs during the same period last season as the 2021-22 campaign began. With four weeks still remaining until the transfer deadline on September 1, the expected frenzy is yet to reach the fever pitch witnessed just a year ago, but top clubs are still poised for major moves. The reduced spending can be attributed to a number of factors, including the ongoing financial uncertainties caused by the conflict in Ukraine, rising inflation, and the delayed return of revenue from live sports betting, which has suffered during the summer break. Additionally, clubs are also being forced to navigate the complex landscape of Financial Fair Play regulations, as well as the push for global wage growth to remain competitive in an increasingly player-driven market. Notably, some of the league's biggest names have been relatively quiet early in the summer. Manchester United and Liverpool have both been linked to multiple high-profile targets, but concrete signings have so far been limited. By contrast, Chelsea — still adapting to owner Boehly's influx of capital — have splurged early, including a reported £100m plus add-ons for Moisés Caicedo, while Manchester City – historically restrained in summer dealings – continue their approach of supplementing their squad with the odd positional upgrade rather than wholesale reconfiguration. The unusually slower pace has already begun to stir debate in football circles. Media analysts have pointed to Premier League TV revenue being spread out over a five-year window rather than a three-year cycle as a key reason for the more measured approach being adopted by most clubs this term. This, they argue, has given teams more time to deploy their finances rather than rushing into major purchases at the first whistle of the transfer window. As it stands, the EPL transfer record is unbroken, but that could be a matter of weeks. With clubs still in high spending mode, and top players at major European clubs aware of their market value, it is believed intense activity is likely to ramp up in the critical final two weeks as managers prepare for the 2023-24 season. At the moment, £500 million represents a reflection of prudence rather than a lack of ambition — and as the weeks unfold, it may well be revised substantially.

Wales captain Sam Warburton has backed his long-time team-mate and legendary forward Gethin Jenkins to take charge in a potential leadership role should the coaching change temporarily shift responsibilities more towards the senior players on the field. With a close contest looming against Argentina in the Rugby World Cup, Warburton, who has been a central figure on and off the pitch for Wales for over a decade, has expressed his confidence in Jenkins’ ability to inspire the squad in a high-pressure environment. Gethin Jenkins, 36, has arguably had a more traditional journey to leadership compared to the athletic and dynamic Warburton, but the veteran hooker has consistently proven to be a calming and authoritative presence on the Welsh team. Known for his relentless work rate and calm execution in the forwards, Jenkins has long been respected as a figure of stability and example, qualities essential for guiding teams in tight matches and under global lights. Warburton, in a recent press conference ahead of the match, said: “Gethin’s experience and leadership in big games are invaluable. He knows what it takes to perform at this level and how to get the best out of the team when it really matters. If we find ourselves in a situation where we need strong leadership from within, Gethin would be someone I’d have total confidence in stepping up.” The comments come against the backdrop of ongoing speculation about the future of Wales’ coaching structure, with some suggesting the interim manager may be looking to test the team’s resilience by potentially rotating key roles or giving more directive input to senior players. Warburton, however, has cast no doubt on the team’s unified spirit, saying that his focus remains on the ambition to finish the campaign with pride and determination. The match against Argentina is considered a make-or-break opportunity for the Welsh team, with both sides searching for motivation and momentum to improve their positions in the group stage. Argentina, known for their fiercely physical style and high-intensity forward play, will pose a stern test. Jenkins, with over 130 caps for Wales and 50 for the British & Irish Lions, is a proven leader in those scenarios. As the world’s rugby eyes turn to Cardiff’s Millenium Stadium, the partnership of players like Warburton and Jenkins will be more than just a collaboration of skill and strength—it may be the key to Wales rekindling the form that has made them one of the most respected teams in the sport.

A leading fertility charity is urging the Scottish government to increase the number of free IVF cycles available to couples struggling with infertility, from two to three, in a significant boost to reproductive healthcare access. The call comes as Scottish ministers prepare to unveil revised funding guidelines for 2024, following years of campaigning by patient groups who argue that two cycles are often insufficient for successful conception. Currently, the National Health Service (NHS) in Scotland offers a maximum of two free IVF treatments per couple under specific criteria, including age limits and diagnosis of infertility. However, charities and fertility experts are now demanding that this limit be raised, arguing that a third cycle could significantly improve the chances of success, particularly for women over 35 and those with complex medical needs. The Campaign for My Fertility, a reproductive rights advocacy group, says the move would bring Scotland in line with recommendations from the British Fertility Society and align the country more closely with England, where access to IVF treatment is governed by local councils and varies significantly across regions. Linda Doyle, chief executive of the Fertility and Reproductive Healthcare Association (FARHA), warned that the current limit "can feel like a cruel deadline for couples who are facing the most emotionally and physically challenging time in their lives". She said many women who use two cycles often face a decline in fertility by the time they exhaust their NHS funding, at which point they must often pay large sums – sometimes thousands of pounds – for further treatment. “It’s not enough to be offered a lifeline and then have it pulled away,” she said in a statement. “For people in Scotland who already face a tough journey, this change could make all the difference.” The charity has received backing from a cross-party group of MPs and MSPs, as well as a number of NHS clinicians, who support the proposal on the grounds of equity and improved outcomes. A recent clinical study showed that for women between 35 and 37, the live birth rate for fertilisation dramatically increased with a third treatment cycle. However, the Scottish government faces a tough balancing act: while acknowledging the emotional and medical importance of IVF, it has pointed to the significant cost implications of expanding treatment. Health Secretary Jeane Freeman has said the topic is under review as part of a wider review of reproductive healthcare funding, but has not committed to changes.

The heartfelt words of Cardinal John Onaiyekan, formerly the Archbishop of Abuja and a respected voice in the Catholic Church, have underscored a deeper tension within the global Catholic community following the election of Pope Francis. A man celebrated by millions as a beacon of humility and progressive change, Pope Francis — the first pope from the Global South and the first Jesuit — has also stirred unease among certain Catholic leaders in Africa and beyond. Cardinal Onaiyekan, one of Africa's most prominent prelates, said in a private interview that while he respected and admired the new pope, his election had arrived in Africa at a time of crisis. "I see a lot of joy and celebration for Pope Francis, but I'm living his election with a lot of pain," he said. "We have enough to deal with in our own churches, and now the world is focused elsewhere." The comment has added nuance to the otherwise widespread optimism about Francis’s papacy. While many have hailed his pastoral style and his calls for simplicity in leadership, his election has also generated anxiety among church leaders who fear it signals a marginalisation of African concerns on the Vatican’s radar. Africa, a continent home to some of the fastest-growing Catholic populations, is grappling with deep challenges: the legacy of colonialism, poverty, political instability, and, in some regions, growing fundamentalist Islam. Local Catholic leaders argue that while the Vatican has shifted its gaze to other regions, Africa continues to fight an internal battle to preserve its voice and mission on the world stage. “Pope Francis, in his infinite wisdom, may have no idea of the difficulties we face here,” Cardinal Onaiyekan said. “But the fear is that his election will further centralise power at the expense of our own struggles.” The cardinal’s words are being closely watched not only by fellow bishops in Africa but by theologians and Catholic observers globally. At a time when the Church is increasingly aware of the need for decentralised leadership to meet diverse regional needs, the response to Francis’s election will resonate for years to come. As the new pope seeks to redefine the tone and mission of the Church, his words on poverty, social justice and the environment have been embraced. Yet as one African cardinal suggests, the joy of a new papacy may come with an undercurrent of pain for those who feel their voice is fading in the chorus of global Catholicism.

The Dartford Crossing, one of the UK's busiest road tunnels and a vital artery for commuters and freight in the Southeast, has been excluded from government assessments of air quality—despite its proximity to residential areas and densely populated commuter towns—because it was classified as a "rural" road, the BBC has revealed. The anomaly has raised concern among local councils, residents and environmental advocates, who argue that the decision undermines air pollution regulations and public health. Data obtained through a Freedom of Information request shows that air quality monitoring at the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge, as it is officially known, was excluded from national pollution assessments by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) due to its classification. This is despite the crossing handling over 90,000 vehicles a day, including numerous heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), whose emissions are known to contribute significantly to localised air pollution in the form of nitrogen dioxide (NO2), a harmful pollutant linked to respiratory illnesses and cardiovascular disease. Residents of Dartford and Gravesham, located near the crossing, have long raised concerns about the area's air quality. Angela Murphy, a local parent and campaigner, told the BBC: “You live in a housing estate a few hundred yards from the crossing and you can still smell the fumes—it’s obvious it’s unhealthy. It’s absurd that it's being treated as rural when it’s surrounded by homes, schools and shops.” Environmental experts have echoed her frustration. Professor Nick Hewitt, from the University of Leeds and a member of the UK's National Air Quality Expert Group, said: “This classification error is a real issue. Air pollution is a local phenomenon—what’s emitted at a road or industrial site doesn’t travel very far. Classifying such key locations as rural and excluding them from national assessments is not just misleading, but potentially dangerous.” Transport for London (TfL), which fails to monitor air quality at the crossing due to Defra's decision, argued that the classification was for the purposes of National Air Quality Strategy reporting only, and that health risks were monitored as part of a separate framework. However, critics argue that accurate data is essential to implement effective measures, such as Clean Air Zones or filters to monitor and reduce emissions. Local MP Gareth Johnson called on the government to re-evaluate the classification: “The air around Dartford Crossing affects the health of thousands.

Tributes have poured in for a grieving family in Caerphilly County following the tragic death of a mother in the horrific terrorist attack in Tunisia. The woman, whose identity has yet to be officially released by British authorities, was among 38 UK citizens who lost their lives in the bombing at the luxury seaside resort of Sousse on June 26, 2015. Confirmed by West Midlands Police as one of the victims, her family now face the devastating task of arranging a return to their home in South Wales as condolences are extended from across the region and beyond. The attack, claimed by the so-called Islamic State (IS), saw a gunman open fire at tourists just before midday, leaving 30 Germans and another eight Britons among the dead, along with local Tunisians. Funerals for the British victims began earlier this week, with the first service held for a woman from the West Midlands. It is now expected that services for the remaining victims, including those from Caerphilly, will follow in the coming days, with the Queen having waived funeral expenses to allow for traditional homecoming ceremonies. Neighbours and friends of the woman spoke of the deep sense of shock and sorrow sweeping through the local community. Steve Davis, a friend and fellow resident, described her as a “kind-hearted, fun-loving mother who lit up the room with her smile,” who was preparing for what he said would be “a dream holiday” with her family. Local politicians and community leaders have also offered their sympathies, with Rhondda Cynon Taf’s MP, Chris Bryant, hailing the Caerphilly family as “a community that gives a lot and deserves so much more.” A local noticeboard and community centre in Margam have been designated as tribute spots, where people are encouraged to place flowers, photographs, and messages in memory of the mother and others lost. As the grieving process continues, family and friends are left to handle the unrelenting grief that comes with such a brutal and senseless act of violence. A multi-faith vigil is expected to be held in her memory, as well as a service of remembrance for all those who perished. As one floral tribute read simply: “You were taken from us too soon.” In the wake of the attack, calls for greater security for British tourists in high-risk travel regions have once again emerged as gove ministers face pressure to reassess risk assessments and policy.

The 2012 Scottish council elections marked a dramatic shift in the political landscape of Scotland, with both the Scottish National Party (SNP) and the Labour Party claiming victories in different parts of the country, while the Liberal Democrats faced a severe collapse in support. The results have deepened uncertainties about the future of the Lib Dems in Scottish politics, and highlighted a divided political environment as the country continues its long-running debate over independence. The SNP, led by Alistair Darling’s successor as First Minister, Alex Salmond, celebrated gains in key areas, particularly in rural and lowland Scotland. The party maintained control of 19 out of 32 council areas, with significant increases in voting share. Labour, meanwhile, retained control of six councils, including its traditional strongholds in central and west Scotland. The left’s performance suggested a cautious realignment of the political centre following the SNP's rising influence. The most striking trend, however, was the Liberal Democrats’ plummeting fortunes. The party lost ground in all but a handful of council areas and, in some places, was reduced to just a handful of councillors. This collapse mirrored similar declines in previous years and has raised serious questions about the party’s future in Scotland. Party leader Sir Menzies Campbell, who only narrowly retained his Westminster seat in 2010, warned of a “political earthquake” in national politics – but it is at the local level where the tremors have been most pronounced. The council elections had initially been seen as a key test of the Lib Dems’ viability after their disastrous general election performance in 2010. But the results have underscored a profound crisis for the party. Many voters in Scotland, who have continued to reject the Lib Dem “third way” approach, appear to be shifting decisively between Labour and the SNP. Analysts suggest that the Lib Dems’ central role in the 2010 Coalition government may be fundamentally alienating left and right voters alike in Scotland. In the run-up to the election, polls had shown steady support for the SNP, with the party gaining momentum as it moved further towards its campaign for an independent Scotland. Labour, on the other hand, struggled to reframe its appeal in rural areas, but sustained strong support in urban seats such as Glasgow and Dundee. The results also brought into focus the growing complexity of Scotland’s political landscape, with the Scottish Greens and various independent candidates making modest gains.

Lewis Hamilton put on a commanding display in the final practice session ahead of qualifying at the British Grand Prix, as F1 drivers made their last-minute preparations for what promises to be a thrilling Saturday at Silverstone. The seven-time world champion topped the timesheet at the end of FP3, lapping the iconic track with precision and speed in a performance that signals his intent as he aims for an eighth British Grand Prix victory.
