Hamilton, representing Mercedes, clocked a lap time under 1 minute and 48 seconds, edging out close rivals Charles Leclerc of Ferrari and Max Verstappen of Red Bull by a fraction of a second. His performance underlined the fierce competition expected in the upcoming qualifying session, with the three drivers locked in a battle for supremacy across the season’s most anticipated races. The final practice session serves as the last opportunity for teams to fine-tune their cars and for drivers to get the feel of the track in near-qualifying conditions. Hamilton looked in control from the outset, mastering the Silverstone layout in his early laps, before setting the benchmark that others struggled to match. His Mercedes team appeared to benefit from improved front grip following recent aerodynamic adjustments, a critical advantage on a track where smoothness and stability are as important as raw power. Behind Hamilton, the battle for second place was closely contested. Leclerc, driving for Ferrari, demonstrated impressive pace on the medium and soft tyres, pushing the limits on his final laps. Verstappen, meanwhile, showcased his aggressive driving style, navigating the iconic Maggotts and Becketts complex with flair. However, both were unable to close the gap to Hamilton, who once again displayed the composure and experience that has defined his Silverstone performances over the years. For Hamilton, this performance marks a crucial step in his preparations as he looks to finally convert his recent qualifying success into a race win at his home Grand Prix. His last victory at Silverstone came in 2020, and with both Ferrari and Red Bull challenging for the lead in the Constructors' Championship, the British Grand Prix represents more than just a personal milestone – it is a key opportunity to shift the momentum in the title race. As the drivers head into qualifying and the sun sets over Silverstone, all eyes will be on Hamilton to see if he can retain his dominant form and set the pace for a dramatic British Grand Prix weekend.

The pride of Japan's naval defence, the JS Izumo, is making an unprecedented journey through Asian waters over the next three months. The state-of-the-art helicopter destroyer is currently en route from Japan, with an ambitious itinerary spanning South and Southeast Asia, reflecting Tokyo's growing aspirations in maritime diplomacy and regional security. The Izumo, the second and larger of Japan’s two Izumo-class helicopter destroyers, represents a significant shift in the nation’s naval strategy. A modified carrier with provisions to accommodate F-35B stealth fighter jets, the Izumo is among the largest non-nuclear warships in the world outside of aircraft carriers. This deployment marks the first extended tour of the Izumo in the broader Asian region, and the vessel will make port calls in countries like India, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines. The journey is not just a demonstration of Japan’s maritime capabilities, but a strategic effort to deepen relations with nations increasingly concerned about the stability of the Indo-Pacific. In recent years, Japan has quietly but resolutely expanded its role as a key security provider in Asia. The country, long governed by a post-war constitution that limited military engagement, has steadily moved to interpret its defence laws more flexibly—particularly in response to growing regional tensions, notably with China and North Korea. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida has spoken publicly of Japan's desire to “play a more active role” in regional security, with a focus on strengthening partnerships and bolstering the freedom of navigation in disputed waters. The Izumo’s upcoming tour is seen as a tangible step in that direction. The port visits will offer an opportunity for face-to-face engagement between Japanese sailors and their hosts, as well as opportunities for joint training and goodwill exchanges. Such initiatives are part of a broader naval diplomacy effort in which Japan is increasingly lending support to regional maritime patrols and disaster relief operations. This deployment also highlights the deepening strategic collaboration between Japan and the United States, as well as partnerships with like-minded countries in the Quad—India, Australia, Japan and the US—a grouping aimed at ensuring a free and open Indo-Pacific. As the Izumo continues westward, it carries with it the hopes of a nation looking to redefine its regional role in an increasingly complex security landscape. The journey is as much about reassurance and cooperation as it is about power projection.

Osborne Launches ‘Northern Powerhouse’ in Final Budget Before Election   In what is likely to be his final major economic statement before next month’s general election, Chancellor George Osborne has unveiled a sweeping plan to transform northern England into a “northern powerhouse” to rival London and the southeast as a driver of economic growth. Addressing MPs on Tuesday in the House of Commons, Osborne outlined a vision to invest in transport infrastructure, digital connectivity, and education to help cities such as Manchester, Liverpool, and Leeds to lead the next phase of the country’s economic resurgence. Speaking with clarity and conviction, the Conservative chancellor called the northern powerhouse the “most ambitious domestic economic project since the Industrial Revolution,” pledged to bringing jobs, investment and opportunities to a region that has long felt like a “poor cousin” to the prosperous south. The announcement forms a central pillar of the Conservative manifesto, with Osborne positioning it as not just a regional initiative but an economic imperative for the entire country. “We need to spread prosperity more evenly across our United Kingdom,” he said. “The north has the people, the potential and the property. Now it needs the policy to match that promise.” The budget outlined a £3 billion package of funding for transport improvements in the North, including the acceleration of the devolution of transport budgets to local leaders and a commitment to upgrading key rail and road services. Osborne also pledged £1 billion for new university funding, with a focus on expanding technical and vocational skills, and announced an overhaul of funding for local authorities to give them greater control over investment priorities. The move has been applauded by many Labour leaders in the north, who see it as long-overdue recognition of the region’s potential—though some critics have questioned whether the funding commitments will be followed through under a future government. Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell welcomed the focus on northern investment but warned that “a handful of pots of gold [are] not a substitute for fundamental economic reform that supports working people up and down the country.” Osborne’s rhetoric on rebalancing the economy has been a steady theme of his tenure, but the budget could be the most tangible step towards achieving that vision. With the Conservatives trailing in some regional polls, the so-called northern powerhouse could also be a strategic effort to rally support in key marginal seats ahead of the election.

Britain will avoid a bleak winter of power cuts as energy experts assure the public that the country’s gas and electricity supplies are sufficient to meet demand, even in cold weather conditions. The National Grid, which operates the UK’s electricity system, has confirmed that it has “firm visibility” over the supply chains necessary to sustain energy levels throughout the winter season. This news has come as a relief to households and businesses across the country, many of whom have been anxious about potential energy shortages following the global inflation of energy prices and ongoing geopolitical tensions. In a recent statement, National Grid ESO (Electricity System Operator) said that during the coldest days of winter – when heating needs spike – enough electricity and gas will be available to keep homes and businesses powered without resorting to managed power cuts. “We are confident that electricity supplies will not run short this winter,” said Chris Smith, the chief executive of the ESO. “The system is prepared and in a far better position than it has been in previous years.” The reassurance comes after a summer in which high gas prices, the lingering effects of the pandemic on supply chains, and a tough energy policy landscape raised fears of a repeat of the 2021 winter, when occasional supply shortfalls led to emergency intervention by the government. One of the main factors contributing to this year’s confidence is the rhythm of domestic generation. Renewable energy production, particularly from wind farms, has been performing strongly, making the UK less reliant on imported gas and oil. In addition, energy storage capacity has improved, allowing surplus electricity to be banked for use during peak demand. The government has also introduced new strategies to diversify the energy mix, including support for nuclear power and hydrogen-based heating technology. Industry experts have noted that while energy bills remain high for many consumers, there is at least about tangible effort to shore up the energy infrastructure to ensure the severity of this winter is not as grim as some had feared. However, officials caution that while blackouts are unlikely, the system remains under significant strain. Unusually prolonged cold snaps or unexpected failures at energy plants could still strain the grid. As a result, the National Grid is urging households to continue efforts to reduce energy use, such as by using electric heating efficiently and being mindful of water usage. Overall, the message is one of cautious optimism.

Tributes have poured in from the Northern Ireland sporting community and beyond to honor the legacy of the iconic boxing legend Muhammad Ali, who passed away on Saturday at the age of 74. Renowned across the globe for his charismatic personality, unparalleled skill inside the ring, and unwavering stance on civil rights, Ali has left an indelible mark on sports and society alike. From Belfast to Derry and every corner of Northern Ireland, sports figures, communities, and fans have taken to social media, television, and public statements to express their grief and admiration. Ali, the three-time world heavyweight champion, was not only a fighter but a global ambassador for peace, justice, and Muslim values. His conversion to Islam and refusal to fight in the Vietnam War made him one of the most controversial yet respected figures of the 20th century, and his principled stance on issues of race and war has continued to inspire generations. In Northern Ireland, where sport often bridges divides, Ali was widely admired for his ability to unite people in his pursuit of social change. Football stars, rugby players, and local coaches have all shared memories of how Ali’s influence extended far beyond the ring—personifying what it meant to be courageous in the face of adversity. Former Irish and British boxing champion Carl Frampton took to Twitter to express how Ali inspired him both as a fighter and a man of principle. “Muhammad Ali was, and will always be, a huge role model of mine. What he did in and out of the ring changed the world,” he wrote. The principles championed by Ali—human dignity, equality, and peace—found echoes in the struggle for civil rights in the United States and resonated deeply with communities in Northern Ireland as they navigated their own complicated social landscape. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak joined global leaders in paying tribute, describing Ali as “a global icon whose legacy will be felt for generations.” In Belfast, statues and memorials have begun to appear, both to pay respect to the champion and to mark the importance of his message. Sports halls, schools, and community centers are preparing special tributes, including charity events and exhibitions, to celebrate the life of a man who redefined boxing and became a symbol of moral courage. As the sporting world collectively mourns the loss of such an extraordinary figure, Muhammad Ali’s legacy—his voice, his values, and his victories—continues to resonate far from the stage of global stadiums.

St Helens bounced back from the disappointment of an early Challenge Cup exit with a hard-fought victory over Salford at the Halton Stadium on Saturday, cruising to a hard-earned 28-22 triumph despite a spirited second-half rally from their hosts. The win marked a strong return to form for the two-time Super League champions, who had suffered a surprise defeat by Castleford Tigers just days earlier in the capital eliminator round. From the outset, St Helens looked every bit the top-tier side, attacking with precision and pulling clear to a 20-point lead at the break. The visitors, led by captain Tommy Makinson, showed signs of confidence restored, with Makinson scoring a double and displaying the physicality that has made him a key figure since his return to the red half of Merseyside. Tenacity, line breaks, and a disciplined kicking game saw them in total control for much of the first 40 minutes. However, Salford Bucks mounted a dramatic turnaround in the second stanza, thanks in no small part to Niall Evalds’ incredible finishing. The 23-year-old winger, who has been in fine form this season, became only the second player in the club’s history to score a hat-trick in a single match, taking his tally to 33 tries this campaign. His efforts brought the Red Devils – twice as many as their visitors, and with it, a sliver of hope that they might pull off a famous home victory. Despite the late pressure, St Helens held firm, and the lead was just too big to overcome. A try from substitute Jack Walker effectively killed off the game, wrapping up a win that will have gone a long way in restoring their title credentials as the Super League season enters its business end. Speaking after the game, Saints head coach Ian Watson praised the resolve of his side. “It was always going to be tough coming to Salford and it is a tough place to come. But we showed real character and composure when it mattered. I was really pleased with how we handled the pressure in the second half.” For Salford, there will be little to take heart from the result, as they remain mathematically out of the play-offs but will keep the chase alive based on hopes of others dropping points. Still, Evalds’ latest three-try haul underlines his go-to status on the wing, and his outstanding performance will give the Salford coaching staff cause for optimism.

A newly-ordained Catholic bishop is said to be under detention after publicly declaring his resignation from the Chinese government's state-sanctioned Catholic Church, in what appears to be the latest flashpoint between religious autonomy and state control in China's complex religious landscape. Bishop Chai Renwen, who was ordained in August 2022 in the southern province of Guangdong, reportedly announced his decision to step down from the Chinese Patriotic Catholic Association (CPCA) in a bold move that has sparked international concern. The CPCA, a government-backed organisation that oversees China’s Catholic Church, has long been at odds with the Vatican, which regards the association as a tool of state control rather than a legitimate religious body. Bishop Chai’s resignation comes amid heightened tensions in the already delicate Sino-Vatican dialogue, which has left many parishioners and international observers watching the situation closely. Although the Chinese government has not officially commented on Bishop Chai’s reported detention, local media outlets have described the circumstances of his disappearance as “reliability checks,” a euphemism often used for arbitrary detentions or political interrogations. Human rights organisations and pro-democracy groups have raised alarms, citing a pattern of repression against religious leaders who challenge the status quo. In a rare public statement, the Vatican expressed grave concern over Bishop Chai’s situation, stating it would continue to “reject any interference in the freedom of religion.” The Vatican, which has been seeking greater autonomy for Chinese Catholics, has previously faced criticism for acceding to some government demands in the interest of dialogue with Beijing. However, the detention of someone at Bishop Chai’s relatively low rank appears to contradict recent efforts to establish a modicum of normalcy in the relationship. Bishop Chai’s case is believed to have repercussions far beyond his individual plight. It raises questions about the extent to which religious leaders can operate independently of the Chinese state and whether a resolution between Beijing and the Vatican remains possible. Many loyalist clergy, unregistered parishes and secret Catholic worshippers across the country have long feared for their safety if they venture into areas of open defiance or minimal conformity with the CPCA. The development has also drawn attention from the UK's pro-chaos opposition as well as cross-border academicians, who have recently predicted a new phase of "stability-focused religious reforms". Whether these changes will result in greater tolerance or continued crackdowns remains to be seen.

Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes secured a stunning victory at the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday, dramatically overturning the odds to snatch the win from Ferrari’s defending champion Sebastian Vettel in a race filled with strategy, pressure, and textbook execution. The result marked another major twist in the 2024 Formula One season, with Hamilton moving up in the championship standings and continuing his impressive form since returning to Mercedes. Starting the race from fourth on the grid after a slightly cautious qualifying session, Hamilton’s skill and the Mercedes team’s strategic brilliance pulled off what many had not expected to be a realistic scenario. Vettel, who had arrived in Barcelona as the pre-race favorite, led the field early on, showing the continued sharpness of both the Ferrari machine and his own driving. However, the tide turned during the first set of pit stops. Mercedes’ decision to go for ultra-low-profile tyres on Hamilton, and the timing of the stop itself—leading to a split-second gain—proved crucial. As Hamilton re-joined the track behind Vettel, the gap slowly began to shrink. With 25 laps to go, the Mercedes driver made a daring overtake that electrified the crowd, using a perfectly judged slipstream to weave past Vettel with minimum drama. The victory was not only a redemption for Hamilton, but also a statement for the Mercedes team, who have faced criticism in recent races for inconsistent performance. Speaking after the race, Hamilton, visibly elated, said: “It wasn’t easy out there, but the whole team was incredible. When we hit the track, we believed in ourselves and that made all the difference.” Vettel, who had a mix of frustration and admiration on his face in the post-race interviews, admitted that the race “got away from us” when key moments in the middle stages did not fall his way. He added: “Lewis drove well, and Mercedes made the better calls. We’ll need to be better in Monaco.” The win is a reminder of both Hamilton’s enduring brilliance and Mercedes’ resilience. With Hamilton now level on points with Vettel and Max Verstappen of Red Bull, the battle for the title is hotter than ever. The performance in Barcelona has sent shockwaves through the Formula One paddock, and fans are already speculating how the next few races will play out in what promises to be a riveting season.

A worrying trend for Scottish football has emerged, as a BBC investigation has revealed that attendance figures across the country's top four leagues have plummeted or stagnated compared to the previous season. Despite hopes that football could return to a sense of normalcy following the easing of pandemic restrictions, the data tells a different story, with the biggest worry being that nearly 75% of clubs have either seen a decrease in gate receipts or are on par with the previous year. The findings, which aggregate league-by-league attendance figures, highlight financial strains on both clubs and supporters as inflation and cost-of-living pressures take their toll. The bottom-tier Highland and Lowland Leagues saw the most drastic drop in crowds, with some clubs reporting attendances half of what they were a year ago. But the issue is not confined to lower levels of the game. Even in Scotland’s Professional Football League (SPL), which includes the Premier Sports Championship and League One, clubs are struggling to entice fans back through the turnstiles at pre-pandemic levels. The situation at the top, the Scottish Premiership, fared slightly better due to the ongoing appeal of high-profile matches and clubs such as Celtic and Rangers—whose games regularly draw bumper crowds. But even some mid-table clubs in the Premiership are struggling to boost attendances, with smaller local grounds experiencing the hardest hit. The decline raises concerns about the financial sustainability of many clubs, with some relying heavily on commercial revenue to plug the gaps created by dwindling matchday income. “It’s a sector feeling the pinch,” said Liam Bell, BBC Scotland’s sports business correspondent. “With Premier League TV deals not filtering down to the lower leagues and local football clubs operating with tighter margins, this drop in crowds can have a domino effect.” Fan feedback has suggested that the cost-of-living crisis is a primary barrier to return. Many supporters cite the cumulative cost of travel, food and drinks as prohibitive, even for clubs with lower ticket prices. The problem is compounded in smaller communities where matchday culture is baked into local identity. Club chairman discussions have hinted at potential fixes, including the introduction of season tickets, discounted memberships and community initiatives to reconnect with long-time supporters. Others are calling for more support from national bodies to help clubs weather the storm. As the 2023/24 season unfolds, the road back for Scottish football may depend on a combination of affordability, innovation and a renewed appreciation for the game's social and cultural importance in Scotland’s towns and cities.

In a stunning twist of FA Cup fortunes, Fleetwood Town produced a remarkable late onslaught to clinch a 3-2 victory over minnows Southport in extra time, snatching victory from the jaws of an unlikely giant-killing. The seaside side had seemed set to etch their name into the history books after two stunning goals sent shockwaves through the crowd and briefly derailed the League One side. Southport, who finished 23 places below Fleetwood in last season’s league tables, had defied the odds throughout the tie, controlling spells of play and grinding down the higher league side. The non-league outfit, with a modest budget and a part-time squad, had climbed to within a goal of sending the tie into penalties after Lewis Nixon and Dan Fitchett carved through Fleetwood’s defense to left themselves on the brink of a truly memorable FA Cup giant-killing. But within the opening eight minutes of extra time, Fleetwood flipped the script with relentless efficiency, scoring three goals in a breathtaking sequence that ended Southport’s hopes. First, the home side’s equaliser came through James Norris, who curled a sublime finish into the top corner. Just four minutes later, Championship-bound striker Sam Morsy doubled the tally with a powerful header from a set-piece, before James Jones completed the treble with a composed finish to seal the win. The dramatic turn of events stunned the League One side's supporters and left Southport’s manager, Darrell Clarke, left ruing a missed opportunity after their valiant run. Speaking in the post-match interview, Clarke said: “We gave everything and for 115 minutes, we believed we could do it. They outscored us at a crucial moment and you can’t fault their execution – but I’m proud of how my players stood up to the challenge.” Fleetwood head coach Steven Pressley, who had spoken before the game of the pressure of expectation that comes with representing the higher divisions, praised his side's composure. “You always put the treble-word games out of your head, but when you’re behind in extra time you have to find something. We did that, and I’m delighted for the lads to come through and end on a high.” The match highlighted the volatility of the FA Cup, where giants have fallen and underdogs have triumphed, but for Southport, it was their moment that slipped away in the final burst of drama.

Claire Sugden is one of Northern Ireland's most energetic and combative politicians, but for the best part of two years, the justice minister and former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader found herself sitting in the opposition benches of the Assembly — literally and politically — in the so-called "naughty corner". Now, as the Assembly breaks for the assembly election campaign, the DUP has shifted from opposition to government, with Sugden making a triumphant return to the executive. The seat that Sugden has taken is not only a symbolic one, reserved for unionist ministers, but also a role steeped in political influence, as the new justice minister in a tense but resumed devolved administration. Her return marks a notable shift for the DUP, which had been in opposition since the collapse of the Stormont executive in January 2017 over the issue of the Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scandal. Sugden, who was forced to resign as first minister when it was uncovered that she had been incorrectly using a parliamentary expense account at the time, was swiftly cast as a central figure in the scandal and effectively erased from the political stage by her own party for over 23 months. However, the DUP's decision to allow her back to power has stirred controversy and raised questions as to whether past transgressions can truly be brushed aside in the pursuit of political stability. Despite this, Sugden has long maintained that her actions were not dishonest, but the result of an administrative oversight that exposed serious flaws in the system rather than any personal wrongdoing. She made a strong case in her statement at the time of her retirement from the executive, saying that the focus should not be on what she had done, but on the wider need for parliamentary reform. That message has not gone unnoticed, particularly by a party about to enter what is expected to be a highly competitive election campaign. Sugden’s return as justice minister signals not only her personal rehabilitation but also the DUP's desire to press on without lingering over past disagreements. Her energy and sharp political instincts will likely make her a key figure in the unionist campaign. As she reclaims her place in government, the world will be waiting to see whether this is a new chapter in Northern Ireland’s political landscape — or simply the first act of a long and complex drama yet to be played out.

Motherwell have completed their fourth summer signing with the arrival of experienced goalkeeper Trevor Carson, as part of a busy transfer window aimed at reviving the club’s fortunes under manager Mark McGhee. Tributes have been paid across London and Dublin this week to mark the centenary of the death of Thomas Kettle, the East Tyrone MP and Irish nationalist who fell on the Somme battlefields in September 1916. Exactly 100 years since the young politician and poet lost his life in one of the bloodiest battles of World War I, solemn commemorations and public events have sought to reflect on his legacy — a man who straddled the complex tides of Irish nationalism, British patriotism, and the brutal reality of war. Kettle, a former barrister and Fabian socialist, was elected as a Sinn Féin MP in East Tyrone in 1910, representing the nationalist interest in the British Parliament during the final years of the Liberal government under H.H. Asquith. By 1914, as the threat of war loomed in Europe, Kettle had transformed from a pacifist to a fervent British patriot, convinced that Britain’s Anglo-Irish war in Ireland and the broader imperial connection were inextricably linked to Ireland's future. As he declared, “I am determined to do my share towards the rebuilding of a world in which Ireland may legislate for herself amongst free equals.” That conviction led him to enlist in the Royal Irish Rifles, and by August 1915, Kettle was preparing for his first major battle in the sweltering heat of Gallipoli. He narrowly escaped death there and was promoted to captain before being transferred to the Western Front. It was at the Somme — in one of the most gruelling engagements of the war — that Kettle was killed on September 9, 1916. The 36-year-old was posthumously awarded the Military Cross for his bravery. In London, a wreath-laying ceremony was held at Westminster Bridge, where dignitaries and Irish community leaders gathered to remember Kettle’s contribution to both Irish nationalism and British military service. Poems he authored, expressing his tragedy and conviction, were read out by students from Dublin’s Trinity College, whose Kettle Foundation has supported them for decades. Meanwhile, in Dublin, a candlelit remembrance at the General Post Office highlighted the contradictions of a man who tried to hold together Ireland’s struggle for independence with his loyalty to Britain. “Tom Kettle’s story is not just one of war,” remarked Liam Kelly, a historian at University College Dublin. “It is a reflection of a divided nation, torn between love and loss, self-determination and sacrifice.

As the new season draws closer, all eyes will be on the Briton to see whether this radical shift in approach can maintain his position among F1’s elite.

For a small nation with a population of just over half a million, Malta’s history is anything but insular. Perched in the heart of the Mediterranean, this tiny archipelago has stood at the crossroads of empires, kingdoms and conflicts for centuries. Nowhere is this more evident than in the ferocious fighting against the Nazis during World War Two, a chapter in Malta’s storied past that remains among its most defining moments. Centuries before that, the Knights of St John had turned the Maltese islands into a bulwark against Ottoman invasion. Then came the British, whose colonial rule from 1800 left a deep imprint on the country’s language, culture and architecture. But it was the Second World War that tested Malta in ways that few places endured, transforming the island into a fortified fortress against one of history’s darkest forces. From 1940 to 1943, during the intense Axis siege, Malta became a linchpin in the Allied war effort in North Africa. The island served as a crucial supply and operations base, enduring relentless aerial bombardment. Luftwaffe and Italian Air Force raids sought to cripple its defences, yet the Maltese people held firm — quite literally. The bravery and resilience of the Maltese people during this period earned the island a unique distinction in British history: King George VI conferred the George Cross to the nation in 1942, an act of the highest recognition of civilian courage. Decades later, the memory of that struggle still lingers. Bullet-scarred walls, abandoned shelters and war memorials stand as testaments to a time of unimaginable hardship. Today’s Maltese, a people of seafaring and stoic pride, speak with quiet dignity of their forebears, whose sacrifices helped tip the scales of a global war. In 2022, Malta commemorated the 80th anniversary of the George Cross Award, sending a powerful reminder of how a small island made an outsized contribution to history. As tourism flourishes and modern economic challenges shape the present, the lessons of the past remain deeply etched in the national character. For all the crises Malta has weathered over the centuries, one truth remains: this is a country that never backs down from a fight. And that spirit, born of hardship and honed by the crucible of war, continues to define it today. Despite its size, Malta has always punched above its weight — and will likely always do so. Time and again, history has shown that.

"We need to have more courage," a Labour MP, newly elected last year, confided to me in the corridors of Westminster. The remark, seemingly offhand, struck a chord in a political landscape desperately in need of bold action. The words came as the UK faced another bruising week in parliament—marked by heated debates over austerity, public sector cuts and the growing divide between the government and the electorate. With his shoulder-length hair and slight swagger, the MP, whose name has not been disclosed for confidentiality, typifies the new wave of Labour politicians who entered Parliament under a fresh mandate in the 2024 general election. But with a political tsunami yet to crash, and even older-than-old challenges still looming, the question is: where can this newfound courage be directed? The Labour Party, after years of left-right infighting and a deeply unpopular leadership, hopes its recent election victory and the return of the 2024 unity pledge will bring about a fresh start. Indeed, prime ministerial candidate Brian Johnson—who ran in his first election, thanks to an 11,000-vote swing in his North London constituency—has promised monumental change, citing a need to "reconnect" with the people. But as one of his backbench supporters explained, courage today might not demand much—it may only require the rhythm of a speech or the staffing of a new ministry. The nation, meanwhile, is watching with bated breath. With soaring inflation, public service funding shortfalls and fears about the generational divide intensifying, the British public is looking for tangible reforms. The new parliament also finds itself at a crossroads with key European Union decisions on the horizon and a looming reshaping of the global economy. Yet as this young MP’s comment suggests, there is a feeling about Westminster that courage is not the same as the boldness of old. It is a phrase used more and more in coffee bar conversations and barely noticed in media soundbites. The kind of courage, once embodied by the likes of Margaret Thatcher or Aneurin Bevan, has been diluted. Today, it is confined to the talking points of press releases rather than enacted in the policies themselves. In this context, as Johnson prepares to present his first budget to a new House of Commons, the path forward is as uncertain as ever. The MP’s whispered words may not yet be a go-to catchphrase for his party, but they are reflective of a deeper sentiment within the new Labour intake: a yearning, perhaps, to be what one commentator described as “not just listeners, but leaders.”

Voters across the United Kingdom are heading to the polls today to cast their decision in a historic referendum on whether the UK should remain a member of the European Union or leave. The vote, which has sparked a deeply polarised national debate, could determine the country’s future relationship with the EU and reshape its economic, political and social landscape for decades to come. The referendum, mandated by Prime Minister David Cameron following intense pressure from his own Conservative Party, comes amid a backdrop of rising Euroscepticism in the UK. The Leave campaign argues that Britain should reclaim control of its borders and laws, and that the EU imposes unnecessary burdens on the economy and democracy. On the other hand, the Remain campaign insists that EU membership offers unique economic benefits and security, and that leaving would risk financial instability and international isolation. Despite numerous high-profile interventions from world leaders—including German Chancellor Angela Merkel and US President Barack Obama, who both urged the UK to remain in the EU—the outcome remains uncertain. Public opinion polls have shown no clear majority either way in recent weeks, with many voters basing their decision on local concerns, political affiliations, or national identity. The EU referendum is the first of its kind for the UK and marks a significant moment in the country’s constitutional history. Turnout is expected to be the highest in any such vote in recent memory, with the government stating it will count all ballots “fairly and transparently” to ensure the results, wherever they fall, are accepted as legitimate. The vote will take place at registered polling stations across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. For the first time in modern history, members of the armed forces serving overseas will also have the opportunity to vote by post. Some students and recent graduates have been granted an extra day off their classes to cast their votes, in a move widely seen as an attempt to boost youth participation in what could be the most significant decision of their lives. As the UK prepares to make its choice, the atmosphere is one of both anticipation and anxiety. The results, expected by early Thursday, will not only define the nation’s immediate future but also have far-reaching implications for the European Union as a whole. Whatever the outcome, history will remember this day as one that marked a turning point for the United Kingdom.

Two brothers have found themselves facing the devastating reality of eviction from the family farm they have called home for more than two decades — all due to what they describe as a legal miscalculation made over 20 years ago. The farming family, led by brothers John and Michael Shaw, had worked tirelessly on the 250-acre site on the outskirts of Newton Abbot in Devon, cultivating crops and running livestock that had become the lifeblood of their community. Now, with documents in hand from their solicitors, they are left stunned as their livelihood is dismantled and their future thrown into uncertainty. The issue, the brothers claim, dates back to 2003, when property rights were supposedly transferred without their knowledge. They insist that despite working on and contributing to the land, they were never officially informed of the change in ownership status. Legal representatives from the current landowner, a private investment firm, argue that the transfer complied with all relevant legal processes at the time. However, the brothers say this happened incorrectly, leaving them in a “tenancy trap” as their legal rights to the property have now been rescinded. John Shaw, 53, spoke outside the farm on Wednesday, surrounded by crop machinery that could soon be sold as their assets were divided. “This is more than just land to us. It's our heritage," he said. “We grew up here, we brought our children up, and now because of a mistake made years ago, we're being thrown out like we never existed.” His younger brother, Michael, 49, added: “We've been farming here for 21 years. We've put everything into it. It feels like a betrayal — not just by the former owner but by the legal system that should have protected people like us.” The situation has sparked outrage among local farmers and community members, many of whom have rallied to support the Shaws. At a public meeting last weekend, dozens of local residents expressed anger at the way agricultural workers and tenants are treated in the UK, calling for urgent reform of land tenure laws. “Too often the law is stacked against the people who actually maintain the farm, not just the ones with the title deeds,” said Richard Dale, a local farmer whose family has been farming in the area since the 19th century. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) has been contacted for comment on the case, although it appears there are currently no legislative measures in line to address the particular issue of long-term tenancy rights on privately owned farmland.

"We were only moved here a few years ago as part of a rehousing scheme for a nearby town that was overfilled and in need of regeneration," she said. HS2 Ltd, the agency responsible for building the national high-speed railway line, has said that the updated corridor is necessary to facilitate the streamlined expansion of the southern terminus and to integrate the line with existing services. Initial discussions have already been held between HS2 and the residents, with offers of compensation and alternative housing being raised. But many remain skeptical, feeling excluded from the decision-making process. Steve Carter, a local councilor and advocate for the residents, said: "These residents are not peripheral to the plans. They are the people affected most by these changes, and yet, they are being treated like collateral damage. We will not rest until we know the full extent of the plans and any alternative routes that might have been considered." The council has since urged the Department for Transport to provide further clarity on the revised corridor and to engage with the affected community more comprehensively. They have also raised concerns over delays in rail projects elsewhere around the UK, suggesting the government is setting unrealistic expectations rather than ensuring well-informed and sustainable development.

Samson Siasia, one of Nigeria's most celebrated football coaches and a key figure in the country's sporting history, has announced his decision to retire from coaching due to his frustration with what he calls a "disrespectful system" in Nigerian football. His resignation marks a significant moment in the landscape of the sport in the country, especially after he guided Nigeria’s U-23 team to a historic bronze medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics — a major achievement that earned him national acclaim. Siasia, 66, who has played and coached at the highest levels in Nigeria and beyond, said his decision was not made lightly. In a statement released on Wednesday, he made it clear that the problems within the Nigerian Football Federation (NFF) and the overall management of the sport have made it impossible for him to continue. "I have given this sport my life, and I have no regrets," he said. "But at a certain point, when you see no progress and witness a lack of respect for those in the game, you have to ask yourself — why continue?" The bronze medal in Rio was a high point for Nigerian football, with the team, affectionately known as the "Dream Team," finishing third out of 16 teams and raising hopes for the future. Siasia was named Confederation of African Football (CAF) Men's Coach of the Year for his efforts. Yet, in the years since, his relationship with the NFF has been strained, with reports of unpaid wages and disputes over administrative support. Siasia, who also led Nigeria to the 2000 Africa Cup of Nations final and coached top-tier teams such as Enyimba and Heart of Africa, has long been an advocate for reform in the sport. He has previously spoken out about corruption, lack of investment in youth development, and the challenges of maintaining professional standards in a game where politics often overshadows passion. “I’m not resigning out of anger, but because the system doesn’t respect the process,” he told BBC Sport. “I can't coach players with no facilities. I can't uplift the sport when there’s no backing. It’s not just about me. It’s about what this country’s players deserve.” Nigeria’s football development has long been held back by various obstacles, including inconsistent management and poor club infrastructure. Siasia’s departure is a reminder of the challenges facing the sport in Africa's most populous nation — and the urgency of reform if the game hopes to remain competitive on the global stage.

Fresh anti-Japan protests have erupted across China as tensions flare over a long-standing territorial dispute involving a cluster of islands in the East China Sea, compounded by rising nationalist sentiment on the 86th anniversary of Japan’s invasion of north-east China in 1931. Demonstrators in cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou have taken to the streets, with some clashing with police and others breaking windows of Japanese government offices and businesses. The protests have been fuelled by historic grievances and a renewed sense of Chinese nationalism, as well as recent diplomatic missteps between the two Asian powers. At the heart of the unrest is the disputed ownership of a group of islets known in Japan as the Senkaku Islands and in China as the Diaoyu Islands. Both nations claim sovereignty over the uninhabited islets, which are located roughly 230 miles from mainland China and around 760 miles from Tokyo. Relations between the two countries have been strained in recent months, particularly following a series of high-profile incidents involving Chinese naval vessels entering the disputed waters and confrontations between coast guard ships from both nations. Chinese state media have accused Japan of "aggressive behaviour" in failing to show deference to historical frustrations over Japan’s imperial-era aggression and its apparent reluctance to issue sincere apologies for wartime atrocities. Protesters have been seen holding banners calling for national pride and demanding the Chinese government protect its territorial integrity, with many accusing Japan of brushing aside its wartime past. In Shanghai, thousands converged at a memorial site dedicated to the 1931 Mukden Incident, marking the start of Japan’s brutal invasion of the north-eastern region of China, then known as Manchuria. The incident, widely seen as being fabricated by Japanese forces to justify occupation, remains a potent symbol in Chinese collective memory. Authorities have deployed police to manage the crowds and prevent further violence. Despite a police ban on gatherings, some protesters ignored the restrictions, and reports indicate that up to 1,000 demonstrators breached security cordon at the Japanese embassy in Beijing. The Chinese government has issued a strong diplomatic statement, urging Japan to show "mutual respect" and to "resolve disputes in a peaceful and rational manner." The situation is seen by some analysts as a potential flashpoint in the region, with risks of escalation not only for bilateral relations but for wider geostrategic stability in the East China Sea.

Glover and Stanning’s breakfast-time start in London has become a source of national pride in recent years, with legions of fans tuning in to watch them kick off the rowing day over tea and toast—this time with puddings and cakes available in the warm-up tent in France. Competing in their third consecutive world championships as a pair, the duo faced a highly competitive field, but their technical precision and experience proved decisive. Yet it was the British pair’s undimmed ambition and ability to outpace a field marshaled by powerhouse nations that underlined the significance of their victory. Reflecting on their achievement, Glover said: “It’s the best feeling in the world to be standing on the podium again. Heather is such a brilliant crew mate and it’s a real privilege to row with her. Their performance at Aiguebeleze not only raises the bar for British rowing but also sends a clear message to the rest of the world: when it comes to the women’s pair, Helen Glover and Heather Stanning remain in a league of their own.

I recently met Greece's former finance minister, Yanis Varoufakis, in the lobby of a five-star hotel in Athens. It was the kind of quiet corner of the capital that still whispers of a bygone era where politics and philosophy coexisted with elegance and entitlement, and it felt fitting for a man whose career has been as much about ideas as about influence. Dressed simply, with a quiet intensity that had once helped him navigate a debt crisis, Varoufakis was in a reflective mood, offering insights into a turbulent period in Greek history that continues to echo across Europe. “I once called the situation a game of poker with a rigged deck,” he began, referring to Greece’s struggle with its creditors during the height of the debt crisis. “If you knew the rules, you could at least play to lose slowly. But most of the time, the other players didn’t care how you lost—only that you did.” These were not the words of a defeated man, but of someone who had refused to yield to the pressure of a system he felt was not designed to save, but to test national resilience. Varoufakis, once a professor of economics at the University of Athens and a vocal critic of austerity, became a symbol of resistance and intellectual courage when he was appointed as Greece’s finance minister in 2015. He quickly gained international attention for his sharp rhetoric and unorthodox approach, and for confronting the European Union’s financial demands with what many called refreshing honesty. Yet the fight for democratic sovereignty in economic negotiations came at a cost. He resigned in 2015, amid growing political pressure from within Greece and external forces that had made clear what the consequences of defying them might be. “I didn’t come out of that fight in a better place,” he admitted. “But I came out of it having shown the world that this was not just a Greek issue—that the battle for economic freedom is one shared by many.” As we spoke, it was clear that Varoufakis still carried the weight of those years, but his mind was fixed on the future—on the lessons that could be learned, and the systems that might yet be reimagined to serve people over profit. His story, once so central to headlines, now seems to belong to the history books, yet no less relevant as Europe grapples with rising inequality, the climate crisis, and a new generation of leaders searching for direction.

Llandrindod Wells, a once-prosperous spa town in rural Powys, has seen its storied past reawakened in a remarkable fusion of history and modern technology. Known in its heyday as a destination where health-seekers came to bathe in the town’s mineral-rich waters, it was also transformed during World War One into a bustling military hub, housing thousands of troops. Now, as the centenary of the Great War fades into memory, the town’s unique past has become the focus of a new digital project that is breathing new life into the echoes of the early 20th century. Local history enthusiasts, supported by the Heritage Lottery Fund, have developed a trail across the town featuring QR codes and augmented reality markers that allow visitors to use their smartphones to access stories, photographs and even audio recaps of what everyday life was like during its military years and as a spa destination. Locals and tourists now walk the same cobbled streets that British and Allied soldiers once marched through, returning via their phones to a time when the town looked very different. “People may have forgotten the extent of Llandrindod’s role during the war, but it is there in the architecture, in the buildings, and in the landscape,” said Dr Elinor Price, a project lead on the initiative. “By using technology, we’re ensuring that the town does not just preserve its past, but actually shares it in an accessible and engaging way.” The project highlights how Llandrindod was not only a stepping stone for troops headed to the Western Front, but also a place of rest and recuperation. At the time, the town had a military hospital and barracks, and it continued to serve as a training base well into the war’s latter years. Its proximity to the Brecon Beacons made it an ideal location, and the tranquil greenery offered a much-needed respite for weary soldiers. The digital trail also touches on the town’s Victorian transformation into a spa, a time when Llandrindod was considered one of Britain's most healthful places to recover. Famous for its ‘azure bath’ believed to have restorative properties, the town was a magnet for the wealthy and the ill alike. Websites and local newspapers of the era mention figures such as politicians and aristocrats taking the waters, reinforcing its reputation. With this new initiative, the town is set to become a living museum of history and innovation — proving that even in the quiet hills of Powys, the past is never far away.

Recent figures obtained by BBC Breakfast reveal a startling trend in England and Wales: fewer than one in five people arrested for begging last year were actually homeless. The data, sourced from police records, sheds new light on an issue often associated with a lack of shelter and support, and raises difficult questions about what drives people to beg and who is being criminalised for it. According to the statistics, the majority of those arrested under anti-begging laws were not sleeping rough or registered with homeless shelters at the time of their arrest. This suggests that many were begging not as a result of housing insecurity, but for other reasons – potentially including coercion or vulnerability within networks of exploitation. The data also highlights disparities in how anti-begging laws are enforced across different regions. In some areas of England and Wales, doorstep arrests for begging have increased significantly in the wake of new legislation introduced under the Public Spaces Protection Order (PSPO) laws. These laws grant local authorities the power to ban certain activities, including begging, in specific areas deemed problematic. However, critics argue that criminalising begging fails to address root causes, such as poverty, mental ill health, and domestic abuse. Campaign groups have long pushed for the decriminalisation of begging, urging local authorities instead to focus on providing support and services to those in need. “It’s time to move away from punitive approaches and adopt a more compassionate and sustainable model,” said Naomi Akabas, a spokesperson for Crisis, the national charity for homeless people. “People don’t beg by choice. They beg because they have no other options.” The BBC Breakfast investigation also revealed that approximately 40% of those arrested for begging had a history of mental health issues or drug and alcohol addiction, yet few had been referred to appropriate services during their arrest. This has fuelled calls for a review of how begging is treated within the criminal justice system, and for greater collaboration between police and support agencies to ensure that individuals are offered help rather than punishment. Local housing charities have welcomed the findings as evidence of a deeper problem. They argue that while addressing high-profile cases of begging on city streets is often a political priority, the focus should instead be on tackling the root causes of poverty and housing crises that leave people in vulnerable and desperate situations. As pressure mounts to rethink the approach to anti-beggary laws, these figures serve as a reminder of the urgent need for a compassionate and holistic response to the challenges faced by some of the most vulnerable members of society.

In a remarkable rags-to-riches story, a football club founded by a 16-year-old in the wake of the 2011 London riots is set to make its eagerly anticipated FA Cup debut this season. The story of Bishop’s Stortford CFC, based in Hertfordshire, has become a symbol of hope, community resilience, and the power of sport to transform lives. The club's creation traces back to a pivotal moment in British history. In the summer of 2011, riots swept through some of London’s most deprived areas, sparked by the fatal shooting of Mark Duggan by police. Amid the chaos, Ethan Ashley, then just 16 years old, abandoned the idea of joining in the violence and instead turned his frustration into action. Inspired by his love for football, Ashley founded Bishop’s Stortford CFC with the support of a local church and community group. It was, by his own admission, an "impulse decision aimed at pulling people’s focus away from anger and towards a shared goal". Ten years on, the club’s journey is the stuff of sporting dreams. Originally starting with a makeshift pitch and players drawn from the local youth, the club has since moved up the tiers of the non-league football pyramid, earning promotion through grit, local support, and a strong emphasis on discipline and teamwork. Now competing at the ninth level of English football, Bishop’s Stortford’s inclusion in the FA Cup is set to attract new attention and fans from across the country. The FA Cup, England’s oldest and most prestigious football competition, is known for its tradition of underdog stories. Matches between top-tier teams and lower-league opposition often serve as a reminder of the deep roots and rich diversity of the game in England. Bishop’s Stortford, with its grassroots origins and the personal story of its founder, is the latest chapter in this tradition. Ethan Ashley, now 26 and working as the club’s director, said the opportunity to play in the FA Cup is not only a dream for him personally, but a source of pride for his community. “This isn’t just about football — it’s about showing that even in the aftermath of darkness and disorder, people can come together to create something special,” he said in a recent interview. The club is no stranger to high-profile attention. In 2017, it featured in a BBC documentary series about football's social impact, and in 2020, it was named one of the most successful non-league developments in recent UK football history by the Guardian.

Buffeted by a freezing wind on a chilly afternoon last April, I accompanied Martin McGuinness and his dog for a stroll around an ancient Irish hill fort just across the border on the Inishowen peninsula in Donegal. It might seem an unusual setting for a politician’s media moment, but as the Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland in his final months in office, McGuinness was keen to remind people of the deeper connections between all parts of these islands. The hill fort, known locally as Grá Keep, has stood for over 2,000 years as a silent witness to the shifting sands of history. Its ancient ramparts revealed under winter’s erosion provided the perfect backdrop for a man who had dedicated much of his adult life to fostering peace and understanding in a region once torn by conflict. As we made our way slowly through the biting wind, the Sinn Féin leader seemed at ease, the tension he often displayed in political settings softened by the presence of his loyal dog and the quiet dignity of the place. Grá Keep is not just a ruin, but a symbol. For generations, it has divided and united in equal measure, standing on shared soil between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. McGuinness, whose political journey from IRA commander to peacemaker is the stuff of modern legend, often spoke of the need to move beyond such divisions. As we walked alongside the crumbling stone walls, he reflected on the hill fort’s endurance and what it meant for the future of the peace process. “It’s easy to forget,” he said, stepping carefully over the wind-swept ground, “that people in this part of the world have always known how to live together. Look at what our ancestors built out of these rocks and wood. They didn’t see borders the way we do now.” The occasion was about more than nostalgia. Just days earlier, the UK Government had signaled its intent to proceed with what many in the Republic of Ireland and beyond viewed as an unprecedented challenge to the constitutional arrangements that have underpinned peace on the island for over two decades. McGuinness, ever the pragmatist, was keen to use such moments to show there were still bridges to be built, symbols to be shared, and a collective effort to be made. As the wind whistled through the ancient stone, the message he seemed to want to convey was clear: the past, like the hill forts of Inishowen, might be weathered and battered, but it endures—if only we are willing to face it.

Scientists detect atmosphere on ‘Earth-like’ exoplanet in major discovery   For the first time, scientists claim to have detected an atmosphere surrounding an Earth-like planet beyond our solar system, heralding a landmark breakthrough in the quest to find potentially habitable worlds. The discovery, announced by a team of international researchers, marks a key step forward in the search for alien life and raises new questions about the conditions that allow planets to support atmospheres — a crucial component for sustaining life as we know it. The planet, known as GJ 1132 b, is located approximately 39 light-years from Earth in the constellation Vela. While not a perfect duplicate of Earth — it is only 1.2 times the size of our planet but significantly hotter due to its close orbit around a red dwarf star — the presence of an atmosphere opens the door to the possibility of studying the chemical compositions of such worlds in greater detail. It is the first time an atmosphere has been identified on a rocky exoplanet roughly the size of Earth, setting it apart from previously detected oversized “super-Earths” or gas-rich planets. Dr. Jason Dittmann of the Harvard–Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, one of the lead researchers involved in the study, described the finding as “exciting and surprising,” pointing out that the planet may have retained a steamy, water-rich atmosphere – or one composed of molten material – due to the star’s intense radiation. The team used data from the Hubble and Spitzer space telescopes to measure the planet’s dimming effect as it passed in front of its host star. The observations revealed that the planet obscured more light than a bare rock would, indicating the presence of a surrounding envelope of gas. “This is a big deal because it confirms that even small, rocky planets can retain atmospheres under certain conditions,” said Dr. Dittmann. “It gives us more confidence that Earth-sized planets with Earth-like atmospheres may be more common in the universe than we had previously thought.” However, experts caution against over-optimism. The extreme temperatures on the surface of GJ 1132 b — estimated to be around 230°C — make it unlikely that conditions are suitable for sustained life. Nevertheless, the breakthrough sets the stage for the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), set for launch later this year, to analyse the chemical makeup of the planet’s atmosphere more thoroughly.

John Higgins marched into a commanding 10-7 advantage over defending champion Mark Selby on the opening night of the World Championship final at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield. The snooker legend Higgins, known for his composure and tactical brilliance, displayed a masterclass in the technical and mental aspects of the game to outmanoeuvre the invincible World number one. The historic venue, filled with the hushed anticipation typical of this most prestigious of tournaments, bore witness to a compelling battle as the two top-tier talents vied for supremacy. Higgins, a three-time World champion, began the night in formidable form, securing the first two frames to assert his authority. Selby, who made history last year as the first player to win six consecutive rankings titles, responded with a gritty display of precision and resilience to narrowly claw back the lead. However, Higgins' ability to remain calm under pressure and make crucial pots in tight moments proved decisive, enabling him to extend his lead when it mattered most. One of the standout moments came in the 13th frame, as Higgins clinched a dramatic 52-minute clash with a meticulous clearance from a complex snooker, drawing loud applause from the Crucible crowd. This victory not only showcased Higgins' unshakable tenacity but also hinted at Selby's growing frustration as the night progressed. The Englishman is no stranger to such challenges: his ability to adapt and rise to the occasion in the face of adversity has been the hallmark of his career and the reason he remains the sport's dominant figure. The first session ended in a tense atmosphere, with both players aware that the second half of the evening could go a long way in determining the overall outcome. For Higgins, the memory of previous title clashes – where he has come close but never quite managed to lift the trophy – will add to the intensity. For Selby, the pressure of defending his crown and maintaining his record of not losing a final since becoming world number one will be immense. The Crucible, with its unique aura and high stakes, is the ultimate proving ground for greatness. As the table was cleared and the players left the hallowed room for the night, the sense of anticipation for session two was palpable. With 14 frames remaining, a new chapter in the history of snooker was far from written, and the minds of fans around the world will remain fixed on Sheffield as the final weekend unfolds.

Ulster have made three high-profile changes as they prepare to face Munster in Saturday’s decisive Pro12 interprovincial clash at Thomond Park in Limerick. With the Pro12 season nearing its climax, the game has taken on added significance for both teams as they fight for continental qualification honours. Andrew Trimble, Chris Henry, and Jacob Stockdale have been named in the starting XV, bringing fresh energy and experience to a squad that has shown mixed form this season. Head coach Neil Jenkins has confirmed the changes are aimed at strengthening Ulster’s backline ahead of what promises to be a fierce contest in Limerick. Trimble, a proven try-scorer who has made a triumphant return from injury, will don the number 14 jersey. Stockdale, the fly-half who has dazzled in previous appearances, will start at 10, while the inclusion of Henry, the winger known for his deft handling and try-scoring flair, adds another dimension to Ulster’s attacking arsenal. The alterations come at a crucial moment for Ulster, who trail the Irish province in the Pro12 table, currently sitting in sixth place with just three matches remaining in the regular season. A win in Saturday’s match would significantly boost their chances of qualifying for the European Champions Cup, something both teams are desperate to achieve after unsuccessful campaigns in previous seasons. Munster, preparing for their own series of pivotal fixtures, will be eager to consolidate their position and potentially secure home advantage in the knock-out stages. Ulster’s backline will be put to the test in what is expected to be a high-tempo encounter. Munster have made their own adjustments, bolstering their pack ahead of a physical clash with the northern province. Paul O’Connell, head coach of Munster, has warned of the challenges posed by the trio of Trimble, Stockdale, and Henry. "Ulster have some dangerous players that can change the game in an instant," O’Connell said. "We need to be disciplined and focused from the outset." Supporters on both sides have been speculating about the implications of this match for the wider Pro12 picture. The performance of Ulster’s newly integrated backline could prove to be a vital factor in their campaign, with the likes of Stockdale offering creativity and playmaking that has been somewhat lacking in earlier fixtures. Saturday's game is set go ahead at 3pm Irish time and will be broadcast live across multiple platforms.

Rapper Rhymefest Invites Donald Trump to Chicago to Highlight City’s Resilience   US rapper and activist Che "Rhymefest" Smith has extended an invitation to Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, urging him to visit Chicago to see the city for himself and challenge the negative rhetoric that has been dominating the national conversation. The offer comes in response to Trump’s recent remarks, in which he painted Chicago as a city in crisis, plagued by crime, violence, and policy failures that reflect poorly on local leadership and, by extension, the Democratic Party. In a social media post that quickly went viral, Rhymefest, a Grammy-winning artist and long-time advocate for education and urban development, wrote: “Mr. Trump, I invite you to visit Chicago and see our city for yourself. There’s beauty here. Hope. Tenacity. We’re not what you describe, and I say this respectfully — your words don’t do us justice.” Rhymefest, whose real name is Che Smith, has frequently used his platform to speak out on social and political issues, especially those affecting the African American community in the Windy City. He is best known for penning the theme song for the acclaimed film  The Butler , and for his contributions to Chicago’s rich musical and cultural landscape. Trump, during a recent campaign stop in Aurora, Illinois, just outside Chicago, criticized the city’s leadership, saying it was in “disarray” and claimed “they don’t know how to run things.” He also pointed to the city’s violent crime statistics and the struggles of its public schools as proof of what he claimed is a failing progressive agenda. Rhymefest’s invitation has been hailed as a powerful rebuke of the rhetoric and a call for a more nuanced understanding of one of America’s most storied cities. Within hours of the post, the rapper received messages of support from politicians and activists across the ideological spectrum, many of whom echoed his sentiment that it is unhelpful and misleading to define a city by its worst problems alone. Chicago Mayor Lori Lightfoot, addressing the issue in a press conference shortly after the invitation was made public, said: “Chicago is a city of contrasts — just like any major city. We have challenges, but we also have innovation, resilience and incredible communities. Mr. Trump can paint the picture he wants, but the reality is far more complex.” The invitation has yet to receive an official response from Trump or his campaign.

Women at high genetic risk of breast cancer could soon have a new treatment option other than undergoing a double mastectomy, with scientists exploring the potential of preventive drugs to reduce their likelihood of developing the disease. This emerging approach, which could offer a less invasive alternative to surgery, has raised hopes among specialists and at-risk individuals who have long sought alternatives that preserve quality of life without compromising on risk reduction. The development is driven by advances in pharmacogenomics — a field that tailors treatments to an individual’s genetic profile. Researchers have identified a group of drugs, including selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), that may considerably lower the risk of breast cancer in women predisposed to it due to inherited mutations, such as those in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These genetic mutations are known to significantly increase the chances of developing breast and ovarian cancers, and for many, a preventive double mastectomy has long been the standard option recommended by physicians. In a recent clinical trial conducted at the universities of Edinburgh and Manchester, women carrying BRCA gene mutations were given a five-year course of a SERM known as raloxifene. The results, published in the  British Journal of Cancer , showed a 42 per cent reduction in the incidence of invasive breast cancer among participants compared to those who received a placebo. Moreover, the side effects were manageable and considerably less severe than previously estimated. Dr Naomi Royal, a leading oncologist at the University of Edinburgh and the principal investigator of the study, said: “This is a significant step toward providing women with more choices, and one that could reshape the way we approach breast cancer prevention. While mastectomy remains a life-saving option, not all women wish to undergo such a drastic procedure. These drugs offer an alternative that could make a real difference.” The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) is now considering whether to recommend the drugs for routine use in high-risk patients. If approved, the provision of preventive medication could significantly change the landscape of cancer prevention in the UK, offering women not only autonomy over their treatment decisions but also a new frontier in the battle against breast cancer. As the debate continues around accessibility, long-term effectiveness, and patient choice, one thing is clear — the landscape of breast cancer prevention is on the cusp of transformation. The next chapter will explore the implications for GPs, hospitals, and the NHS, as the system prepares for a potential shift in patient care.

Sighs of happiness, I imagine, filled the upper echelons of British horse racing, especially amongst officials at Royal Ascot, on the famous fixture's fifth and final day. After months of tight regulations, widespread uncertainty, and a global health crisis that seemed set to puncture the very fabric of traditional events, the much-loved Epsom Derby meeting and the Royal Ascot festival have regained their celebrated groove. Royal Ascot, a cornerstone of the British sporting and social season, this year marked a triumphant return to its usual form, as it drew spectators from across the country—and once again graced the fashion world with its traditional display of hat-clad elegance. The event, which is known not only for the thrill of horse racing but for the sartorial splendour of its attendees, appeared to reflect a much-needed lift in the national mood. From the manicured lawns of the world-famous enclosure to the cheers echoing across the parade ring, there was no doubt that the community found solace in the rhythms of a festival long steeped in tradition and pageantry. Behind many of the grins and glasses of champagne, there was relief and, undoubtedly, hope. For those involved in the sport—trainers, jockeys, race officials, and, of course, the watching public—this year’s Royal Ascot provided more than just entertainment; it was a symbol of resilience, and, perhaps, a long-awaited sign that normality was beginning to return. Jimmy Stewart, a British racing expert and veteran commentator at the BBC, noted: “This festival wasn’t just about racehorses. It was a celebration of community, of culture, and above all, of perseverance. Whether you won a race or lost a bet, there was a feeling in the air today about moving forward.” With a packed schedule featuring the prestigious Gold Cup and the Queen Anne Stakes, the final day of Royal Ascot provided dramatic finishes and poignant moments. Among the highlights was the impressive victory of Burgoo King in the Gold Cup—a triumph that not only highlighted the talent present on the track but also served as a reminder of how deeply beloved this sport is in Britain. As the sun set on the fifth day of Royal Ascot and the grounds were finally vacated, it was hard not to feel the air was filled not just with the excitement of competition, but the shared joy of a country hoping to rediscover its pageantry and identity.

A newly promoted health minister has sparked a new national debate by calling for people seeking help to end their lives to be allowed to obtain assisted dying in the UK. The comments, made in a surprise public statement, signal a dramatic shift in tone from recent government policy and have divided opinion across the political and medical spectra. The minister, who was recently elevated to the role, argued that the state should not stand in the way of individuals in "endless suffering" who wish to die with dignity. Such a stance has not previously been formally supported by a sitting minister of state and is likely to reignite the long-standing debate over the legalisation of assisted dying. Currently, the UK criminalises even the act of helping someone die, unless the individual is terminally ill and in the final six months of life under the current legal framework left in place by the Assisted Dying for the Terminally Ill Act of 1994. However, this bill was not passed into law and remains hypothetical. The minister’s remarks come at a time of growing pressure on the government to modernise laws surrounding end-of-life care. Campaigners have long argued that the current legislation is outdated and places unbearable emotional and ethical burdens on patients, their families, and medical professionals. Supporters of the move welcomed the minister’s bold stance, with one leading advocate stating, "It is about time our laws reflected the reality of modern medicine and human dignity." Opposition, however, has been swift. Religious leaders and some conservative MPs have condemned the statement as a dangerous precedent that could undermine the sanctity of life and open the door to unchecked euthanasia. They argue that vulnerable people, particularly those with disabilities or mental health conditions, could be at risk if legal barriers to assisted dying are lowered. Healthcare professionals are also divided. While some have expressed sympathy with the minister’s views, others fear it could create a rift in clinical practice and weaken the trust between doctors and their patients. The government has not yet issued a formal response to the minister’s comments, but the development is expected to influence ongoing discussions about the future of end-of-life care legislation in the UK. With parliamentary elections looming, this issue is set to become a major political battleground. Whether the UK will follow in the footsteps of countries like the Netherlands, Belgium, and Canada—where various forms of assisted dying are legal—remains to be seen.

Sheffield Wednesday Topple Newcastle to Spark Championship Title Hopes   Sheffield Wednesday have signaled their intent in the Championship play-off race with a crucial 2-1 victory over second-placed Newcastle United at Hillsborough. A physical and often tense contest saw the hosts grab a morale-boosting win — one that could prove pivotal in the race for the top two — against a Newcastle side dealt yet another major blow by injury as their star striker Dwight Gayle left the field with what appears to be a significant setback. The Owls started the brighter of the two sides and took the lead after just 13 minutes when Liam Palmer converted a penalty after Gayle had brought down Aaron Ramsdale. The Newcastle skipper, who has been in prolific form this season and has been the focal point of Rafa Benítez’s side, was destined to leave the field early, with assistant referee and the Premier League head of medical performance all assembling for a lengthy wait at the corner flag, sparking fears of a serious injury. Despite a lack of initial alarm being shown, the player was eventually stretchered off to be replaced by Paul Dummett. Newcastle struggled to cope without Gayle, whose absence left a gap in both flair and power in their attack. The Toon responded bravely, with Joelinton and others stepping up, and they equalised just before half-time through a clinical finish from Kieron Freeman, who fired home from close range after a low cross from Mohamed Diamé. But it was Sheffield Wednesday who regained the lead in the second half, with Billy Sharp netting his 13th goal of the season from close range after a well-worn through ball from Adam Reach. The Owls, marshaled expertly by Paul Heckingbottom, defended resolutely in the closing stages, with goalkeeper Keaton Dixon making a crucial last-ditch block to preserve the lead. The result sees Sheffield Wednesday climb into the top half of the Championship table, a reminder of their ambitions as they target a return to the Premier League after nearly a decade away. With seven games remaining, their win further tightens the title race, particularly with Newcastle now facing an uncertain run-in without Gayle.
