Benítez, who has enjoyed a sustained wait for the title since his return to English football in 2021, will be delivering a terse dressing room address after the setback. Meanwhile, Heckingbottom’s men are riding a wave of confidence at home.

Former Newcastle United Star Nile Ranger Cleared of Rape in High-Profile Court Case   A former Newcastle United footballer walked free from court last Thursday after being cleared of a serious rape charge in a trial that has gripped both the footballing world and the public. Nile Ranger, 30, who played for the Magpies between 2011 and 2013, was found not guilty by a jury at Newcastle Crown Court following a week-long trial. The case had sparked significant media attention, with many watching closely as it unfolded in a city still deeply connected to the Premier League club. Ranger, whose career also included spells at West Ham, Wigan Athletic, and League One side Shrewsbury Town, faced allegations of rape and assault that reportedly occurred in 2021. The charges were later withdrawn by the Crown Prosecution Service, following a review of the evidence. A spokesperson for the CPS stated that while there was sufficient evidence for a prosecution, there was “no realistic prospect of a conviction in the criminal courts.” However, as part of a re-investigation, the case was re-committed for trial by the Director of Public Prosecutions under new legislation designed to encourage victims to come forward. In court, Ranger strongly denied the allegations, with his legal team arguing that the accusations were unfounded and that their client had “acted responsibly at all times.” Speaking after the verdict, Ranger, who was visibly emotional, said: “I’m incredibly grateful to have been found not guilty. This has been a very difficult and distressing time for me and my family. I remain committed to making a positive contribution in football and in the community.” The case has reignited debate about reporting procedures and athlete conduct. The Crown Prosecution Service has since announced it is reviewing its handling of similar cases to ensure clarity and consistency. A spokesperson for the CPS said: “We take all allegations of sexual violence very seriously and are committed to supporting victims. This case highlights the complex nature of such trials and the need for robust, well-judged decisions based on the evidence available.” Newcastle United distanced themselves from comment on the specific charges, but issued a statement reaffirming their commitment to holding players to high professional and moral standards. “We fully support all initiatives aimed at promoting the safety and well-being of individuals in and around the sport,” the statement read. Ranger, who signed with Australian A-League club Sydney FC earlier this year, has made just one appearance for the club so far.

Hungary has found itself at the heart of an incendiary public debate over its role during the Second World War, with historians, politicians, and citizens re-examining the events that unfolded between 1939 and 1945. The renewed discourse comes amid rising tensions as centrist and far-right parties clash over how best to represent the country’s wartime past, an issue that has long been mired in controversy and political manipulation. At the heart of the controversy is the extent to which Hungary was complicit in the Holocaust, which saw tens of thousands of Jews sent to Nazi death camps under the direction, or at least with the knowledge, of the Hungarian government. Though Hungarian forces did not initiate the mass slaughter, many now point to the administration of Miklós Horthy, who ruled as regent from 1920 to 1944, as having enabled the systematic removal of Hungary’s Jewish population, particularly after the country entered the war on Nazi Germany’s side in 1941. The debate has been reignited by recent legislative proposals, including a motion from the governing Fidesz party to revise aspects of the 2011 Historical Responsibility Act, which criminalises the denial of Nazi crimes. Critics argue that the original law failed to assign sufficient responsibility to Hungary for its role in the persecution of Jews and Roma. The proposed amendments have been met with fierce resistance, with some accusing the government of seeking to sanitise history or shift blame to other wartime actors. Public memory is also being challenged by education reforms. Last month, the Hungarian Ministry of Education announced revised history curricula for secondary schools, which will place renewed emphasis on the country’s “victims” of the war and its “sacrifices” to democracy, rather than its wartime alliances with the Axis. Critics have decried the move as an attempt to rewrite history and weaken the emphasis on Hungary’s direct involvement in the Shoah. In a statement last week, the Jewish Community of Hungary (MAZSIHISZ), the country's largest Jewish organisation, warned against further historical revisionism. “We are not enemies of national pride, but Hungary must face its past to move forward. Silence on these issues only breeds division,” said János Grünhut, the community's president. Meanwhile, Fidesz leader Viktor Orbán has positioned his proposed revisions as part of a broader effort to restore national dignity. “Hungary was a country in the middle of brutal conflict,” he said in an address to the Hungarian Parliament.

A man found guilty of causing the death of an 18-year-old university student while driving under the influence has been handed a seven-year prison sentence. James Harrison, 27, of Birmingham, was convicted earlier this month after a three-week trial at the city’s Crown Court. The tragic incident occurred on the early morning of November 3, when Harrison, with more than twice the legal alcohol limit in his system, crashed his car into a pedestrian crossing on Digbeth High Street, where the student, Connor Edwards, had just started a new course in engineering. According to testimonies from witnesses and forensic evidence, Edwards, whose family revealed he came from a military background and had recently won a scholarship, was crossing the street at a marked junction when Harrison's silver Vauxhall Astra veered off the road and struck him with such force that his body was thrown into the bonnet of another car. A statement from Edwards’ family, read by his mother at the trial, described the moments of “pure horror” as she ran to his side and attempted to perform CPR while paramedics fought to gain access. Harrison was treated for minor injuries at the scene before being jailed, despite a reading of 88 microgrammes of alcohol per 100ml of breath – well above the 35-microgramme legal limit. West Midlands Police praised “the relentless efforts of officers” who pressed the Crown Prosecution Service to pursue a charge of causing death by dangerous driving, rather than the lesser charge of causing death while driving under the influence. Harrison had previously held a learner’s driving licence but was driving without supervision at the time of the crash. Sentencing him on Friday, Judge Juliet Lodge QC condemned Harrison's actions as “utterly reckless,” and said the prison sentence reflected the “frankly astonishing” negligence of a young man “who should have appreciated the dangers [his drinking] posed to others.” She also ordered Harrison to undergo a driving disqualification and a rehabilitation programme to treat his alcohol dependency. A response from the education provider expressing “profound sorrow” and announcing plans to increase student safety on campus was read during the sentencing hearing. Meanwhile, neighbours and friends described Edwards as an “enthusiastic and hard-working young man” who was recently awarded a new role with a top engineering firm and whose death has left a “huge hole in our community.” The case has reignited calls for stricter penalties for drink-driving and increased police patrols in city centre areas popular with students.

Shakila Ghabring, the Afghan woman whose powerful portrait appeared on the cover of National Geographic's October 2016 issue, has been denied bail by a court in Afghanistan after being arrested on fraud charges. The arrest has stunned both local and international observers who celebrated the image as a symbol of female resilience in a country long plagued by conflict and restrictive gender norms. Ghabring, who is believed to be in her 30s, became an overnight sensation following the photo shoot with renowned Australian photographer Tim Hetherington. The image, taken in a small village in the western Herat province, depicted a woman whose piercing gaze and elegant headscarf conveyed both strength and vulnerability. The photograph was later used in the publication’s powerful "The Afghan Women’s Photograph" campaign, which aimed to highlight the struggles and agency of women in Afghanistan. However, the emotional resonance of the image and the global recognition it brought came to an abrupt halt earlier this month when Ms. Ghabring was taken into custody in Kabul. According to court officials, she was arrested on allegations related to fraud, reportedly concerning property transactions and forged documents. While details of the case remain murky, her legal team has argued that the charges are baseless and politically motivated. In a press statement, Ghabring’s lawyer, Asma Farid, described the arrest as a “tragic misuse of national resources and power,” adding that her client, like many Afghan women, faces huge challenges accessing justice and basic freedoms. “What Ms. Ghabring is accused of is a small financial matter, and the seriousness with which state authorities are treating it is unjust and out of proportion.” The court’s decision to deny bail has drawn criticism from human rights organisations and international media. The National Geographic Society has not officially commented on the situation but has been urged by campaigners to use its global standing to support the case and secure Ghabring’s release. This case has once again brought attention to the fragile legal and political landscape for women in Afghanistan. While the country made international headlines for progress in women's rights, many activists argue that laws often fail to protect them, particularly those from marginalised communities. As protests grow in both Kabul and abroad, one question remains at the forefront of public consciousness: What price do women pay for standing in the spotlight in a society where visibility often comes with vulnerability?

Amid growing concerns over the welfare of the public and the integrity of the criminal justice system, assurances are being sought by MPs, charities and legal professionals that the significant restructuring of the probation service will not leave communities more vulnerable to reoffending and criminal activity. The Probation Service, which operates as a critical bridge between the courts and the rehabilitative support of offenders, is currently undergoing one of the most sweeping changes in its history as part of a government-led shake-up aimed at modernising the system and reducing taxpayer costs. Under the new proposals announced by the Ministry of Justice last year, the existing service will be replaced by a network of independent public-private partnerships bidding for contracts to supervise offenders. The government claims that this flexible, competitive model will promote innovation, improve outcomes and reduce reoffending, which currently stands at an average of 48% over the first two years after release. But Opposition and civil society groups are raising alarm. They point to risks of fragmentation, loss of specialist knowledge and a lack of accountability in contracting out a service that holds such a crucial role in safeguarding both individuals and the public. Labour Shadow Justice Secretary Emily Thornberry has called the plan "a gamble with public safety" and warned that the impacts of short-term cost savings could be disastrous. She cited the recent example of private sector involvement in managing bail hostels – where concerns about understaffing and inadequate support for prisoners preparing for release prompted urgent parliamentary scrutiny. At the core of these concerns is a fear that in the drive to reduce costs, high-quality supervision will be compromised. Smaller, less-resourced contractors may struggle to offer the same level of guidance and support to offenders, particularly those with complex needs – including mental health issues, substance abuse or histories of domestic violence. Probation officers speak of a key role in identifying and intervening about such risks, preventing not only reoffending but the potential spread of harm to vulnerable members of the public. The Crown Prosecution Service and the National Probation Service have both highlighted that the system, for all its flaws, has developed over decades into a sophisticated network that supports thousands of people a year to reintegrate into society. Charities, including the Howard League and the Prison Reform Trust, are calling for strong oversight bodies to be established ahead of the shake-up to ensure that offender management remains the top priority – not profit maximisation or cost efficiency.

The Scottish National Party is currently redoubling its efforts to secure greater control over tax and welfare powers as part of the ongoing Scotland Bill negotiations, but the UK government has responded with a firm rebuke, telling the SNP to “stop talking and start doing.” The escalating tensions between the two sides have once again brought the issue of Scottish devolution and the limits of Westminster authority into the spotlight, with political rhetoric heating up ahead of potential parliamentary debates on the revised legislation. The SNP, which has long campaigned for a more autonomous Scotland, is seeking to increase its fiscal and social policy powers through the Scotland Bill currently under consideration in the House of Commons. Among the proposals under the party’s agenda are plans to allow Holyrood to set the rate of income tax for non-savers and the self-employed, as well as to fully administer benefits in specific circumstances. The demands from the SNP argue that these powers would allow Scotland to tailor its economic policies and welfare systems to better suit local needs, a core argument in its broader push for independence. However, in a clear challenge to the SNP’s approach, a senior Conservative minister has told the party that its focus should now be less on negotiating and more on delivering on promises made in recent years. The short, sharp message from the UK government is seen by many as a calculated attempt to force the SNP back to the negotiating table with a more conciliatory stance – or to face increasing criticism over stalled progress on devolution. Political observers are monitoring the exchanges closely, with some predicting that the row will continue to play out in the media and the corridors of power in both Edinburgh and London. SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon has already signalled that her party will continue to press its demands, stating that “maximum flexibility” and “progressive devolution” remain key principles as the Scotland Bill moves through its parliamentary stages. Meanwhile, Conservative MPs are using the dispute to highlight what they see as the lack of unity and cooperation that has characterised the devolution process under SNP rule. As the debate intensifies over the scope and scale of Scotland’s powers, one thing is clear: the relationship between the UK government and the SNP remains fraught with tension, and the outcome of these discussions could shape the political landscape for years to come.

The UK government has unveiled proposals to grant new powers to regulators to fine mobile network operators and pornography website owners for failing to take sufficient action to protect children and vulnerable users from harmful material. The announcement, made in a statement by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), forms part of a broader strategy to make the digital space safer and more accountable. Under the proposed measures, Ofcom, the UK's communications regulator, would be given the authority to investigate and impose financial penalties on broadband suppliers, mobile providers, and online pornography platforms that do not comply with new safety and protection guidelines. The fines could range from thousands to millions of pounds depending on the scale of non-compliance and the potential harm caused. Justice Secretary Dominic Raab, who outlined the proposals in a press briefing, said: “We are not allowing the internet to become a lawless space where the risk to vulnerable and underage users is ignored by those who profit from it. This move is about holding providers and platforms to account and ensuring they are not just reactive in their approach to safety, but proactive in preventing harm.” The government’s plan comes in the wake of increasing public concern over the ease with which children and other vulnerable individuals can access inappropriate or explicit content online. Recent studies have revealed high levels of exposure to adult content among minors, much of it accessed inadvertently while browsing mobile devices. The government is also facing pressure from MPs and child welfare experts, who have called for stronger legal frameworks to protect users. The proposed powers are part of the government’s upcoming Online Safety Bill, which will require social media companies, messaging apps, and video-sharing platforms also to implement age verification systems and algorithmic safeguards to prevent the proliferation of harmful material. Industry bodies have reacted cautiously to the news, warning that the proposals could be complex and costly to implement, particularly for smaller firms. However, they have largely backed the principle of enhancing online safety and said they welcome clearer guidance from regulators. The Details of the proposals have not yet been finalized, and the government has indicated that it will consult further with telecom providers and digital rights groups before the legislation moves to the parliamentary stage later this year. If passed, the measures would mark a significant shift in the UK’s approach to online regulation, putting safety considerations at the heart of the digital economy.

When I said hello to Rupert Murdoch outside the Manhattan headquarters of his media empire last month, he told me he was "not worried at all" about Ofcom. The 93-year-old media mogul, dressed in a tailored suit and holding a cane, exuded his trademark confidence as he addressed a gathering of reporters and analysts. His assurance stands in stark contrast to the growing scrutiny his empire, News Corp, faces from regulators in the UK, a key market for its major newspapers and streaming services. Ofcom, the UK’s communication regulator, is currently conducting a comprehensive review of how the media landscape is shaping up in the digital age. The inquiry looks at whether the market is fair, open, and provides consumers with enough choice and security, particularly in the wake of growing concerns over misinformation, media concentration, and foreign influence. Murdoch, whose News Corp empire spans the Guardian, Sky, HarperCollins, and the New York Post, is one of the most powerful figures in global journalism. He arrived at this meeting reeling from recent blows — layoffs at Sky, the collapse of merger talks with the House of Representatives in the UK, and increasing demands from lawmakers for greater transparency. Yet, for Murdoch, it is business as usual. “I’ve been through this many times,” he said with a wry smile, watching the passing traffic on Park Avenue. “The only thing that counts is what the reader wants. I’ve always known that.” Behind his composed façade, however, there are signs of unease. Sources within the company suggest that the regulatory climate in the UK has led to internal strategic reviews and a rethinking of investments. Ofcom is not alone in its scrutiny — the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has also raised concerns about News Corp’s expansion plans in the online news and entertainment sectors. Murdoch’s remark echoes the headstrong spirit that has marked his 60-year reign in media. Yet, with shareholders demanding profitable growth and governments tightening the regulatory screws, the old rules may no longer apply. Whether he will survive the next wave of challenges — and at what cost — remains to be seen. For now, as he turned and disappeared into the skyscraper lobby, the world’s most unassailable media tycoon looked unshaken. Whether his empire can remain so is another question entirely. Manchester United set a club-record transfer fee by purchasing Paul Pogba from Juventus for £89m in 2016.

The planned closure of the Forensic Science Service (FSS), once a national asset in the UK's criminal justice system, may prove to be far costlier than initially estimated, according to new research by a leading academic. A study led by Dr Lucy Heath, a forensic science expert at the University of Surrey, suggests the true cost could be more than three times the government’s current projection of £35 million. The FSS, which for over a decade provided forensic testing to police forces across England and Wales, was under government ownership until earlier this year, when it was sold to the private sector and renamed LEC Services. The decision to privatise the FSS, which had long been valued for its scientific integrity and national standard, was controversially announced in 2011 by then-Home Secretary Theresa May. The official rationale was to reduce the cost of forensic services for local authorities and to improve efficiency. However, critics warned of a potential decline in the quality of forensic work and a widening gap in regional support for investigations. Dr Heath’s analysis, published in the  Journal of Criminal Justice Policy , challenges the cost-benefit claims made by the Home Office over the years. According to her research, police forces have been forced to outsource forensic testing to private companies across the country since the FSS was dismantled. These companies have varying levels of accreditation and access to national databases – resources once centralised under the FSS. The result, Dr Heath argues, is an increase in duplicated work, delays in processing evidence, and higher operational costs for police. “We’ve looked at the outlay incurred by four major police forces over the past three years and found that the cost of forensic testing alone had risen by an average of 217%,” Dr Heath said in a recent interview. “This is about more than money. Cases are taking longer to resolve, and forensic evidence is being lost or misinterpreted due to fragmentation in the system.” The government has defended its decision, citing initial savings of £17 million per year. However, these figures have drawn heavy scrutiny. The Home Office declined to comment on Dr Heath’s findings, directing questions to a press release issued in April 2014, which reaffirmed its confidence in the sustained benefits of the FSS’s closure. The controversy has reignited calls from legal reform groups and parliamentary committees for a review of the decision.

Lewis Hamilton secured a record-equalling seventh world championship in thrilling fashion on Sunday, winning the US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, and claiming his fourth title with one race still to go in the 2021 season. The Mercedes driver edged out his title rival Max Verstappen in what turned out to be a dramatic and high-stakes battle at the Circuit of the Americas, an event that has fast become synonymous with dramatic racing over the past decade. A masterclass in composure and precision, Hamilton, 36, started the race in third place behind Verstappen and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc before undercutting the Red Bull car on a tense lap 13 pitstop to retake the lead. What followed was a nail-biting final 20 laps, during which numerous late pitstops left the track teeming with strategy-changes, safety cars, and a flurry of overtaking maneuvers that kept even the most seasoned motorsport fans on the edge of their seats. The Mercedes driver held firm despite a late charge from Verstappen, who looked desperate to bridge the gap in the final few corners. However, Hamilton’s superior pace in the closing stages, combined with aggressive race strategy from the Silver Arrows garage, proved decisive. As he crossed the line, the Brazilian flag unfurled on the pitboard – confirming a first Grand Chelem (pole position, fastest lap, fastest race lap, and race win) and extending his lead in the drivers’ championship to 18 points over Verstappen. The win marks Hamilton’s 88th in Formula One, drawing him level with the legendary Michael Schumacher for the second most in history. For the Briton, it was a deeply personal and symbolic victory. Hamilton has long spoken about his desire to make history in motorsport, not just for the sport, but as the first Black driver to cement his name in its annals. This win was widely seen as the culmination of a decade-long journey to not just challenge for titles, but to dominate them. Historic moments are rarely celebrated without controversy, and this weekend was no exception. Prior to the race, intense speculation surrounded whether Verstappen – just one point behind Hamilton as the reigning world champion – could still overtake the Briton with the final race of the season in Abu Dhabi remaining. Many fans, analysts, and even some drivers on the grid predicted go-kart rivalries and fierce verbal exchanges would culminate in a tense final line in the desert.

There was an underlying new buzz of excitement in the corridors and bars and cafes of the House of Lords this week, as speculation mounted over a potential shift in the political priorities of the Conservative government. This rare sense of anticipation has spread beyond the hallowed halls of Parliament to the media, the public, and even among opposition leaders who have noted an unusual hesitancy from the government to address the flurry of recent leaks. At the heart of this intrigue is a widely reported internal memo, attributed to one of the Prime Minister’s senior policy advisors, which suggests a radical rethink of the government’s economic strategy. The memo, said to have emerged from within the Treasury itself, hints at a pivot from austerity to a stimulus-driven plan, involving the reallocation of billions of pounds in funding towards renewable energy, housing, and education. Though the memo is purported to be internal and has not been officially endorsed, its very existence has caused ripples across the political landscape, with some commentators likening it to the famous 1975 Anglo-French memorandum in which a profoundly radical idea was first introduced to cabinet, only to remain secret—and unacted upon—for months. The House of Lords, long seen as a place of quiet debate and occasional rumbles, has become a hub for high-level informal meetings, with peers seeking confirmation of the possibility that the government may indeed be preparing a major announcement. Some senior crossbench Lords have been overheard discussing the implications of the potential policy shift, with one prominent peer telling a journalist, “If the government is serious, this could be the most significant reversal in fiscal policy this country has seen in decades.” But not all are convinced. Senior members of the government have declined to comment specifically, and some within the Cabinet have reportedly expressed their disapproval of the memo’s contents, fearing it could derail public confidence in the government’s existing economic standing. Meanwhile, the Treasury remains silent, and a senior civil servant briefed yesterday described the memo as “a suggestion, not a plan.” Still, within Parliament, the energy is palpable. Lunchtime passed quickly in the Members’ Dining Room on Tuesday as MPs and peers debated the potential impact of the leaked document, while waiting for the Prime Minister to address the House. As one junior minister put it, trying to sound nonchalant but clearly embroiled in the excitement: “You don’t get these buzzes every day.

The festive season has never felt quite so magical as it does this year for Emily Clark, who has just announced she is to become Mrs Emily Smith after a whirlwind year of unexpected events, heartache, and finally, a romantic whirlwind that culminated in a Christmas miracle. Her boyfriend, Radek Smith, surprised her with a proposal during a quiet evening at home, a moment that, by all accounts, brought tears to her eyes — a rare but heartfelt reaction from the usually composed marketing executive. Emily, 28, described 2023 as a year of “intense emotional ups and downs” — a rollercoaster that included a tense three-month separation from Radek after he was unexpectedly deployed to a supply mission in Prague, and a well-publicised promotion at work that placed her under the corporate spotlight. But despite the demands of her career, which saw her relocate to London temporarily for six months to take on a senior role at a media firm, the couple remained committed and reconnected more frequently via video calls, slowly planning for the future they both longed for. The proposal, however, came entirely out of the blue. “We were just lying on the sofa, surrounded by the half-decorated tree and unopened presents, and Radek suddenly stood up, got on one knee, and said, ‘Emily, you’re the most amazing partner I could have wished for, and I want to spend the rest of my life with you.’ It was so romantic and so unexpected,” she said. Radek, 30, a software developer originally from the Czech Republic, has been based in Manchester for the past two years, where he met Emily at a mutual friend’s birthday party. The couple, who will tie the knot next summer, said the engagement made about half their December significantly brighter — especially given the touch of fate that led to Radek being back home at all. “I think it was the perfect way to close the year,” Emily said, her eyes sparkling with joy. “And now, I can’t wait to have my first real Christmas with a ring on my finger and a wedding to look forward to.” Friends and family who have followed the couple’s journey over the years are also celebrating their happy news, with many noting that the proposal happened at the perfect time, just as the world around them seems to be slowing down to enjoy the cooler season.

British Cycling has announced a comprehensive overhaul of its medical services following an independent review, in what the organisation has described as a ‘timely’ update to safeguard the health and performance of its elite athletes. The review, conducted by external experts, was launched in the wake of growing concerns over the physical and mental well-being of cyclists competing under high-pressure international schedules. In a statement released on Monday, British Cycling confirmed that it had taken immediate action to implement a series of reforms across its medical provisions, including the introduction of new protocols for injury prevention, concussion management, and athlete welfare. These changes are expected to set a new benchmark in sports medicine and athlete care not only for the UK but potentially for other national governing bodies. The review highlighted the intense physical demands placed on cyclists and underscored the need for a more holistic approach to athlete health. It found that while British Cycling had an excellent record in terms of performance and safety, the pace of elite sport meant that risks were evolving at a rate that required more dynamic responses. At the heart of the revisions is a new system of athlete-led health monitoring, which empowers cyclists to report concerns in real time through streamlined digital platforms. These tools will allow for quicker interventions, better communication between medical staff and athletes, and a focus on early warning signs of overtraining and fatigue. British Cycling CEO Ian Drake praised the work of the independent panel and said the reforms were a “necessary step forward” for the sport. “Our priority has always been the well-being of our athletes,” he said. “This review gave us a clear framework for improvement, and we are committed to embedding these improvements in everything we do.” The overhaul also includes the appointment of a new lead medical officer and the expansion of a sports science and medicine team. The organisation will also be increasing its investment in mental health support, recognising the toll that elite competition can take on psychological resilience. With the 2024 Paris Olympic cycle now in full swing, these changes are expected to bolster British Cycling’s efforts as it continues its pursuit of excellence on the world stage while ensuring athletes are supported both on and off the track. The reforms have been welcomed by riders, coaches, and medical professionals alike, with many viewing the updates as a significant vote of confidence in the sustained future of the sport.

Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has called on UK ministers to do more to involve people in Wales in the Brexit process, saying they must be given a “bigger stake” in determining the country’s post-EU future. Speaking ahead of a major UK government review into devolution and the relationship between Wales and Westminster, Davies warned that continued neglect of Welsh voices could damage trust in both institutions and fuel support for his party's political opponents. Davies, leader of the Welsh Conservatives and one of the most prominent Tory figures in Wales, stressed that the Brexit negotiations must reflect the “diverse and complex needs” of Wales rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach. His comments come as tensions continue to rise between the Welsh Government and UK ministers over the execution of the post-Brexit agenda, including the application of English regulations to Welsh devolved areas and the management of agricultural support and trade deals. The call for increased participation in the Brexit process echoes concerns raised by Welsh MPs and stakeholders who argue that decisions are frequently made in Westminster without sufficient consultation with Wales. With 45 per cent of those who voted in the 2016 EU referendum in Wales choosing to remain in Europe, the sense of alienation in some corners of the country is palpable. For many Welsh voters, the decision to reject Brexit during the UK-wide vote was ignored by UK ministers who proceeded – with Wales held to the same timeline and approach as the rest of the UK. Davies acknowledged the frustrations but urged caution, insisting that Welsh Conservatives remain committed to a Brexit that works for the people of Wales. “It is essential that Wales is not just a spectator in this process, but an active participant,” he said. “Welsh ministers and politicians must be at the table when future frameworks are negotiated, and people across Wales must feel they are not being left behind.” The remarks follow a recent debate in the Welsh Assembly over the need for greater devolution of powers in areas affected by Brexit, such as the environment, agriculture, and transport. First Minister Mark Drakeford has consistently called for Wales to have a distinct approach to Brexit, arguing that it should not be bound by English-only policies. His pro-Remain stance and calls for a more flexible relationship with the EU have recently prompted a new surge of support for Welsh nationalist party Plaid Cymru, something Davies has sought to counter.

A new government study has revealed the alarming figure that approximately 1,300 children under the age of 17 in the United States die each year from gun-related injuries, sparking renewed calls for stronger gun control legislation and improved measures to protect young lives. The report, compiled by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), underscores the urgent need for a national conversation on firearm safety and prevention strategies to address this persistent and preventable crisis. The statistics highlight a tragic but often overlooked side of the country’s gun violence epidemic, with firearms accounting not just for homicides and suicides, but also for accidental discharges and other unintentional injuries among young people. According to the CDC, firearm-related deaths remain one of the leading causes of death for children and adolescents in the US. The study breaks down the fatalities by age group and cause, revealing that while homicide rates remain the highest, a significant number of children lose their lives due to accidents involving guns, often in homes where weapons are stored improperly. The debate over gun safety laws has intensified in recent years, particularly after a wave of mass shootings, but the CDC’s report emphasizes that the crisis is not confined to public spaces—it is also unfolding quietly within communities and families. Advocacy groups have pointed out that as many as one in six American homes contain a firearm, often stored unsecured, increasing the risk of domestic accidents. “Every single gun death is a tragedy, but when it involves a child, it strikes at the very heart of our communities,” said Dr. Rochelle Walensky, Director of the CDC. She called for expanded efforts to promote responsible gun storage, increased access to emergency services, and preventative education for families. In response to the findings, some lawmakers have redoubled their efforts to pass federal legislation that would require background checks for all gun purchases, limit access to certain types of firearms, and fund mental health and violence prevention programs. Meanwhile, civil liberties groups continue to emphasize the right to bear arms while advocating for improved safety measures to ensure that firearms do not fall into the wrong hands. Across the country, parents, educators, and healthcare professionals are also pushing for more awareness and education about the dangers of firearms for children. As the debate persists, the study’s findings serve as a stark reminder that the issue of gun violence in America is not confined to high-profile mass shootings—it is a heartbreaking reality for thousands of families who lose their children to gun-related injuries on an annual basis.

The heartbreak of families bereaved by the devastating effects of drug abuse is sharply in focus in Tuesday's newspapers, with real-life tragedies serving as a painful reminder of the ongoing crisis tearing through communities across the UK. Behind every statistic are parents, siblings, and children who have lost loved ones to addiction, overdose, or the long-term consequences of substance abuse. For many of these grieving families, the loss is not only emotional but all-consuming, with a fight that spanned years often ending in death too soon. The stories shared in the press this week are as varied as they are harrowing. They feature young lives snuffed out before they had a chance to bloom, others lost in the grip of dependency after a single misstep. The stark reality is that no one is immune—addiction spares neither privilege nor poverty. The papers highlight the growing need for better support systems, from frontline care and mental health provision to community-based recovery programmes. For far too long, the burden has fallen disproportionately on families already reeling from grief and anger. Joanne Thompson, whose 23-year-old son died from an opioid overdose in Manchester, described how she and her husband spent years trying to get him the help he desperately needed. “We did everything we could think of. We begged, we researched, we moved in with him. But it wasn’t enough,” she told one broadsheet. Her story is one of many, with each family confronting the same questions: why wasn’t there better access to treatment? Why did the system fail them? The press also shines a light on those fighting for change. Charities and organisations are tirelessly campaigning for government investment in preventative action and early intervention. They argue that addiction is not a criminal issue, but a public health emergency requiring compassion and funding. As the Prime Minister remains under pressure to address the crisis, the voices of the bereaved continue to echo through the headlines — demanding action and not fading into oblivion. The provision of better support does not come without cost, but for grieving parents like Ms. Thompson, it is a small price to pay to ensure no other family suffers the same fate. With every story published, another heart is laid bare. The hope is that these acts of remembrance might also be acts of hope — for a future where addiction can be halted in its path and lives no longer lost in silence.

Morrisons, one of the UK’s leading supermarket chains, has confirmed that 720 jobs will be lost at its headquarters in Bradford, marking a significant blow to the local economy and workers in West Yorkshire. The announcement, which stunned staff at the retail giant’s South Bank offices, brings fears of a larger-scale restructuring within the company and adds to a growing list of job cuts across the British retail sector. In a statement, Morrisons said that the move is part of a wider organisational review designed to “streamline operations” and ensure the company remains “competitive and efficient in the long term.” The affected roles, which span a variety of departments including finance, human resources, property and digital, will be subject to redundancy procedures, with employees advised to continue working until the process is finalised later this year. The announcement is the most dramatic escalation to date in what has been a challenging period for Morrisons. Earlier this year, the firm reported a 9.5% drop in sales and has faced increasing pressure to match the operational efficiency and technology investment of its rivals Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Asda. The supermarket is currently exploring new ways to reduce costs, including the potential closure of stores and impacts on its regional offices. Unions and local MPs have voiced deep concern over the impact on Bradford, a city that has long been a focal point of Morrisons’ operations. Labour MP David Ward said, “This is devastating news for the employees and their families. It shows that big corporate decisions have devastating consequences for working people and local communities.” He called on the government to urgently review the policies supporting regional employment and business resilience. The move also highlights the growing challenges facing traditional retailers as they contend with continued consumer shifts to online shopping, intense competition and rising operational costs. Morrisons has suffered in particular from poor customer satisfaction scores in recent years, prompting the company to overhaul its supply chain and improve standards in stores. As the company now shifts more functions to digital platforms and combines back-office roles with regional delivery units, the response from employees has been one of disbelief. A number of union representatives said it is a “desperate move” that prioritises profits over people. Morrisons has offered to support affected staff with redundancy payments, outplacement services and retraining packages. It has also reiterated its commitment to the regions, insisting that its “footprint across the UK remains vital to the success of the business.”

Calls have been made for harsher penalties to protect ambulance control room workers from the increasing wave of abusive and threatening calls they receive in the line of duty. As emergency call handlers strive to remain calm and professional in their high-pressure roles, a growing number of incidents involving verbal and even physical threats are being reported — prompting calls from unions and health professionals for stronger legal protection. In recent months, the incident rate has risen alarmingly. Control room staff, often the first point of contact for emergency services, are now reported to be facing a staggering number of abusive or threatening calls. According to the National Emergency Services Federation (NESF), ambulance control operators receive hundreds of abusive calls each week — a 40% increase compared to the previous year. In one case last December, an operator working a night shift for the East Midlands Ambulance Service reportedly received a string of demands from an intoxicated caller, ending with threats of violence towards the worker’s family if she did not cancel an ambulance dispatched for a minor incident. The abuse does not always come from members of the public. Organised groups of hoax callers, some even assisted by social media, have been accused of targeting emergency services for fun or political reasons. Last year, a network of hoaxers in north-west England were found to be supplying fake numbers and scripts to encourage others to make malicious 999 calls — leading to staff being verbally abused or – in one case – mistreated with racial slurs. Trade union leaders are growing frustrated. “These workers are already under immense stress trying to deal with real emergencies, but now they are also being treated like someone’s punchbag,” said Gary Tee, a union representative for ambulance staff. “This isn’t just about rude words. It’s about real psychological harm, burnout and even the future viability of people choosing to work in this vital sector.” Existing laws are seen as insufficient to deter abusers. Current legislation allows for fines and even imprisonment for wasting police or emergency time, but it does not specifically address verbal abuse towards workers. Campaigners are calling for a new set of offences targeting threats, intimidation, and harassment against emergency call handlers — backed by stronger penalties including mandatory repeat offender programmes or increased prison tariffs. With the pressures of winter and the expected rise in emergency calls, calls for action to protect the “unsung heroes” of the emergency services have never been louder.

A Breath Test That Could Detect Parkinson’s: Breaking Through Long-Standing Barriers   The promising prospect of identifying Parkinson’s disease through a non-invasive, quick breath test is gaining more than just scientific interest—it is sparking hope among medical professionals and patients alike. Experts believe they have taken a crucial step forward in simplifying the diagnosis of this progressive neurological condition, which often has a long and complex diagnostic process involving multiple tests and specialist consultations. Currently, diagnosing Parkinson’s is notoriously difficult in its early stages, as symptoms can be subtle and vary widely between individuals. Today, neurologists rely heavily on clinical observation, symptom monitoring, and occasionally expensive imaging tests to confirm a diagnosis. The process can be lengthy, and early detection remains a challenge—especially before irreversible damage has occurred. Now, a group of researchers are claiming to have found specific volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the breath of Parkinson’s patients that are not present in healthy individuals. This discovery is the foundation for a new breath test that may allow doctors to spot early signs of Parkinson’s, potentially enabling treatment to begin before symptoms even appear or worsen significantly. One early trial has already shown strong results, with the test being able to distinguish between Parkinson’s patients and healthy individuals with an impressive accuracy rate. Dr. Emily Carter, a neurologist at the Royal Free Hospital and lead researcher of the project, commented on the breakthrough. “This could be a game-changer for how we diagnose Parkinson’s. A breath test is not just quick and non-invasive—it could be done in a general practitioner’s surgery, in a nursing home, or even in the future at home using a handheld device. It gives us an earlier entry point to this condition than previously possible.” The test is based on the idea that the body produces distinctive biomarkers in response to the progression of Parkinson’s disease. These biomarkers can be present in the breath long before visible symptoms take hold. If further trials confirm the initial findings, the test could be rolled out within a matter of years—offering not only an easier way to detect Parkinson’s but also a potential tool to monitor the disease as it progresses. Such a development is particularly welcome given that the number of people living with Parkinson’s is expected to nearly double in the next 20 years.

In a thrilling encounter at Victoria Stadium on a chilly Bank Holiday afternoon, Accrington Stanley clinched a vital 2-1 victory over promotion-chasing Colchester United, lifting their hopes of securing their EFL League Two status this season. The win came despite the Lilywhites managing the game for over an hour with just 10 men, following a first-half red card for captain Shane McLoughlin. The visitors had arrived in Lancashire with ambitious intent, sitting comfortably within the top six and looking to continue their push for a promotion berth. However, Accrington, perched precariously just outside the relegation zone, made it abundantly clear they would not be pushed aside easily. The hosts opened the scoring in the 21st minute through a moment of individual brilliance from Marco Matias, whose solo run culminated in a composed finish past the outstretched legs of Colchester goalkeeper Kean Bryan. It was a goal that sent the home supporters into raptures and offered a timely lift for a side in desperate need of points. Just as Colchester looked to settle into the match and respond, Accrington were dealt a major blow when McLoughlin was shown a straight red card for a two-footed challenge in the box. The dismissal sent shockwaves through the Lilywhites’ ranks, but rather than capitulate, Accrington grew in confidence and intensity as the game progressed. Their resilience was tested in the 55th minute when Colchester equalised through a penalty, following a foul in the box by Matias, which he also missed appealing for. Premier League loanee Will Badodi sent Accrington goalkeeper Sam Slocombe the wrong way to level the score and inject fresh energy into the Colchester side. Yet Accrington, fully aware of the stakes, refused to buckle under the pressure. With 18 minutes left on the clock, substitute Kiko Martinez produced another moment of quality, latching onto a long clearance from Slocombe and finishing clinically to give the home side a deserved advantage. From that point on, Colchester threw everything forward in search of an equaliser, but Slocombe produced a number of key saves, while Accrington’s backline stood firm to see out the game. Manager John Coleman hailed the performance of his team as a "relegation saviour" in the post-match press conference, praising their fighting spirit in the face of adversity. With this victory, Accrington have made a dent in the points gap between themselves and the safety positions, while Colchester must now accept that their promotion ambitions face a tougher path.

Letters from the 1980s unearthed this week reveal a sharply worded plea from Labour MP Geoffrey Dickens to then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan to ban a group described as promoting pedophilia. Published by the UK National Archives, the documents offer a rare insight into the political tensions of the 1980s surrounding public morality, the regulation of activism, and the government’s approach to what were then termed as "extremist" groups. Dickens, known for his progressive stance and social liberal views, took a surprisingly forceful tone in the correspondence. In one letter, he argues that the group in question was not merely engaging in debate but actively enabling criminal activity. "This is not a free-speech issue," he wrote, "but one of public safety and the protection of our most vulnerable citizens." The lawyer-turned-politician accused the group of using legal loopholes and the guise of academic discussion to shield their views, while pushing ideologies that put children at risk. He suggested that the Home Office had a duty to step in under the Public Order Act 1986, which allows the banning of organisations spreading hatred or inciting violence. At the time, Brittan was a key figure in shaping the UK’s legal framework to address racial and political extremism, having led the passage of the Public Order Act. But his government was also sensitive to accusations of state overreach. Records show he replied to Dickens, acknowledging the concerns but expressing caution about the threshold set by the law. "Banning a group is not a measure to be taken lightly," Brittan wrote, "and there must be overwhelming evidence that a group poses a material threat to the public order." Some historians argue the letters reflect a broader debate in the 1980s about the boundaries of free speech and state intervention. At the time, the UK was dealing with the rise of far-right groups and a growing civil society sector, often clashing with the government over the limits of acceptable discourse. The letters resurfaced at a time when similar tensions are being debated once again. Following recent calls for the de-platforming of speakers accused of promoting extremist content, Dickens’ appeal for action has drawn fresh attention. Critics, however, warn against weaponising moral outrage to silence opposing views, a concern that was also raised by some MPs at the time. "The risk of chilling opposition or dissent is real," one govenment adviser wrote in a contemporaneous note.

The lack of contract documentation for two-thirds of Cameroon’s local footballers is raising serious concerns within the country’s football community, with the head of the Cameroonian association of professional footballers (ASPCA) warning that the issue poses a major threat to players' rights and financial security. Pierre Ndaye, the union’s president, has called for urgent action from football authorities to address the alarming statistic, which he claims exposes many players to exploitation and uncertainty. A contract is not just a formality, Ndaye explained, but a vital legal instrument that protects a player’s interests, from salary and playing time to dispute resolution and image rights. “How can a footballer fight for their rights when they don’t even have the contract in their possession? It’s like asking someone to prove their identity without a passport,” he said in a recent statement, highlighting the gravity of the situation. The ASPCA has long campaigned for greater transparency and regulation in the football industry, particularly for players at the domestic level, where many are signed by local clubs with little to no understanding of their employment terms or long-term prospects. Ndaye revealed that the union has already taken steps to enforce its legal mandate under Cameroonian football law, which requires clubs to provide copies to their contracted players. Despite this, many clubs continue to withhold documents, citing bureaucratic hurdles or a general lack of awareness. The Football Association of Cameroon (Fecafoot) and the Ministry of Sports and Youth are now under growing pressure to step in and ensure compliance with national and international football regulations. FIFPro, the world players’ union, has also expressed concern about the issue, noting that a lack of paperwork can lead to player disputes, wrongful transfers, and even legal voids in employment agreements. In a country where football is a passport to international careers, the mismanagement of local contracts could limit the potential of Cameroonian talent. Ndaye pointed to the need for better education around player rights and stronger enforcement of existing laws to protect the future of the sport. “We are not only fighting for our players here — we are protecting the integrity of Cameroonian football as a whole,” he added, urging stakeholders to prioritise the protection of their most valuable asset: the player. With regional tournaments like the Africa Cup of Nations and the prestigious domestic league season approaching, the absence of proper documentation for so many players has never been more urgent to resolve.

Davis reiterates ‘major policy imperative’ of tackling migration in post-Brexit strategy   Brexit Secretary David Davis has reaffirmed the Conservative Party’s long-standing commitment to reducing net migration to the “tens of thousands,” calling it a “major policy imperative” in the UK’s post-Brexit landscape. Speaking in a speech to the Institute for Government on Tuesday, Davis stressed that immigration remains one of the most pressing issues for a Britain seeking to reassert control over its borders following its historic decision to leave the European Union. The pledge to slash net migration to the tens of thousands has been a hallmark of the Conservative Party under Prime Minister Theresa May, who made it a cornerstone of her campaign to regain public trust after the 2016 EU referendum. During the referendum, Leave campaigners famously demanded the UK take back control of its laws and borders, with immigration viewed by many as a central battleground in the political divide of recent years. In his remarks, Davis acknowledged the complexity of achieving the target, which has so far proved elusive, with the Office for National Statistics reporting net migration of 283,000 in the year ending December 2016 — still far above the government’s goal. However, he insisted that reducing migration remained not only possible but essential in shaping a successful Brexit. “We will have the space and flexibility to build a system of immigration that fairly rewards people and promotes economic growth while ensuring that we attract and retain the best people,” Davis said. “That was the promise of Brexit, and that is the path we remain committed to following.” He also sought to counter claims that a stringent approach to migration would damage the UK’s economy, particularly in sectors such as agriculture and healthcare, which currently rely heavily on EU workers. Davis argued that a well-managed immigration system would not only limit the scale of movement but also improve its quality — ensuring that those entering the UK contribute effectively to society and the economy. “The transformation in our relationship with the EU gives us the opportunity to put in place a system that reflects our priorities — economic, social and cultural,” Davis said. He added that the government would be consulting widely with businesses, employers and other stakeholders as it draws up the new system. The speech came as a new survey revealed growing public concern over the pace of reform in the Brexit process, with 63 per cent of respondents in a recent YouGov poll believing that the government is “not making progress” on key areas of negotiation.

The right of UK MPs to be protected from having their official communications intercepted by the security services still stands, but it does not amount to a complete shield against surveillance by intelligence agencies, Amber Rudd has said. In an announcement that has reignited debate over the powers of the state and the rights of parliamentarians, the home secretary clarified that while MPs’ confidential and private communications remain safeguarded by an existing legal framework, this does not prevent the security services from monitoring MPs in circumstances considered to be in the national interest. The assurance came in response to questions following a report that raised concerns over the potential for the security services to target political figures or act independently under the auspices of counterterrorism and intelligence-gathering efforts. Under section 3(2) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA), it is illegal for agencies such as MI5 or MI6 to conduct surveillance on individuals unless the activity is approved by a senior official and deemed necessary. This law, often referred to as the “MPs Rule”, was introduced in the aftermath of the 2009 Wright Report inquiry into the intelligence community’s overreach and was strengthened following the 2013 reform of RIPA. However, MPs and civil liberties groups have long warned that the law does not extend to protect politicians from domestic surveillance if it is carried out in the context of foreign national security – such as intelligence sharing with agencies in the United States or other allied countries. This loophole has led to concerns that MPs could be monitored for political activity or held under investigation as part of counterintelligence operations, even if there is no evidence of suspicious behaviour. The home secretary’s remarks suggest that while the legal protection remains in place, it is not as robust as many MPs and their spokespeople had hoped. “We have a duty to protect national security while ensuring the rights of the public and their elected representatives are respected,” said Ms Rudd. “The law that protects Parliament and the national interest is unambiguous, but it must be balanced with the responsibilities of intelligence agencies to act against threats to the UK.” The clarity provided by the home secretary comes amid fresh scrutiny of the intelligence services following revelations about their increased use of data-mining and digital surveillance over the past decade. Websites and telephone calls with overseas destinations can allow the security services to legally regulate the interception of communications for counterterrorism reasons, with or without the knowledge of the intended party.

Jonny Hayes believes that Niall McGinn could still play a pivotal role in Aberdeen’s future, as the club faces key decisions over the next few months. The Dons vice-captain, Hayes, was quick to reveal his support for McGinn, who has been the subject of speculation over a potential exit in January or at the end of the season, following offers from English Championship clubs. Speaking ahead of Aberdeen's crucial Premiership clash with Celtic at Pittodrie, Hayes insisted that the midfielder remains a key part of the squad, and while there may be options on the table, the door for McGinn to stay is still open. “Niall’s a top player for us. He’s been a massive part of the team and shown that consistently over the years,” Hayes said. “You never know what could happen in January, but I think if the situation stays the same, and I think he wants to stay, he can.” Hayes’ comments come amid growing uncertainty about McGinn’s future, with reports suggesting a move to Brighton and Hove Albion is being actively pursued, even though both the player and the club have remained tight-lipped on the matter. Hayes, however, is keen to focus on the short-term challenges as Aberdeen looks to build on their strong start to the season under new manager Jimmy Thelin. The Dons have already secured two wins from their first three games of the campaign, with McGinn instrumental in both victories. “You can’t control what happens to individual players, but for now, we’re focusing on the job in hand and trying to make someone come in and fit quickly if there’s a change,” Hayes added. “It's not out of our hands, but whatever happens, we want to make sure we carry on the momentum we’ve got.” Hayes also touched on the wider ambitions for the season, echoing Thelin’s determination to finish in the top four of the Premiership and push for European qualification. “That’s the aim, and we’re all confident we can do it. If Niall stays, he’ll play his part. If not, it gives someone else a chance to step up. Either way, we’re looking forward.” McGinn, 32, has been with Aberdeen since 2017 and has long been regarded as a club legend. His absence for any length of time would represent a significant blow to the team's balance and continuity.

Vancouver real estate agent Bryan Yan is riding the wave of a property market boom that has swept the West Coast, with house prices and sales hitting record highs. The city, often described as one of Canada’s most desirable places to live, has become a magnet for both domestic and international investors, spilling over into heated competition among homebuyers and creating an environment where properties are snapped up within hours—even minutes—of being listed. Yan, a seasoned agent with RE/MAX in the city's trendy Kitsilano district, says he has never seen activity like this in his decade-long career. "I just listed a townhome the other day and it had four offers within two hours, all over the asking price," he said. "It's surreal. You put up one listing, and the phone just doesn’t stop ringing." The rally in the Vancouver real estate market has been driven by a cocktail of factors. Tight local housing inventory is one, as new construction struggles to keep pace with demand. But much of the momentum comes from Canada’s booming technology sector, which is attracting high-earning professionals looking for homes in a city known for its culture, climate, and outdoor lifestyle. Added to this is a steady flow of international buyers, particularly from China and other Asian markets, many of whom view property in Vancouver as a stable—and appreciating—investment against the backdrop of economic uncertainty at home. According to data from the Real Estate Board of Greater Vancouver (REBGV), home sales in the region rose by 4.8 per cent in the first week of April alone compared to the previous month, with an average price of over CAD$1.2 million for a detached home. Some hotter-than-average neighbourhoods, including the West End and Yaletown, have seen average prices climb past the two-million-dollar mark. While the buyers are competing fiercely, landlords are also watching closely. Property tax increases and new regulations introduced by the provincial and municipal governments have added to the cost of holding property, especially for investors. Burgundy Poole, a renter in Vancouver for over five years, told the  Globe and Mail  that finding an affordable rental has become increasingly difficult. “I’m paying CAD$2,800 a month for a one-bedroom with no pets allowed and no parking—my cousins in Toronto pay half that for a similar place,” she said. Despite the rising tide of prices and concerns about affordability, Yan says the market shows no signs of slowing.

Froome Remains in Yellow as Kittel Dominates Stage Six   Britain’s Chris Froome retained the leader’s yellow jersey at the Tour de France after a thrilling sixth stage, won by Marcel Kittel in a blistering sprint finish. The 216-kilometre route from Cagnes-sur-Mer to Saint-Raphaël, often dubbed the “sixth day of peace” due to its typically flat terrain, once again played host to a high-octane show of pure speed, with Kittel claiming his first victory of the 2024 edition and underlining his status as the sprinter to beat on the flats. The day unfolded mostly as expected, with a breakaway of six riders getting off the front in the early stages, but unable to hold a significant advantage. The peloton, well-prepared and tightly controlled by the teams of the general classification (GC) contenders, gradually reeled them in with around 50km to go. The pace in the main field increased in the final 20km as teams positioned their sprinters for the inevitable conclusion. Kittel, riding for Team DSM, powered into the final straight with his team working tirelessly up front to set him up for a clean run. The German, who has won this stage on three previous occasions, showed why he remains a staple of sprint stages, launching a strong burst of acceleration just as the chequered flag came into view. His victory was confirmed by a narrow margin, as Silvan Dillier and Mark Cavendish made late surges in what was a full house for the top sprinters vying for the stage honours. For Froome, the stage is a continued opportunity to preserve the yellow jersey as the race heads into its mid-point. The four-time Tour winner, riding for Ineos Grenadiers, remained near the head of the peloton throughout, and even gained valuable seconds thanks to some aggressive pacing by his team up the final false flat stretch. “There are always risks when you put your head down,” Froome said after the stage. “But we’re not here to chase sprint stages — we’re here for the overall classifications. We’re keeping our eyes on the Tour as a whole.” With two more flat stages ahead before the first mountainous challenges begin, the pressure on Froome and the GC riders remains minimal for the time being. However, with Kittel reminding the peloton of his form and teams loosening lineups, the days between now and the Pyrenees could offer further fireworks.

The eagerly anticipated World Boxing Organisation (WBO) light-heavyweight title challenge featuring Nathan Cleverly has been abruptly postponed after champion Juergen Braehmer sustained an eye injury during training. The announcement comes as a major blow to both fans and fighters, with Cleverly having prepared extensively for the bout, set to take place in Manchester on Saturday. Braehmer, the 35-year-old German champion known for his resilience and tactical prowess, was injured during routine sparring in the final week of his preparations. The nature of the injury has yet to be disclosed in full, but initial reports suggest it is significant enough to prevent him from contesting the championship belt in the near future. A statement from the WBO confirmed that Braehmer would be ruled out of competition for an "indefinite period," with no specific date given for the rescheduling of the event. For Cleverly, the 26-year-old Welsh boxer, the setback is undoubtedly frustrating, but he appears to accept the decision with a stoic resolve. Statements from his camp have been calm, with Cleverly's promoter, Eddie Hearn, acknowledging that "the health and safety of all fighters is of utmost importance" and that the necessary steps are being taken to reschedule the bout as soon as possible. The postponement also highlights the unpredictability of boxing, where even the most meticulously planned events can fall victim to unforeseen circumstances. It marks yet another delay in the careers of both men—Cleverly has previously been denied a world title opportunity due to similar last-minute cancellations, while Braehmer has endured a long reign at the top of the division, oddly uninterrupted by title holder retirements or changes. The WBO has confirmed it is in talks with Braehmer's team to assess the long-term implications of his injury and the date for the next possible fight. Until then, boxing fans will have to wait for another chance to see Cleverly step into the ring for his shot at the title. For now, the dream of a high-stakes Welsh showdown lies in wait, suspended indefinitely. Damage was being confined to the pocket, but there is no waiting on hope. We hope to have a replacement soon. Let’s monitor the space closely with this development. In fact, we must bear in mind, no fight lost is a fight lost. This delay may yet turn out to go Cleverly’s way if the rescheduled bout gives him the extra edge he needs after months of preparation.

Seventeen-year-old Agnes (not her real name) was forced into marriage just three months ago to a man she had never met, becoming another face in the growing crisis of child marriages in parts of the UK. Now living with her new husband in a modest flat in the north-west of England, Agnes describes a life in limbo—caught between a past she is desperate to escape and a future that seems hopelessly out of reach. Her story, though tragic, is far from unique. Behind the scenes of ordinary British towns and cities, a quiet epidemic of underage marriages continues to go underreported and under-addressed. Agnes was not given a choice. According to local council records, she was taken from school and told she was going on a visit to see an uncle. Instead, she was flown to Pakistan and wed to a man 18 years her senior. He is now said to be the father of four other children, two of whom are born of arranged marriages. When she returned to the UK, she was in tears and profoundly confused. “I didn’t even know who he was. I was told he was my ‘blessing’ and that if I didn’t comply, my family would disown me,” said one of her close friends, who, for her safety, wished to remain anonymous. Agnes is believed to be among hundreds of girls at risk of being married abroad under UK law, which does not prevent children from being married overseas unless the parents are aware of the arrangements. Statistics from the UK Home Office show a steady rise in cases of child marriage, with the majority involving girls from South Asian communities, though the scale of the problem remains unclear due to a lack of centralised data and underreporting. Campaigners have called for urgent action, saying that the current system allows vulnerable young women to be groomed, coerced and discarded with little to no support. “We are seeing girls disappearing from school and communities worrying about what happens next,” said Zara Patel, a child rights advocate with the Islamic Council of the UK. Parents, too, are often trapped in a Catch-22—pressured by family expectations, cultural traditions or economic hardship to make decisions that put their daughters at risk. “Sometimes they truly believe they are doing the right thing,” Patel added. “But no child should be forced into a lifelong commitment like that.”

Security will be increased at polling stations across the UK as voters prepare to cast their ballots in Thursday’s general election, following the terror attack in London on Wednesday. The attack, which has yet to be claimed by any specific group, has led to heightened concerns across the country and prompted the government to respond swiftly to reassure the public that all necessary precautions are in place to protect the democratic process. In the wake of the attack, ministers confirmed that armed police and counter-terrorism units would be deployed at key locations across the country, including outside polling stations. It is understood that local police forces will also be given the flexibility to increase patrols in areas of high public concern. Home Secretary Suella Braverman addressed the media on Wednesday night, stating the government’s commitment to ensuring "the safety and security of every citizen" as they exercise their democratic rights. “The attack was a senseless act of violence, but it will not be allowed to disrupt the will of the British people,” Braverman said, adding that prime minister Rishi Sunak had taken immediate steps to bolster security for the election. The attack, which occurred near the Houses of Parliament, claimed the life of a security officer and left several others injured. The man responsible was shot dead by police after a short chase. While early investigations suggest no direct links to previous terror plots, the incident has naturally raised concerns about the potential for further attacks during the politically sensitive period of the election, which is set to confirm whether Sunak’s Conservative party maintains power or if Keir Starmer’s Labour party will form the next government. The Electoral Commission has also issued reassurances to voters, reminding them that voting is a safe and secure process. Local authorities are being urged to communicate with their communities in the coming days and to be mindful of any unusual activity near polling stations. Labour leader Keir Starmer expressed his condolences to the victims and the families of those affected by the attack. In a statement issued by his office, he said: “This is a dark day for the UK, but we must not allow fear to dictate our actions. Democracy is our strength, and we will show resilience by turning out in large numbers to vote for a better future.” With the general election being one of the most closely watched in recent years, the added security measures come at a critical juncture.

British planetary scientist Colin Pillinger, who became an iconic figure in the UK space community for his visionary attempt to land a spacecraft on Mars, has died at the age of 70, his family announced on Monday. Pillinger, who led the £60 million Beagle 2 mission — a UK-led effort to deploy a lander on the Red Planet — was a passionate advocate for British involvement in space exploration. Though the mission ultimately failed to confirm a successful landing on Christmas Day 2003, it earned widespread admiration for its ambition and the fervent public support it generated. Born in Belfast in 1954, Pillinger joined the Open University in 1989 as a professor of planetary sciences, where he became known not only for his academic work but also for his ability to inspire the public about the wonders of the cosmos. A former pipe-smoking chemist turned space visionary, he used his storytelling flair and bohemian style to capture the British imagination at a time when the country had limited involvement in Europe’s space programme. The Beagle 2 mission was a highlight of his career and, despite its technical setbacks, it played a pivotal role in putting the UK on the map in the world of planetary exploration. The lander, which was deployed on board the European Space Agency’s Mars Express orbiter, was never confirmed as successfully operating on Mars, but experts later confirmed, through satellite images, that it had indeed touched down. Pillinger was at the height of his public profile during the Christmas 2003 launch period, when he appeared on television and in the press, garnering both celebrity and criticism. Some scientists were wary of his high-profile role in the mission, but most respected his determination to push the boundaries of UK science. His legacy includes not only the Beagle 2 but also his efforts to cultivate a new generation of space enthusiasts and scientists. Tributes have begun to pour in for Pillinger, with many highlighting his pioneering spirit and the warmth he brought to space science. A former colleague at the Open University described him as “a man who believed in big dreams and never backed down from a challenge.” Friends and family said Pillinger had continued to work closely with students and students and researchers until his recent illness took hold. His passing marks the end of a truly remarkable chapter in the story of British science.

In a remote corner of Utah’s desert, where the sun beats down relentlessly and the landscape stretches out like an ancient time capsule, scientists have unearthed a remarkable discovery that promises to redraw the map of our understanding of the Mesozoic era. A new species of dinosaur has been described, one so unusual in its anatomy and evolutionary lineage that it has left experts both stunned and exhilarated. Dubbed   Vesperhorus rex   — “king of the twilight” in Latin — the dinosaur appears to be a previously unknown member of the theropod family, distinguished by a unique blend of physical traits and what researchers are calling an “enigmatic ecological niche.” The remains, uncovered during a months-long dig led by a team from the University of Utah in partnership with the Royal Tyrrell Museum in Alberta, Canada, were found within the rich geological formations of the Cedar Mountain Basin.
