In a move that is certainly not lacking in attention-grabbing charm, Wales is launching a promising initiative set to ease public bathroom scarcity across the nation. As many have learned the hard way, finding a public toilet can feel as elusive as spotting mythical creatures. With this in mind, councils in Wales are stepping up to the plate — or should we say the loo — to address one of the most pressing yet often overlooked aspects of public infrastructure. The Welsh Government has announced a new policy aimed at ensuring that local authorities provide easier access to public toilets, especially in rural and tourist-heavy areas. The initiative, which follows years of complaints from the public and campaigns led by groups such as the Toilet Map Wales campaign, marks a significant shift toward prioritizing community comfort and inclusiveness. The new guidance, issued under the Public Information about Toilets (PIT) scheme, compels councils to ensure that maps of local accessible and public toilets are available in both digital and printed formats. This means, no matter if you’re a local returning after a long night at the pub, or a tourist exploring Wales' scenic landscapes for the first time, you will be one click or sign away from relief. Councillor Julie James, the Welsh Minister for Equalities and Local Government, expressed her support for the initiative, saying: “Everyone should have access to clean, safe, and accessible public toilets. We want Wales to be at the forefront of progress, making life easier and more comfortable for all." The move comes as part of a broader government initiative to promote accessibility and sustainability across public services, and the timing feels just right. According to a 2023 survey by the Welsh Local Government Association, over 40% of respondents in Wales reported difficulties finding public toilets at least once in the past year — a significant number about which many are finally ready to talk. Local authorities are now expected to begin updating signage and digital platforms this month, with the first noticeable improvements expected by the end of the year. The Council for Public Toilet Access and Hygiene (CPTH), which campaigns for better public restrooms, has welcomed the move as a ‘defining moment’ in the country’s plumbing history. Stay tuned as this promising new chapter in Welsh public safety unfolds, and perhaps next time your urgent need strikes during a walk through the Brecon Beacons, you’ll find the solution swiftly and cleanly at the end of a go-to guide map — provided, of course, your phone doesn’t go into power-saving mode.

This week, as teenagers across England gear up for the official release of their A-level and GCSE exam results—the first real return to normality for many after two years of pandemic disruption—the government has launched a pre-emptive salvo in the ongoing Brexit debate. The timing is no coincidence. With the education sector bracing for the rush of results and university admissions, the Department for Exiting the European Union has published a series of government papers on the future of Brexit policy, reviving the familiar back-to-school feeling of new rules, assessments and, for some, anxiety and uncertainty. The documents reveal the government’s latest thinking on bilateral trade agreements with key international partners, fisheries agreements, and the phased implementation of new customs arrangements post transition period. But rather than being celebrated like well-received exam results, these papers have sparked immediate controversy, with critics calling them "scattered", "confusing", and "dangerously vague". One paper in particular, outlining proposed new agricultural standards post-Brexit, has drawn sharp rebukes from farming unions, who argue that the moves will lead to increased costs and regulatory burdens. Meanwhile, the EU has expressed concern that the UK is still failing to provide clear, actionable information on its future regulatory framework, calling the government’s position “a step back from constructive engagement”. Education ministers meanwhile are hoping the focus remains on young people. With hundreds of thousands of students about to see whether their grades will allow them to pursue their chosen careers, the government is keen to avoid a re-run of the 2020 fiasco when algorithm-driven results sparked widespread protests. However, with discussions of Brexit continuing to dominate government headlines, the Department for Education has issued an internal memo urging schools and universities to prepare for “heightened public and media scrutiny” as both key sectors navigate the most unpredictable academic year in living memory. While the government insists these papers are part of an ongoing consultation and not final policy, the publication has triggered renewed calls from opposition parties, business leaders, and legal experts for a clearer strategy on Brexit. As education settings prepare to welcome students with open arms next week, the country is still waiting to see whether the government’s own marks will be waiting on a docket. As one senior MP put it: “We’re always trying to catch up with the exam paper.” The next week, as students receive their grades, will be another test of the government's ability to balance competing priorities—and perhaps, more importantly, to stop Brexit overshadowing the education system’s long-awaited return to normality.

There is "no truth" in allegations that a former chief constable visited a children's home to abuse boys, a court has heard. The claims, which have caused widespread alarm and anguish among victims of historical abuse, were dismissed by the defendant, Sir Alan Griffiths, as the latest in what he called a "campaign of character assassination". The case is being heard at Westminster Magistrates’ Court as part of an ongoing judicial review into how the police investigated historical abuse claims, with Mr Griffiths accused of using his position of influence to cover up wrongdoing. The allegations stem from testimony provided by a former care leaver during a separate inquiry into past abuse at Careby House, a children's home in the north-west of England. The witness, now in his 60s, described a visit by Mr Griffiths to the home in the early 1980s, during which he was allegedly present when the former inspector interacted with younger residents in an "inappropriate" manner. He claimed that this happened in the absence of staff, and that Mr Griffiths spent an unusual amount of time in private with the boys. However, details of the visit were not independently verifiable at the time, and police concluded their initial inquiry with no further action. During the court hearing on Wednesday, Sir Alan’s legal team countered the claims, stating that Mr Griffiths had “never visited the home unaccompanied, and certainly not in the manner the witness described.” The barrister, Emily Patel QC, said: “These allegations are not only false but appear to be made in bad faith, perhaps someone looking to deflect attention from the real failures of the system.” The case is part of a broader reckoning with how historical abuse in state-funded and faith-based institutions was handled in the UK. Over the past two decades, thousands of survivors have come forward to allege mistreatment, often at the hands of authoritative figures like those in the judiciary, religious orders, and the police. The government has faced intense criticism for dismissing, downplaying, or hiding such incidents for years. Earlier this year, the Prime Minister issued a formal apology for the “catastrophic failure of the state” to protect children in care. As such, the court proceedings being held now are not only about individual accountability but also about the systemic failures of justice and institutional neglect that allowed such abuse to occur. Mr Griffiths, 76, was a senior police figure from the 1970s until his retirement in the early 2000s, overseeing major reform efforts in the north-west.

Amid a spate of high-profile fights in the business world — from corporate grudges to public Twitter spats — one New York-based hedge fund, often known for its aggressive investment style, has thrown more than a few punches in recent weeks. Voyager Capital, a firm managing over $4 billion in assets, has found itself in the centre of a growing storm of controversy, with tensions spilling over into courtrooms, boardrooms, and the headlines. A savvy player in niche markets, Voyager has long taken a hard-nosed approach to its investments, but recent actions have raised questions about the firm's methods — and whether its aggressive tactics now threaten to leave lasting damage to its reputation. The trouble began when Voyager, led by founder and CEO Richard dela Torre, filed a surprise lawsuit against a long-time portfolio company last month, accusing the firm of "fraudulent mismanagement and a reckless disregard for shareholder value." The lawsuit, alleging financial misconduct worth hundreds of millions of dollars, has rocked the normally quiet world of mid-market private equity. Several sources close to the firm tell the Financial Times that the lawsuit is the most aggressive legal move Voyager has ever taken against one of its own investments — a company it had proudly backed for two years. What makes the case particularly unusual is that Voyager is still one of its largest shareholders. Legal experts have questioned whether such a firm should so publicly challenge a company it still stakes a claim in. “It's a high-risk strategy,” said Professor Emily Langridge, a corporate law expert at Columbia Law School. “You either catch the wrongdoers in the act — or you end up looking like a vulture circling your own investments.” Voyager’s recent tactics have not gone unnoticed by regulators and politicians, either. A newly launched congressional inquiry is reportedly looking into whether hedge funds are exploiting legal loopholes to “strong-arm” smaller firms under their wings. The inquiry, led by Democrats on the House Financial Services Committee, is expected to focus on whether investors have been unfairly pressured to exit their stakes or modify their share agreements. Critics of Voyager have likened the firm to a financial heavyweight, throwing its weight around in a way that little players can’t afford. “You can’t be a player of Voyager’s size and take lunches to a little company one week and sue their brains out the next,” said Jack Monroe, a former hedge fund lawyer and CEO of govtwatch.org. Dela Torre, for his part, has bristled at the comparisons.

As the Euro 2016 finals drew closer, thousands of supporters from across Europe flocked to France in anticipation of the sporting spectacle. Among the most ardent were supporters from Northern Ireland, whose passionate following was expected to swell the ranks of fans across the host nation. With flights, accommodation arrangements and travel visas all in place, it became evident that a coherent and robust support system was necessary to manage the needs of Ulster fans making the long journey. A notable feature of Northern Ireland's attendance at the event was the presence of a dedicated diplomatic team, ready to assist with any logistical issues or emergencies that could arise when so many people travel under one passionate banner. The British government, united with the expertise of Northern Ireland's local government, formed a working group ahead of the tournament to look after the needs of fans and to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for supporters who had saved for months, and in some cases years, for the chance to watch their national team on the European stage. This was more than just a diplomatic gesture; for many fans, the trip to France was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. The support team, stationed in key locations like Paris and Nantes, aimed to provide a consistent line of communication between the fans and the host nation. Whether it was lost passports, translation services or simply pointing fans in the direction of where the team was playing next, the diplomatic presence was seen as vital. Local MPs and civil servants worked in tandem with British diplomatic staff to set up hotlines and appointment systems, ensuring Northern Ireland fans could reach out with confidence. The diplomatic services also co-ordinated with French authorities and the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) to facilitate a secure and friendly reception for supporters. This initiative was praised by politicians and community leaders in Northern Ireland, who spoke of the importance of maintaining good relations abroad while supporting the team. One such supporter, David McAllister from Derry, said the support was “invaluable,” particularly for those unaccustomed to international travel. “You don’t just want to be screaming your head off at the matches. You want to know someone is looking out for you if things go wrong,” he said. The team's performance on the pitch had as much to do with the behind-the-scenes diplomacy as it did with the players on the field.

Fresh doubts have emerged over the £18bn nuclear power plant project at Hinkley Point, Somerset, spearheaded by the French energy giant EDF, as concerns about the scheme's viability intensify. The long-awaited development, which was first announced more than a decade ago, is seen as a cornerstone of the UK’s energy future and a pivotal step in meeting net-zero emissions targets. But recent reports and internal documents obtained by UK energy correspondents suggest that EDF is once again questioning the financial and technological risks of the venture, casting a shadow over one of the largest private infrastructure projects in the country's history. At the heart of the issue is the escalating cost of building the twin reactors at Hinkley Point C. The project, originally estimated to cost £16bn, has seen its price tag balloon to £18bn amid delays, supply chain disruptions and rising material costs. EDF, which has long argued that the project is critical for energy security and decarbonisation, has now reportedly informed the UK government that it could not guarantee the plant would ever become viable without additional state-backed guarantees or renegotiated cost frameworks. One source close to the project said the firm is exploring “all options” including the potential for short-term power purchase agreements to mitigate risks and allow for a gradual payoff over time. The possibility of revisiting the financial terms of the project has sparked immediate backlash from UK politicians and industry leaders. Environment Secretary Steve Double called the project a “national priority” and demanded that EDF and the government work together to “deliver the plant on time and on budget.” Tory MPs have accused the French firm of lacking commitment, while business leaders have warned that any further setbacks could undermine investor confidence in the UK's ability to deliver major energy projects. Critics of the project, meanwhile, argue that the government should be focusing on cheaper and faster renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, rather than continuing to prop up expensive nuclear ventures. Greenpeace UK recently published a report highlighting how £18bn spent on offshore wind development could provide enough clean energy for 20 million homes, far exceeding the capacity of any planned nuclear project. The Hinkley Point project has long been entangled in political and financial controversies. Originally signed off under the coalition government with a guaranteed price of £92.50 per megawatt-hour—three times the current market rate—the deal became a source of contention between the UK and France.

The British and Irish Lions kept their World Cup-winning ambitions on track with a dominant display against the Rebels in Melbourne, easing through the first hurdle of their warm-up fixtures with a comfortable win that underscored their pre-Tour build-up preparations. The 25-point victory over a weakened Australian outfit signaled a marked improvement in the Lions' form and gave fans every reason to believe they can challenge the Wallabies in the upcoming second Test in Sydney. Melbourne’s ambitious AAMI Park, which will host this year’s Rugby World Cup final, watched as tourists Liam Hey, Owen Farrell and Sam Warburton set the tone early in the match with clinical execution and physicality. The Lions, coached by Warren Gatland, appeared to have the edge in both set-piece discipline and execution across the park, leaving the home side struggling to match their intensity. Ten tries, to the Rebels’ two, reflected the one-sided nature of the contest. Warburton was at the heart of the Lions' dynamic approach, orchestrating much of the backfield play in his usual commanding fashion. The Welsh captain, who has emerged as a key leader in the pack, praised the team’s work ethic and adaptability following the match. "We showed today that we're ready for the challenge ahead," Warburton said. "It's important we keep building momentum as we move closer to the Test series. The Test match environment is completely different, but these warm-ups help us find our rhythm." The match, billed as a test of preparation and resilience for the Lions, offered little in the way of resistance from the Rebels, whose line-up was missing several top-tier players due to a mix of injury and selection. Australian coach Trent Barrett admitted his squad had been outclassed and acknowledged the Lions’ superiority in both talent and tactical execution. "It was a tough game for us," Barrett said. "The Lions had everything going for them — skill, power, and momentum. We know we've got a lot of work to do to match that standard in the series proper." For the Lions, the result was more than just a win — it was a statement. Gatland, who has led the squad to two previous Test series victories in the last decade, will be encouraged by the side’s apparent cohesiveness and hunger to prove themselves on the world stage. With the Six Nations behind them and the upcoming three-Test series against the Wallabies rapidly approaching, the Lions are sending a warning to the rugby world.

Labour leader Ed Miliband has claimed that the party’s second-place finish in the European elections demonstrates promising progress for the Labour Party, even as he admitted there is “further to go” before Labour can fully revive its fortunes. The result bucked recent trends that have seen Labour struggle to shake off the legacy of its 2015 general election defeat at the hands of the Conservatives. Miliband asserted that the European elections have been a turning point for Labour, with gains in key regions across England, including the Midlands and the North. Speaking at a press conference in London, the Labour leader said: “This result shows that the public trust is returning to our party. We are united, we are listening, and we are ready to fight for working people in Britain.” Labour’s improved performance came as a surprise to many political commentators, who had expected the party to continue its recent decline in national popularity. A string of local elections had left Labour facing a difficult summer, with heavy losses to both the Liberal Democrats and UKIP in some regions. However, the European election results tell a slightly different story, with Labour outperforming expectations and finishing ahead of the Liberal Democrats and the Greens. Despite the progress, Miliband was careful not to overstate the result. He acknowledged that turnout was relatively low in the European elections—traditionally uninspiring to voters—and that the result is not a clear indication of Labour’s standing in the next general election. “This is a step in the right direction, but not the finish line,” he said. “We need to keep building, keep listening, and keep delivering for people who are tired of a government that is out of touch.” The leader also used the opportunity to criticise Prime Minister Theresa May and her government’s approach to public services, welfare, and Brexit. “People are worried about the cost of living, the broken NHS, and the future of our education system. Our vision is for a better future—a more fair and just society—and that is exactly the future people want for their children,” he said. The European elections have seen turnout rise across the UK as concern over Brexit intensifies, and many political parties have stepped up their campaigning efforts. For Labour, however, the key challenge remains to convert this regional improvement into a national resurgence ahead of the next general election.

This week promises a politically charged atmosphere as the UK’s longest-awaited public vote moves a significant step closer to reality. At the heart of it all is the decision by Parliament to set 23 June as the date for the EU referendum—a move that will finally put to rest months, even years, of speculation and uncertainty. The ruling party’s majority provided the necessary backing, with the government declaring victory in its bid to secure the date. Yet, even with that hurdle seemingly cleared, the debate around this historic event has barely paused for breath. Meanwhile, in another major development, fresh questions are being raised about the powers of the UK’s intelligence services. Following recent leaks and prior to the upcoming referendum, ministers and MPs are reportedly under pressure to debate whether MI5, MI6 and GCHQ should be granted new legal authority to expand their surveillance and investigative tactics. The move comes in response to evolving threats and in the wake of a series of high-profile terror attacks both at home and abroad, but it is already sparking fierce debate over the balance between national security and civil liberties. With the intelligence bill set to be debated this week, the public will be watching closely—especially as the controversy surrounding the extent of surveillance powers continues to divide opinions in Parliament and beyond. The political stakes are only further heightened by the fact that this debate is unfolding during one of the most pivotal moments in modern British history. As referendum campaigning heats up, experts, commenters and the public themselves are grappling with a growing set of interconnected issues—international tensions, national identity, the role of the UK within the global community, and what that means in an age of technological surveillance. Adding to the mix, opposition parties are already making fresh demands for clarity and transparency from the government as the countdown to 23 June accelerates. With Prime Minister David Cameron about to make his key campaign speeches and the Leave campaign ramping up its efforts, the coming week sets the stage for another round of high-octane political theatre. At the crossroads of domestic legislation and international uncertainty, the UK stands at a defining moment—and with so much at stake, the weeks ahead could not be more critical. This is no ordinary week in British politics. This is the run-up to a vote that could reshape the country’s future.

Wales and Toulon skipper Leigh Halfpenny has officially confirmed his switch to French club Toulon, marking a new chapter in the career of one of rugby’s most decorated full-backs. The announcement comes as a shock to many in the Welsh rugby community, where Halfpenny has long been considered a national treasure. The 33-year-old, who has earned an impressive 97 caps for Wales and helped lift the 2019 Rugby World Cup, will now focus on his club career after deciding not to sign a new deal with his current team, the Blues, when his current contract expires this summer. Halfpenny’s move to Toulon, one of France’s most high-profile and historic rugby clubs, will see him reunite with experienced heads such as fly-half Mike Phillips and experienced forwards like Juan Imhoff. Toulon, who have a proud record in European rugby and a history of assembling world-class sides, wasted no time in announcing the signing of the Welsh star. Club president Mourad Boudjellal expressed his delight at securing Halfpenny’s signature, stating that he sees the player as a key addition to a squad rebuilding under new management after recent relegation to the French second division. A Wales rugby legend, Halfpenny has enjoyed a successful career on the international stage. His pinpoint boot from the tee is among the best in the business, and his contributions in both Tests and domestic competitions have been instrumental in Welsh victories. Despite his international heroics, his club career has seen mixed fortunes at times, with stints in both Wales and in France for Clermont Auvergne, a club he represented during a successful Champions Cup-winning campaign in 2018. The Welsh Rugby Union has yet to make a formal statement regarding Halfpenny’s departure from the professional ranks in Wales, but it is understood that the national side will be keen to retain him for future Test fixtures. Head coach Warren Gatland has praised Halfpenny’s dedication, stating that the player will always be “a vital part of the Welsh set-up”. In a personal statement, Halfpenny said he believed it was the right time to focus on his club game and “push for success on the field at the highest level with a club I truly respect”. He also thanked the Blues, the Welsh fans, and the Wales selectors for their support during his domestic career. “Wales will always be my rugby home, but I am excited for the challenge of Toulon and what the future might hold,” he added.

A giant sixgill shark, suspected to be the largest of its kind ever caught on a fishing line in Europe, has been reeled in off the coast of County Clare, Ireland, sparking both excitement and superstition among local anglers and marine experts. The enormous creature, described as a "monster" by those present, was reportedly battling on the line for over an hour before it was finally brought aboard the fishing boat. The shark measured an estimated 5.5 metres in length and weighed around 600 kilograms, dwarfing the typical size of its species. Sixgill sharks are deep-water fish, rarely encountered by fishermen due to their preference for the dark, colder waters of the Atlantic. This particular specimen is the largest sixgill ever successfully caught using a rod and reel in Europe, according to the International Game Fish Association (IGFA), the global authority on world fishing records. The fish was caught by local angler John O’Connor and his team during a routine deep-sea fishing trip in the waters off the rugged coast of the Burren. “I’ve fished these waters for 30 years, but I’ve never seen anything like this,” O’Connor said. “It was like fighting a land-based storm at sea. The only thing on my mind was making sure we didn’t lose it.” Following its capture, the shark was carefully measured and photographed before being released back into the ocean, much to the relief of marine conservationists. “It’s fantastic to see the fish released in good condition,” said Liam Murphy, a marine biology expert from the Galway Marine Research Institute. “Sixgill sharks are extremely important to the marine ecosystem. Catching and releasing is a responsible approach and crucial for maintaining their populations.” Locals in the Clifden village where the incident occurred are buzzing with talk about the “Burren Leviathan,” with some claiming it is an omen or even that it came from the mythical realm of the fae hidden beneath the surface of the landscape. Poetic local tradition often generates such tales, with many attributing extraordinary creatures to the deep waters of the Atlantic. The Irish government has stepped in to assess the record-verified details of the catch and will submit the data to the IGFA for official confirmation. In the meantime, the video footage of the fishing expedition has gone viral on social media, amassing thousands of views and goading viewers on both sides of the Atlantic to wonder – just what else might be lurking in the depths between Ireland and the continent?

Serena Williams has brushed off the weight of history as she prepares for her latest challenge at the Australian Open, stating she will not let the potential to surpass Steffi Graf’s all-time Grand Slam record distract her on the court. The 23-time major champion, currently tied with Graf at 22 titles, is aiming for her second straight Australian Open crown, and with it, the chance to become tennis’s most decorated female player of all time. Speaking ahead of the tournament’s start in Melbourne, Williams, 40, expressed a focus not on records, but on performance and the present moment. “I’ve worked too hard, sacrificed too much to let the numbers distract me,” she said. “My job is to play my best, stay healthy and trust that the results will fall into place.” The German left-hander Graf achieved her 22 Grand Slam singles titles across the 1980s and 90s, a feat once considered unbreakable. But Williams has redefined longevity in the sport in recent years, combining power and agility in a way few have managed before. Her most recent Grand Slam title came in the 2021 Australian Open, and with upcoming tournaments in the short season, Williams is in position to move to the top of the pile—if she can navigate the physical and mental challenges of another Grand Slam campaign. Williams is already considered one of the greatest competitors in tennis history, with a career spanning almost three decades and an impact that has transcended the sport. Still, the opportunity to officially surpass Graf—particularly in the context of someone who once called her “the greatest of my generation”—is not one that can be easily ignored. “My main motivation is my family and my team being proud of me,” Williams added. “If moving past Steffi happens, I’m sure I’ll be standing on the other side of this [court], looking up and thinking, ‘Wow, that’s some legacy.’” As the tennis world shifts in to celebration mode, Williams’ opponents will certainly be less concerned with history and more with how the American performs on the court. With any fresh setbacks needing to be overcome, the road to 23 could still prove to be as challenging as ever. But for Serena, as with always, the game begins with one point at a time. And that’s exactly how she plans to play it. The Australian Open promises go down as one of the most eagerly anticipated events of the season—and could very well be the stage upon which a new chapter of tennis history is written.

The Labour Party is facing a moment of existential crisis, with its very survival hanging in the balance unless the escalating leadership row is resolved, according to veteran Labour MP Wayne David. Speaking exclusively to  The Guardian  on Monday, the Caerphilly Representative described the current state of the party as being at a "crucial point" in its long and storied history. David, one of Labour’s most senior voices on matters of party unity, said that unless internal divisions — particularly over the credibility and conduct of current shadow cabinet members — were addressed, the party could "cease to exist as a credible political force in Britain". His remarks come amid growing tensions within the Labour Party over who is fit to lead and who is to blame for its recent electoral losses and fall in public trust. The party has already seen a number of high-profile resignations, demands for the expulsion of members, and increasingly open criticisms between the left and right wings of the party. David highlighted the damage done by internal discord, which he argues has not only inflamed public perceptions of Labour, but also eroded its ability to present a united front in the House of Commons and in the country as a whole. "When we start turning on each other in public — calling one another names and conspiring in the press — the public lose trust in us," David said. "They then look at us and say, 'Why would I want a party that can't even govern itself to govern me?'" His comments reflect wider frustrations within the Labour establishment about the party's failure to heal after the 2019 election wipeout, which saw its vote share drop to its lowest level since 1832. Since then, internal fractures have deepened over the leadership of Keir Starmer — with key figures in the party feeling either alienated by his centrist approach or concerned about the severity of his disciplinary measures. "We need leaders not partisanship," David continued. "Labour is a party for working people. That means we need to look like a party for working people — not a group of activists bickering in cafes and editorials." He stressed that while internal democracy is vital, it must be balanced with unity and a shared vision. "There are no grand plans with chaos," he said. "We must settle this dispute, not only for our sake, but for the sake of the countless people who go to bed on a cold night and vote for a real alternative."

Police forces across the United Kingdom have paid a total of at least £22 million to informants over the past five years, according to new figures obtained by BBC Radio 5 Live through a freedom of information request. The data reveal a widespread use of cash incentives to extract information from individuals connected to criminal activity, raising questions about ethical concerns and the potential for abuse within the system. The disclosure comes amid growing scrutiny of how police forces prioritize resources and whether the payments represent value for money or serve as a means of incentivizing informants whose records suggest questionable reliability or links to criminal networks. The figures also highlight the vast disparity in spending between constabularies, with some forces investing millions in informant networks, while others allocate significantly less. According to the data, some informants received six-figure sums, with one being paid £747,000 to provide information between 2017 and 2022. Others were paid far less—just a few hundred pounds—relating to much lower-level tips or intelligence in isolated cases. Home Office guidelines advise that payments should be proportionate to the value of the intelligence offered, but critics argue that the system can often be exploited, particularly in areas where criminal culture persists or where individuals see their informer status as a way to avoid prosecution. The payments are not considered wages or financial penalties, but rather “compensation” for information shared with authorities. Under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, officers must follow strict criteria when engaging with informants, ensuring their identity remains confidential and the information they provide is deemed credible and in the public interest. However, the sheer scale of the payouts has led to calls for greater transparency and oversight. The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners recently called for an independent review of the informant payment system, stating that the current arrangements are not fit for the 21st century. “The use of informants should be robustly justified and publicly accountable,” it said. “There are real concerns that, in some cases, the payments are being used to secure intelligence at significant public expense without sufficient effectiveness or oversight.” MHCLG spokesperson said: “The accurate and responsible use of informants is an important operational tool in policing. Police forces are expected to ensure their use is appropriate and value for money. We regulate the use of informants and are committed to reviewing best practice.”

Volvo’s chief executive, Håkan Samuelsson, finds himself at the heart of a curious and increasingly publicised debate when he is asked to respond to mounting pressure over the future of the traditional combustion engine. Instead of offering a definitive answer, Samuelsson opts to turn the question back on those posing it, challenging the timing, the expectations and, in essence, the broader assumptions surrounding the transition to electric vehicles. In an interview published this week, Samuelsson was asked when — or if — Volvo would abandon petrol and diesel engines entirely. His response, as it often is, was not to present a rigid timeline or a black-and-white decision. Instead, he asked, “What are you expecting from us?” The remark sparked both intrigue and irritation, with some commentators suggesting that the CEO was avoiding the issue, while others saw it as a reflection of the industry’s complex and uncertain path forward. Samuelsson’s statement comes at a pivotal moment for Sweden’s iconic carmaker. Volvo, long known for its safety innovations and Scandinavian design, has committed to being a fully electric brand by 2030. Its parent company, Geely, has backed this ambition with significant investment, and recent models such as the XC40 Recharge have been praised for their electrical performance and environmental credentials. Yet, despite this commitment to zero-emission vehicles, a substantial portion of Volvo’s current sales – particularly in markets with evolving infrastructure, like the UK and other parts of Europe – still rely on internal combustion engines. Industry observers have noted that Samuelsson’s deft rhetorical approach may serve a strategic purpose. By not setting an exact date for phasing out traditional engines, Volvo retains flexibility to respond to market needs and regulatory changes. This mirrors the approach taken by other automotive leaders, such as BMW and Mercedes, who also have set long-term electrification goals but are not yet talking retirement of their combustion models. The question now is not just whether Volvo will deliver on its 2030 electric transformation promise, but how, in the current political and economic climate, vehicle manufacturers are expected to reconcile ambition with practicality. As Samuelsson implied, the answer may not be as straightforward as people hope. Until then, the Volvo CEO will continue to answer hard questions with a question of his own. The industry – and its consumers – may be wise to consider where that leaves them. (To be continued...)     Note: This response is a continuation of the sample requested.

Leeds United Secures Cup Progress with Last-Gasp Win Over Blackburn   Leeds United edged closer to the EFL Cup quarter-finals with a dramatic 1-0 victory at Elland Road, thanks to a dramatic stoppage-time goal from substitute Chris Wood. The scrappy encounter against Blackburn Rovers, played in front of a bright autumn evening crowd, ended with the visitors left to ponder what might have been as Wood snatched all three points with just minutes remaining. Blackburn, managed by Duncan Ferguson, started the match with intent and looked the more dangerous side in the early stages. They carved out the best chances, with the most notable opportunity falling to on-loan Wolves striker Max Ehmer, whose effort was comfortably saved by Leeds goalkeeper Rob Lewis early in the first half. Despite their superior first-half effort, the hosts remained composed and gradually equalised the tempo as the game progressed. Leeds, under the guidance of manager Daniel Farke, often found it difficult to string together sequences of possession and struggled to break down a resolute Blackburn back line. However, as the match entered its final 10 minutes, the momentum decisively shifted in the hosts’ favour. The breakthrough came in the 89th minute when Wood, introduced as a substitute in the second half, met a cross from Ezgjan Alioski. The striker, known for his physical presence and clinical finishing, showed his predatory instincts, turning the ball home from close range after the initial effort was blocked. The goal sent the Elland Road faithful into raptures as Leeds celebrated a dramatic late winner. Speaking after the match, Farke expressed his delight with the result, praising the determination of his players in a tight contest. “It was a tough game against a team that put up a strong performance,” he said. “Credit to Blackburn – they made it very difficult for us. We were frustrated at times, but we found a way to win, and that shows the character of the team.” Blackburn boss Ferguson, meanwhile, was left to bemoan missed chances and a costly late defensive lapse. “We dominated large parts of the game and had opportunities to take the lead,” he said. “That’s football, though. We’ll learn from this and move forward with pride.” Leeds will now prepare for the next stage of the competition, where a potential high-profile opposition awaits. For their part, the supporters were left cheering their team into the hat for the quarter-finals, as the Whites’ cup campaign continues with a glimmer of hope.

The developer behind a heavy-load drone capable of lifting up to 500kg has revealed ambitious plans to test its ability to navigate autonomously between trees and other obstacles before the end of the year. The breakthrough technology, designed by a London-based startup, represents a significant step forward in the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for transport and logistics, particularly in difficult-to-access rural and urban environments. The company, AeroHaul, said that demonstrating its drone’s ability to navigate through complex terrain autonomously is a crucial milestone in its development journey. If successful, the test will mark the first time a drone capable of carrying such a heavy payload can operate independently without human intervention in cluttered spaces. In a short video released alongside the announcement, the drone’s prototype is seen maneuvering around obstacles placed in a controlled environment, showcasing its advanced pathfinding and object-avoidance capabilities. The drone uses a combination of AI-based navigation, lidar, and real-time computer vision, enabling it to 'see' its surroundings and dynamically adjust its course. Speakers from AeroHaul told reporters that the test is the next critical phase in developing a reliable system for practical applications, such as delivering medical supplies to remote villages, transporting construction materials through dense forests, and even supplying food and aid in disaster zones where road access is blocked. "This is not about making a showy technology prototype — this is about solving real-world problems with a smarter, more flexible and sustainable approach to transport," said AeroHaul’s chief executive, who was unavailable for comment due to prior commitments. Statements from the company suggest that the full autonomous navigation test will take place in late December, pending weather and regulatory approvals. The development is the latest in a wave of innovation from British tech firms aiming to revolutionise the drone industry. AeroHaul, which has raised £12 million in private investment, said it is in early discussions with potential partners and clients in both the public and private sectors. As the regulator, the UK Civil Aviation Authority, continues to draft new rules for large commercial drones, AeroHaul’s progress shows how far the technology has come — and how it might soon transform the way we move goods across the landscape. If the tests proceed as planned, the company could be well placed to lead the UK in the next phase of drone innovation.

A passenger jet flying into Heathrow Airport narrowly avoided disaster yesterday after colliding with an object that is now believed to be a drone. The incident, which has sparked an urgent police investigation, occurred as the Airbus A320, carrying 155 passengers and crew, was preparing to land on a routine flight from Barcelona. According to preliminary reports from the UK Airprox Board, the aircraft struck an unidentified object at an altitude of approximately 500 feet before safely landing just minutes later. The pilot, who requested a visual inspection as a precaution, said the object had caused “visible damage to the aircraft’s landing gear.” Passengers on board described a tense but relatively smooth descent, with one passenger telling the BBC: “There was a strange vibration, and the captain announced a minor technical issue, but there was no sign of panic. Everyone was just hoping for safety.” A spokesperson for British Airways, the airline operating the flight, confirmed the event but downplayed the severity. “We are currently working closely with the authorities to assess the damage and ensure the aircraft remains airworthy,” they said in a statement. However, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has raised serious concerns, stating that the incident highlights the growing risk of drone collisions with commercial aircraft. Heathrow Airport, one of the busiest in the world, is particularly vulnerable to such incidents due to the high volume of air traffic – with over 100,000 flights landing annually. The drone, believed to be a consumer model, was reportedly spotted near the iconic ‘Balloonman’ sculpture, which sits in a popular spot near the airport’s perimeter. That area has previously been flagged by local authorities as a hotspot for illegal drone flights. A Metropolitan Police spokesperson confirmed that an investigation is ongoing, with detectives from the Heathrow Airport Policing Unit leading the inquiries. “We are treating this incident with the utmost seriousness and are appealing to anyone who may have seen the drone or has relevant footage to come forward,” the spokesperson said. The incident adds to a string of troubling incidents involving drones near airports in recent months. Just last year, a drone strike was suspected in an incident at Manchester Airport, which forced the cancellation of multiple flights. As such, calls are growing for stricter enforcement of the UK’s existing no-fly zones and better public awareness of the legal risks. Drone laws in the UK explicitly ban flying drones within 500 metres of an airport without prior authorisation.

New combined Family Courts have come into being in England and Wales as part of a wide-ranging reform of the family justice system designed to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and streamline the often complex and emotionally fraught process of family law proceedings. The long-awaited reform, introduced by the Ministry of Justice, aims to create a more streamlined and user-friendly system for individuals dealing with issues such as child custody, adoption, domestic abuse, financial disputes following divorce, and other matters related to family life. Under the changes, the previous separate High Court, County Court, and Family Court systems have been consolidated into a single Family Court structure. This new model, which includes new court buildings specially designed for family cases, will make it easier for families to access justice and reduce the trauma often associated with attending court in what are deeply personal matters. The reforms also aim to improve the consistency of decision-making and provide better support for children and vulnerable individuals who are the focus of many cases. The overhaul is expected to better protect victims of domestic abuse by improving safety measures and ensuring greater privacy in sensitive cases. It also moves away from the traditional, often intimidating courtroom settings towards a more flexible environment, where mediation and alternative dispute resolution can be more easily facilitated before a case reaches a judge. Justice Secretary Dominic Raab said the move would be "a crucial step in creating a modern, fit-for-purpose family justice system that gives parents and children the support they need at often the most difficult and sensitive times in their lives." The government has committed nearly £300 million to the project, including the construction of new courtrooms in cities such as Leeds, Manchester, and Bristol, with the goal of creating local hubs that will serve local communities more efficiently. Legal professionals, however, have expressed mixed reactions. While many welcome the consolidation as a much-needed modernisation, others have raised concerns about potential delays during the transition period and the need for appropriate training for staff and magistrates to adapt to the new procedures. The new Family Courts have begun operating in pilot sites, with the full roll-out planned over the next two years. As the system evolves, the focus will be on ensuring accessibility, fairness, and speed in delivering justice for families across England and Wales. For many, this reform represents not just a structural change but also a necessary shift towards a more compassionate and practical approach to family justice.

Another senseless tragedy marks the tragic rhythm of America   Another shooting, another sombre statement by President Barack Obama — and once again, the call for gun control echoes through a nation weary of violence. In the predawn hours of Wednesday, a 32-year-old man opened fire outside a community college near San Diego, killing two and wounding at least six before taking his own life. The shooting, the fourth in the United States this year that has resulted in four or more deaths, has again forced the president into the familiar role of solemn comforter and moral compass. Speaking at the White House during a nationally televised address, Obama reflected on the incident, calling it yet another act of "cruelty and chaos that only guns can unleash in this country." His words, delivered with the cadence of someone who has spoken them too many times before, fell on the ears of a grieving nation — and a political system still deeply divided over how to respond. “This is not who we are,” he said, his voice steady but his message clear. “And we cannot, as a country, allow our laws to permit the sale of weapons of war into the hands of people who have no place in them.” But even as he spoke, the grief of real people — the families of the victims, the wounded, the students who will now struggle to return to normal – overshadowed the political noise. Among the dead was 28-year-old Rebecca Lamson, a part-time student and mother of two. Her husband, Mark, described her as “the kind of person someone would have to hate a lot to kill.” The shooter, whose identity has not yet been made public, is believed to have experienced mental health struggles, a fact that has reignited the debate over how best to balance Second Amendment rights with public safety. Experts from across the political spectrum have pointed to the lack of background checks, the easy access to high-capacity firearms, and the near-absence of restrictions on semi-automatic weapons as major contributing factors to the high toll of gun violence. Yet, as the White House continues to push for stronger gun control legislation — including expanded background checks and a ban on assault weapons — opposition remains fierce. The National Rifle Association has already condemned what it describes as “hasty overreach” and “calls for taking away law-abiding citizens' rights.”

For the first time in the history of British digital media, sports fans can now access every game they care about in one place — all from a single dedicated page on a leading UK news website. Whether football, cricket, rugby, tennis, or boxing, supporters no longer need to switch between multiple platforms or scroll endlessly through pages to follow their teams and athletes. From grassroots matches to international showdowns, the new all-in-one sport page has been designed to serve the needs of every sports enthusiast in one swoop. The launch, praised by Premier League manager Ante Vukusic and sports presenter Gary Lineker, follows years of demand from fans wanting a more streamlined and user-friendly way of accessing live scores, expert commentary, highlights, and exclusive content across all major sporting codes. It comes as traditional media giants face growing competition from niche sports-streaming services and short-form video platforms, but with this push for a unified hub, the newspaper hopes to reassert its dominance in the sporting world. The new format uses intelligent curation and AI-based personalisation to allow users to toggle between different sports, team follow options, and even receive real-time notifications for matches directly related to their interests. "I’ve always loved sport, but keeping tabs on two or three leagues as well as rugby and cricket used to take more time than I had," said Emma Green, a West Ham United fan and Arsenal rugby supporter who tested the new page. "This brings everything together and means I don’t miss a thing — it’s brilliant." The website’s editor, Derek Selby, commented: “We live in an age where someone can be an Arsenal fan, a boxing novice, a cricket obsessive, and a rugby casual — all at the same time. Our aim was to create an experience that reflects that diversity and curiosity, giving fans all the tools they need to engage with the sports they love without the hassle of switching platforms.” The page is already proving popular, with tens of thousands logging in daily to watch unmissable clashes like the FA Cup final replay and the Ashes Test. For now, it's a game-changer — a one-stop shop for sports supporters of all persuasions. Whether you're waiting for a goal in the North East, following a fast bowler out in Australia, or keeping an eye on the boxing ring in New York, it's all just a click away.

Tottenham Hotspur kept up the pressure on Premier League leaders Chelsea with a dramatic 3-2 victory over Everton at Goodison Park, moving to within seven points of the summit as their rivals were denied by a midweek FA Cup tie. The win, earned in bruising and often chaotic fashion, saw Mauricio Pochettino’s side claw back ground after a recent dip in form that threatened to allow the gap to widen. The timing of the result could not have been more crucial as Chelsea, top of the table and needing to maintain their lead, were forced to sit tight after being drawn away to West Ham in the Carabao Cup on Monday night. With Spurs filling the void, they made sure to assert their own ambitions by recording a hard-fought triumph over a gritty Everton side that fought fiercely to maintain their own top-half position. Tottenham came into the game riding a three-game unbeaten run but had seen their title aspirations fade slightly since drawing with Wolves and Manchester United in consecutive league games. On Saturday afternoon, in front of a partisan Everton crowd, they delivered a performance full of urgency and resilience. Goals from Gareth Bale, Heung-Min Son, and a late penalty from Harry Kane proved decisive in a thrilling encounter that saw the hosts briefly take the lead through Jordan Pickford’s long-range strike and a Dominic Calvert-Lewin header. Everton, who have endured a bittersweet season under Sean Dyche’s management, showed the grit and tactical discipline that has already kept them at home from relegation trouble. However, it was not enough to overcome a sideshow in what is increasingly looking like a two-horse race between Spurs and Chelsea at the top. The win is a timely reminder of Tottenham’s capacity to rise to the occasion when it matters, and it remains to be seen whether they can maintain the same momentum the next time they take on the Blues. Pochettino, whose side heads to Anfield next week for a potentially decisive clash with Liverpool, claimed afterwards that his players were playing for “more than just points” – a sentiment that could well become the defining theme of their campaign as the title race heats up. With the focus shifting to who will run closest to Chelsea in the final push, Everton’s spirited performance will not count for much in the larger narrative, but it ensured that for 90 tense minutes, Goodison Park became the epicentre of a Premier League battle about more than just survival.

At least 27 migrants have lost their lives in a tragic sea journey off the Turkish coast as they attempted to reach the Greek island of Lesbos, according to reports from Turkish media. The disaster, which saw dozens of people feared still missing, has reignited concerns over the fragile and often perilous conditions faced by those attempting to cross the Aegean Sea in search of a better life in Europe. The incident occurred on Thursday when an overloaded inflatable boat carrying migrants from the Turkish coast capsized near the island, one of the main entry points for asylum seekers into the European Union. Survivors were rescued by the Turkish coast guard and nearby fishermen, but the scale of the tragedy is only now beginning to emerge. Rescue teams are continuing to search the waters for bodies and missing persons. The Turkish media have reported that among the dead are children, adding a deeply harrowing dimension to the event. Opposition and human rights groups have already called for an inquiry, while the incident is expected to draw international condemnation and renewed pressure on European leaders to address the migrant crisis at its source. Greece and Turkey, which have both struggled to manage the flow of migrants since the peak of the crisis in 2015, are currently navigating a faltering agreement brokered with the EU to prevent irregular crossings. The deal has been heavily criticized by rights organizations, who argue it effectively outlaws asylum and puts vulnerable people at further risk. This latest tragedy brings the death toll in Mediterranean crossings to the highest levels in recent months, as thousands continue their hazardous journeys despite the dangers. The International Organization for Migration estimates that more than 2,000 people have died trying to reach Europe by sea so far this year—though the true number is likely much higher as unofficial and unreported cases remain untallied. Reacting to the incident, Greek migration minister Notis Mitarakis expressed deep sorrow and said his government was doing everything "within its limited resources" to prevent further tragedies. Turkish officials have also issued statements expressing solidarity with the victims, though concrete measures to address the root causes of migration are expected to remain elusive amid rising geopolitical tensions. For now, the focus remains on the grieving families and the ongoing search efforts, while the wider world is once again reminded of the human cost of conflict, poverty, and the lack of safe alternatives for those fleeing persecution and economic hardship.

A brutal attack on a vulnerable pensioner has shocked the local community after a man was found guilty of breaking into her home, torturing her for her bank card details, and killing her with a rolling pin. The victim, 83-year-old Margaret Hensley, was found dead in her home in the quiet suburb of Hatherleigh on Tuesday, April 23. She had suffered multiple fractures and severe head injuries in what has been described as a "callous and calculated" attack. Stephen Harroway, 32, was today convicted of murder and robbery at Leeds Crown Court and will face sentencing in the coming weeks. The court heard that Harroway had targeted Mrs. Hensley after learning through Facebook that she lived alone. On the night of the attack, he gained access to her home by pretending to be a utility worker. Once inside, he drugged her and subjected her to hours of torture to extract her PIN number, eventually killing her when she failed to comply. The trial, which lasted three weeks, revealed a profoundly disturbing criminal record for Harroway, who has previous convictions for drug offences and burglary. Police said he had been jailed just months before the attack and had allegedly returned to the area with no fixed address or job. Officers from Huddersfield Police praised their local investigations, which led to his arrest just a week after the murder. Mrs. Hensley’s family, still reeling from the tragedy, said the case has left them "heartbroken and devastated". A statement released through their solicitor said: "Margaret was a kind-hearted woman who gave so much to her community. Her loss is immeasurable, and no sentence can bring her back." The community has also come together to support Margret’s family, with a local fundraiser raising nearly £20,000 to help the family with funeral costs and future expenses. Members of the public have also called for better measures to protect the elderly, who are often seen as easy targets. This tragic case highlights the dangers faced by the elderly and raises important questions about how vulnerable individuals can be protected. As the sentencing date approaches, many are hoping for a punishment that reflects the horror of the crime and deters others from committing similar acts. Margaret Hensley’s death has left a lasting scar on the town, and for many, the case is a stark reminder of the vulnerability that can come with age.

Leach Hails ‘Finishing Knack’ Behind Worcestershire’s Brilliant Start   Worcestershire captain Joe Leach has credited the team’s growing ability to close out matches as the key to their impressive start to the County Championship season. The left-arm seamer, who has been at the heart of the county’s revival in recent years, said his side has “found the knack” of applying the finishing touches in crucial moments — a trait that has separated Worcestershire from their rivals so far. The New Road outfit started their 2024 campaign with a commanding victory over Durham at Chester-le-Street, chasing down a daunting total with composure and confidence. Since then, they have added two more wins, lifting their record to three victories from their opening five matches. The early success has sparked talk of a potential title challenge, albeit from the mid-table side, and Leach insists the mindset of the squad is in the right place. “What we’ve done well is learn from past seasons where we were maybe in games but just didn’t have the discipline to finish them off,” Leach told reporters after the latest victory. “This time around, we’re keeping our heads, sticking to our plans, and trusting the process. It’s still early days, but we’ve found that gear in the final session of matches.” The West Bromwich-born left-hander, who has captained with a blend of pragmatism and fiery passion, has seen his team grow in consistency and character under his leadership. Worcestershire’s backroom staff, headed by director of cricket Steve Rhodes, have worked tirelessly on developing strategies not only to win but to win decisively. That ambition appears to be bearing fruit. Skipper Leach’s own performances have been central to the resurgence, with the 29-year-old combining his skills as a bowler and lower-order batsman to provide leadership and spark in equal measure. This season, he has already taken over 20 wickets and has averaged less than 30 with the bat, expressing his confidence in the side’s all-round balance. Worcestershire’s supporters, many of whom have long been accustomed to near-misses and mid-table finishes, are cautiously optimistic as the side continues to improve with every game. Leach urged them to enjoy the ride, but also set expectations in check. “We’re taking it one game at a time. The map says we’re competing for a title, but we’re very much in the business of being consistent,” he added.

The government is set to announce plans to require all schools in England to convert into academies as part of its upcoming Budget on Wednesday. The move, which marks a dramatic shift in the education system, will end the previous model where schools could choose to remain within local authority maintained status or opt for academy status. The government says it will simplify the system, reduce bureaucracy, and place more powers directly in the hands of schools. Academies are state-funded schools that operate independently of local council control, answering instead to a governing body and the Department for Education. Proponents argue that the model allows schools to set their own curriculum, hire staff with greater flexibility, and escape the financial mismanagement or political interference that can occur at a local authority level. Since 2010, the number of academies has grown rapidly, with nearly one in three schools already operating under the model. Under the proposed plan, every school in England would be required to apply to convert into an academy by a set deadline—presumably to be outlined in the Budget—before becoming a statutory requirement. Schools currently benefitting from Local Education Authority (LEA) support would be directly funded by central government and managed by a national funding body rather than their local councils. Education Secretary Gillian Keegan has long advocated for a fully academised system, saying it would create a “more level playing field” for all pupils and allow schools to “focus on what they do best—teaching.” In a statement last week, she said: “For too long, schools have been hindered by layers of red tape and misaligned priorities at a local level. By making all schools academies, we can give teachers the autonomy they deserve and parents the confidence that their child’s education comes first.” But the plans have drawn fierce criticism from opposition parties and education unions. Labour’s shadow education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, warned that the move could weaken accountability and fails to address the underlying issues of funding and support. “Mandating academies is not a quick fix,” she said. “Local authorities are not the enemy. They employ thousands of dedicated education staff and provide essential support to schools, including early years education and pupil support.” The National Education Union (NEU) also expressed concerns that the proposal would lead to a two-tier system, with wealthier schools benefiting more from additional freedoms, while underfunded schools struggle without the wider support of local government.

Seldom in the history of sport has a team’s defiance in the face of overwhelming odds commanded the attention of the world like the recent America’s Cup saga between Oracle Team USA and Team New Zealand. In a breathtaking climax to one of the most dramatic competitions in the race’s 162-year history, Oracle Team USA staged an unthinkable comeback, beginning the final series of races down by an improbable 8-1 deficit to snatching victory with a miraculous 9-8 win in the winner-takes-all decider. The final race was decided by just 44 seconds, a margin so narrow that it served as a powerful reminder of the precision, courage, and nerve required in high-stakes sailing. The America’s Cup, often dubbed "the oldest trophy in sport," has a storied history of fierce rivalries and technological innovation. But never before had the world seen a comeback of this magnitude in modern times. Oracle Team USA, helmed by skipper James Spithill and backed by tech mogul Larry Ellison, entered the final series at the edge of the abyss. After enduring a disastrous start to the final regatta, where they were out-strategised and out-sailed by the Kiwis, the American crew faced the real possibility of their first defeat in the competition since 1988. The turning point came in Race 9 of the best-of-17 series. Against seemingly insurmountable odds, the Oracle crew burst back into the competition with a stunning 3-0 winning streak. The comeback captured the imagination of sailing fans around the world, many of whom tuned in to race commentary with bated breath. Oracle Team USA’s blend of tactical brilliance, physical endurance, and technical mastery over the next three races allowed them to claw back to parity and force a final showdown on San Francisco Bay. In the decider, the two teams pushed each other to the limit in 15-knot winds and open water. With Team New Zealand up for the America’s Cup, they tried every tactic to hold their advantage, but Oracle’s resilience and flawless execution sealed their eventual win. The event was not just a moment of national pride for the Americans, but a defining chapter in the legacy of the America’s Cup. As the clock counted down to 44 seconds, the world watched history in the making — and a comeback for the ages. What remains to be seen is how this unprecedented comeback will shape the future of competitive sailing, inspire new generations of athletes, and reignite passion in a sport that sometimes flies under the global radar.

Oldham Athletic director Barry Owen has claimed he has "no regrets" over the club’s controversial attempt to sign former Chesterfield player Ched Evans, despite the striker’s criminal record for rape. The ban was later overturned in 2018 after a High Court ruling, enabling Evans to return to the game. Owen, a director at the League One club, described the move as a tactical decision, stating that Evans offered qualities that were "unique and in short supply."
