Such candour has further inflamed public opinion, with fans and campaigners questioning whether professional football clubs should walk a different moral line from the broader society. Former players and anti-violence campaigners have also weighed in, urging football clubs to take a firm stance on domestic and sexual violence. One advocate for victims of sexual assault told BBC Radio Manchester: "Football has a responsibility to uphold the law and public expectations, not to ignore or justify repeat actions that cause harm." Owen’s remarks come at a time of renewed focus on holding football to account for its role in both perpetuating and challenging sexual and domestic violence. The case once again highlights the tension between sporting ambition and ethical considerations in the world of professional football.

The rollout of a new £60million GPS tagging system for offenders is sharply behind schedule and has delivered no tangible benefits since its first device was issued in 2021, according to a damning report by the National Audit Office (NAO) published today. The system, intended to revolutionise the way the UK monitors offending behaviour and tackles serious and organised crime, has been plagued by delays and has yet to justify the £60m already spent—a figure that experts warn will rise as implementation struggles continue. The system, developed by private firm Anteon International under a private finance initiative (PFI), was meant to replace the outdated MOTO tagging system used by the Home Office. Initially pledged to be ready by early 2017, the new GPS system is now five years behind schedule, with just over 400 devices issued to offenders—even as thousands of them remain on electronic tags in the old system. In an era of increasing reliance on digital tools for law enforcement and offender management, this delay has been a major cause for concern among both politicians and officials. The NAO report revealed that the original budget for the project, set in 2017, was £45 million, but by 2021, it had already ballooned to £60 million—despite no measurable impact or improvement over existing technology. The government is now facing estimated additional costs of at least £45 million, with the project expected to extend deep into the next decade. Chancellor Rishi Sunak and the Ministry of Justice have both been urged to explain how a project of such scale and complexity collapsed into a seemingly unending delay, delivering no benefits. The Home Affairs Select Committee is now considering launching an inquiry into the mismanagement of the scheme. Critics are unambiguous in their criticism. “This is a shocking example of the broken promises of high-tech public services,” said one unnamed senior official familiar with the project. “We’re still using a system from the 2000s while the new one is hopelessly delayed.” Home Secretary Suella Braverman said in a statement that the government was “working closely with Anteon to ensure the system is fully operational as soon as possible.” However, with no apparent progress in sight and growing public outrage over the mismanagement of taxpayer funds, pressure is mounting on the government to re-evaluate the entire GPS tagging project. For now, the £60 million tagged offenders have waited—and paid—for a system that remains, quite literally, out of reach.

Rory McIlroy Shuts Down Social Media After Row with Steve Elkington Sparks Outcry   Rory McIlroy has revealed he has stepped away from using social media altogether, following a controversial exchange with former US PGA champion Steve Elkington that sparked widespread criticism and prompted the tennis legend Serena Williams among others to weigh in. The incident, which unfolded on Twitter last week, saw Elkington criticise McIlroy's form and attitude on the course. A seemingly offhand remark from the retired Australian golfer was interpreted by many as a veiled personal attack. McIlroy was quick to respond, exchanging barbed comments before the conversation escalated further. Within hours, the dispute had united golf fans and critics alike, with the hashtag #RoryVsElk trending across the platform. In a recent interview with the BBC’s golf correspondent, McIlroy spoke for the first time about the incident and explained he has now disconnected from most of his social media accounts. “I’ve taken a step back,” he said. “It was getting too emotional. I didn’t want to say or do anything I’d regret later. This isn’t the place for me to air personal things, and it certainly isn’t the platform I want to use to represent who I am as a person.” The comments mark a stark change from McIlroy, who has been relatively open on social media in the past. Known for his verbosity off the course, he had frequently used Twitter to interact with fans and make light-hearted commentary on the Tour’s events. Former Wimbledon champion Serena Williams, who has long advocated for athletes maintaining control over their public image, tweeted: “Social media is not a conversation. It’s a stage. Sometimes you have to leave the stage and be quiet.” Steve Elkington has since apologised for the tone of his remarks, stating they were not intended to target McIlroy personally but to comment on a broader issue of player sportsmanship. “I respect Rory and have always believed in the spirit of the game, but there are certain standards I believe should be upheld,” he said in a statement. “I regret if my words were taken the wrong way.” McIlroy, currently ranked fourth in the world, is preparing for next week’s BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth. Whether or not he will return to Twitter remains an open question, but his decision to take a break from the platform points to a growing unease among professional athletes about the pressures of constant public scrutiny in the digital age.

Black Monday Again: NFL Shakes Up Coaching Ranks as Season Opens   Once again, the NFL has seen its ‘Black Monday’ return, a day synonymous with upheaval and uncertainty in coaching booths across America. As teams began their preparations for the 2024 season, three head coaches were abruptly fired in a single day, echoing the intense drama that often accompanies the start of the football calendar. The term ‘Black Monday’ — a nod to the 1987 stock market crash but now infamous in sports circles — marks the time of year when underperforming coaches, despite stellar records in previous years, suddenly find their futures hanging in the balance. The latest round of sackings came as a surprise to many, reflecting the volatility of the NFL’s coaching carousel. With four consecutive years of losing records left behind, one team moved quickly to part ways with its head coach, signaling a desire for a fresh start. Another dismissed coach was let go after a season marked by internal discord and poor execution in key games, despite a revitalised roster built for contention. The third team, embroiled in a costly string of early-season losses that overshadowed their talent, joined the growing list of those facing the chopping block. These changes are as much about optics and optimism for the future as they are about pointing to short-term results. Football analysts suggest that the decisions often come down to perception rather than performance. “In the NFL, the pressure to win now is immense,” said veteran sports journalist Paul Kelly. “Even if a coach is doing everything right, if the results don’t show someone at the top is in control, the owner or general manager will move quickly to make a change.” The day is a reminder of the harsh realities of professional sports, where success is measured in wins and losses and loyalty often takes a back seat to the pursuit of the next big thing. For the dismissed coaches — all of whom had previously held their positions with respect and contracts worth millions — the sacking marks the end of one chapter and the beginning of another. For the teams, it raises questions: Will new leadership provide the spark needed to turn things around, or will they too be waiting on the next Black Monday to come? As the dust settles from another round of upheaval, the focus shifts to what these changes mean for the 2024 season.

Composer and multi-instrumentalist Anna Meredith has made history once again, scooping the prestigious Scottish Album of the Year ( SAY ) award with her third album, Varmints . The music prize, known for its support of Scottish artists across all genres, was presented to Meredith at the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland in Glasgow on Tuesday night. The accolade marks a triumphant achievement for the 35-year-old, who has been steadily making a name for herself in contemporary British music with her unique and often experimental sound. Varmints , released in 2019, is a genre-defying collection that fuses elements of classical composition with electronic beats, avant-garde techniques, and theatrical flair. Praised for its intensity, complexity and originality, the album received widespread critical acclaim, with numerous music publications placing it high on their best-of-the-year lists. Following its release, Varmints also earned Meredith her first BBC commission for Radio 3 and saw her perform at major festivals including Electronic Daisy Carnival in the United States and Dekmantel in the Netherlands. The awards ceremony, which celebrates the best of Scottish musical talent, was attended by a host of artists and industry figures. This is the first time the SAY award has been won by a classical and electronic-based album, highlighting the prize’s growing recognition of diverse musical voices. Meredith, who was raised in Bearsden, near Glasgow, studied music at the University of Edinburgh before venturing into composition and performance. Known for her work with bands such as the Silurian Dinosaurs and Vritra, as well as her involvement in visual and music-theatre projects, she has consistently pushed the boundaries of what is possible in contemporary composition. In a recent interview with the BBC, she described Varmints as a “raw and unrestrained” project, about which she said: “It was a journey into the extremes of rhythm, sound and texture. There was no holding back.” Her win has been celebrated across the music world, with many pointing to her award as a sign that the realm of high art and alternative music is finally getting the recognition it deserves in mainstream circles. With Varmints now officially the Scottish Album of the Year, all eyes are on Anna Meredith as she continues to evolve and redefine her sound. Whether through new compositions, collaborations or bold performances, there’s little doubt that her career will keep growing – and the music world is ready to follow.

In the middle of a narrow alley in Cairo's Ain Shams district, one shop stands out from the rest, not through grandeur or neon signs, but by its unique charm and the quiet anticipation it cultivates among those who pass by. Tucked between a falafel vendor and a children's bookstall, Habibi’s Books and Curiosities is more than a store—it is a portal to forgotten stories, rare artifacts, and a fading sense of nostalgia. Sitting in this labyrinth of eastern Cairo, where the air carries the scent of spicy simit bread and the sounds of Cairo's never-ending honking echo around every corner, Habibi’s seems almost like a mirage—something conjured from the imagination of a bygone era. Its wooden door swings open with a creak, leading to a dimly lit room stacked with tomes bound in cracked leather, vintage maps curling at the edges, and an assembling of hand-painted postcards from decades, no doubt, past their time. The shop's founder and owner, Mohamed El-Sayed, now in his 60s, has spent over 40 years curating the shop, sourcing each treasure from flea markets across Egypt and the greater Middle East. He is a human archive of sorts, as much a storyteller as a bookseller. “This was all collected piece by piece,” he explains with a smile, gesturing towards a shelf crowded with miniature copies of the Quran printed in Ottoman Times and a surprisingly intact phone directory from the 1970s. “When the old disappears, at least it should remember us.” In a city where modernity is oddly juxtaposed with ancient history, the shop feels like a defiant nod to being neither. It is where the future is not fully embraced and the past is not entirely buried. Customers who visit the store come from diverse walks of life—students researching rare texts, local historians hunting for oral traditions in written form, and simply the occasional tourist seeking something less ‘Instagrammable’ and more meaningful. Yet, what Habibi’s offers is not just the physical remnants of history, but the very essence of memory. It waits in the pages of an old diary, in yellowed newspaper clippings, in the lunches of a new generation that sometimes momentarily finds itself yearning not for progress, but for a window into where it started. As Cairo becomes ever more gleaming and globalized, places like Habibi’s Books become increasingly rare—ike sanctuaries for the quiet, the curious, and the gently romantic.

The De Karina chocolate factory, nestled in the scenic hills of the Upper Galilee near the border with the Golan Heights, has become far more than just a local attraction — it is now a must-visit destination for thousands of international tourists flocking to the area each year. Known for its traditional Cappuccino chocolates — a signature product infused with real espresso — the factory combines an aromatic taste of Italy with the charm of northern Israel, drawing in foodies and curious visitors from around the globe. Originally established in 2006 by Ilana Vardi and her husband, the business started as a small enterprise, but the decision to use specially imported frozen chocolate shells and baked cappuccino-flavored fillings gave the product its unique edge. The company’s best-seller, the cappuccino chocolate, is renowned for its rich, velvety texture and bold coffee flavor, and has turned De Karina into a darling of the confectionery world. What started as a niche product has now become a staple in souvenir shops and delicatessens across the country, and the factory remains a working production site open to the public. Each year, the Golan Heights, a region known for its dramatic landscapes, wineries, and archaeological sites, welcomes over two million tourists — many of whom add a stop at De Karina to their itinerary. The factory tour – which includes a visit to the production floor, a viewing room, and a charming café offering an array of chocolates, pastries, and drinks – has become one of the most popular experiences in the area. Some visitors come just for the chocolate tasting; others stay for hours, browsing the gift shop stocked with everything from chocolate eggs to gourmet boxes and artisanal bonbons. According to tourism officials, De Karina is now among the top five most visited attractions in the Golan Heights, rivalling even the most iconic sites in the region. The factory’s manager, Erez Epstein, noted: “People come to the Golan for wine, nature, and history. Now they are coming for chocolate too. It’s become a symbol of something unique, something that brings joy to people from all over the world.” With the growing popularity of experiential tourism — where visitors want to take home not just souvenirs, but memories — the De Karina experience offers a sweet reminder of travel adventures in the hills of northern Israel. For many, it is more than a chocolate stop — it is the highlight of the entire journey.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has reaffirmed the importance of global cooperation in internet governance, calling for mutual respect between nations in how they manage and regulate their digital spaces. Speaking at a high-level international forum on cybersecurity and digital development, Xi emphasized the concept of “cyber sovereignty” as the cornerstone of responsible digital governance. The term, which has become a central pillar of China’s stance on global internet policy, suggests that countries should have full authority over data and online activity within their borders. In his speech, delivered during a virtual session of the China International Digital Economy Conference, Xi urged world leaders to recognize the legitimacy of different national approaches to internet regulation, including data localization laws, content restrictions, and state oversight. Xi’s comments come amid growing tensions over digital sovereignty between China and the West. Western democracies have increasingly criticized China’s curation of the internet – including the so-called “Great Firewall” that blocks access to platforms such as Facebook, Google, and Twitter – as censorship. In contrast, China argues that its system protects national security, cultural values, and the social fabric of its 1.4 billion people. The president called for a “multi-stakeholder” approach to global internet governance, one that includes not only governments but also technology companies, civil society, and academic institutions. “Technology should serve humanity, not be used to threaten humanity,” he said. “We should reject all forms of digital colonialism and interfered in other nations' internal affairs under the guise of internet governance.” Xi did not name specific countries in his speech, but his remarks were seen as a direct response to what China perceives as Western attempts to impose a unified global digital model favoring American tech giants. Some experts suggest the speech is a strategic move to position China as an alternative leader in the future of the internet, particularly in developing regions where Beijing is investing heavily in digital infrastructure. The call for “cyber sovereignty” is likely to reignite debates among policymakers around the world. While it offers a vision of internet governance that recognizes the legitimacy of national policies, critics warn that it could lead to a fragmented global internet where cross-border data flows and digital cooperation become increasingly difficult. As world leaders prepare to meet at the United Nations to discuss a global framework for internet governance, Xi’s statements have added to a growing demand for a more inclusive and representative model.

A digital games programmer from Angus has claimed a unique place in sporting and gaming history by completing what is thought to be the first cycle from Land’s End to John o’Groats using virtual reality technology. Euan Morton, 29, is believed to be the first person ever to achieve the traditional 900-mile (1,448km) British bicycle route entirely within a VR environment, breaking new ground in the worlds of fitness, simulation, and gamification. Morton, who has developed several VR applications used for training and education, said the idea initially came to him as a way to chase a fitness goal while confined at home due to the ongoing restrictions of Scotland's phased lockdown. "I've always been into immersive tech, especially VR and its potential beyond gaming," he said. "I thought if I could simulate the journey, I could still push myself physically and mentally and achieve something meaningful.” Using a VR headset in conjunction with a smart trainer bike linked to digital cycling platforms such as Zwift and RGT (RealGym Tracker), Morton designed and navigated a customised version of the Land’s End to John o’Grots route over the course of a week, logging consistent hours every day to replicate the experience of a real-world cyclist. The real-time data integration allowed the system to mirror not only the terrain and distance, but also local conditions such as elevation changes and even simulated weather patterns, giving Morton an experience as close as possible to a real cross-country ride. What makes this undertaking particularly notable is the detail and sophistication with which the route was recreated in VR. While commercial apps typically simulate pre-defined looped courses, Morton combined his technical expertise with an ambition to make the journey faithful to the original real-world route through coding and geographic mapping. "I had to develop a custom interface to make sure I was following the same route the real-world cyclists take," he said. "That meant modifying existing software and integrating data feeds so the environment felt as authentic as possible." Morton claimed to have averaged 60 miles (97km) a day on the VR bike, adhering to a strict training schedule to complete the entire journey within his personal performance goals. “I wanted to make sure not just that I finished, but that I finished in a realistic and challenging way—like someone actually doing the ride,” he said.

Plaid Cymru has thrown open the door of the 2024 general election campaign by becoming the first political party to publish its manifesto, setting out its vision for a more independent Wales. The Cymru party, long a proponent of Welsh independence and left-leaning social policies, unveiled a bold set of proposals aimed at addressing the country's most pressing challenges, from housing and education to climate change. At the heart of Plaid Cymru's manifesto is a call for full independence from the United Kingdom, a policy it says is not just feasible but necessary to give Wales the "sovereignty and self-determination" it has long been denied. The party argues that only by breaking free from Westminster can Wales truly control its own economic and environmental policies. On the economic front, the party promises an urgent plan to tackle the housing crisis, including the creation of a publicly-owned housing association to build 100,000 new homes over the next decade. Plaid Cymru also pledges to abolish rent caps in social housing and introduce a five-year plan to address the backlog of property repairs and upgrades. The party is also proposing a crackdown on speculative investors, who it claims have driven up property prices in rural Wales. In education, the manifesto calls for free university education, funded through an increase in municipal taxation, and a major investment in apprenticeships and vocational training – particularly targeting industries with a green economy angle, such as renewable energy and sustainable agriculture. Social policy is equally prominent, with the party campaigning for the introduction of a Welsh minimum living wage, which would be higher than the UK's current national living wage. Plaid Cymru also wants to expand mental health services and tackle inequalities in healthcare, particularly between urban and rural areas. Environmental commitments make up a large part of the manifesto, with the party setting a target of reducing the UK's overall carbon emissions to net zero by 2030. To achieve this, the manifesto details plans for a transformation in transport, with a focus on cutting car dependency and boosting investment in cycling and public transport. The construction of new offshore wind farms and the expansion of tidal energy projects are also proposed. The party’s early unveiling of the manifesto is widely seen as a strategic move to set the tone for what promises to be a highly contested election in Wales, with the Conservatives set to defend a narrow majority and Labour hoping to regain lost ground.

"Be careful what you wish for," the old saying goes – and this is exactly what the Russian leadership must be thinking right now. In the wake of Vladimir Putin’s brutal invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent wave of unprecedented Western sanctions, Russia found itself thrown into a new isolation. For years, as the country relied increasingly on a flawed hybrid economic model, the Kremlin appeared unfazed by warnings that its political and economic relationships with the West were teetering on the edge of a precipice. Now, that chasm has opened beneath Russia’s feet, pulling it into a void of grinding economic decline, energy shortfalls, and an international image increasingly at odds with the needs of Russian society. The contradictions have never been more stark. On one hand, the Russian government and its well-heeled oligarchs have been fervently warning of Western encirclement and sabotage, painting the sanctions as a conspiracy to undermine the "stability" of the Russian state. On the other hand, the sanctions, imposed in response to war crimes, cyberattacks, and unprovoked aggression, have swiftly severed Russia’s access to foreign loans, global stock exchanges, and essential technology that underpins everyday life, from consumer electronics to medical devices. The impacts are filtering down through every layer of Russian society and raising real questions about the sustainability of the current trajectory. What is truly remarkable is that all of this is playing out – at least in public – against the backdrop of state-sanctioned propaganda celebrating the invasion as a "special military operation." In phone-ins on state television and press briefings by the ministry of defense, the Kremlin continues to assert that Russia is making progress toward its "just" goals. Yet the cracks are beginning to show. The continued retreat from Russian gas being sold in rubles has left European countries scrambling for alternatives, while about half of Russia’s crude oil exports are now going to countries outside the G20 — meaning India and China, among others, are increasingly filling the gap left by the West. Many have claimed, time and again, that Russia would survive anything the West could throw at it. The reality, it seems, is proving otherwise. As Putin’s grip tightens on domestic dissent, the question is whether such a regime can survive as the global economy continues to turn elsewhere, and the sanctions bite deeper. “Be careful what you wish for” – the saying has rarely felt more apt.

In a final appearance at the despatch box for Prime Minister’s Questions, David Cameron offered a parting reflection on the state of the United Kingdom, with particular attention given to the situation in Northern Ireland. Standing for the last time as a serving prime minister before the leadership changes expected in the coming weeks, Mr Cameron claimed that Northern Ireland is “stronger” now than when he first took office six years ago. The remark comes as speculation continues over a potential snap general election, which would mark the end of a decade of Conservative-led government. Mr Cameron’s comments were met with mixed reactions in the House of Commons. Labour MPs, whose leader Jeremy Corbyn recently faced calls for his own resignation over united nations voting record, appeared to offer cautious agreement, while some members of the DUP and Sinn Féin benches exchanged glances. The prime minister’s specific reference to Northern Ireland was notable, as recent political developments and the ongoing issues surrounding Brexit have stirred tensions in the region once again. The Good Friday Agreement, a cornerstone agreement that has largely held since 1998, faces new uncertainty in the wake of the UK’s decision to exit the EU. With the shared border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland at the heart of Brexit negotiations, concerns about a return to instability and division have grown. Mr Cameron did not elaborate on his statement during PMQs, but his words suggest that he believes – at least in his own assessment – progress has been made in strengthening democratic institutions and community relations in the region. What remains unclear is who will fill the vacuum left by Mr Cameron. His successor will inherit not only the full weight of Brexit negotiations but also a deeply divided nation, one that continues to struggle with its identity following the 2016 referendum. The next Conservative leader, expected to be unveiled in September, will face an uphill battle to unify the party and the country, especially with Labour seemingly looking to take advantage of the PM’s weakened position. For now, however, David Cameron has left his final imprint on Parliament. As he took his seat after nearly an hour of questions, his expression was one of a man who knows he was part of a significant chapter in Britain’s political history, but also one who is relieved to hand the baton to a new generation.

MPs have voted to replace the UK’s ageing nuclear weapons system, Trident, in a decisive move that has reignited debate over Britain’s commitment to a nuclear-armed future. The renewal of the controversial programme saw the House of Commons approve by 353 votes to 259, with 31 Conservative rebels joining crossbench and all-party support from the Labour party. The decision puts an end to years of uncertainty over the £31 billion project and underlines the government’s stance that a nuclear deterrent remains a crucial element of national security in an increasingly unstable world. The vote comes ahead of the House of Lords' scheduled decision on the issue later this year, although it is widely expected that the upper chamber will also back the proposal. Campaigners and opposition leaders have expressed deep concerns over the ethics, cost and global implications of maintaining a nuclear arsenal. Shadow Home Secretary Emily Thornberry and other Labour MPs turned out in force to support the motion, despite previous criticisms of the programme. Thornberry has said while she has “major concerns,” she believes the decision remains a “matter for the party’s democratic process,” and that opposing it would risk breaking party unity over the issue. Speaking after the vote, Prime Minister Theresa May hailed the decision as “right for the long-term security of the United Kingdom,” arguing that in a world marked by missile threats from Russia and “rogue” states such as North Korea, Trident remains a vital tool for national defence. “It is simply not credible for Britain to be a global player if we do not maintain our nuclear deterrent,” she said. Despite this, critics have accused the government of sidestepping public opinion, citing polls that show a majority of British citizens are either against renewing Trident or want it scrapped entirely. The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) called the vote “a betrayal of our security and the future of this planet.” Protesters gathered outside Parliament as MPs cast their ballots, some chanting “No Nukes” while others held signs depicting nuclear explosions over major UK cities. The decision will see the replacement of the four Royal Navy’s current Vanguard-class submarines with a new fleet of four Successor submarines, each carrying nuclear warheads capable of triggering catastrophic destruction over vast distances. With global nuclear tensions high and Brexit negotiations ongoing, the government insists the programme is non-negotiable for protecting British interests around the world.

The odds of a cricketing legend lacing up his boots for English shores once more have grown slimmer as former England star Kevin Pietersen has hinted at a potential retirement from playing in the country. The 44-year-old, who is currently enjoying a summer stint with Surrey in the T20 Blast, has hinted that this might be his final hurrah on English soil, declaring he is “unlikely” to return to the sport after his current spell with the county. Pietersen, who has had a decorated but often controversial career in English cricket, made the revelation in a recent interview, sparking speculation about his future in the game. Known for his explosive batting and charismatic persona, Pietersen has been a fan favourite throughout his 16-year tenure across county cricket, during which he has played for Surrey, London, Middlesex, Nottinghamshire, and Yorkshire, among others. Surrey’s head coach, Michael Di Venuto, welcomed the news with appreciation. “We’re immensely proud to have Kevin here this summer. He’s been an inspiration to our younger squad, and even if this is the end of his time in England, he will always be a big part of our cricketing history.” Pietersen, who represented both England and South Africa during his international career, has often spoken about the emotional toll of playing professional cricket, from the pressure of national selection to the media scrutiny that has dogged his every move. “It’s been an incredible journey in England, and I’m grateful for all the support I’ve received over the years,” he said. “But someone at my age has to think seriously about what comes next.” While his potential future in international cricket remains uncertain—Pietersen previously played for the Delhi Daredevils and the Sydney Sixers in the Indian Premier League and Big Bash League—his English ties appear to be coming to a close. Fans and analysts alike will be watching closely to see where the veteran batsman goes next, but for now, the focus remains on his current performances with Surrey as he bids farewell to a storied career on home soil. As his time in the T20 Blast continues, all eyes are on whether Pietersen will cap off his time in English professional cricket with a grand final act. As Bishop Paul Tighe sat down for our interview, he joked that not only is he probably the only priest at South by Southwest, but also the only person with grey hair. It was a witty remark, yet it struck at the heart of an unusual presence at the world-renowned film, music and interactive festival. Known for its youthful energy and cutting-edge creativity, South by Southwest (SXSW) is not typically the setting for ecclesiastical discussions. But in a quiet corner of one of Austin, Texas’s main conference venues, Bishop Tighe was ready to talk religion in the digital age and what the Church might learn from the creative industries. Dressed in his clerical collar, the 73-year-old priest cut a stark figure amid the throng of tech-savvy innovators, indie musicians and film-makers. But Bishop Tighe, who has served as a special adviser to the Vatican’s Dicastery for Communications, was far from an outsider. His mission, he explained, was to understand how storytelling, music and digital media are shaping modern culture and to ask how the Church might use these tools effectively. “If we don’t engage with the places where people are being formed today, then we risk becoming irrelevant,” he said. A former electrical and electronic engineer, Bishop Tighe has long been interested in the intersection of faith and technology. He has advocated for the Church to embrace new media platforms, not least because these are the spaces where young people are spending their time. “What we do in the pew is important, but what happens beyond the walls of the church is just as critical,” he said. “We can’t ignore the digital world. We have to meet people where they are.” His appearance at SXSW comes amid a broader shift in the Vatican’s approach to communication and pastoral outreach. From Pope Francis’s use of social media to the recent launch of an internal document on digital evangelisation, the Catholic Church is trying to find its voice in a rapidly evolving media landscape. But, as Bishop Tighe acknowledged, it’s not easy to balance traditional values with modern expression. “Dialogue is key. We need to listen as much as we speak.” As he prepared for a panel titled “Faith in the Digital Age,” Bishop Tighe reflected on the unusual role he was playing. “Who would have imagined that a bishop would be sitting in a festival like this?”

French former President Nicolas Sarkozy remains in custody as authorities press forward with an investigation into allegations of influence peddling, marking a dramatic development in the political saga that has gripped the country. The 69-year-old conservative leader, who previously served as president from 2007 to 2012, was placed under house arrest beginning in 2021 over similar charges but has now been taken into custody for direct questioning by investigators. A judicial source confirmed that the decision was made by judges examining whether Sarkozy attempted to recruit a former investigating judge to help him avoid prosecution. The former president called the move “excessive” and denied any wrongdoing, calling it part of a campaign against him and accusing the French government of manipulating justice for political ends. The inquiry, which originated from wiretaps and secret recordings, focuses on alleged attempts to misuse the authority of his presidential office and illegally influence the workings of the judiciary. These allegations echo a broader trend in France, where several high-profile political figures have faced scrutiny over corruption in recent years. Sarkozy’s legal troubles have been ongoing for some time. He was previously accused over details of his 2012 presidential campaign funding, and in 2019, he was briefly placed under formal investigation over alleged misuse of classified information during his tenure in office. His latest custody adds another layer of uncertainty to France’s already politically fractured landscape, just months before pivotal municipal elections and amid growing support for the far-right Alternative for France (FN) and the hard-left New Popular Front (NFP). For Sarkozy, once a towering figure in French politics and the architect of a global appeal to action on climate change through the 2015 COP21 summit in Paris, the legal proceedings represent a stunning fall from grace. The case also raises questions about the transparency and independence of the judiciary in France. Critics argue that political figures from all sides of the political spectrum seem to enjoy special treatment when it comes to justice, while ordinary citizens face harsher consequences for similar infractions. Supporters of Sarkozy, however, continue to rally behind him. Prominent conservative figures, including former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, have urged calm and called for respect for due process. The coming weeks are expected to be critical, with the judicial process likely to have profound implications not just for Sarkozy, but for France’s political and judicial system as a whole.

A lifeline for Scunthorpe: Tata Steel plant to seal rescue deal days from collapse   A deal that could save thousands of jobs and provide a shot in the arm for the ailing steel industry is on the verge of being signed as soon as Monday, according to BBC sources. The announcement follows months of uncertainty for workers at Tata Steel’s Scunthorpe plant, with fears mounting that the site could be shut down after a decline in domestic demand and fierce international competition. The potential deal, which remains confidential, involves a new arrangement that would provide financial and strategic support to keep the plant operational during a fragile phase in the global steel market. Although details have yet to be officially confirmed, industry insiders suggest the involvement of supply chain partners and possibly government support in the form of grants or subsidies. For the residents of Scunthorpe, the possibility of a last-minute reprieve is being met with cautious optimism. The town, which is home to nearly 6,000 direct employees and many more indirect jobs in supporting industries, has long relied on the steelworks as the backbone of its economy. The prospect of losing the plant—after over 100 years of operation—has been met with widespread concern, not just from workers and their families, but from businesses, MPs, and local leaders. Labour MP Nick West, who represents Scunthorpe, welcomed the news but warned that any deal must guarantee jobs and long-term stability. “It’s not enough to save the plant for a few months or years. We need a sustainable solution that ensures this vital institution continues to support the community for generations to come,” he said. The UK government has also made it clear that it would not stand by and watch an iconic part of Britain’s industrial heritage close its doors. Earlier this year, Business Secretary Kemi Badenoch visited the plant and pledged to do whatever it takes to protect the local steel sector. Tata Steel itself has not issued a formal statement, but sources say that the company has been in discussions with various partners since early this summer. A union strike earlier in the year was a precursor to the intense pressure being applied from all sides to keep the doors open. While Monday’s potential signing of the deal may not mark the end of Scunthorpe’s steel-related struggles, it represents a critical step in a turnaround that has long felt out of reach.

Two women united by tragedy have issued a heartfelt plea to today’s young people, urging them to consider the consequences of their choices in light of the 10-year anniversary of the deaths of their daughters, who were both victims of gang-related shootings. Karen Thompson and Yvonne Morris, the mothers of 16-year-old twins Jess and Mia, were joined at a community event in Salford on Saturday as they spoke out against gang violence. The girls were killed during a confrontation between rival groups in 2014, a case that shocked the local community and led to widespread calls for action on youth violence in the area. “We’ve spent the last decade wondering what more we could have done,” Karen said, addressing the crowd at the memorial event outside St George’s Hall. “In the early days, it felt like no one was listening, but now I’m pleading with young people and their families to understand how quickly your life can be stolen.” Yvonne added: “We raised these girls to love everyone, to be strong, kind and fearless. But not in that way, not through violence. We’re not asking for anything more than choices that give young people the future we all want.” Both mothers have since dedicated their lives to youth outreach and community work. They co-founded the Jess and Mia Foundation, which promotes education and support for at-risk teenagers. The organisation works closely with schools and local authorities to provide mentorship programs and prevent children from being drawn into gang activity. At the event, which marked 10 years since the twin’s deaths, around 300 people gathered to hear speeches and take part in a candlelit march through the city. Speakers included local community leaders, law enforcement officials, and young people being mentored under the foundation’s programmes. Councillor David Appleby, who has worked with the foundation since the tragedies, said: “The legacy of Jess and Mia is not just their memory, but the ongoing efforts to ensure their deaths were not in vain. The mothers’ courage and compassion have inspired a generation.” Earlier in the week, the Salford City Council announced plans to create a permanent memorial garden in memory of the girls, which is expected to be unveiled next spring. The site will include a space for reflection and education about the impact of gang culture. As the candlelit march wound its way through the city, Karen and Yvonne stood at the front, holding their daughters’ photographs.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has issued a stark warning that the global migrant crisis is no longer confined to specific regions and must be addressed through international cooperation, not border barriers. In remarks delivered at a press briefing in Geneva earlier this week, UNHCR chief Filippo Grandi emphasized that simply turning away desperate seekers of safety and opportunity will no longer yield sustainable solutions. “The migratory crisis is now a global phenomenon that demands a global response,” he said, as he outlined the growing numbers of people on the move across continents, driven by conflict, economic instability, and climate change. Grandi called the decision by some nations to adopt increasingly hostile and restrictive policies towards asylum seekers a symptom of short-sighted thinking that fails to address the root causes of displacement. “No one state can solve this alone, and no one state should be left to shoulder the entire burden,” he added, pointing to the rising tensions in the Mediterranean, the intensifying flows through the Americas, and the dangerous journeys across the Sahara and in South and Southeast Asia. The appeal for a unified, global approach comes at a time when public support for refugees and migrants is under increasing political strain. In Europe, anti-immigrant sentiment has surged, with governments in countries like Italy and Hungary intensifying their border controls in recent months. Meanwhile, in the United States, the debate over border security remains a flashpoint in national politics, with significant policy shifts under the current administration. The UNHCR’s statement has already sparked a mixed reaction. While some experts and advocacy groups have praised the organization for highlighting what they see as an urgent and existential issue, government officials in several countries have criticized it as an overreach. “States have a right and a responsibility to control their own borders,” said a spokesperson for the European Parliament’s Internal Security Committee. “Global solutions are not the problem, but solutions that respect national sovereignty and security are.” The UNHCR data cited by Grandi shows that the number of forcibly displaced people worldwide, including refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced persons, now exceeds 120 million. This is a figure that has nearly doubled in the last decade, driven by protracted crises in Syria, Afghanistan, and Ukraine, as well as regional conflicts in the Central African Republic and South Sudan. Grandi also pointed to the growing impact of climate change as a growing driver of displacement, citing floods in Pakistan and droughts in the Horn of Africa as examples.

The residents of Mexico City will be woken by an unusual alarm clock this weekend, as part of a bold new initiative designed to disrupt the city's deep-rooted culture of traffic congestion and noise pollution. Beginning on Saturday, a cascading “sound wave” will echo across the capital at dawn as a collaboration between urban planners, sound artists, and environmental activists aims to awaken the public with an acoustically diverse 15-minute performance of natural and ambient sounds—including birdsong, wind chimes, and even recordings of ancient pre-Hispanic flutes. According to project organisers, the soundscape will be broadcast from a network of strategically placed amplified devices specially installed on bridges, rooftops, and public spaces. The idea is to replace the city's usual early morning clang of car horns, sirens, and street vendors with a more serene and culturally resonant alternative. Mexico City, home to over 21 million people within its metro area, is renowned for its relentless breakfast-time traffic and sky-piercing noise levels which exceed 90 decibels in some areas—equivalent to the sound of a passing freight train. The project, titled “Despertar Nuevo” (New Awakening), is the brainchild of urban design firm EcoAurora and has received support from the city’s mayor, Claudia Sheinbaum. Sheinbaum has praised the initiative as “a creative step towards reimagining the soundscape of our city and reminding citizens of the beauty of our natural and cultural heritage.” The first performance will begin at 7 a.m. on Saturday, with a further two in the following days. Each soundscape has been curated to represent different regions of Mexico—starting with the lush tropical tones of the Yucatán Peninsula, followed by the arid desert melodies of the northwest, and culminating in a weekend finale featuring the high-altitude birdsong of Chiapas. Critics and residents alike are divided. Some city dwellers have expressed concern that the early morning sound installation could disrupt sleep patterns or create confusion among those who rely on traditional cues for waking up. Others, however, have hailed the project as an innovative and necessary way to reduce the city's dependency on the honking horns and rushed routines of urban life. Environmental campaigner Luis Ortega, one of the project’s consultants, said: “What we are trying to do is awaken not just the senses, but the soul of the city. It's not about replacing one noise with another—it's about making people conscious of the silence they might have lost.”

The Crown Prosecution Service has confirmed that a Labour peer at the centre of a decades-long child sex abuse scandal will not face charges due to his "advanced" mental state. Peter Janner, 86, was himself a member of Parliament for 33 years and a prominent figure in children's charities, yet the inquiry into alleged historic abuse claims against him has been concluded without charges being brought. The decision, announced on Thursday, marks the end of a judicial process that has spanned more than a decade, beginning with a 2009 police investigation. In a statement, the CPS said that Janner, whose full title is Lord Janner of Braunstone, will not face trial because he is "unfit to do so due to the severity of his dementia." The service added that he is “incapable of participating in his defence and would not be able to assist in the preparation or conduct of his defence.” The news has sparked anger among charities and campaigners who have long called for accountability in historic child abuse cases. Several testimonies from the 1970s and 1980s alleged that Janner abused children in care, often at his home in Leicester. The claims were never proven in a court of law, and the decision not to pursue charges has been met with accusations that it may set a problematic precedent. Former national newspapers – most notably the Daily Express – broke the allegations in the 1980s, but faced fierce criticism from MPs and the government of the time, who slammed the reports as defamatory. A formal inquiry in 1981 concluded that there was “no case to answer”. Since then, the cases have continued to resurface and be re-examined by both police and prosecutors. Janner was about to face trial in 2016 when the CPS overturned its initial decision to charge him, citing the same grounds that are now preventing a prosecution: his unfitness to stand trial. That decision was heavily disputed, with some lawmakers suggesting that Janner was being treated differently due to his political status. The current ruling adds to a deeply controversial legacy for a man once described as a “champion of children”, who served as a children’s rights advisor and held a prominent role in the charity world. Janner stepped down from the House of Lords in 2014 amid the goings-on of the inquiry, and his assets were later frozen in a separate legal case, though that issue was eventually resolved with a modest financial settlement.

Universities Paid Out Hundreds of Thousands in Compensation to Students – Official Data Reveals   Universities across England and Wales paid out more than £400,000 in compensation to students last year after handling complaints over a range of issues, including poor teaching standards, inadequate support, and breach of contract. The revelation, based on data provided to the Office of the Independent Adjudicator (OIA) for Higher Education, has sparked a fresh debate over the accountability and quality of university education in the UK. The OIA records indicate that a total of 248 complaints from full and part-time students in 2023 resulted in monetary compensation. The figures reflect growing dissatisfaction among students, many of whom are paying soaring tuition fees and expecting a correspondingly high standard of service and education. Among the most common complaints were issues relating to the guidance provided to disabled students, the absence of promised support services, and teaching quality concerns, particularly among those on online and postgraduate programmes. In one notable case, a student was awarded £33,000 in compensation after a university allegedly failed to make appropriate adjustments to support their neurodiverse condition. The OIA serves as a final independent appeals body for students who feel their complaints have not been adequately addressed by university authorities. As a result, the amount of compensation awarded is a stark indicator of how often institutions are failing to meet their obligations under student contracts and accessibility policies. A spokesperson for the OIA said: “These figures underscore the increasing awareness among students of their rights and the willingness of universities to provide redress where mistakes have been made. However, they also reflect an underlying concern that more institutions are at risk of breaching the expectations of their students and the standards expected of higher education providers.” Universities UK, the sector body representing about 140 universities in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, acknowledged the findings and said universities were “continually working to learn from feedback and improve the student experience.” In response to the data, Labour MP for Poole, Nicolle Feeley, said: “This shows that far too many students are not being treated as the priority they should be. With the cost of living crisis placing such enormous financial pressure on students, they deserve more than empty promises and compensation payouts after the damage has been done.” Shadow Education Secretary, Rebecca Long-Bailey, added: “Tuition fees have go up dramatically in recent years, and our students are rightly expecting much more in return.

Lee Smith has insisted there are no lingering tensions with his former club London Wasps ahead of his emotional return to Adams Park on Saturday. The Newcastle Falcons full-back, who spent five successful seasons at the Berkshire club, will take to the field against his old side for the first time since leaving in 2021 and has put concerns about on-field and off-field disagreements to rest. Speaking to   The Times   ahead of the Aviva Premiership clash, Smith said: “I have no issues with Wasps, past or present. It was a mutual decision to move on when I was ready for a new challenge. Playing against them now is just another game, even if it carries a bit more personal weight. I’m here to play for Newcastle first and foremost.” The 31-year-old, who made 87 appearances for Wasps between 2016 and 2021, has become a key figure for Falcons, forming a strong connection with fly-half George Dell and contributing to the team’s improved form this season. His departure from Wasps came amid a turbulent period for the club, which was expelled from the Premiership in early 2021, a decision later reversed after significant restructuring. Smith never expressed strong public criticism of the club and has remained on good terms with many of his former teammates. He added: “I always got on well with the lads. We had a good, tight-knit group during my time there. The club went through a lot, but that’s for the board to handle. I’m not in a position to comment on that side of things. I’m just glad my experiences are positive.” Fans at Adams Park are likely to make their feelings known when Smith takes to the pitch, as clashes like this are among the most anticipated of the season. The match is expected to draw a sell-out crowd, with many supporters keen to see how the new-look Wasps fare under ex-England forward Dean Ryan, who took over as head coach in November. Wasps’ new identity under Super League company LDN Holdings and their recent move to the Championship has sparked fresh interest in the club’s progress, and Saturday’s game will be one of their first major tests as they look to re-establish themselves in the top tier of English rugby. For Smith, the return is not only a personal milestone but a chance to help Newcastle continue their push up the table.

Calls for the reintroduction of a post-study work visa system for international students in Scotland have been firmly rejected by the UK government, sparking disappointment and concern among university leaders and business groups. The proposal, which had been championed by a coalition of Scottish universities and industry representatives, aimed to allow international graduate students to remain in the UK for two years after completing their studies, providing a pathway to permanent employment and settlement. The system had been in place until 2012 but was abolished in a bid to curb immigration numbers. In its absence, many graduates have struggled to find work in the UK and have instead returned home, depriving Scottish employers of valuable talent. The reintroduced system, which still exists for students in England and Wales, was backed by Education Secretary Angela Constance, who argued that it was an “essential tool” for growing Scotland’s economy and attracting high-calibre graduates from around the world. The government’s refusal came in response to a request made by Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon during a meeting with Prime Minister Theresa May last week. First Minister Sturgeon had argued that the absence of the post-study work visa was having a “devastating impact” on Scottish universities, which rely heavily on international student fees, and was deterring global talent from choosing Scotland as their destination for higher education. The current policy, which applies to all of the UK except Scotland, allows international students to stay for up to four years after graduation—two years while the graduate visa is in place and an additional two under a new global talent visa scheme. However, the two-year requirement in Scotland is currently in limbo, with no resolution in sight. Universities Scotland, which represents the sector in the country, condemned the decision as “out of touch and short-sighted” and warned it could damage Scotland’s global reputation as a hub for research and innovation. The organisation said it would explore all options, including legal and constitutional routes, to secure agreement on the issue. Critics of the current policy have claimed that it undermines the investment made by international students in their education and leaves talented individuals at risk of being lost to other countries’ workforces. At a time when the UK is looking to rebuild its economy post-Brexit, supporters of the system argue that retaining global talent is a key priority that the UK cannot afford to ignore.

Two men have been found guilty at the Old Bailey of smuggling a cache of firearms, including five rifles and three sub-machine guns, into the UK from the Netherlands in a shipping container described as "a smuggler's textbook operation." The trial, which concluded earlier this week, revealed the alarming level of sophistication used to bypass UK customs and security checks and transport weapons that could have been used for mass violence. The prosecution described the seizure as "one of the largest quantities of military-style firearms ever to enter this country illegally." The men, identified as 30-year-old Adrian Rahman and 40-year-old Christopher Warren, were convicted of conspiracy to import prohibited weapons under the Firearms Act 1968. Both appeared in court to hear the verdict, with Rahman composing himself well while Warren, who had previously served in the armed forces, showed visible emotion, blinking back tears as the jury returned their unanimous guilty verdict. Sentencing is expected to take place in the coming weeks. The weapons, intercepted in March 2023 after customs officers detected unusual activity during routine checks at a distribution centre near Heathrow Airport, included a total of 19 firearms—among them three Uzi sub-machine guns and two AR-15 rifles, both of which are commonly used in serious and deadly attacks. A forensic report submitted to the court showed the firearms were fully functional and capable of firing at a high rate of speed. The case was part of an ongoing investigation codenamed Operation Citadel, led by the Metropolitan Police and the National Crime Agency. Detectives revealed Rahman and Warren had conspired for at least 18 months, sourcing the weapons from an international dealer believed to have links to an Eastern European crime network. The men transported the firearms in a sealed container under the guise of importing ballet costumes, a ruse described by prosecutors as "a chilling deception" to mask the severity of their actions. During the trial, the Crown argued that the pair had shown "a complete disregard for public safety," with the potential for catastrophic consequences had the weapons reached the hands of criminal groups or lone actors. A senior police source said: "The seizure of these weapons could have ended in tragedy for innocent people. Convictions like this are essential in deterring weapon smuggling and preventing future violence." Family members of both defendants told the court they had "no prior indication" of their sons’ involvement in criminal activity, with Warren's wife describing her husband as a man who "loved firearms but never wished to do harm."

The European Council president, Charles Michel, has called for a proposal to restrict in-work benefits for newly arrived EU migrants, aiming to reduce the impact of the UK's historically high migration figures since 2004. Speaking at a press conference in Brussels, Michel argued that such targeted measures are necessary to address public concerns over welfare dependency and economic pressure caused by continuing inflows of migrants from the European Union. The proposal forms part of broader EU discussions on migration reform, which have gained urgency amid growing calls from several member states for a more coherent and regulated asylum and employment policy. Currently, EU citizens who move to the UK are entitled to access a range of in-work benefits, including working tax credits and housing support, after meeting the relevant residency criteria. However, critics argue that the criteria are too lenient and insufficient to deter high levels of migration destined for the UK's labor market. According to recent statistics from the Office for National Statistics, the UK’s net migration figures have fluctuated, but the total number of people arriving has remained significantly in excess of pre-2020 levels, with the majority coming from the EU. Michel’s comments follow strong advocacy from British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who has repeatedly stressed the need for both the UK and the EU to address migration as a shared challenge. In February, the UK government announced plans to cap certain benefits for EU migrants arriving after a new date, with further details expected to be finalised following the conclusion of Brexit-related negotiations with EU institutions. Earlier this month, the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford noted that in 2023, the net migration rate stood at 262,000—more than double the predicted pre-pandemic average. The UK government has set a net migration target of 100,000 by the end of the next Parliament. Michel defended the proposal as being in line with EU solidarity and the principle of shared responsibility. “We must not close borders, but we must ensure the sustainability of our guest countries,” he said, insisting that the reform would uphold the principles of fairness and proportionality. The idea has received backing from some Eurosceptic politicians who argue that such steps will help shift the burden of sustained migration from the UK to a more balanced EU-wide approach. However, opposition voices, including members of the House of Lords and some minority rights groups, have warned of the potentially discriminatory impact of such restrictions.

Lana the Labrador, once known to the world as the “saddest dog in the world” after her former owners left her on a park bench in Shanghai with no way to return home, may have finally found the third chance at happiness she so desperately needed. The 11-year-old dog, who became an international internet sensation in 2016, has been the subject of much heartbreak and hope over the years. Now, a miraculous twist in her story has touched the hearts of dog lovers across the globe once more. Lana’s journey began in China when she was abandoned by her elderly owners outside a supermarket in the city of Suzhou. Photographs of the dog, sitting alone on a bench with eyes full of longing and sadness, went viral across social media, prompting an outpouring of sympathy and interest in her welfare. Thanks to the efforts of foreigners living in China and animal welfare charities, Lans came to the attention of a rescue group working with international adoption, and in 2017, she was flown to Spain to begin a new life. In 2023, the news that Lana had been returned to China after separating from her second owners sent shockwaves through the global animal community. Her well-worn face and mournful appearance once again dominated headlines, but this time, the reaction was sharper, with many questioning the way she had been treated twice. However, just weeks after her return, the news emerged that Lana had been found by a new and very caring family in Chengdu. Lana’s new owner, who wishes to remain anonymous, says the dog has been hesitant but gradually warming to her new surroundings. Small but significant changes are being made each day — a fresh bed, delicious new food, and most importantly, the presence of a family who vow to never let her feel alone again. "She's learning to trust again," the owner said in a recent Facebook post. “She looks tired and a bit worn, but every time she sees me, her whole face lights up.” For Lana, who passed 500,000 social media followers long ago, this moment represents not only a rare canine redemption story but a powerful tale about loyalty, resilience and the enduring bond between humans and animals. As she adjusts to her latest chapter, the world is watching with hope that for once, the ending truly is happy. For the first time in her life, it seems, Lana may be about to write a story of comfort and love without a sad finale.

The man convicted of murdering a four-year-old boy in what prosecutors described as an "incomprehensible brutality" has been found dead in his cell at HMP Wandsworth, one of London’s most high-security prisons. Police confirmed that Kieran McEvoy, 21, was discovered unresponsive at about 10.30pm on Monday, and has since been pronounced dead. Post-mortem tests are scheduled to determine the exact cause of death, though no foul play is currently suspected. The tragic news comes just four months after McEvoy was sentenced to a minimum of 30 years in prison for the brutal killing of Leon Smith, the son of a close friend. The incident shocked a community in Sutton, South London, where the boy’s death was described by a local MP as an “unspeakable crime” that left the public “numb with horror.” Leon’s death came to light in February 2022 when paramedics were called to a domestic property following reports of a serious assault. The four-year-old was found with catastrophic head injuries, which were allegedly inflicted after he was beaten and struck with a large object. Court proceedings revealed harrowing details, including evidence that McEvoy had expressed no remorse as he described the attack. Leon died in hospital two days later, on 3 March. During the trial, the court was told that the child had been with McEvoy and other members of Leon’s family while the boy’s mother was out of the home for just 40 minutes. The case sparked an outpouring of grief and anger throughout the UK, with vigils held in memory of the child and renewed calls for action on child protection and domestic crimes. Leon’s father and mother, Paul and Lydia Smith, have been vocal in their efforts to raise awareness about child safety and the need for better monitoring of vulnerable children in shared care situations. Sutton Council has since undertaken an extensive review of child protection procedures, citing the case as a catalyst for change. A local charity has also been established in Leon’s name to support bereaved families and raise awareness about child safeguarding. Speaking tobbc, Councillor Ged Latimer described the case as a “never-ending nightmare for the family involved” and praised the couple for their “courage and determination to do the right thing, for Leon, for their other children, and the wider community.” McEvoy had been serving his sentence in a special unit at HMP Wandsworth for violent offenders, where he had been placed under close supervision due to reports of self-harming behaviour.

Donald Trump’s campaign has once again proven a polarizing force in American politics, with his sharp-edged rhetoric and unfiltered style deepening the nation’s divisions in a way not seen in recent memory. As the 2024 election edged closer, citizens across the country have found themselves firmly entrenched on either side of a growing ideological rift, largely fueled by the former president’s combative approach to both opponents and the media. Trump, known for his no-holds-barred style, has sparked fierce reactions, both positive and negative, as he re-enters the political arena. His campaign events have drawn massive crowds, but also protests and heated debate, often splintering even united communities. "He's fearlessly speaking out, and that's what politicians are supposed to do," said one lifelong Republican who attended a rally in Scottsdale, Arizona. "This country needs a fighter, and I think he's doing what's best for America." In contrast, several Democrats and even some Republicans have voiced concern over the tone of his campaign, which they claim has emboldened misinformation, fueled hostility, and eroded political norms. “There’s nothing like civility or decency in his message,” remarked a voter in Boston who refuses to support Trump. “It's like the whole campaign is based on belittling others and pushing people further into their bubbles.” Political commentators have drawn comparisons to the 2016 election, when Trump first ran as a presidential candidate and similarly fractured public opinion with his unorthodox rhetoric. “What we’re seeing now is the evolution of that divisive style. It’s no longer just polarizing—it’s tribal,” said political analyst Professor Emma Rice of Oxford University. “His strategy seems to be to position himself as the underdog while continuing to push boundaries that make most people flinch.” Despite the controversy, Trump’s message appears to be resonating with key demographics in what many see as a campaign that is as much about national identity as policy. His supporters praise the clarity, even if they bristle at the harsh language. Critics, however, fear the damage to the country's political fabric is becoming irreversible. As the campaign intensifies, Americans are increasingly segmented not just by party lines, but by attitudes towards civil discourse, truth, and the role of leadership in a democracy. Some wonder whether Trump's adversarial style will come with a cost at the ballot box or go on to define another election cycle rooted in division.

The National Health Service is to take drastic new steps in tackling underperforming hospitals and health services across England, as the chief executive of NHS England, Amanda Pritchard, announced today that entire areas will be placed in special measures if services are found to be “failing” the public. This announcement follows mounting pressure on the health service during the winter period, with emergency departments, ambulance response times and elective care all coming under intense scrutiny. Pritchard confirmed that a “systemic approach” will be taken to identify regions where performance targets are not being met, and where patient care has been compromised. Such areas will be subject to urgent intervention plans led by the NHS Improvement team. Special measures—previously used as a last resort for individual hospitals—will now be applied at a regional level for the first time. The move is intended to accelerate reform and bring about co-ordinated improvements in areas suffering from long-standing underperformance. It is understood that the north-west and parts of Yorkshire are among the initial regions under consideration for this measure. The announcement has split opinion within the NHS and political circles. Some have welcomed the bold step, calling it a long-overdue response to a crisis that has highlighted deep inequalities in healthcare across the country. Labour health spokesperson Emily Eldridge said the move “confirms what we have long been saying—that standards have plummeted in certain corners of the NHS and decisive action is required.” However, others warned that placing areas in special measures could provoke unintended consequences, including staff burnout and the risk of vital services being diverted from other parts of the country. Dr Sarah Kreps, consultant in emergency medicine, expressed concern that “the rush to intervene may not always address the root causes of underperformance and could lead to a tick-box mentality.” NHS England insists that the special measure intervention will be paired with increased funding and support to help the affected areas rebound. “This is not a punitive measure,” Pritchard said in a statement. “Our goal is to restore public trust, improve safety and ensure every patient receives the high-quality care they are entitled to. We will work closely with local leaders and staff to achieve that.” The government has yet to comment publicly on the decision, though sources suggest that ministers will support the initiative as part of their broader strategy to stabilise the NHS during the critical next year.

For over 400 years, a haunting yet enigmatic face with a grizzled moustache has stared solemnly from a stone block on Hamworthy Beach, overlooking Poole Harbour in Dorset. The visage, long thought to be the remnants of a 16th-century cannon — one of the many placed in the area to defend against potential invasion — has stood the test of time, becoming a local curiosity and a symbol of the harbour's turbulent past. Now, after centuries of weathering wind and tide, the mysterious face is set to journey once more across the waves — and this time, it will be returned to its rightful place. The cannon is one of only two still intact from a set of three erected in 1623 by Sir Myrcius Hopton, an eccentric local figure who fortified the Hamworthy shoreline against the looming threat of Spanish Armada-type invasions. The cannon had lain in near-oblivion for several centuries when, in 1978, local historian Jack Costello identified the moustachioed figure, rekindling public interest in the cannon’s origins. Despite attempts to locate the other two, only fragments remain of those, leaving the moustachioed one to become a humanistic relic, as much a part of local lore as the Pendle Witch Trials or the D-Day landings at nearby Portland. Heritage officers, in collaboration with Poole Harbour Conservancy and local community groups, have now secured £200,000 in funding to restore and reposition the cannon in a newly created coastal heritage display on Hamworthy’s foreshore. The project is not merely an act of preservation, but a reimagining of the cannon’s role — as a guardian of history, rather than a soldier about to fire. “It's not just the cannon we're saving,” said Dr. Eliza Harper, a maritime historian working on the project. “It's a reminder of how closely the lives of coastal communities like Poole have always been tied to the sea — for better or worse.” The cannon will be reconstructed stone by stone and installed in a way that allows visitors to see the moustache from as close as a few feet away. Some locals have likened the face to that of the “Fortune Teller of Hamworthy” — a quirky but stoic man known to have goaded sailors on the coast about their destinies. Others suggest it could simply be the smiling visage of Sir Hopton himself, cast in stone to watch over his latest attempt at preparedness.

The sweetest part of Glasgow’s famous victory in Paris was indeed the almost utter unlikelihood of it. Few, if any, would have dared to dream it possible—that a group of players largely overlooked, underestimated, and occasionally overburdened with expectation based on past glories, would rise as they did to deliver a moment etched in sporting folklore. For a city used to both triumph and tribulation, this victory was as much of a surprise as it was a celebration. Glasgow’s journey to Paris had not promised much in terms of hype or expectation. Unlike their high-profile rivals, whose preparations had drawn feverish media attention and public anticipation, the team limped into the spotlight trailing behind losses, injuries, and a stark lack of form. Their performances in the run-up to the final had been inconsistent at best, raising questions over their credentials and fitness to withstand the pressure of Parisian football. Yet, what unfolded in the final was a demonstration of raw character, grit, and an indomitable team spirit that stunned onlookers and rekindled belief in the enduring magic of the underdog story. The match itself became a moment of catharsis, not just for the players, but for the thousands of fans who had followed their journey with a mix of hope and resignation. Glasgow, a city known for its tenacity and resilience, saw in its national team a reflection of its own evolving spirit—scrappy, determined, and often underestimated. The final whistle in Paris did not just mark the end of a game; it marked the culmination of a stirring redemption arc. Sport at its best is about moments like this—when a narrative defies the odds, when ambition outpaces expectation, and when a victory is all the sweeter for having come when it was least expected. For Glasgow, this was more than a win. It was a resurgence of something deeply felt and widely shared. And perhaps that is why the taste of triumph in Paris lingers a little longer in the hearts of those who witnessed it. Moments like these remind us that in sport, as in life, greatness is not always fashioned in the spotlight, but often discovered in the shadows. The question now is what lessons from such an unheralded triumph can be carried forward with the same quiet confidence that led to the moment in the first place. That, perhaps, is the best course of the future.

Turkey has called for an urgent meeting of NATO ambassadors in Brussels to discuss ongoing military operations against both the Islamic State (IS) terror group and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), as part of its broader strategy to address security threats on its soil and beyond. The meeting comes amid rising tensions as Turkey continues its military campaign against Kurdish forces in northern Syria and Iraq, often citing the PKK as a key threat to national security. The government of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has long accused the PKK of being responsible for numerous attacks on civilians and military personnel, branding it a terrorist organisation and vowing to eliminate its presence in regions along the Turkish-Syrian and Turkish-Iraqi borders. In recent weeks, Turkish airstrikes and cross-border operations have intensified, drawing international concern and prompting calls for de-escalation. In a statement, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said the meeting would provide a platform for NATO members to align their positions on the most effective way to counter both IS and PKK. Turkey has been a key NATO partner in the broader fight against IS and has contributed troops and aircraft to the US-led coalition against the group since 2015.
