A Florida officer shot and wounded an unarmed black therapist while responding to a request for help from a man with autism, local media reported on Monday, sparking an investigation into the use of force and raising concerns over policing practices in the state. The incident occurred in Largo, a city outside Tampa, after 31-year-old Ricardo Baumbach, an employee at the Gulf Coast Center for Autism and Developmental Disabilities, was called to assist a distressed man who had not been sleeping or eating in days and appeared to be emotionally overwhelmed. Mr Baumbach, a licensed therapist and advocate for the autism community, was working with his client, whose identity has not been disclosed, when a 911 call was made to report the situation, according to reports. Chad Myrum, a Hillsborough County sheriff’s deputy who responded to the call, arrived at the scene, where he reportedly confronted Mr Baumbach and demanded to know who he was. Tensions escalated rapidly when, according to witnesses and video footage obtained by the Press in Tampa Bay, Mr Baumbach attempted to explain his role, but the officer fired multiple shots, striking the therapist in the legs and rendering him unable to walk. Mr Baumbach was taken to a local hospital and is said to be in non-critical condition. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that the shooting was under investigation and stated that it was “collecting facts and evidence surrounding the incident.” The agency said it would “determine if any policy was violated.” The video footage, which has since been widely shared on social media, has cast sharp focus on the deputy’s response to a clearly non-threatening situation. Mr Baumbach had no weapon and continued to walk away from the officer as he was shot, according to the Press in Tampa Bay. The autism community has expressed deep concern over the incident, with many reacting to the fact that an individual supporting vulnerable people was harmed by police. Autistic individuals often face unique challenges in interactions with law enforcement due to differences in communication and sensory processing. Mr Baumbach’s union, the Florida Scholastic Press Association, called for a full and transparent investigation into the shooting. “Ricardo was trained to de-escalate situations like this with people on the spectrum. It’s alarming to see an unarmed, professional worker be shot by a police officer,” a union representative said in a statement.

Young man found in possession of Nazi paraphernalia during school visit to Holocaust Museum sparks outrage   A pupil at a London secondary school has drawn widespread condemnation after arriving at the school dressed in a costume evoking Nazi themes, including a black uniform, a Darth Vader-like mask, and a stylised sword, during a visit to the Holocaust Memorial Centre in Manchester. The 15-year-old, identified only as Anton L., has been temporarily suspended from the Aneurin Bevan Community School in Oldham, Greater Manchester, pending an internal disciplinary investigation. The disturbing incident was captured on mobile phone video by other students and later shared on social media platforms, swiftly going viral. In the footage, Anton is seen stomping aggressively through the school corridors, pointing at and singling out students with darker skin tones to confront. One witness described the scene as “terrifying,” adding, “It felt like he was trying to make us feel like we were his enemies.” The school, which serves a diverse community, has condemned the act in the strongest possible terms. Headteacher Kathy Baker released a statement saying: “We are deeply shocked and disgusted by the behaviour of one of our students. This is totally unacceptable and contrary to our school's ethos of respect, equality and human dignity. We are collaborating closely with the local authority and the police to ensure a thorough investigation takes place.” The school’s visit to the Holocaust Memorial Centre, an educational initiative aimed at teaching students about the Holocaust and the importance of standing against hatred and discrimination, was meant to be a profoundly solemn and reflective day. Now, many question whether the trip will also serve as a lesson in the very intolerance it was designed to combat. The Metropolitan Police is now investigating the incident as a potential hate crime under the Race Relations Act. A spokesperson for the force said: “Anyone who uses clothing or symbols to intimidate or offend another person on the grounds of their race, colour or ethnic background is likely to be prosecuted. We are taking this complaint very seriously and are carrying out investigations.” Parents of pupils at the school are demanding answers. One parent told the  Manchester Evening News : “This isn’t just about a costume. It’s about a message of hatred being delivered in full view of our children. We want to know how such a thing was allowed to happen and what the school plans to do beyond a suspension.”

Scottish politicians are ramping up their efforts as they hit the streets to meet voters this weekend, with just five days remaining until the general election on Thursday, July 4. Across Edinburgh, Glasgow, and the Scottish Borders, candidates from all major parties are engaging in door-to-door campaigning, town halls, and public events in a final rush to influence the electorate ahead of polling day. For many voters, this weekend is expected to be the most decisive of the campaign so far. With the result in Scotland widely seen as a key battleground for determining whether a majority government is formed at Westminster, the stakes for all parties are high. The Scottish National Party (SNP), seeking to build on its 2019 dominance, has been emphasizing its record on devolved issues like the NHS, education, and climate change. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, meanwhile, has called for a return of "national unity," urging voters to unite behind the Conservative Party to address economic challenges and "clean up" British politics. Opposition leaders are not standing idly by. Keir Starmer, leader of the Labour Party, has been campaigning heavily in key marginals like Edinburgh East and Glasgow North East, where he is facing strong challenges from the SNP. Labour has stressed the need for a strong, stable government to fix the economy and bring an end to what it calls the “disastrous” policies of the Conservative Party. The Liberal Democrats, Greens, and Reform UK are also making their presence felt, with each party pushing their own visions for Scotland’s role in the UK and on the global stage. Localised issues are also dominating the political narrative. In areas like Ayrshire and the Borders, debates over healthcare access and infrastructure have been central to politicians’ pitches. Meanwhile, education reform, rural broadband expansion, and public transport improvements are key themes in urban centers like Glasgow and Edinburgh, where candidates are facing a generational and often fiercely contested electorate. As turnout projections remain tight, the focus for all political leaders is on persuading undecided voters and ensuring that their core supporters are motivated to cast their ballots. With the election looming, any ground gained during the final days of campaigning could prove decisive in determining which party forms the next government and how much of Scotland’s voice is represented in Parliament. The coming five days will test not only the stamina of the candidates but also the resilience of the political landscape itself.

Facebook, the social media giant, unwittingly hosted an online exchange between one of the men who later murdered Fusilier Lee Rigby and far-right extremists, five months before the 2013 murder, the BBC has revealed. The conversation, which took place in May 2012 — well before the terrorist act in Woolwich, London — appears to have included racist and anti-Muslim rhetoric, as well as boasts about plans for a "jihad" against those perceived as enemies of Islam. The details, obtained through records and interview sources, suggest Facebook was used as a platform for radical discussion among individuals who would later coalesce under the banner of the terror organisation Islamic State, orISIS. Fusilier Lee Rigby, a 25-year-old British soldier, was brutally killed by MI5-surveilled extremists Michael Adebolajo and Michael Adebowale, who used knives and a hammer to carry out the attack in broad daylight. The horrific scene was live-streamed by Adebolajo, with the footage later appearing across the internet, including on Facebook pages linked to extremist groups. Investigators have since revealed that the platform was more than a passive host — it played a role in connecting and radicalising those involved in the crime. A Facebook group and private message thread reportedly included Adebolajo and others who would later form part of the plot. The conversation, which appeared to predate any direct radical grooming by known terrorist networks, involved calls to arms and graphic descriptions of violence against “infidels.” One unnamed participant is quoted as saying that the military and the police were “legitimate targets for the global war on Islam.” The exchange, which came to light following a months-long investigation by the BBC, highlights the growing concerns over how social media can be used to spread extremist ideologies and radicalise individuals who might otherwise not have access to such material. Facebook officials were quick to respond, stating that they take reports of such content “very seriously” and have procedures in place to remove posts that violate their community guidelines. A spokesperson said, “We are committed to creating a safe environment on our platform and collaborate with law enforcement to support investigations into terrorism and other illegal activity.” The discovery has reignited calls for tighter regulation of online platforms, especially in preventing the spread of extremist content. MPs and security experts have long argued that companies like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube must do more to identify and remove dangerous material before it can be used to radicalise or incite violence.

For once, that overused word turmoil is amply justified. The southern African kingdom of Lesotho, a small, landlocked nation nestled within the borders of South Africa, has found itself engulfed in an unprecedented political crisis that has thrust it into the international spotlight with alarming urgency. At the heart of this unfolding drama is Prime Minister Thomas Thabane, who has fled the country for South Africa, accusing his own military of staging a coup and placing his life in peril. The situation in this oft-troubled nation is tense, uncertain, and increasingly dangerous. Speaking to the BBC from his temporary refuge in South Africa, Mr. Thabane described a military takeover that had rendered his government “dysfunctional,” adding that he had only left Lesothu to preserve his safety. “I came into South Africa this morning and I will return as soon as my life is not in danger. I will not go back to Lesotho to get killed,” he stated, his voice carrying the gravity of a man who has seen too much instability in his homeland. The events began early on Monday morning, when the first gunshots echoed through the capital, Maseru, jolting the capital from its familiar rhythm into chaos. By morning, as news of troop movements and apparent military takeovers of key government buildings spread, the city had fallen silent, with residents confined to their homes – unsure of what to expect next, and distrustful of the authorities. “It’s a media blackout,” said Basildon Peta, publisher of the Lesotho Times, who is currently in Maseru. “This is a military coup. There can be no other reason for the soldiers' actions other than to seize power.” What started as a quiet early morning soon escalated into a situation that Prime Minister Thabane now calls a coup. He has not ruled out the possibility of further violence. Thabane, who has led a unity government since the election in May 2012, has faced significant political pressure from within his own party. He suspended parliamentary sessions in June 2013 due to internal conflicts within his coalition. His government has long been on tenuous grounds, but the current crisis appears to stem from a power struggle within the military itself. According to reports, the army’s actions followed an attempt by Thabane to remove the head of the armed forces, Lt Gen Kennedy Tlai Kamoli. The military, for its part, has denied the rumors of a coup, with spokesman Maj Ntlele Ntoi insisting that all was well.

Three years ago, Andy Murray arrived at the Roland Garros tournament in Paris with a significant cloud hanging over his career. Suffering from a persistent and nagging back injury, Murray had seen his dream of competing at the French Open disappear after it flared up only 10 days earlier during the Italian Open in Rome. The injury not only sidelined him from one of the most prestigious Grand Slams on the tennis calendar but also raised serious questions about his long-term prospects in the sport. At the time, many experts and fans alike watched Murray's career with bated breath, wondering whether the two-time Wimbledon champion could recover his form. Fast forward to 2024, and the story is immeasurably different. In the past few months alone, Murray has experienced a career renaissance that has taken the tennis world by surprise. Recently, Murray completed what many are calling the most dramatic comeback in the history of the sport, making a victorious return to the top when, somewhat miraculously, he happened upon a net cord in his semi-final match. This not only provided a crucial turning point in the match but also demonstrated the full measure of his skill and resilience. The satisfaction of his win is not limited to the short-term glory of tournament victories. It is also a redemption for the years of injury and watching other peers move forward without him. For Murray, it's a validation that years of intense focus, rigorous physiotherapy, and an unwavering belief in his ability have not gone in vain. The British number one is back, not only in terms of form but also in stature, and his return has reignited a sense of excitement and pride across the United Kingdom. Murray's journey back to the top has been nothing short of extraordinary. From slipping down the rankings in 2021 to making key finals in 2022 and 2023, his progress has been measured and consistent. Whether it's the media, his coaches, or his family, everyone is quick to point out the sheer determination that has led to this exceptional comeback. As fans reflect on his recent achievements, one can't help but wonder: is this the start of a new era for one of Britain's greatest tennis players, or is this the peak of a truly remarkable second act in his career? As he takes to the court once again this week, the man from Dunblane is more than just a competitor.

The Great Barrier Reef is at the heart of an escalating crisis that could see Australia grapple with both a significant dent to its global reputation and a potential collapse in one of the most important sectors of its economy—tourism. Faced with mounting pressure from environmental advocates and international organizations, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is considering placing the Reef on its “List of World Heritage in Danger” following reports that have highlighted a decline in water quality, mass coral bleaching events, and ongoing threats posed by climate change and human activity. According to a recent assessment by the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, the Reef has deteriorated to a critical state, with sections suffering extensive damage from back-to-back mass bleaching events linked to rising sea temperatures. Scientists have repeatedly warned that if these trends persist, the Reef could be beyond recovery within decades. This looming threat has sparked a national conversation in Australia, with environmental groups and scientists urging the government to take immediate and decisive action to protect the Reef. Currently, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee meets once a year to consider whether to add, remove, or keep the Great Barrier Reef on the danger list—set for review this July. Should the decision be made to list the Reef as "in danger," the consequences could be far-reaching. Australia’s tourism industry, which generates billions of dollars annually and supports tens of thousands of jobs, is particularly vulnerable. In 2023 alone, the Reef attracted over two million tourists, contributing an estimated A$6.4 billion to the economy. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has pledged to take all necessary measures to protect the natural wonder. “The Great Barrier Reef is not just a point of national pride, but a global treasure,” he said in a recent statement. “We are committed to doing everything in our power to preserve it for future generations.” But the opposition has accused the government of moving too slowly on environmental protection, with some MPs arguing that stronger climate policies and stricter regulations on land-based agricultural runoff are essential. Meanwhile, the coal industry, which generates significant revenue for the country and whose activities contribute to environmental degradation, is being scrutinized under intense public and political pressure. As Australia prepares for what could be one of the most defining environmental decisions of the decade, the fate of the Great Barrier Reef—both as an ecosystem and as an economic and cultural asset—hangs in the balance.

Celtic manager Ronny Deila has praised the performances of midfield stars Callum McGregor and Scott Allan as the Glasgow giants claimed a 3-1 victory over Inverness Caledonian Thistle in their Scottish Premiership clash at Celtic Park. The win extended Celtic’s dominance in the league as Deila highlighted the pivotal role played by his midfield duo in securing a key three points. McGregor and Allan were instrumental in all three of Celtic’s goals, demonstrating the technical and physical quality that has made them key components of Deila’s side. Both players were tireless in their energy, contributing to attacks and breaking up opposition play with well-timed interventions. Their influence was particularly noticeable in the second half, when Celtic turned the match in their favor with two quickfire goals. Speaking after the match, Deila said: "Callum and Scott were outstanding today. They are both special players and I think they turned the game for us in the second half. They have been working really hard for the team this season and they are playing in a team that’s demanding the highest standards every week, and they have both delivered." The Norwegian manager, who took charge of Celtic in 2014, has often spoken about the need for strong central midfield to support the creative play of his wingers and forwards. The performances of Allan, signed from West Bromwich Albion earlier this season, and McGregor have often underpinned that approach, providing both control and protection in the middle of the park. Allan has been a revelation since making the move to Glasgow, with his versatility and composure marking him out as a valuable asset. Deila has frequently rotated his central midfield partnership, but with McGregor and Allan displaying such fine form, it is likely they will retain their starting roles for key matches coming up in the league and Europa League. The win brought Celtic to within one point of second place in the table, thanks to their superior goal difference. Deila, however, is unimpressed by league positions and insists the team must keep focusing on performance. "We are not here for just league points," he said. "We are here to play with intense determination, enthusiasm, and performance – and we are doing exactly that." Celtic’s next challenge is a crucial Europa League tie, and with the form of their midfield looking as sharp as ever, Deila will head into that game with confidence.

Sudan’s history is one of resilience—etched into its parched landscapes, its turbulent politics and its songs of dissent passed down from generation to generation. And now, as the nation grapples with yet another bout of political upheaval, a new group of young poets is rising to keep that legacy alive. In cafes, on social media, and at grassroots gatherings, Sudanese youth are reclaiming the power of words as tools of resistance. Among them is Yousra Elbagir, a Sudanese-British journalist and documentary filmmaker who has been journeying across the country to document this revival. Elbagir’s recent piece for the BBC’s  Africas  series delves into how a new generation of poets, often trained in literature and philosophy, is weaving protest into verse, echoing an age-old tradition of lyrical rebellion. From the backstreets of Khartoum to the remote villages of Darfur, these poets are challenging censorship, inspiring resilience, and finding new ways to express outrage against a regime in flux. Their words, often as bold as they are beautiful, have become anthems for a movement determined to see democratic change through to the end. This is not the first time poetry has played a pivotal role in Sudan’s narrative. The country once boasted a proud literary culture, with poets like Mahjoub Saleh lending their words to national struggle and transformation. But with the rise of authoritarianism and the repression of free speech, that tradition nearly faded into obscurity. Now, thanks to the internet and the growing reach of social media, young poets are able to circulate their work more widely than ever before. Their verses—mixing traditional Arabic with the vernaculars of Nubian, Beja, and Darfurian languages—speak of hunger, oppression, and dreams of freedom. As Elbagir notes, their poetry is “not just a form of expression, but of survival.” Whether performed in the shadow of a military checkpoint or shared on TikTok, their words carry the same punch. For many, it is a way to remember who they are, where they come from, and what they are fighting for. The question now is whether these voices, as strong as they are, can pierce the silence of a country on the cusp of transformation. In a nation that has seen so much bloodshed and so many broken promises, Sudan’s young poets are once again proving that even in the darkest of times, the line between language and liberation runs thinner than it seems.

The Belfast Giants mounted a stunning third-period comeback to beat the Nottingham Panthers 7-4 in a dramatic Elite Ice Hockey League encounter at the SSE Arena on Saturday night. With the game locked at 4-4 heading into the final 20 minutes, the home side showed remarkable resilience and firepower to score three goals in quick succession and steal a thrilling victory. The triumph capped a night of high drama and intensity at the Ulster capital's world-renowned indoor ice rink. The Giants, who suffered a 3-2 home defeat to Nottingham in their previous meeting just two weeks ago, were eager to settle the rivalry, and they left no doubt in a tense but exhilarating final stanza. The Panthers had taken a 4-3 lead into the third period thanks to an early goal from captain Marco Cuda and a solo effort from Anton Karlsson to cap off their most disciplined and clinical display of the campaign. However, the Giants, displaying a blend of composure and urgency, roared back with goals from Brian Costello, in his first season with the club, and a brace from Jordan Mintz, whose performances have continued to divide opinion among fans. The turning point came at the 13-minute mark when Sean Richards controlled the puck in the offensive zone and found Mintz with a pinpoint pass. The American forward, known for his endurance rather than his finishing abilities, potted the equaliser with a simple, but decisive, slapshot to the back of the net. It was to be the moment that sparked a wave of momentum in Belfast’s favor. Just two minutes later, someone dislodged the puck from Panthers’ defenceman Kyle Rau, allowing Costello to capitalise with a breakaway opportunity and extend the home side’s lead to 5-4. The momentum didn’t let up as Steve Savard notched a crucial insurance goal with just over five minutes remaining. Nottingham, despite their best efforts to plug gaps in their own zone, could not close the deficit and found themselves chasing the game for the closing stages. The Panthers did manage a late goal from Daniel Brennan to make it 6-5, but it was too little, too late, as the Giants held firm and added a seventh to seal a thoroughly deserved victory. Post-match, Belfast head coach Adam Dyck heaped praise on his team's poise under pressure and their desire not to be written off in a game they looked to be losing.

The Boy Scouts of America has confirmed that a decision on ending its long-standing ban on openly gay scouts and leaders will be delayed, following a last-minute adjournment of the organisation’s national board meeting. Originally scheduled for September, the long-anticipated vote has now been postponed as the leadership seeks what it called a “more comprehensive approach” to address the issue. The Scouts’ current policy, which prohibits youth members who are openly gay and adult leaders who are openly lesbian or gay, has drawn increasing criticism and legal challenges over the past decade. Last year, the American Civil Liberties Union and the Human Rights Campaign called the policy discriminatory, arguing that it conflicts with the organisation’s founding principle of being open to all young people regardless of their background. In 2013, the ban on scouts was lifted after seven years of intense activism, but the rule surrounding adult leaders has remained in place, prompting continued pressure from supporters of LGBTQ+ inclusion. The postponement has sparked frustration among advocates, who accused the board of using delays as a tactic to avoid hard decisions. “This delay is unacceptable,” said Ken Montoya, national director of the Gay, Lesbian and Straight Education Network (GLSEN). “It is clear that the Scouts are prioritising tradition over the needs of young people and the real-world values of inclusion and equality.” Yet, the move may also reflect concerns from more conservative elements within the organisation about the potential impact of changing the policy, particularly on affiliated religious youth groups. The Boy Scouts of America has long operated through partnerships with a wide range of faith-based organisations, many of which have their own views on matters of sexuality and gender. Critics of the ban have argued that the Scouts are out of step with the mainstream values of young people in the 21st century, but supporters insist the group must remain faithful to its original mission and constitution. A representative from the organisation said the board had instructed committees to review all options thoroughly before another vote is scheduled. “This is not a matter of turning to the left or the right,” the representative stated. “We are trying to remain centrist and true to the values that have guided the Scout movement for over a hundred years.” The waiting game continues, with the nation watching as one of America’s most iconic youth organisations comes to terms with a new social and political landscape.

A new Palestinian unity government has been sworn in, marking a pivotal moment in the long-standing political divide between rival factions in the West Bank and Gaza. The formation of the Cabinet is seen as a critical step toward reconciliation between the Fatah and Hamas movements, who have maintained a fragile and often bitter separation for over a decade. The swearing-in ceremony, held in Ramallah, the West Bank administrative capital, was attended by senior officials representing both sides. Among those present were President Mahmoud Abbas of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority and Ismail Haniyeh, the Hamas political leader, who has for the first time in years taken a public step toward collaboration with Fatah. The united government, led by Muhammad Ishhag, a former aide to Abbas and considered a centrist figure, aims to establish an interim administration that could pave the way for broader reconciliation efforts and, ultimately, reconciliation and reform in governance. The initiative was brokered with the backing of key regional and international actors, including Egypt and Qatar, who have long played a role in mediating between the two factions. The move reflects a growing sense of urgency in the face of Israeli military operations in Gaza and the increasing volatility of the situation in the occupied territories. While Fatah, which is aligned with the internationally recognized Palestinian Authority, has traditionally controlled the West Bank, Hamas has been in charge of governing Gaza since 2007, following a violent coup. The division has long frustrated efforts toward a unified Palestinian state and has hindered the prospects for peace talks with Israel. The unity government, which is described in public statements as a "national salvation government," is expected to focus primarily on delivering basic services, easing humanitarian crises, and rebuilding infrastructure across the divided territories. However, overcoming years of mistrust between the two groups is expected to be an immense challenge. Analysts note that the success of the government will depend on its ability to enforce control not only in the West Bank and Gaza but also in the disputed areas of East Jerusalem and the southern West Bank. "This is not an easy task," said Wa’el Abu al-Khair, a political analyst based in Ramallah. “Both groups have deeply ingrained positions and regional backers. The unity government is being asked to balance the interests of Palestinian citizens with the demands of foreign powers.” Some observers also warn that Israeli and US concerns around Hamas' militant wing could complicate the govt’s efforts to gain international legitimacy or support.

The long-awaited independent review into the future of tidal lagoon energy in the UK has sparked renewed debate over its environmental viability — a sector once hailed as a cornerstone of renewable energy now under intense scrutiny. Conducted by Scottish consulting firm Mott MacDonald, the review was commissioned by ministers in the wake of the government’s controversial decision to reject the second tidal lagoon project, proposed by Simec Atlantis Energy off the coast of Swansea in 2018. A year later, policy changes in May 2019 formally ended state support for new lagoon developments. Now, the findings present a complex picture — balancing the potential of tidal energy with concerns over its ecological impact and cost-effectiveness. At the heart of the environmental discourse are the potential consequences for marine ecosystems. Tidal lagoons rely on the ebb and flow of water between the lagoon and the sea, which is used to drive turbines and generate electricity. But scientists and environmental groups have raised alarms about the effects of altering natural tidal patterns. Studies suggest that blocked inlets and the construction of large concrete barriers could disrupt sediment transport, damage habitats and affect the survival of key species such as fish and crustaceans. Dr. Emily Rhys, a marine biologist at the University of Wales, warned that the long-term effects of tidal lagoon operations on estuaries and coastal habitats are still not fully understood. “We know alterations in water flow can have knock-on effects on biodiversity,” she explained. “We saw similar concerns with other coastal developments, and the ecosystems can take years to recover — if they do at all.” Fish migration patterns are another area of concern. Marine biologists have pointed to potential barriers caused by lagoon structures, which could hinder the movement of species like salmon and eels — both of which are already under significant conservation pressure. Some have even cited the example of the Scolt Tail Z barrier in Cumbria, where adverse effects on water quality and species were detected following its construction. On the economic side, opponents of tidal energy argue that construction costs remain high and are not yet competitive with more mature renewable technologies such as wind and solar. The Swansea lagoon, for example, was estimated to cost £1.3 billion and generate electricity at 240p per kilowatt-hour — over three times the cost of recent offshore wind contracts. The review appears to reinforce these economic concerns, while also recommending that future consideration of tidal energy must involve more rigorous environmental impact assessments and better engagement with local communities and environmental bodies.

President Jacob Zuma’s long-awaited release of the 600-page Marikana report has reignited a deeply entrenched national debate over the rule of law in South Africa, more than six years after a violent confrontation between police and striking miners left 34 dead and 70 injured outside a platinum mine near Rustenburg in the North West province. The report, compiled by former judge Ian Farlam and his panel of investigators, offers a detailed account of the events of 16 August 2012, but its release was met not just with anticipation, but also with skepticism. Many South Africans are still grappling with the slow pace of justice and the lingering impact of one of the most tragic episodes in the post-apartheid era. The Marikana massacre has since become a symbol of the systemic failures within the South African state—from the demands of the labor sector for fair wages and better working conditions, to the violent response by the police, and the perceived lack of accountability from those in power. The report has been criticized in some quarters for not being as robust in its findings or as clear in its judgment as many had hoped, with some sections heavily redacted, citing national security concerns. These omissions have fueled accusations that the report undermines transparency and the public’s right to know, especially in a country where the rule of law is a cornerstone of democracy. The national conversation that has followed is as much about the past as it is about the present. Civil society groups and opposition parties are calling for the establishment of a special prosecuting unit dedicated to the Marikana case, in what they argue is an attempt to avoid political interference. At the same time, survivors and the families of the victims are demanding not just legal accountability but practical justice—reparations, education for the children of the dead, and tangible support for communities still reeling from the trauma of that day. In releasing the report, President Zuma has been praised for showing some commitment to transparency, but also criticized for delaying its publication for so long. Some observers suggest that the timing coincided with broader political maneuvering, including the ongoing battle for democratic legitimacy as the African National Congress (ANC) seeks to reassert its dominance while dealing with internal divisions. Others propose that Zuma is trying to draw a line under the scandal before the 2015 general elections, delivering something akin to a political olive branch to the public.

In a spellbinding display of T20 batting, Alex Hales carved a record-breaking 95 from just 30 balls to lead Nottinghamshire Outlaws to a stunning win over Durham Jets at Trent Bridge. The game, played in front of an electric crowd, saw Hales unleash a whirlwind innings in the Powerplay that set a new benchmark in the shortest format of the game. Notts' remarkable total of 195-2 in six overs — the highest Powerplay score in T20 history — stunned the cricketing world and underlined Hales' reputation as one of the most fearless hitters of his generation. Hales' masterclass included seven boundaries and eight towering sixes as he and fellow opener Lewis Gregory pounded the Durham attack well beyond its capacity. The duo stitched together a partnership of 136, accounting for the majority of Nottinghamshire's total within the opening six overs. Hales, in particular, was at his relentless best, launching the first ball of the innings for a six and showing no sign of slowing down as he strode effortlessly to his near-century in a blistering over per 100 balls strike rate. Nottinghamshire’s record-breaking Powerplay score puts them a step ahead of previous records set by teams such as Hampshire in 2023, and it will undoubtedly be etched into the annals of T20 history. Durham, who had entered the game as one of the competition's stronger sides, were left scrambling at the slower scoring required to chase down such an aggressive onslaught. Their chase was further hampered by a clinical bowling display from Notts' pacemen, who stifled the run flow and ensured the game never inched into the mouths of the Durham batters. Speaking after the match, Notts captain Chris Nash praised Hales' “flawless execution and vision during the Powerplay” and described the innings as “unreal and a masterclass in modern T20 batting.” The performance has put Hales firmly back in the spotlight as England's top international players continue to monitor standout domestic showings. With the T20 World Cup on the horizon, such explosive powerplay performances are as crucial as they are rare. As the cricketing world digests what may well have been the defining T20 innings of the season, one thing is certain: Alex Hales has reminded all onlookers why he remains one of the most electrifying performers on the circuit today. His 30-ball 95 may already be classified as a record, but for fans, it will live on as a moment of pure T20 brilliance.

Middlesbrough have parted ways with manager Aitor Karanka after three and a half years at the helm, marking the end of a challenging and ultimately unsuccessful tenure for the Spanish manager at the Riverside Stadium. The announcement comes as the club sits near the relegation zone in the Premier League, having struggled for consistency this season. Karanka, who took charge in June 2013, departs with his legacy at the club defined more by promise than achievement, despite his efforts to bring a brand of attractive, attacking football to the Teesside side. The decision to sack Karanka coincides with the run-up to the January transfer window, as owner Steve Gibson seeks a change in direction to steer Boro away from the danger of relegation. Karanka’s tenure began with a strong start, including an impressive Europa League run in the 2014-15 season, and a Premier League campaign that saw them finish in mid-table. However, the following seasons proved more difficult, with several early exits from European competitions and inconsistent league form, culminating in a squad that has shown signs of disunity in recent weeks. After guiding Middlesbrough into the top flight for the first time since 2009, Karanka was widely praised for raising the club’s profile and instilling a distinctive identity during his early days in charge. However, fans have grown increasingly impatient as injuries, evolving squad needs and fluctuating performances have hampered progress. His reputation as a tactical innovator has also been questioned following what some perceive as a failure to adapt to the changing dynamics of the Premier League. Aitor Karanka’s sacking is the second managerial change of the season in the top division, following Crystal Palace’s decision to replace Sam Allardyce in October. The club now faces the challenge of finding a replacement quickly to provide stability as the season enters a pivotal phase. Current assistant manager Ronny Deila has been mentioned as a potential interim candidate, while a number of high-profile names from across Europe are being considered for the permanent role. Fans are now turning their attention to the January transfer market, where any fresh investment will be vital in turning Boro’s season around. For Karanka, the move ends a chapter of his managerial career that, while ambitious, ultimately failed to meet the expectations of a fanbase desperate for progress beyond a return to the Premier League. Further developments are expected in the coming days as Middlesbrough look to restore their fortunes and climb away from the drop zone.

Scotland were dealt a heavy defeat by Italy in an emphatic World Cup qualifier at Wembley Stadium on Sunday, with the Azzurri dominating from start to finish. The match, part of their crucial pre-Euro 2024 campaign, left the Tartan Army bemused as their side struggled to cope with the intensity and precision of the Italian side. Despite the one-sided nature of the contest, there was a grim consolation for Scotland in that the final scoreline—4-1—was not as damaging as it might have been. Italy came out with attacking clarity and purpose, and their superiority was evident within the opening 20 minutes, when three quick goals left Scotland reeling. Captain Lorenzo Insigne, in only his sixth game in international football since returning from injury, was instrumental in the early bursts, providing the assist for the first Italian goal, while Gianluca Scamacca turned in a fine team move for the second. The third, a thunderous 25-yard strike from Nicolo Barella, left the Scottish keeper with no chance and effectively ended the contest before the break. Italy, under manager Roberto Mancini, pushed forward throughout the second half and could easily have extended their lead, with a number of chances falling to veteran striker Domenico Berardi. The hosts, meanwhile, were rhythmless and without the fluency that has marked their recent matches, offering little in response to the relentless Italian pressure. The only bright spot for Scotland came when substitute James Forrest scored a consolation goal in the final ten minutes with a crisp low finish from just outside the box. Manager Steve Clarke was left to pick through the wreckage after the match, acknowledging what he described as “an extraordinary performance from Italy and a concerning one for us.” Speaking to BT Sport, Clarke said, “We were outplayed in all areas of the game, and it’s clear we need a major rethink.” He refused to be drawn on blame but admitted it is a reminder for his squad of just how tough the competition will be in the upcoming European Championship qualifiers. For Italy, the win was a further indication of their status as one of Europe’s elite sides, while Scotland must now regroup quickly to avoid slipping further behind in the group. Next up for the Scots is a challenging trip to Slovakia in their next fixture, as they look to salvage something from this bruising stretch of their campaign.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has launched an incendiary appeal to the European Union, urging it to channel €3 billion (£2.2 billion; $3.4 billion) in financial assistance to Syria’s immediate neighbours — Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq — to help alleviate the humanitarian crisis among those displaced by Syria’s devastating civil war. In a speech delivered at the Hungarian parliament in Budapest on Wednesday, Mr Orbán reiterated his long-standing position that Europe should not bear the burden of refugee absorption but rather support frontline states directly. His comments came as tensions over migration policy continue to strain the unity of the EU, with several member states under political pressure to reduce the influx of asylum seekers. Mr Orbán, whose national-conservative Fidesz party has built its political career on a hardline stance against migration, argued that the EU’s failure to provide sufficient funding to countries on the frontlines of the conflict has led to an "unfair distribution of burden" across Europe. He accused the EU of neglecting its "moral responsibility" and insisted that redirecting financial support to Syria’s immediate neighbours would be a more effective way to manage the crisis than relaxing border controls or increasing quotas for asylum seekers in Western Europe. The Hungarian leader’s call follows recent statements from human rights groups and non-governmental organizations, which have also urged the EU to increase aid to the region. The European Commission has already allocated significant funding to these countries, but critics say it is insufficient given the scale of the humanitarian needs. More than 6.8 million Syrians have been displaced within the country’s borders, while approximately 5.7 million have fled abroad, according to the United Nations. Turkey hosts the largest number of Syrian refugees, with over three million registered as of 2024. Mr Orbán, whose rhetoric about migration has often drawn sharp criticism from Brussels, framed the €3 billion demand as a "reasonable and dignified solution" that would address the root causes of the problem without opening European borders. His statement is likely to reignite the ongoing debate within the EU about how best to manage the flow of refugees while balancing democratic values with concerns about national sovereignty and security. The European Parliament is expected to discuss migration policy as early as next month, with Mr Orbán’s proposal predicted to gain attention from Eurosceptic and far-right parties, who broadly support his approach.

The chair of Kick It Out, the organisation dedicated to tackling discrimination in football, has called for sanctions against English Football League (EFL) clubs that fail to commit to interviewing black, Asian and minority ethnic (BAME) candidates for coaching and management positions. Speaking to the  Guardian , Kick It Out chairman Lord Ouseley urged greater accountability in the hiring process, stressing that meaningful progress on racial diversity in football leadership roles must be enforced with a "tougher stance." This comes in the wake of ongoing criticism about the lack of ethnic diversity in coaching positions across English football. Despite the EFL's “Minimum of Two BAME Applicants” policy — introduced in 2019 to encourage clubs to consider at least two BAME candidates for senior roles — its voluntary nature has been seen by some as insufficient to drive significant change. Ten years after the Rooney Rule was first adopted in the EFL in a pilot format, only 8 per cent of managers at the top four tiers of English football are from a BAME background. Lord Ouseley’s comments have swiftly sparked debate, with some calling for the policy to be made compulsory, backed by financial penalties for non-compliance. “If a club says they are looking for the best person for the job and they only interview white candidates, we have to ask: are they truly committed to inclusivity?” he said. “Sanctions should be a last resort, but they may be necessary to ensure that these policies aren’t just token gestures.” The Football Association has long supported initiatives to increase diversity in senior roles, with former FA chairman Greg Clarke recently apologising for the pace of progress. However, the call for enforced sanctions has not yet been formally adopted by either the EFL or the FA, and officials have so far maintained that encouraging culture change remains a priority. Football agents and former players have largely supported the idea of making inclusion policies more enforceable. Ex-England cap and Kick It Out ambassador Dwight Yorke said: “We’re not just talking about opportunities for the sake of it. BAME candidates have the experience and qualifications. If a club won’t give them a shot, they should be held to account.” Clubs such as Manchester City and Arsenal have already committed to academies and coaching pathways with a focus on diversity, whileournemouth have proudly cited the recent appointment of Tom Gillingwater as their head of recruitment, the EFL's first BAME man to be appointed to such a role at a top club.

The Premier League is set to return this weekend as fans across England and beyond prepare for another electrifying season of high-stakes football. With anticipation building in the weeks leading up to the opening fixtures, football lovers are keen to see which teams will rise to the occasion and which will struggle to adapt to the relentless pace of the top tier. Manchester City, the defending champions, will aim to make a strong start to their title defense as they welcome a host of new faces from their summer signings. Meanwhile, Liverpool continue to be tipped as serious contenders after strengthening their squad under manager Jürgen Klopp. The Merseyside derby, which traditionally takes place in early October, is already generating talk of a fiercely contested race at the top. For clubs looking to secure a Europa League spot or mount a surprise challenge, the opening weeks of the season could be crucial. London is once again home to some of the league’s heaviest hitters. Arsenal, Chelsea, and Tottenham have all made tactical moves, and the debate over whether any of them can challenge in both domestic and European competitions remains as lively as ever. Off the pitch, the Premier League remains one of the most lucrative leagues in the world, with global broadcast deals worth billions of pounds. The attention from a worldwide audience is high, and for players and managers alike, the pressure is on to deliver compelling football from the very first whistle. Other than the traditional powerhouses, the battle in and around the relegation zone promises to be intriguing. New managers, new signings, and under-pressure clubs will all look to hit the ground running, aware that missteps early in the campaign could prove costly. This weekend sets the tone for what is expected to be another thrilling Premier League season. As the floodlights come on and the first match kicks off, fans are ready for the rollercoaster ride that is English football’s premier competition. From Anfield to the Etihad, from Stamford Bridge to the Hawthorns, the new era of the league has begun. The action, the drama, and the storylines are already taking shape. And for football fans everywhere, the wait is finally over. The 2023–24 Premier League season is here. We are live. Now. Let the games begin. Stay tuned. And enjoy the show. The first whistle blows today, and with it, a season of dreams, rivalries, and the magic of the game.

If you find yourself with a skip in your step and a grin on your face, it’s likely you just made a real estate purchase... or perhaps bought some new gear. Otherwise, your good mood may need an explanation. A new survey by Consumer Reports has found that 40% of Americans would be happier if they bought a home or made a major purchase, and 35% feel good just thinking about buying something they need. The findings came from a listing by the research organization of what makes us feel happy, with home buying arguably coming out as the top activity to increase happiness. "People get excited during the process of home buying. You start with needs, then wants, and soon everything is wrapped up with anticipation and emotion," said Rob Gschwind of Consumer Reports. "In the home buying process, you reflect on what you want, where you want to live, and how and with whom you want to live. It is a very personal and exciting process." However, researchers warned that happiness does not last for everyone — in fact, the happiest people were not necessarily those who had indulged in the most costly pleasures. That would be the case for over-purchasing and under-spending, which showed impacts in short-term happiness only. The report also found that charitable giving can boost happiness levels in the long term, as can exercising and spending time with family. "In the long run, people who help others and value time with family and themselves are the ones who are happier overall,” said Ms. Silletti, who is the editor at Consumer Reports, and co-author of the report. "We also saw that people who live a balanced lifestyle are the happiest. That’s not about excess, it's about having real and meaningful connections in life," she added. The study found that most people about to make a major purchase — be it the home of their dreams or an exciting new gadget — felt more positive than those who had recently made a purchase. The unifying theme in the study is that people are happier when they feel they are expressing their values, giving back and creating meaning in their day to day. What all scientists relied on is that accurate accounts from Americans themselves, which were tallied into a ranked list of what makes them happy. "We're not making new discoveries with this study," Silletti conceded, "but delivering something that people are feeling and the context of how go about feeling it."

A man has been sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Irish student Karen Buckley, who was found dead on a remote farm four days after she disappeared from Glasgow city centre. The 27-year-old, originally from Donegal, was last seen at a fast-food restaurant in the city’s west end on 21 April. She was reported missing after she failed to return home the following day and was found later that week in a remote field in Kirkintilloch, North Lanarkshire. At Glasgow High Court, Ali Hashim, 35, was convicted of the murder after a harrowing trial that lasted several weeks. The court heard that Hashim had been in a short-term relationship with Buckley, who was studying supply chain management at Glasgow Caledonian University. Their relationship, marked by jealousy and possessiveness, ended just days before the incident, with Buckley expressing concerns over Hashim’s controlling behaviour. Buckley’s body was discovered by a farmer while he was carrying out normal duties on the morning of 25 April. The cause of death was later confirmed to be multiple stab wounds. detectives from the Police Service of Scotland (PSOS) said that the body had been placed in a crop of grass in a field. During the trial, prosecutors revealed that Hashim had lied to police and others about Buckley’s whereabouts and had previously deleted messages between himself and Buckley – efforts they argued were attempts to cover up the crime. Haylie Longmuir, 32, Hashim’s partner at the time, was found not guilty of any involvement, including perverting the course of justice. Buckley’s family, who attended the trial from Ireland, praised the police investigation and the medical staff who supported them during the traumatic process. In a victim impact statement, her father, Kevin Buckley, expressed his devastation and thanked the public for the messages of support he had received. The sentencing marks the conclusion of one of the most high-profile cases in Glasgow in recent years. The community has come together in the wake of the tragedy, with tributes continuing to pour in for Karen, who was described by friends and lecturers as kind-hearted, ambitious, and full of life. A memorial fund has been launched in her name to support young people studying in Scotland. Lord Advocate Jackie Baillie QC, who led the Crown case, stated after the verdict that the sentence reflected the seriousness of the crime and the brutal nature of the killing.

Are You Happy at Work? The Quiet Crisis in British Employment   In a post-pandemic world, where mental health has risen to the top of both public and corporate agendas, more and more Britons are questioning a simple yet profound question: am I happy at work? According to recent surveys by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD), employee satisfaction remains as low as it has been in over a decade. With over one in five employees reporting feeling emotionally drained or unmotivated, the workplace is emerging as a silent battleground for mental wellbeing. Employers, too, are under pressure to address the issue. Recent legislation, including the Health and Safety (Mental Health) Amendment Bill, suggests that governments are finally recognising the toll that dissatisfactory working environments take not just on individuals, but on the economy at large. Despite this, many businesses remain unaware—or unwilling—to confront the problem at its core. Dr Lucy Jenkinson, a leading organisational psychologist in London, says, “We’re in a generational shift in expectations. People are no longer willing to put up with toxic environments for the sake of job security.” This sentiment is echoed in the words of a 28-year-old marketing executive from Manchester, who requested anonymity due to current employment constraints. “I was offered a promotion last year, but it came with burnout. I had to take time off and rethink my priorities. I’m now in a better place, but it was a hard road getting there.” The rise of the “quiet quitting” phenomenon in 2023 further underscored a growing sense of disillusionment. Defined as employees doing the bare minimum required in their roles and no more, it has sparked fierce debate in boardrooms and living rooms about how far employees are expected to go “for the company.” Some argue it is a necessary reclamation of work-life balance; others see it as a reflection of unmet expectations in leadership. The cost for businesses is tangible. A study by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) estimates that employee disengagement costs UK businesses around £27 billion per year. Poor morale leads to absenteeism, staff turnover, and a decline in productivity. So, what is to be done? Experts stress the importance of open conversations, mental health support, and the need to redefine success in the workplace. But if employees continue to wonder “am I happy at work?”—without that question being met with real change—then the crisis will persist.

Kodjia Fires Villa to Fourth Straight Win   Aston Villa accelerated their revival under manager Steven Gerrard with a emphatic 2-0 win over Queens Park Rangers at Villa Park, with Jonathan Kodjia continuing his stunning recent form by scoring his seventh goal in seven games. The result extended Villa’s winning streak to four matches, and has reignited belief in a team many had written off at the start of the season. The Nigerian forward, who has become one of the standout performers in the Championship this season, once again proved to be the difference-maker. Kodjia netted Villa’s opening goal in the 19th minute, finishing coolly after being played in by Jacob Ramsey, who continues to shine in midfield under Gerrard’s system. The second came four minutes later, an improvised left-foot strike from just outside the box that left QPR goalkeeper Marcus Bettinelli stranded. It was a piece of quality that underlined why Kodjia is now attracting transfer interest from several Premier League clubs. The victory not only saw Villa climb five places in the Championship table to 12th, but also marked another encouraging chapter in Gerrard’s tenure, which has already seen a significant upturn in morale and performance. Speaking to the press after the match, Gerrard praised the character and confidence of his players. “These games are building blocks. The players are starting to believe in themselves, in each other, and in what we are trying to achieve here. Jonathan has been exceptional for us, but credit to the team – every department of the squad has contributed this season.” The win also provided a psychological boost over QPR, who have been inconsistent under their new manager Liam McAlinden. The former West Ham and Celtic coach took charge in September with the aim of securing a return to the Premier League after a frustrating season last term ended with relegation on the final day. Kodjia’s heroics are now drawing comparisons to some of the most prominent names in the division, with many supporters and pundits arguing that he should already be a regular on the radar of Premier League scouts. His form has raised questions about how long he will remain at Villa, with transfer fees soaring due to his blistering run of scoring form. With four consecutive victories now under their belt, Aston Villa have shown the potential to become a genuine promotion contender come January and beyond.

The European Commission has abandoned proposals to impose new time limits on surcharge-free roaming for mobile phone users within the European Union, in a reversal of its earlier outlined plans. The move has sparked reactions from consumer rights groups, telecoms companies, and politicians across Europe, who had differing expectations and concerns about the implications of the EC’s original proposals. For over a decade, the EU has ensured that all citizens enjoy the right to use their mobile services — including calls, texts, and data — at no extra cost while traveling within member states. Known as “roam like at home,” the policy has been seen as a major step forward in the EU’s digital integration and a key benefit of being part of the single market. However, the European Commission had initially proposed capping this benefit at five consecutive weeks per year, an idea that generated widespread unease among both everyday users and advocacy groups. Under the revised stance, the EC has now decided not to introduce any time restrictions on surcharge-free roaming, following feedback and lobbying from various sectors. A Commission spokesperson said the decision was taken to “preserve the rights of EU citizens and to support the free movement of people and digital services within the Union, which are fundamental pillars of European cooperation.” Consumer groups, including the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), welcomed the decision, praising it as a safeguard against regulatory overreach and a win for travelers. “Roam like at home has empowered Europeans, and now it will continue to do so without arbitrary restrictions,” said a BEUC representative in a statement. Telecom companies, on the other hand, had expressed reservations about the full extent of the cost burdens associated with supporting free roaming, particularly amid rising mobile data usage and the rollout of 5G networks. While they did not oppose the EC’s eventual decision, they urged for a balance between consumer protection and the sustainability of the mobile market. The decision is likely to be a relief for frequent travelers, students, and small business owners who have come to rely on mobile connectivity as part of their daily operations. With no time limits in place, EU citizens can continue to use their mobile services without fear of being confined to a rigid weekly cap — ensuring the policy remains a practical and meaningful benefit for years to come. The Commission’s decision confirms its commitment to protecting a policy that has been widely supported since its introduction in 2017.

In a landmark ruling that has reignited a decade-old controversy, an Indian court has ordered Bollywood superstar Salman Khan to face charges of culpable homicide for a hit-and-run incident involving a motorbike rider in 2002. The decision, announced earlier this week, marks the latest twist in a case that has long been mired in legal and public debate, and has the potential to significantly impact Khan’s celebrated career. The incident in question occurred in Mumbai on June 16, 2002, when a motorcyclist, Nitin V. Saxena, was hit by Salman Khan’s chase car, or  gadi , as these high-speed convoy vehicles are colloquially known. Saxena sustained serious injuries, and despite treatment, he died in 2013 after complications. For years, the case languished, with appeals and procedural delays stalling progress. Now, the Sessions Court in Mumbai has dismissed all prior legal hurdles and referred the matter back to the trial court to frame charges, which includes the serious criminal offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Salman Khan, 58, has maintained his innocence over the years, and his legal team is expected to continue challenging the charges. In previous statements, Khan and his lawyer, Rajeev Dhawan, have argued that the actor was not in the car at the time of the collision. However, the court has ruled that because the star was the “mastermind” of the car chase, he bears legal responsibility under the law. The case has drawn considerable public interest, in part because of Salman Khan’s status as one of India’s most popular entertainers. His films are consistently box-office hits, and he has a commanding presence in Indian cinema. The incident had briefly tarnished his image at the time, but his subsequent public shows of remorse, such as performing at charity events and spending a night in jail as part of an apology to the victim’s family, helped soften the impact to some extent. Critics of the Bollywood star argue that high-profile figures such as Khan often receive preferential treatment in the justice system, and that the slow progress of his case symbolises broader issues with judicial delays and inequality in prosecution. Others have praised the court’s decision as a sign of the judiciary resisting the powerful influence of the film industry and holding celebrities to the same legal standards as any other citizen. The go-to  gadi  system, often used by Bollywood celebrities for high-speed travel in Mumbai, has previously drawn criticism for causing chaos on the city’s roads and contributing to road accidents.

Schools across Scotland are facing a growing crisis as an increasing number of pupils arrive hungry for more than just lessons, with some children stealing food from classmates in dire need of sustenance, teachers have revealed. Concerns are mounting over the scale of child hunger, with staff in classrooms reporting alarming cases of pupils skipping meals or failing to bring lunch due to financial hardship at home. The issue has been highlighted by education unions and school staff as government support for free school meals faces reductions under new policy changes affecting eligibility. In many areas, only children from families receiving specific benefits are now entitled to free school meals, leaving a gap for those just above the threshold who still struggle to afford three decent meals a day. As a result, teachers say the burden of feeding hungry children is increasingly falling on the shoulders of schools and staff, who are left scrambling to provide emergency food parcels or distribute meals discreetly. A primary school head in Glasgow described how a growing number of pupils are arriving at school with empty breakfast bags and even taking food from others. "It's heartbreaking," she said, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the issue. "Some of these children are so embarrassed about not having a packed lunch that they try to hide it, or even admit to stealing food from a friend’s lunchbox. As a teacher, watching that play out in front of you is devastating." The national leaders of the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS) echoed these concerns, saying the problem is no longer isolated to certain communities but has become a widespread issue. EIS General Secretary Larry Flanagan noted: “This is not about one or two schools. We’re seeing a pattern emerge across the country. Children are being sent to school hungry, and the impact on their concentration, wellbeing and future education is clear.” Local initiatives have attempted to fill the gap. In the Highlands, the Food for Kids campaign provides free meals during school holidays, and some local authorities have introduced school breakfast provision for all pupils. However, without consistent, nationwide funding, many schools remain left to fend for themselves. Earlier this year, Scotland’s First Minister Nicola Sturgeon pledged to provide all primary school pupils with free school meals, regardless of income. However, funding for secondary school students beyond the most deprived households has been limited.

French presidential hopeful François Fillon has fallen under the weight of a growing political scandal, as prosecutors have announced that he is now the subject of a formal investigation over allegations of misusing public funds. The announcement comes after months of mounting controversy surrounding the employment of his wife, Penelope Fillon, as a parliamentary assistant. French media first raised questions about the legitimacy of Penelope Fillon’s role in 2011, but the matter has since resurfaced in a scandal that has shaken Fillon's political fortunes and thrown his path to the presidency into doubt. According to judicial sources, the investigation—which could run through the French presidential election in April—is examining whether Fillon and his wife used public funding for personal, non-political purposes. Penelope Fillon’s well-documented absences from her role, including to nurse ailing parents and serve on the jury of the prestigious Goncourt literary prize in 2014, have been at the heart of the controversy. As details of these absences emerged, critics accused the Fillon couple of benefiting from the financial perks of political office without fulfilling the required duties. The case has taken on even greater significance as it coincides with one of the most competitive presidential races in recent French history. Fillon, a long-standing figure on the right-wing UMP and now leading the centrist La République En Marche list in the 2017 legislative elections, was once seen as a strong contender for the presidency. However, recent opinion polls have shown a marked decline in his support, with younger voters, in particular, distancing themselves from the campaign. Former prime minister Alain Juppé and centrist mayor Emmanuel Macron are now leading the race, with the former commanding the support of traditional right-leaning parties and the latter drawing in a coalition of centrist and left-wing voters. Fillon's legal team has denied wrongdoing, describing the allegations as an “abuse of power” by judges who are biased against the candidate. The president of the Paris Bar Association, Jean-Louis Montagnon, meanwhile, has called the judicial inquiry into the Fillon case politically motivated, suggesting it could be an attempt to undermine the right-wing candidate’s campaign. The scandal has already forced Fillon to cut short appearances with his wife, and Penelope Fillon has since retreated from public view. Last week, she issued a statement saying the couple believed in the integrity of the judicial process but urged voters not to allow one case to define their campaign.

When a sense of understatement has long defined her political persona, Theresa May’s uncharacteristic directness during her leadership campaign sent a clear signal to the Westminster establishment—and the British public—that she was ready to throw her hat into the ring. As the then home secretary took to the floor in what would become one of the defining moments in her campaign to replace David Cameron as Conservative Party leader—and, by extension, as prime minister—she announced with a rare display of assertiveness: “I’m Theresa May and I’m the best person to be prime minister.” The statement, stark in its simplicity, marked a striking departure from the measured and composed tone that has typically characterised May’s political communications. Known for her methodical approach and reserved style, such bluntness caught many of her colleagues by surprise, and it left an indelible mark on the race for the top job in British politics. At the time, May had been in the role of home secretary for almost five years—during which she had been instrumental in shaping some of the most controversial policies of the Cameron government, including the handling of immigration and the UK’s approach to counter-terrorism. By positioning herself as the most logical candidate to lead the party into the next phase, May sought to assert her experience and pragmatism as crucial assets in an era of uncertainty. Her bold declaration also set the tone for a campaign characterised by a focus on stability, continuity and, crucially, her long experience in government. It was a message that resonated with a party searching for a steady hand at the helm, particularly in the wake of the EU referendum, which would soon test the UK's very political and economic foundations.
