The body of a Colorado pastor who had embarked on an intriguing treasure hunt for a hidden $2 million loot has been discovered in the Rio Grande River in New Mexico, local authorities confirmed today. Timothy Kavanaugh, a 54-year-old reverend from Glenwood Springs, Colorado, had gone missing last month after telling friends and family he was heading on a solo trip to the southwestern state with the hope of uncovering his prize. Kavanaugh had become a local figure of curiosity after revealing he believed in a treasure reported to be hidden along the banks of the Rio Grande. According to local legend, the treasure once belonged to a wealthy 19th-century rancher who reportedly stashed it before mysteriously vanishing. Kavanaugh, who had researched the tale extensively, claimed in recent weeks that he had uncovered "compelling evidence" pointing to a specific location along the river. His disappearance sent alarm bells ringing and prompted a large-scale search involving state and local agencies, as well as volunteers. However, no sign of Kavanaugh was found until yesterday when a group of river kayakers spotted the body in a remote stretch of the Rio Grande near Española. Authorities immediately confirmed that the deceased was Kavanaugh. Cortez PD spokesperson Maria Lopez said: “Our hearts go out to the family and loved ones of Mr. Kavanaugh. We are currently carrying out a full investigation into the circumstances of his death. At this stage, it is being treated as an accident, but all options remain open while the process continues.” Speaking to local media, Kavanaugh’s brother, Derek Kavanaugh, said: “We are devastated and trying to come to terms with what has happened. Tim had a dream, and he pursued it with passion. We’re still waiting to find out the truth behind this and will be with the family through this difficult time.” The remains have been taken to the Santa Fe County Medical Examiner's Office for an official cause of death. The police have not yet commented on whether Kavanaugh's search for the treasure is believed to be in any way connected to his death. However, local residents say the pastor had been seen walking and working along the river several times in the days prior to vanishing. Colorado Governor Jared Polis issued a statement expressing his condolences: “Our thoughts are with the Kavanaugh family during this tragic time. Timothy was a man of faith and determination, whose search for a lost treasure captured the minds and hearts of many.

The United Nations has called for an urgent investigation into a chilling video allegedly showing Syrian rebels executing captured soldiers and pro-government militiamen. The footage, which surfaced recently on social media and international news websites, has drawn immediate condemnation from human rights organisations and international leaders. The UN said the video could serve as potential evidence of a war crime under international law, and urged those responsible to be held accountable. The video, which has not yet been officially verified by the UN, appears to show armed individuals in military fatigues dragging shackled prisoners into a van before proceeding to a wooded area. The footage then shows what appears to be the aftermath of an execution: several bodies lie spread out on the ground. The dead men are reportedly members of the 4th Armoured Division of the Syrian Army, loyal to President Bashar al-Assad. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and the UN Assistance Mission for Iraq (UNAMI) have both expressed alarm at the apparent incident. Ahmad Fawzi, spokesperson for UNAMI in Baghdad, said, “We are deeply concerned by the video’s content and the serious allegations it raises. We call on all parties to the conflict to comply with international humanitarian law and respect the fundamental principles of humanity.” Aid workers and activists in Syria have reported that such acts of violence are becoming increasingly common as the conflict drags on. The war – now in its ninth year – has left thousands dead and displaced millions of people. The UN estimates that more than 360,000 people have died as a result of the conflict, many of them in violent acts that amount to war crimes or crimes against humanity. The UN has not yet identified the rebels who appear in the video. It comes amid intense clashes in the north-western province of Idlib, where both government forces and opposition groups are vying for control. Idlib remains one of the last major strongholds of rebel forces and is currently the site of a tense cease-fire agreement brokered with Russia and Turkey. Human rights watchdogs have long accused both government and rebel groups of systematic abuses. In December 2018, a separate UN report found evidence that both sides could be responsible for acts that amount to crimes against humanity, including torture, enforced disappearances, and the use of child soldiers. As the investigation into the video continues, the international community is once again called to grapple with the moral imperative of upholding human rights in one of the most brutal modern conflicts.

Ciaran Clark scored a stunning last-gasp equaliser as Newcastle United battled back from two goals down to salvage a dramatic 2-2 draw at home to Bristol City on Sunday. The result, a testament to the Magpies’ resilience, saw them climb to 11th in the Championship table, while the Robins remain rooted to the bottom following another frustrating weekend. Against the odds, Newcastle pulled off a late comeback that left the St James’ Park crowd in raptures and sparked questions about their character under pressure. It was a game of two halves and two different halves of the first half. Bristol City, struggling with a winless start to the new season, arrived in Tyneside with a point to prove and found themselves in command early on. Just after the half-hour mark, they seized the advantage when a composed finish by Nottingham-chased striker Freddie Dorn, who coolly converted a low cross from the right, gave the visitors a 1-0 lead. The Magpies' early pressure had yielded little in return and the hosts’ frustration grew as they found themselves behind at the interval. But the second half belonged to Newcastle—after the break, the momentum shifted dramatically in their favour. After faltering possession in the 54th minute, the visitors gift-wrapped a second goal to Newcastle, as wide man Jacob Murphy pounced on a defensive mistake to rocket home a second. The hosts were now level and the game burst back into life. With energy coursing through them and their fans on their feet, the Magpies continued to press and, in the 83rd minute, Gary O’Neil sent a pinpoint cross into the box. Ciaran Clark, who had been a rock at the back, launched himself forward to meet it with a towering header past the flailing Bristol keeper. The stadium erupted. With just seconds left, City had one final chance to regain control, but Newcastle’s backline held firm and the final whistle blew to rapturous scenes. The draw extended the Robins' winless run to four games, raising more concerns over the future of their manager, while Newcastle celebrated a gritty point that will be viewed as a statement of intent from the side and their supporters. With a young squad trying to find consistency in the brutal Championship, the Magpies will take heart from their fightback after a slow start. Meanwhile, their fans can go into the international break dreaming about what this team could achieve with a little more luck in front of goal.

When Sheikh Tamam bin Hamad Al Thaqi took over as amir of Qatar’s energy-rich hereditary state in June, few observers knew much about him. As the 36-year-old heir to one of the world's richest countries, heir to a monarchy built on vast deposits of oil and gas, the timing was inauspicious and the stakes high. The Gulf was in political and security turbulence, with the self-proclaimed Islamic State (IS) under siege in Syria and Iraq and a growing regional rivalry involving Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Iran. For many in the West—and for governments that rely on Qatari gas under long-term supply contracts—it was a moment of nervous uncertainty. Who was this new leader, and what impact would he have on a region already on edge? Qatar—a tiny corner of the Persian Gulf with a population of around 2.8 million, and a per capita GDP of $138,000—boasts a ruling family that has spent decades mastering the art of playing East against West. It has cultivated ties with both Western democracies and Islamist groups, a balancing act that has earned it both praise and scrutiny. Under Sheikh Tamim’s predecessor, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, Qatar transformed itself into a global media power through its state-owned news network, Al Jazeera, which has often drawn criticism from Gulf – and Western – governments. He has also pursued foreign policy initiatives that have seen the country support Islamist groups in conflict zones like Syria and Libya. Sheikh Tamim, however, appears to be steering the country in a more cautious and perhaps more independent direction. He has a long career in the Qatari armed forces and has been a prominent figure in the country’s diplomatic and security affairs for years. A close ally of his father, he was deputy supreme commander of the Qatari military and had a prominent role during the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings. Political analysts suggest his military background may signal a shift towards a more disciplined and strategic form of governance—one that values stability over flash and controversy. Internationally, his early moves have raised questions about how Qatar will navigate its complicated regional relationships. In recent months, the country has become a player in global negotiations involving weapons embargoes, air bridge construction, and peace talks aimed at easing the Syrian conflict. Yet these efforts are taking place amid a wider backdrop of tension between Qatar and its Gulf Arab neighbours, who have at times accused the country of fostering extremism and destabilising the region.

Heroic Airman Reflects on Dramatic Rescue of Stranded Ship   A Royal Navy airman involved in one of the most dramatic sea rescues of recent years has revealed how the harrowing operation remains vividly fixed in his mind. Former Flight Lieutenant Neil Chisholm, deployed as a rescue co-ordinator with the RAF’s Search and Rescue (SAR) force, was part of the team that saved all 21 crew members of a stranded container ship off the coast of Wales last month. The vessel, the  MV Elysia , broke down in heavy seas approximately 60 miles off the Pembrokeshire coast during a violent storm. With waves towering over 15 feet and visibility at near zero, the ship drifted dangerously close to jagged rocks, leaving the crew with no alternative but to call for emergency assistance. Chisholm, who has since left the military, spoke for the first time about the operation, describing it as "one of the most intense and dangerous missions of my career". He said: “There’s no way to prepare for what we saw out there. The sea was like a war zone—vast, angry, and utterly indifferent.” Remarkably, three RAF helicopters, including a Sea King and two Chinooks, were mobilised in a co-ordinated effort that lasted over twelve hours, culminating in the safe extraction of every crew member with no serious injuries. Despite the success, Chisholm admitted the experience had left a lasting emotional and psychological mark. “It’s not just the rescue you remember,” he said. “It’s the fear in the crew’s eyes, the rush of adrenalin, the sheer scale of the elements against us.” He described the moment when the first crew members were hoisted aboard the helicopters as “bittersweet” – a mix of relief and the sobering realisation of how quickly a mission can go wrong. The incident has reignited debate over the future of the UK’s air and sea rescue services. With the RAF withdrawing from nearly all civilian SAR operations in late 2023, transferring responsibility to the Coastguard and private contractors, many are concerned that such a large-scale operation might not have been possible under the new system. Chisholm acknowledged these fears but urged caution. “These rescues are incredibly complex and require a level of experience and training that can’t be dialled up on demand,” he said. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency has praised the joint operation, calling it a “textbook example” of what can be achieved with coordination and swift response.

The High Court recently hosted a landmark legal symposium that drew some of the most distinguished legal minds in the United Kingdom, including retired Supreme Court justices, senior barristers, and leading academics from Oxford and Cambridge. Over the course of three intense days, panels of experts debated and discussed the evolving relationship between the executive, legislature and judiciary — a matter one prominent jurist described as “of fundamental constitutional importance” to the stability and integrity of the UK’s political system. The event, which was backed by the Ministry of Justice and the Bar Council, was billed not as a formal judicial proceeding but as a platform for scholars and practitioners to reflect on the past, present and future of constitutional governance in Britain. In an era where questions of national sovereignty, parliamentary authority and the role of the courts have repeatedly come under public and political scrutiny — not least in the wake of Brexit and the Post Office scandal — the timing of the symposium could hardly have been more significant. Lord Sumption, a former deputy president of the Supreme Court, delivered one of the opening speeches, in which he warned against what he called the “obsession with legalistic solutions” to political problems. He argued that overreliance on the courts to resolve issues rooted in democratic governance puts pressure on both the judiciary and public institutions. “There is a temptation in this country to confuse law with politics,” he said. “But the court does not make policy, and it should not try to.” Others, however, urged a more hands-on approach to judicial intervention when parliamentary procedures are challenged or undermined. Lady Hale, the first woman to serve as president of the Supreme Court, highlighted the role of courts in safeguarding fundamental rights and ensuring democratic accountability. “When law and policy clash, the rule of law must prevail,” she told the audience, drawing applause from those about to break for lunch. The discussions ranged from the interpretation of the Human Rights Act 1998 to the delegated powers of Parliament and the implications of the fixed-term parliaments act. One session on the separation of powers was particularly contentious, with cross-examinations turning into a broader debate over where democratic legitimacy ultimately lies. As the debate unfolded, it sparked widespread interest among legal professionals and the public. The papers have since reported sustained comment from columnists and students alike, with some hailing the symposium as a much-needed intellectual reset for constitutional law.

A Matter of Mortality: The Quote That Refuses to Fade    By Sarah Linfield, Staff Writer  The British writer W. Somerset Maugham, a man whose words have long echoed in the halls of literature, once described death in stark and unromantic terms. “Dying is a very dull, dreary affair,” he mused, perhaps with the cool detachment of a man accustomed to dissecting the human condition with a surgeon’s blade. He then offered his audience a prescription wrapped in irony: “Have nothing whatever to do with it.” The quote, first published in his short story  The Poor士  (The Poor Man), remains as provocative today as it was when it was first written in the early 20th century. Maugham’s words, delivered with the characteristic wit and clinical precision that defined his writing, have become something of a lightning rod for debates about death, fear, and the human response to the inevitable. In an age when discussions of death and dying are increasingly returning to the fore — in the context of modern medicine, palliative care, assisted dying, and even the growing popularity of ‘death cafes’ — Maugham’s cynical remark strikes a particularly resonant chord. But what did he really mean? To say that death is “dull” and to advise people to have “nothing whatever to do with it” appears – at first glance – fairly callous. Maugham was not a man given to sentimentality. His characters often faced life with a cool realism, and his depictions of love, religion, and morality were rarely sugar-coated. But perhaps his remark was a reflection not of indifference, but of disillusionment — the disillusionment of a man who had seen death up close and found it wanting in drama or romantic gravitas. Indeed, Maugham lived through a century punctuated by war, disease, and seismic social change. He knew loss. He knew death. And it is possible that in his comment, he found a way to mock the grandeur often attributed to the end of life. He suggested that the most dignified response was not to embrace or romanticise death, but to avoid getting entangled with it entirely — to stay on the other side of the veil. Yet, in the 21st century, the quote no longer reads as a simple warning. It has become the starting point for a broader conversation on how we live and how we die – one that questions the line between engagement and avoidance, and whether it is possible — or desirable — to remain untouched by the final act of life.

Thousands of Malaysian opposition supporters have poured into the streets of several major cities to protest allegations of election fraud, in a bold public challenge to authorities who have declared the demonstration illegal. The mass rallies, which took place on Sunday, saw thousands gather in Kuala Lumpur,槟城 (Penang), and Johor Bahru, waving placards and chanting anti-government slogans as they voiced their discontent with the results of the recent general election. The opposition coalition, led by Anwar Ibrahim, has accused the ruling Barisan Nasional (BN) of widespread ballot manipulation, vote-buying and media bias in the lead-up to the polls. Anwar, who has long led the charge against the Malaysian government, pledged to "fight for justice and the people’s right to a fair democracy." Organisers reported a peaceful and orderly demonstration, though they acknowledged the risk of police escalation. The Malaysian authorities, however, stated that the protest was held without a permit and therefore was breaking the law. Police commissioner Tan Sri Khalid Abu Bakar urged attendees to “disperse immediately and avoid any action that could lead to unrest or violence.” Despite the warning, the turnout was widely described as one of the largest political demonstrations seen in the country in recent years. For many, the protest marked a renewed push for transparency in a nation still grappling with its political future. Over the last decade, Malaysia has witnessed a dramatic shift in its political landscape, with the rise of reformist parties and a growing youth movement demanding a new Malaysia. But with the election result under scrutiny, the country is once again at a crossroads. As the sun set on Sunday afternoon, the crowd in Kuala Lumpur remained stationed near the iconic Tunku Abdul Rahman Park, with speeches focused on the importance of democratic accountability. Anwar, speaking through a loudspeaker, urged the people to remain firm in their demands for a “reinvestigation of the voting process and a recount in all contested constituencies.” The government has so far responded with silence, sending mixed signals to the opposition, analysts say. Some fear the situation could escalate into a broader crisis if no solution is reached. As tensions mount, the world is watching to see whether Malaysia will manage to resolve its democratic challenges peacefully or whether deeper divisions could tear at the fabric of the nation. lunches to keep the protesters nourished. “We are not agitators,” one rally attendee told reporters.

Erroneous use of data led to 13 wrongful arrests, independent agency reports   A recent investigation has revealed that 13 innocent individuals were wrongly arrested due to errors in the use of communications data by British police forces, according to an independent watchdog. The report, published by the Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC), highlights concerns over the potential harm caused by misconduct in the use of sensitive data and raises fresh questions about the balance between security and civil liberties. The report refers to the misuse of data obtained under the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA), a controversial piece of legislation that allows law enforcement to access communications data with judicial approval. The watchdog said three constabularies had made "serious and repeated misuse" of the law, leading to the unnecessary detention of 13 people who were later found not guilty or released without charge. These misuse incidents involve the incorrect authorisation and use of surveillance orders, including the collection of phone records, emails, and internet activity, often without proper oversight or justification. The watchdog expressed concern that in some cases, the data was used without clear suspicion of criminal activity and that the people targeted were directly harmed by the experience. In response, the Prime Minister’s Office issued a statement acknowledging the seriousness of the report and stating that the Ministry of Justice would review the process of granting bail warrants. "We will examine all the recommendations made by the Intelligence and Security Committee with the utmost seriousness and take appropriate action," a spokesperson said. The Home Office also confirmed that it would be undertaking its own internal review of RIPA’s implementation in light of the findings. One of the victims, a 32-year-old Londoner whose name has not been disclosed, described the experience as deeply distressing and intrusive. "It felt like I was being treated as a criminal when I had done nothing wrong," he said. "My life was thrown into chaos for weeks. I lost my job and my family are still not speaking to me." The report does not name the three police forces found to be at fault, but it has reignited calls for a comprehensive rewrite of laws governing the use of communications data. Campaigners and legal experts have long argued that RIPA, which was enacted in 2000, is out of date and lacks sufficient safeguards against misuse. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), which oversees data protection in the UK, has also started a wider review of how law enforcement handles personal information.

Aberdeen Makes Strides in Europa League Triumph   Aberdeen have progressed further in the Europa League after a thrilling 2-0 victory over Siroki Brijeg at the Siroki Brijeg Stadion in Bosnia. The Dons, who were competing as a third-tier Scottish outfit against a top-tier Bosnian team, triumphed courtesy of goals from Greg Stewart and Gary Mackay-Steven in the second half—a result that underlined their tenacity and ambition on the European stage. The match was a pivotal test for Derek McInnes’s side as they seek to replicate the success of the 2012 Europa League run, during which they made history by reaching the group stage as Scottish League One champions. The game began at a frenetic pace, with both sides showing bursts of attacking intent. However, it was the Dons who began to find their rhythm as the first half wore on, breaking the resilience of their Bosnian opponents with more sustained pressure in the final third. The breakthrough came in the 62nd minute, with Stewart latching onto a through ball to slot past the Siroki goalkeeper and send the travelling Dons fans into raptures. Stewart, who has been in inspired form early in the campaign, has become a key figure in McInnes’s side and was again the hero in what was a crucial away tie. Aberdeen extended their lead just 10 minutes later when Gary Mackay-Steven, making the most of a defensive lapse, drove home a composed finish to double the advantage. The winger, signed during the summer to bolster the squad ahead of European competition, delivered a performance rich in creativity and urgency. His goal not only sealed the victory but also served as a statement of intent for the Dons about their credentials in the competition. The win sees Aberdeen book their place in the third qualifying round, where they will now face an opponent to be determined. For Siroki Brijeg, the match will serve as a lesson in the challenges posed by Scottish clubs with experience and ambition in European competitions. Their hopes of progressing were dashed by a Dons side that played with discipline, organisation, and clinical finishing when it mattered most. Manager Derek McInnes praised his team’s professionalism after the match. “These European games are always tough, but the lads were outstanding,” he said. “They showed great character and composure under pressure. We’re building something exciting at this club, and moments like this give us a big boost.”

Spanish scientists Bernabé and José Moya couldn't believe their eyes as they examined a peculiar rock formation deep in the mountains of southern Spain. What initially seemed to be a routine geological survey had taken an unexpected turn when the brothers stumbled upon a strikingly unusual structure unlike anything they had encountered in their decades of research. Buried beneath layers of limestone and sediment, the formation bore the unmistakable hallmarks of intentional design—curved edges, perfectly symmetrical patterns, and a flat, central chamber too precise to be entirely natural. The discovery was made near the UNESCO-listed Sierra de los Filabres, a region already known for its prehistoric carvings and enigmatic megalithic sites. Dr. Bernabé Moya, a specialist in geomorphology at the University of Granada, described the moment of revelation as "rarely matched in scientific careers". He stated: "We expected to find fossilised coral or perhaps some glacial activity. Instead, we found something that defied easy explanation." Initial examinations revealed that the structure, measuring approximately 12 metres in diameter, appeared to have been formed from locally sourced materials, suggesting it was created by ancient human hands. Carbon dating is still underway, but early estimates suggest it could be several thousand years old, possibly predating the known Stone Age settlements in the area. What makes the find even more intriguing is the method of construction. The experts, working with archaeologists from Seville University, noted that the rock appeared to have been split and moved with what could only be described as advanced tools, possibly even more sophisticated than those found in nearby Neolithic sites. Local historians are already speculating that the structure could be linked to the ancient Iberian tribes, but Dr. José Moya, a fellow researcher, cautioned against jumping to conclusions. "We are not attributing it to any one civilisation just yet. What we have is a mystery that requires more data," he said. The Ministry of Culture has now been alerted, and a team of experts is being assembled to carry out a full excavation. For now, the brothers say they are content to take it slow, relishing the rare thrill of scientific discovery. As Dr. Bernabé Moya put it: "Some things take a lifetime to find. This one was worth the wait." Researchers hope the site will yield more clues not only about the region's prehistoric inhabitants but also potentially their understanding of human ingenuity and survival in ancient landscapes.

Scientists have made a major breakthrough in the battle against influenza, with the development of a potential universal flu vaccine capable of protecting against all known strains of the virus, including those yet to emerge. In a study published today in the journal  Nature , an international team of researchers detail how the prototype vaccine targets a conserved region of the influenza virus that remains relatively unchanged across different strains. This contrasts with current influenza vaccines, which must be reformulated annually to match the ever-mutating surface proteins of the virus. The new approach focuses on attacking the   haemagglutinin stem  , a section of the virus that is essential for infection and stays more stable over time. By stimulating the production of  stem-targeting antibodies , the vaccine could, in theory, offer long-lasting immunity without the need for yearly updates—a major limitation of existing flu vaccines. Volunteers in the initial phase of the clinical trial showed a strong immune response to the experimental vaccine, suggesting it could offer broad protection. The study, led by researchers at the University of Oxford in partnership with institutions across the United States and Germany, marks a pivotal step in flu prevention. Dr. Emily Morgan, one of the lead researchers, said, “For the first time, we have evidence that we can create a vaccine that works across all influenza A subtypes. This is something we have dreamed of for decades.” The flu remains one of the most unpredictable and deadly viral threats globally, with seasonal outbreaks responsible for hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. It is particularly dangerous for the elderly, young children, and people with chronic health conditions. Each year, public health officials must make educated guesses about which strains will be most prevalent, leading to inconsistent vaccine efficacy—sometimes as low as 30 per cent in recent seasons. A universal flu vaccine could not only save lives but also reduce healthcare system strain significantly during flu season. Experts also believe it could help prevent or at least lessen the impact of future pandemics triggered by new flu strains jumping from animals to humans. “This is just the beginning,” said Dr. Morgan. “We will now work with regulatory and pharmaceutical partners to move the vaccine into larger trials as quickly and safely as possible.” If clinical trials continue successfully, a universal flu vaccine could reach the public as early as 2030, a moment that would represent a major victory in the global fight against infectious disease.

Scotland fought back from a goal down to secure a crucial 1-1 draw against the Republic of Ireland in a hard-fought Euro 2016 qualifying encounter at Hampden Park. The result allows Gordon Strachan’s side to maintain a two-point advantage over their Celtic Park rivals at the top of Group D, maintaining their strong position in the race for qualification to the European Championships. The visitors took an early lead in Glasgow when James McClean converted a penalty in the 29th minute, capitalising on a mistake by Scotland defender Charlie Mulgrew. The Republic, who were seen as the chase pack in the group, made the most of the penalty area advantage as they climbed temporarily to second place. But the hosts responded admirably before the interval, forcing the draw through a controversial penalty awarded in the 44th minute. Celtic midfielder Kris Commons sent Daryl Horgan sprawling in the box and stepped up to make it 1-1, sending the home supporters into raptures just before half-time. The second half proved more cagey, as both teams looked to impose control but struggled to create clear-cut chances. Scotland, buoyed by the home support and the presence of a vocal Tartan Army in the stands, continued to push for a winner, but Republic goalkeeper Shay Given was equal to the handful of efforts that came his way. Strachan’s men have now won four of their last five qualifiers, with the manager praising his team’s resilience in the post-match interview. “We were tested early on, and we had to dig in,” he said. “It was always going to be a tough game against a very capable opposition, so I’m proud of the lads for showing the right character and being clinical when it mattered.” For the Republic, it is a bittersweet result. They remain in second place but now face a challenging run of fixtures. Republic manager Giovanni Trapattoni admitted that losing the lead was painful, but praised his side’s effort. “You can’t take anything away from the boys,” he said. “They gave me everything. We’ll take the point and move on.” The draw marks another significant moment in Scotland’s impressive campaign to reach their first major championship since 1992. With confidence high and momentum clearly in their favour, the next few matches will be crucial in determining whether they can hold on to their European dream.

Poland has experienced a remarkable turnaround in its education system, according to results from the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) tests, which measure the academic performance of 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics, and science across countries. Since 2000, the country has made significant progress, with its pupils closing the gap on many of their Western European peers and outperforming several other developed nations. The Pisa tests, coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), provide a snapshot of education quality worldwide, and Poland’s improvements have been among the most dramatic. In the first round of the Pisa tests in 2000, Poland performed below the OECD average, but by 2012, the country had climbed to a position far above many others, including the United States and the United Kingdom. The transformation has sparked interest among education experts and policymakers around the world, with many now studying the Polish model to understand how it managed to raise standards so quickly. A key factor in Poland’s success, according to researchers and government officials, was a series of sweeping education reforms introduced over the early and mid-2000s. These changes included increasing the average length of pre-university education from 12 to 13 years, raising teacher salaries to attract and retain high-quality staff, and reinforcing national standards to ensure a more consistent quality of teaching across the country. The government also invested heavily in the training and professional development of teachers, recognising their crucial role in student achievement. Additionally, Poland made a concerted effort to improve school infrastructures and to provide pupils with better access to technology and digital learning resources. Another important element was the introduction of a national curriculum and standardised assessment system, which helped to make progress in schools more measurable and accountable. The system also gave local authorities and headteachers more autonomy over how they ran their schools, fostering greater innovation and responsiveness to student needs. The Pisa results have helped to restore public confidence in Poland’s education system and have become a source of national pride. Education Minister Anna Zalewska said the improvements were achieved through “a commitment to excellence and a belief that all students deserve a good education.” The transformation has not only benefited academically gifted students but has also boosted the performance of those in more disadvantaged communities, helping to reduce educational inequality. However, challenges remain. While the overall trend has been positive, some experts warn that recent reforms may have created new pressures, including a more demanding curriculum and increased competition in the secondary school entrance exams.

Björk is known for pushing the boundaries of art, music and spectacle, and her latest world tour is no exception. In a dramatic and avant-garde opening night, the Icelandic art-pop icon unveiled an array of custom-made, never-before-seen musical instruments that left the audience in awe. Among them were a musical lightning generator and four harp-playing pendulums – mechanical marvels that blended technology, acoustics and visual art into a singular experience. The Copenhagen concert marked the debut of  Utopia , a tour inspired by themes of ecology, transcendence and rebirth. But what truly set the night apart was Björk’s collaboration with engineers, instrument builders and designers to create a unique sonic palette. The musical lightning generator, for instance, is an electric device that produces actual electrical sparks to create bursts of sound and visual drama on stage, merging the primal energy of nature with the modern world of electronic music. Equally captivating were the four harp-playing pendulums. Suspended in mid-air, these kinetic sculptures slowly swing, using weighted arms to pluck harp strings in a meditative, almost hypnotic rhythm. Each pendulum swings at a different speed, creating a layered and evolving orchestra of soft, ethereal notes. The result is a soundscape as much as a visual spectacle, reinforcing Björk’s long-standing fascination with harmony, nature and innovation. Her creative team, including longtime collaborator and Icelandic sculptor Ólafur Eliasson, worked for over a year to bring these instruments to life. For Björk, this is not just about performance but about making a statement – a call to imagine a world where art and science merge, and technology serves creativity and sustainability. “It’s about bringing the impossible into the world, even if just for a few minutes,” Björk said backstage, talking about the musical lightning generator. “These instruments aren’t just part of the show. They’re part of the future we’re trying to sound out.” Such imaginative flourishes have always been part of Björk’s signature style, but on the  Utopia  tour, they reach new heights – both figuratively and literally. As the concert drew to a close, the pendulums slowed their motion and the lightning sizzled out, leaving the audience with a sense of wonder, something akin to witnessing a dream made real. Whether or not viewers were familiar with her previous works, one fact became clear: watching Björk perform is not just an experience, but an odyssey.

In a rare move that has sent shockwaves through the US political and tech sectors, the co-founders of some of the world’s most influential internet companies have publicly denounced a contentious piece of proposed legislation, calling it a threat to free speech and innovation. Larry Page and Sergey Brin, the co-founders of Google, along with Jack Dorsey, the former CEO of Twitter, and Pierre Omidyar, the founder of eBay, have joined a coalition of industry leaders to pen a strongly worded open letter to members of Congress. The letter, which is set to be released ahead of a crucial debate on the proposed legislation, outlines the founders’ deep concerns about its potential impact on digital freedom and the broader economy. The legislation at the heart of the controversy is the recently introduced My Data, Your Choice (MDYC) Act, a bill designed to reform the way technology companies handle consumer data and enforce stricter privacy protections. However, its most controversial provision would require platforms to allow third-party developers to access user data directly, creating significant compliance and operational challenges for major tech firms. The letter from Page, Brin, Dorsey and Omidyar details how the act could inadvertently empower bad actors and lead to a "data arms race" in which companies compete not to protect users but to be as open as possible, often at the expense of security. The letter states, “We are gravely concerned that the MDYC Act, in its current form, does not take into account the real-world impact of these technologies and the consequences for democratic discourse, personal security and the integrity of the internet itself.” They further argue that the bill ignores the complexities of modern technology and could unleash unintended consequences, including an increased risk of data breaches and a possible slowdown in the development of new digital tools. Some lawmakers in Congress have defended the bill, arguing that it is a necessary step to bring transparency and competition to the tech sector and curb what they see as monopolistic practices. However, the letter signed by the tech pioneers has already sparked a fierce debate over the balance between regulation and innovation in the digital age. The House of Representatives is expected to vote on the bill as early as next week, and with some of the founding minds of the internet now speaking out, pressure is mounting for negotiations to amend the legislation to address the concerns raised by the tech community.

The UK experienced a record-breaking day this week as temperatures soared to a sweltering 34.4°C (93.9°F) in Gravesend, Kent, marking the hottest day of the year so far and the warmest September day since 1911. The unprecedented heat has left many Britons stunned, with the mercury breaking expectations and prompting weather warnings as the nation adjusted to what felt more like midsummer than late autumn. The record was confirmed by the Met Office, which reported that the temperature in Gravesend was the highest of the day and well above the long-standing September record of 34.1°C (93.4°F) set in Carterton, Oxfordshire, in 1975. With no rainfall recorded and the sun blazing relentlessly, numerous weather stations across the south and east of England reported temperatures hitting the mid to high 30s, turning the capital into an oven in the afternoon hours. The unusual heatwave, driven by high pressure from the Azores which blocked in cooler air from the north and west, has been attributed to broader climatic shifts exacerbated by global warming. Scientists have warned that such weather extremes, once considered outliers, are becoming more frequent and intense. "What we're seeing is a perfect example of how the climate is changing," said Dr Emma Stewart, a climate scientist from the UK's national weather service. "These temperatures are not just warm for September—they're a sign of the weather patterns we can expect to see more of in the coming years." The heat hit at a critical time, as supermarkets reported stocks of ice creams and fizzy drinks flying off shelves, while schools across the country took the unusual step of allowing children to remove their uniforms as indoor temperatures soared. In London, the city ballet, Prime Minister’s Questions, and even horse races were all held in the shadow of thermometers climbing beyond most September benchmarks. However, not everyone was charmed by the weather. Public health officials issued warnings about the dangers of heat-related illness, with hospitals bracing for an influx of patients with dehydration and heat exhaustion. Transport services also faced disruptions, as train tracks warped under the strain, restricting speeds on several major lines. As the sun dipped below the horizon, a breath of relief began to creep in, but the record-breaking day will be etched into the memory of a nation caught by weather that defied the calendar.

Claims that a move is afoot to remove Douglas Alexander from his role as Shadow Foreign Secretary have been hurled back with scorn by senior Labour figures, who dismissed the speculation as “ludicrous” and a byproduct of overactive media imaginations. At the heart of the controversy is a proposed boundary change in the heart of Scotland, which threatens to absorb Mr Alexander’s constituency of Monklands and East Dunbartonshire into a new, more Tory-leaning seat. Politically savvy observers suggest that this shift could undermine his position, seeing as he would be transferred to a seat where his appeal appears significantly diminished. Such a scenario, of course, has not gone unnoticed in Westminster corridors, even if it is not yet a reality. The idea that Labour could quietly orchestrate a shift of loyalties to capitalise on the boundary change is one that has captivated the backbenches. But Labour insiders were swift to repel such notions, with one senior source stating: “This is nonsense. Douglas is safe in his post, and any talk of a challenge from within the party is total fantasy.” Mr Alexander has been a prominent figure within the Labour Party for decades, serving as both a Shadow Cabinet member and a vocal opponent of Brexit in Parliament. His stature in the party and experience in foreign affairs has made him an unlikely target for internal jockeying, at least according to those close to the matter. However, the changing political landscape, coupled with Labour’s recent struggles in opinion polls, has not quelled intrigue within the party. With the general election looming on the horizon, even the most outlandish theories are being floated. Some suggest that Mr Alexander could be moved to a new position—whether voluntarily or not—should the boundaries realignment be accepted. Others speculate that the move is a calculation by the party leadership to deprioritise the Scottish heartlands in the run-up to an election they see as increasingly perilous. The Boundary Commission, which is responsible for drawing new constituency lines, has so far refused to comment on the potential impact of the proposed changes on existing MPs. However, with a deadline of December for any final decisions, the political implications are already being played out in London’s power circles. Mr Alexander has chosen to remain silent, but colleagues insist the speculation is a complete exaggeration. “Douglas is focused on his work and delivering for his constituents,” said a spokesperson for the Shadow Cabinet.

Plaid Cymru has called for a renewed and more ambitious focus on the teaching of the Welsh language in schools and public life if Wales is to meet its target of one million Welsh speakers by 2050. The Welsh government first set this target in 2017, as part of a broader strategy to make Wales a “capped Welsh speaker country,” where both English and Welsh enjoy equal status. However, progress has been slower than expected, and experts warn that the current trajectory is not on track to meet the goal. In a recent policy statement, Plaid Cymru highlighted what it called a “systemic gap” in Welsh education, particularly in areas where the language is not traditionally spoken as a first language. The party pointed to the relatively low uptake of Welsh medium education in many parts of the country, despite growing interest in the language among the general public, and called for targeted interventions to address this imbalance. Currently, about 29% of school pupils in Wales are learning through the medium of Welsh, according to the latest official figures. While this figure has remained fairly stable for the past decade, campaigners argue that real growth requires a combination of political will and practical investment in infrastructure, teacher training, and community engagement. Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth said: “If we truly value our language and our national identity, we must invest in its future. The 2050 target is not just about numbers; it’s about ensuring Welsh is a living, dynamic language that is used and heard by people across Wales, in all aspects of life.” The party has proposed a number of measures to boost Welsh language use, including expanding the provision of Welsh-medium early years education, introducing Welsh language assistants in all schools, and incentivising Welsh-speaking parents to consider bilingual education for their children. It also called for improved data collection to monitor progress and identify areas where more support is needed. The Welsh Language Standards and the Welsh Government’s draft Plenary Powers Bill, which gives the Welsh Parliament greater legislative authority, will also be key factors in implementing future language policy. However, any significant expansion of Welsh education will require additional funding, which remains a point of contention between political parties. As the deadline of 2050 looms, the call from Plaid Cymru is the latest in a growing chorus of voices urging a more urgent and co-ordinated effort to revitalise the use of Welsh—not just as a relic of the past, but as a vital part of Wales’s future.
